News.title: Eight passengers rushed to hospital after severe turbulence on flight as plane forced to make emergency landing
News.content:
Next

EIGHT passengers have been rushed to hospital after horror turbulence hit a New York-bound plane, forcing an emergency landing.

The Avianca aircraft plunged 25,000ft after striking an area of bad turbulence just three hours into the flight from Medellin, Colombia.

Multiple passengers were injured with eight people rushed to hospital after the plane made its unexpected landing at Miami International Airport.

Ambulances were already waiting on the tarmac when the plane landed yesterday evening.





Maria Paula Jimenez, a passenger, told CBS Miami: “When we arrived, when we landed, we saw that very close to where we were going to disembark, there were more than five or six ambulances.

“Seven of them with their lights on as if they were waiting for something. When we arrived, well, you know, it wasn’t normal.”

The extend of the eight patients injuries have not been disclosed but at least one of them is in a serious condition.

News.title: UK hits out at ‘disturbing’ US plan to LIVESTREAM terrorist’s firing squad execution as countries set to ban broadcast
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN has hit out at a “disturbing” US plan to livestream a terrorist’s firing squad execution as several countries are set to ban the broadcast.

Convicted mass murderer Nidal Hasan, who slaughtered 13 people at a US military base, is due to face a hail of bullets live before the world on December 3.



But the Pentagon‘s decision to broadcast his final moments has triggered a furious international debate over the limits of state punishment.

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the execution was a “matter for the US Government” but stressed Britain’s “long-standing” opposition to the death penalty.



The Cabinet minister admitted she personally found the prospect “rather disturbing”.

Her intervention risks igniting a fresh diplomatic row with Donald Trump, as Andy Burnham struggles to make advancements with Transatlantic relations.



US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has defended the firing squad execution as a “no-brainer”.

He insists the public must understand there are “serious consequences for these types of things.”

Trump personally signed off on Hasan’s death sentence on Monday following a recommendation from Hegseth.

The disgraced former Army major, 56, is scheduled to be executed at 1pm local time (7pm GMT) in the first week of December.



But the decision has also raised alarm over whether countries can stop the footage reaching their citizens.

New Zealand has already warned it may be powerless to stop the gruesome footage being streamed across the country.

Its Classification Office admitted it has no authority to block a live internet broadcast, despite growing pressure to shield viewers from violent content.



A spokesperson said: “The Classification Office cannot classify a livestream event as it is taking place, and we, nor any other body, has the authority to block access to a livestream event.”

Chief Censor Caroline Flora warned that banning disturbing material required a delicate balance between public safety and freedom of expression.

She said: “Distressing as content may be, it is not always unlawful.”

The controversy has struck a particularly raw nerve in New Zealand, where a gunman massacred 51 worshippers at two mosques in 2019 while livestreaming his rampage on Facebook.

The bloodbath prompted then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern to spearhead an international crackdown on violent online content.



Now, the prospect of the US Government broadcasting a firing squad execution has reignited fears over graphic footage spreading unchecked across the internet.

Amnesty International Australia has also condemned the decision, urging Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to demand Washington abandon the broadcast.

Campaign manager Kyinzom Dhongdue said: “The suggestion that an execution by firing squad should be livestreamed for public viewing is an appalling disregard for human dignity.”



She added: “Turning a state-sanctioned killing into a public spectacle only compounds the cruelty of the death penalty.”

The White House has refused to say whether Trump personally supports televising the execution, instead directing questions to the Pentagon.

Public executions have become increasingly rare worldwide, although Iran and Taliban-controlled Afghanistan are among the countries known to have carried them out in recent years.

Hasan’s looming death marks another chapter in one of America’s most notorious military massacres.

The former Army psychiatrist unleashed a murderous rampage at Fort Hood in Texas on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others.



Armed with a laser-sighted handgun, he stormed a medical building where soldiers were queuing for routine vaccinations and deployment checks.

He bowed his head several times before shouting “Allahu Akbar” – Arabic for “God is great!” – and opening fire.

Witnesses described scenes of sheer terror as Hasan sprayed bullets across the crowded building before deliberately targeting individual soldiers.

Sergeant Michael Davis recalled: “The rate of fire was pretty much constant shooting. When I initially heard it, it sounded like an M16.”



Investigators later recovered 146 spent shell casings inside the building and another 68 outside, where fleeing soldiers were shot at as they raced towards the car park.

Prosecutors revealed Hasan had spent weeks preparing for the bloodbath, repeatedly visiting a shooting range in Florence, Texas.

He had also visited a gun shop in Killeen, demanding “the most technologically advanced weapon on the market and the one with the highest standard magazine capacity”.

Hasan later claimed he carried out the ten-minute killing spree to stop American troops being sent to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims.



But a military judge refused to allow him to use that argument as a defence.

During his trial, the killer made little attempt to deny responsibility, describing himself as a “soldier who had switched sides”.

He was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder before being sentenced to death.

If the execution goes ahead, Hasan will become the first US service member to be put to death since Army Private John Bennett was hanged in 1961.

It would also mark the first military execution by firing squad since the Second World War.



Hegseth has shown little sympathy for the condemned killer.

Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests or contacted the Trump administration, he snapped: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3rd.”

But the execution could still be thrown into legal turmoil.

Military law experts warn Hasan could launch further appeals or file a habeas corpus petition in a civilian court, potentially delaying his death for years.

Eugene R. Fidell, a Yale Law School visiting lecturer specialising in military law, said: “It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The controversy comes just days after convicted murderer Christa Pike, 50, survived a botched lethal injection in Tennessee on September 30.

Her survival following two rounds of lethal injection has plunged the state into a legal battle over whether it can attempt to execute her again.

News.title: Why do the clocks change? The reason the UK has British Summer Time – and when clocks go back in October 2026
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN has been changing its clocks for more than a century, and the system was originally introduced for very practical reasons.

The annual change marks the end of British Summer Time, meaning darker evenings are on the way. Here’s everything you need to know.



Why do the clocks change in the UK?

The UK moves its clocks forward in spring to make the most of longer daylight hours during the spring and summer.

Making better use of sunlight goes back hundreds of years, with Benjamin Franklin first discussing it in a satirical essay written in 1784.



The idea was later championed in Britain by builder William Willett, who published The Waste of Daylight in 1907.

But his original plan was far more complicated than the system eventually introduced: he proposed moving the clocks forward in four separate 20-minute stages.



A number of attempts to bring in daylight saving legislation were rejected by Parliament between 1908 and 1916.

That changed during World War I, when The Summer Time Act received Royal Assent on May 17, 1916.

The clocks were moved forward for the first time four days later, on May 21.

The wartime measure was introduced in part to improve productivity and cut fuel consumption.



Britain went a step further during World War II, when Double Summer Time meant the clocks were two hours ahead of GMT for part of the year.

The system was abandoned after the war, but briefly returned during the 1947 fuel crisis.

Britain later experimented with keeping the clocks permanently one hour ahead.

British Standard Time began on October 27, 1968, meaning the UK stayed on GMT+1 through the winter instead of turning the clocks back.

But the experiment ended on October 31, 1971, after Parliament voted against making the change permanent.



The move faced particularly strong opposition in Scotland and other northern areas, where it led to much darker winter mornings.

Will the UK stop changing the clocks?

There have been repeated calls to scrap the twice-yearly change or keep the UK permanently on BST.

But in March 2026, the House of Commons Library confirmed the Government had “no plans to make any changes to these arrangements”.

Roughly 70 countries use some form of daylight saving time.

What is British Summer Time?

British Summer Time (BST) is the period when UK clocks are one hour ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).



It begins when the clocks go forward at 1am on the last Sunday in March.

BST ends when the clocks go back on the last Sunday in October.

When do the clocks change in October 2026?

The clocks go back by one hour on Sunday, October 25, 2026.

At 2am BST, the time will move back to 1am GMT, meaning most of us get an extra hour’s sleep.

Once the clocks have gone back, sunrise and sunset will both happen roughly an hour earlier by the clock, bringing lighter mornings and darker evenings.



In the UK, BST always ends on the last Sunday in October, which falls on the 25th in 2026 – the earliest possible date for the switch.

The clocks went back on October 26 in 2025, while next year’s change won’t take place until October 31.

This year’s BST started on March 29, when the clocks moved forward by an hour.

When do the clocks go forward again?

The UK will remain on GMT throughout the winter before the clocks go forward again on Sunday, March 28, 2027.

At 1am GMT, the clocks will jump forward one hour to 2am BST.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

That means losing an hour in bed — but the switchover brings lighter evenings as the country heads towards summer.

An easy way to remember which direction the clocks move is “spring forward, fall back.”

News.title: My family were paedo ring tormentors – I was abused by brother, cousin, grandad and uncle… then mum betrayed me
News.content:
Next

WHEN she was a little girl, Fiona Seath wanted nothing more than a normal, happy childhood – in a loving home where she felt safe.

She would play out happy scenarios with her Barbie dolls, but behind closed doors lay a living hell – a vile, incestuous paedophile ring where she was preyed upon by her brother, cousin, uncle, and sick ringleader grandad.





To make matters even worse, her own mother Mary Seath subjected her to physical abuse and terrorised her with kitchen utensils.

Now, after a courageous battle for justice which saw warped sibling John Sime, 35, and trans cousin Serenity Johnston, 34 – formerly known as David – put behind bars along with her mother, the brave 28-year-old lifts the lid on the horrific campaign of terror.

Fiona, of Fauldhouse, in West Lothian, Scotland, told of the intense pain she suffered as her little body was abused by Sime and Johnston, as well as granddad Alexander Sives, and uncle Robert Sives – who are both dead.

She said: “I grew up in a family of horrors, living out every kid’s worst nightmare.

“They robbed me of my childhood… I was absolutely terrified.

“My abusers can all rot in hell, along with the rest of my family who have disowned me for telling the truth.”





Fiona had some fond memories of growing up before her abusers pounced, including strawberry picking and country walks – but life inside their semi-detached home was “erratic and toxic”.

She said: “I was exposed to drugs and alcohol addiction from a young age.

“I saw things children shouldn’t see or experience.”

From the age of nine, her eldest brother started giving her “special attention”.

Then, one evening, while her mum and stepdad were out, Sime pinned her down to a bed and raped her, after inviting her to watch Disney mermaid movie Aquamarine in his bedroom.

Fiona said: “He just pounced on me. I was wearing a nightie. I just froze and felt pain.

“My other brother was banging at the door. He must have known something was wrong and John jumped up to unlock it.”

The terrified child later confided in her mum – only to be left even further traumtised and confused.

She said: “I was really sore and told my mum. She put me in the bath and told me I was allergic to the bubble bath.”

Sime – who stands well over 6ft tall – struck again when he asked Fiona to go into his room to spell the word ‘the’ on his computer.



As he sat at the keyboard, he grabbed her by the hair and forced her to carry out oral sex on him.

Fiona told how the monster would also spread malicious rumours about her, saying she did sexual favours for cigarettes and juice.

She added: “I was a young girl. It went around the whole village. Can you imagine what that does to a child? The humiliation, the shame.

“He was blaming me. I was blaming myself.”

Sicko Serenity Johnston – then living as David – would be round at the house often.

It was when the family were all helping put boxes into the loft that he first sexually assaulted Fiona.

She said: “We were up in the attic alone and he touched me down there. I didn’t know what to do and was embarrassed.”

On another occasion, the fiend raped the schoolgirl.



Fiona said: “I was round at my granny’s changing her bedding and David came up behind me, pushed me on to the bed. It happened all so quick.

“After that, I was just back and forth to the doctors in pain because I was being sexually abused and raped. I still ask myself how the doctors missed this?”

A year after her brother and cousin began abusing her, beasts Alexander – or Alex as she calls him – and Robert Sives started targeting her. She was ten.

Fiona said: “It was an incestuous paedo ring.

“All of a sudden they were all abusing me – it was as if they’d all spoken, swapping notes.”

She dubs Alex the ‘ringleader’, recalling how he carried out a host of sex attacks including rape and other vile acts over 15 years.

Fiona said: “Again, it started off with sexualised comments about how I’d grow up and have ‘big boobs’. I was ten. He was just obsessed.

“When I hit puberty, he started taking photos of me. I was told what to wear and remember being dressed in a corset for the first one.



“Then he groped me in his kitchen, I wasn’t really sure how to take it, because at this point, I’d already been raped by my own brother and cousin.

“Alex was just another monster, acting in a way which was normalised in my twisted household.”

She says her grandad would carry out further sick attacks in his car, while he ran his pals back and forth to the bingo in the evenings.

When Fiona started a pre-college course in third year at secondary school, Alex picked her up and drove her to secluded country roads to abuse her.

She said: “This would happen twice a week… I basically held my breath and let my mind go somewhere else.

“He would make me do and say things to play out his sick fantasies. And he turned his dash cam round to film it all. I lie awake worrying where these images and videos have ended up.”

Robert targeted her in his bedroom when she was sent round to carry out errands for her relatives.

She said: “Robert was a fat, greasy and lazy slob. He used a mobility scooter to get around, but got around on crutches inside.



“I’d always be sent round to my grandads to clean and help, so I’d be sent upstairs with a tray of food for him.

“He’s call me inappropriate name and make me watch porn. He was very forceful and would trap me into situations, by asking me to get something from under his desk or he’d trap me against his desk and bed, so I couldn’t get out.

“He would touch me and made me perform oral sex.

“When I told him about John raping me, he said it was normal for siblings to have sex.

“All four of them – my brother, cousin, grandad and uncle – were ripping my childhood apart. I just went within myself.”

As all of this was turning her world up side down, the one person who should’ve been protecting her, was making her life a misery too.

The constant fear she felt around her mother Mary was exhausting.

One foot out of line, one command not followed and she was beaten with a wooden spoon – she dubbed a “b***h stick”.

She says: “I was walking on eggs shells all of the time, scared I’d be hit – they were weapons.

“She knew what pain I was going through mentally and physically – she’d even made me take pregnancy tests on holiday after my brother raped me – yet she wanted to inflict further pain on me.”



Fiona told how kitchen utensils filled her with dread – and she can’t even keep them in her home.

She said: “The simple sound of a wooden spoon tapping against a pot didn’t mean dinner was being made – it meant terror.

“I grieve for the mum she should have been.”

Fiona told how she lashed out for years as she struggled to deal with her dark secret.

Eventually, Fiona went to stay with a family friend aged 16 in 2014, and then secured a place of her own.

And the following year, she gave birth to her first child.

She said: “I thought things would change, but I had relatives saying, ‘Get your boobs out’, while I was breastfeeding. It was all sexualised.”

Explaining why she didn’t report the ongoing hell during her childhood, Fiona says she feared she wouldn’t be believed.

She said: “I tried to tell a social worker and they didn’t believe me.

“I told a teacher but nothing happened and then a counsellor but she made it worse by sending a letter home and I got beaten.



“I was also worried about uprooting my other siblings, if they went into care.”

Brave Fiona told how she “cries” for her younger self when she looks at old pictures.

The mum said it’s taken a lot of time for her to process and recover from what happened to her – and a lot of counselling and medication.

She said she thinks she deserved better, adding: “I just feel very sorry for younger me. I would give her a big hug.”

The relationship with her first child’s dad broke down, but in 2016, Fiona found her “soulmate”, who encouraged her to move away and go to the police – she was now in her mid 20s.

She broke down to officers about her suffering at the hands of her brother and cousin – and later she opened up about her grandad and uncle.

Her courageous decison to report them led to her brother and cousin both being convicted and jailed for a total of 16 years after separate trials.

Sime, of Uphall, and Johnston, of Broxburn, both West Lothian, denied all allegations against them in separate cases at the High Court in Livingston last September and January.

But juries returned guilty verdicts on both, over their depraved crimes.

Johnston was caged for nine years and Sime seven years. Both were placed on the sex offenders register for life.



Sime, a convicted domestic abuser, was also convicted of using lewd, indecent and libidinous practices and behaviour towards his sister when she was a child.

He was also found guilty of behaving in a threatening or abusive manner towards a relative’s female partner by refusing to leave her home when asked and repeatedly demanding that she go upstairs to a bedroom with him.

Johnston was found guilty of abusing another victim when she was aged between nine and 11 years old.

Fiona said: “It took the juries less than 50 minutes to find them guilty. I just burst out crying. I’m grateful.”

Grandad Alexander Sives had been due to stand trial next year accused of raping her, but the 83-year-old died in June. Uncle Robert Sives was under police investigation before he also died in January 2024.

Fiona says she feels “mixed emotions” that both her grandad and uncle died before she got “justice”.

She said: “I no longer have to worry about looking over my shoulder. I hope they all rot in hell for what they put me through.”

Mary Seath was last month wheeled into Livingston Sheriff Court to learn her fate for abusing Fiona and also physically attacking a boy during a 16-year reign of terror from 2009.

The court heard the bully slapped a five-year-old lad when he refused to go to nursery.

When he was around 11, the thug grabbed his hair, hit him with both fists and chased him with a toy lightsabre before the terrified boy called 999 for help, branding him a “wee p****”, “little b******” and a “c***”.



She then went on to breach bail conditions in 2024 by phoning Fiona more than 20 times and leaving voicemails calling her a “fat c***”.

She was jailed for 11 months after she pleaded guilty to physical abuse and threatening behaviour.

Fiona said: “I couldn’t help but feeling sorry for her looking frail and helpless, but I’m glad the sheriff saw through that and saw her for what she was.

“I deserved better and she taught me how not to be a mother. I am proud of the mother I am. My kids are so loved , in a happy safe home, as they should be.”

Fiona has found a circle of friends who have been a huge support, as well as her partner and kids.

She added: “My partner and I have been together for ten years, share four kids together, and he’s my absolute rock. If it weren’t for him, I wouldn’t be here.”

Fiona also credited a council-run Domestic and Sexual Assault Team (DASAT) with saving her life.

Although she still suffers bouts of anxiety and depression, Fiona is now looking to the future, as she continues to rediscover who she is.

She said: “I feel proud of the woman I am today. I can finally hold my head up high, knowing my truth and that I survived.

“I finally feel believed and heard. I just want to pave the way for my kids to have the nice childhood that I didn’t have. A house full of love.”



And she encourages anyone struggling alone to tell someone.

She’s even launched her on TikTok channel, as a way of sharing her story in a bid to help others

She said: “I just want to create a safe space and help anyway I can.

“Reporting your abusers is a very frightening prospect at first, but it’s worth the freedom at the end of it.”

News.title: Who is Navi Pillay? Everything you need to know about Nobel Peace Prize Winner
News.content:
Next

SOUTH African-born jurist Navi Pillay has been awarded the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize for her lifelong dedication to international law.

The 85-year-old legal heavyweight and former UN human rights chief received the honour on Friday, October 9.



Her victory is widely viewed as a rebuke to world leaders who have clashed with international courts, including US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Pillay beat out 287 other candidates to secure this year’s prize.



The veteran judge received the news while attending a legal gathering in Nuremberg, Germany, the historic location of the Nazi war crime trials that helped create modern international law.

Receiving a standing ovation, she said: “Your applause means a great deal to me.

“You don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this.”

She added: “But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”

Her win follows the 2025 victory for Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who made headlines by symbolically handing her Nobel medal to President Trump after the US ousted Nicolas Maduro.

Pillay joked: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”



From her anti-apartheid roots to her investigations into the Gaza conflict, here is everything you need to know about the new Nobel laureate.

Who is Navi Pillay?

Born in South Africa in 1941, Navanethem “Navi” Pillay is a lawyer and judge who has built her career taking on some of the world’s most sensitive legal battles.

During the apartheid era in her home country, she worked with Jewish lawyers to fight systemic racial segregation.

She later served as the UN’s human rights chief from 2008 to 2014 and currently works as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the highest court of the United Nations.

Why did she win the Nobel Peace Prize?

The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded Pillay the prize, which comes with 12million Swedish kronor (around £950,000), for her efforts to promote peace and international law.



Jorgen Watne Frydnes, Chair of the committee, described her as a “source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

The committee made it clear that the award is a defence of the international justice system.

At a time when global conflicts are rising, it said that resolving wars without violence relies on the international rule of law.

Pillay’s victory comes after she chaired a UN-backed commission investigating the conflict in Gaza.

Last year, the commission concluded that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza, with an intent to destroy Palestinians.



It also said Israeli leadership had “incited” genocide.

Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since 2021, denied the charges.

Her win is also seen as a direct challenge to Donald Trump’s administration, which is locked in a feud with international tribunals.

The Trump White House recently sanctioned 13 staff members at the International Criminal Court (ICC), while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio launched a campaign to “dismantle” the court.

Last month, Trump slammed the ICC at the UN as an “out of control” and “anti-American tribunal.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

What is she working on now?

Pillay is serving on the ICJ panel in a major genocide case against Myanmar.

She was selected by The Gambia, which launched legal proceedings in 2019 accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority.

News.title: Woman found dead in burning van ‘may have been alive when fire began’ – as man, 38, appears in court for ‘murder’
News.content:
VAN 'MURDER' Woman found dead in burning van ‘may have been alive when fire began’ – as man, 38, appears in court for ‘murder’







Next

A WOMAN who was found dead in a burning van might have been alive when the fire started, a court heard.

Emergency services rushed to a vehicle blaze in the seaside town of Prestatyn, North Wales, in October, after receiving reports of a vehicle fire.



The victim, who has still not been identified, was found inside the van by responding emergency services.

A murder investigation into the horror was launched as officers attempted to piece together what had happened.



Thomas Matthew Hammond Bell, 38, was arrested on Monday, October 5, in connection with the incident.

He was subsequently charged with murder and appeared in court today.



Judge Geraint Walters said it is understood the victim was alive when the van fire started and that the defendant’s case was that he did not start the fire.

The victim has not been publicly identified but the court heard she was known to Bell.

His legal team have indicated that he will enter a not guilty plea when he next appears in court on November 27.

A provisional trial date has been set for April next year and is expected to take place in either Mold or Caernarfon Crown Courts.



A Home Office post-mortem has been carried out, but officers are still urgently working to uncover who the victim is.

Local councillor Gerry Frobisher said the community was in complete shock over the tragedy.

“This type of incident, as far as I am aware, has never occurred in Prestatyn before,” he said.

“Prestatyn is a safe place to be. My thoughts go out to the family and friends of the deceased.”

Detective Chief Inspector Zoie Dunkerley said: “I understand this incident will have caused concern to the local community, and our officers will be maintaining a visible presence in the area should anyone need to talk to us.



“I would like to thank the members of the public who have already contacted us, but if you have any information that could assist our investigation, and you have not already spoken to us, please get in touch via our live webchat or on 101 quoting reference 26000816112.”

The Coroner is being kept informed as inquiries into the death continue.

News.title: Drought is declared in ANOTHER part of England despite recent rainfall
News.content:
HIGH AND DRY Drought is declared in ANOTHER part of England despite recent rainfall

Credit: Getty Images







Next

DROUGHT has been declared in another part of England despite recent rainfall hitting the UK.

The announcement follows prolonged dry weather over the spring and summer this year.

The Environment Agency has declared a drought in Yorkshire due to “low water levels in reservoirs and rivers” despite recent rainfall.



Area environment manager, Vicki Townsend, said: “The Yorkshire area has had the fifth driest April to September on record.



“This ongoing lack of rainfall means the flow in rivers and groundwater levels in certain parts of our area are very low and have now reached our trigger for declaring a drought.

“Even if we receive a few weeks of rain, we cannot quickly reverse the effects of the lack of rainfall during a very dry spring and summer.”

She has encouraged people to be aware of how the drought can impact the community and to “use a little less water to speed up the recovery from drought”.



Drought status has been declared for central, southern and eastern England, with the Yorkshire region now joining this list.

The North East and North West still remain in prolonged dry weather.

The government and the Environment Agency are continuing to “scrutinise water company actions” and make sure they “are adhering to their statutory drought plans to conserve supplies and support communities”.

Water Minister Emma Hardy said “recent rainfall is not yet enough to replenish all the water” used in spring and summer this year and news of the Yorkshire drought “highlights the situation is still serious”.



She continued: “The Government is carefully monitoring the actions of all water companies, and expect them to follow their drought plans, quickly fix leaks, and reduce demand.”

Droughts are caused by a shortage of available water due to low rainfall over a period of time.

In July, the first parts of the UK to be hit by droughts were announced as North Wales and the Upper Severn.

Drought was then declared across half of England following prolonged dry weather.

Areas included in this announcement were East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire & the Isle of Wight, Devon & Cornwall, the West Midlands and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, and South Gloucestershire).



The droughts followed a series of hosepipe bans introduced this summer which placed 23million Brits under restrictions.

News.title: Luxury eight-bed home looks normal from the outside – but buyers are put off by neighbour’s ‘House of Horrors’
News.content:
The three-storey home in Gloucester can be poached for just £350,000.

DARK SECRET Luxury eight-bed home looks normal from the outside – but buyers are put off by neighbour’s ‘House of Horrors’







Next

A NORMAL-looking eight bed-home has seen £75,000 slashed off its asking price as the sellers struggle to find a buyer – due to a neighbouring “House of Horrors”.

The three-storey townhouse in Gloucester can be poached for just £350,000, which appears to be cheaper than other similar properties in the area.



And it may be because it sits just two doors down from where serial killers Fred and Rose West lived at 25 Cromwell Street.

Their home was dubbed the ‘House of Horrors’ after nine victims were found under its patio and cellar.



The property was later torn down and the site is now a pathway.

In 1995, Rose was convicted of 10 murders, while Fred who admitted 12 murders hanged himself while on remand in prison.

He had confessed to killing up to 30 victims.



Estate agent Adam Clegg said the infamous location has been “factored into the price” of the home for sale.

He added: “Gloucester is a city that often gets overlooked, and I genuinely don’t understand why.

“It has a cathedral that rivals any in England, a historic docklands, real community spirit, and people who are fiercely proud of where they live.

“Cromwell Street carries a dark chapter in its past, but that was over thirty years ago.

“This city doesn’t deserve to be defined by it, and in my experience, most people agree. Gloucester has a bright future, and the people here know it.”



The 1,394 sq ft home is being sold by estate agents Keller Williams and is on Rightmove.

It first went on the market around a year ago for £425,000, but the asking price dropped to £375,000 in February.

It has now dropped to £350,000- making the house much cheaper than similar properties in the area, which can fetch around £525,000.

The property listing does not mention its close proximity to where the Wests buried their victims.



It reads: “A substantial terraced property positioned in the heart of Gloucester.

“As a family home, the two ground floor reception rooms stay as reception rooms, giving five bedrooms upstairs plus the separate studio, which suits letting out for extra income, a home office, or space for family.”

The property for sale has been redecorated and has new carpets.

Three of the bedrooms are on the ground floor along with a kitchen and bathroom.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

There are another three on the first floor of the house – one with an en suite – and two on the second.

There is a small garden out the back and off-road parking.

News.title: Polanski vows to stay on as Green leader as criticism mounts after by-election defeat
News.content:
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.

The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he "should resign", adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Lichtenstein's comments come after former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.

Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that.

The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year.

Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.

In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with â it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee."

Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.

The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom".

News.title: 'Deeply personal moment': Watch Sagal Abdi-Wali's by-election victory speech
News.content:
Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, securing 45% of the vote and beating the Green Party which came in second place.

In her victory speech, the Camden Council leader reflected on how the borough had given her family a home and shaped her life.

"My commitment to this community runs deep," she said, adding that she hoped people who looked like her would see themselves reflected in Parliament.

News.title: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
News.content:
Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in February, in the middle of a storm of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The former Prince Andrew was moved to Sandringham, with his brother the King using his own money to provide his upkeep and accommodation.

Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested later that month on suspicion of misconduct in public office - and a court ruling on Thursday found fault with the search warrants used by the police.

But despite moving to Sandringham, Mountbatten-Windsor's lease on Royal Lodge had remained until October - and as that officially ends, the Crown Estate is revealing the terms on which it concluded.

When Andrew had taken on the 75 year lease in 2003, he had made considerable up-front payments, including about Â£7.5m for repairs, which meant that he did not have to pay a monthly rent.

It also meant that if he gave up the lease within the first 25 years he would be legally entitled to some compensation - with that amount reducing each year.

Leaving in October 2026 would have meant that the Crown Estate would have had to pay him back about Â£302,000.

However that amount has been overshadowed by what he owes to the landlord for the state of the building - and so the Crown Estate says it has now received a net amount of Â£1.5m.

It's understood that the payment of that money by the King is to avoid leaving the Crown Estate out of pocket.

Whether Mountbatten-Windsor will repay his brother is said to be a private matter - and there are no further details of what this might say about Andrew's personal finances.

There was also no comment on how the King feels about this arrangement - and there is said to be no connection between this payment and the King making clear this week that his financial support should not go to cover Andrew's legal costs in his battle over search warrants.

It has so far not been decided how the 30-room mansion in Windsor will be used in future, but it is expected to be used to deliver a commercial return - and at present there are no plans for another royal occupant.

"The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return," said a Crown Estate spokesperson.

A report by the National Audit Office had revealed earlier this year that Mountbatten-Windsor had been sub-letting buildings at Royal Lodge, although the amount was never revealed.

That report from the public spending watchdog also showed that Andrew's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Eugenie, had accommodation inside royal palaces which they did not pay for, with the cost being covered privately by the King.

News.title: Alison Hammond: 'I thought I was having heart attack on air'
News.content:
Alison Hammond has said she feared she was having a heart attack on air when she had to rush off ITV's This Morning midway through the programme last week.

The presenter appeared to clutch her chest as she left the show last Friday, and was taken to hospital to have a heart check-up.

She turned out to have suffered a panic attack, and said the experience was "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through".

Returning for her weekly slot on Friday, she told viewers: "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack. I'm so glad I'm here. I feel so grateful. I feel so thankful to God, to everything in life."

She added: "It felt like a heart attack. It was very real."

News.title: £15m spent cleaning illegal waste supersite in ancient woodland
News.content:
The Environment Agency-led clean-up operation began in June 2025 and has seen 2,500 lorry loads of waste removed from the woods by specialist contractors to a landfill site in Essex.

The countryside charity CPRE Kent, residents and Kent Wildlife Trust joined forces in 2024 to campaign for the clearance of the waste, which was piled up to 15ft (4.6m) in places.

They welcomed the work's completion but some are concerned the criminal gangs may return to dump waste.

One of the organisers of the 'Rescue Hoads Wood' campaign said the cleared site would now be "catnip" to both organised gangs and opportunist fly-tippers.

He told the BBC: "Our biggest fear now is people are going to be able to access this site and start dumping on it again and unless the authorities are quick it will happen again."

The Environment Agency (EA) said it was extending the current restriction order in place that prohibits access and had dug ditches to make the site inaccessible to waste trucks.

Matthew Higginson, the EA's area environmental manager, said the regulator, police and local authorities had a joint "trigger plan" in place.

"That will bring all law enforcement partners to work together closely and much more quickly to stop anything like this happening in the future," he said.

News.title: Watch: Fleeing Kyiv for the countryside ahead of winter
News.content:
Kyiv resident Olena Konoplia has decided to move to Ukraine's countryside, as Russian attacks on the city have intensified and the prospect of another cold winter looms.

Russia has been targeting Ukraine's power grid leaving locals without electricity and heating, and they will soon face prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures.

Olena told the BBC she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.

"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explained.

News.title: Autism, ADHD and mental health review: What you need to know
News.content:
The report is clear that there is an increasing risk of over-diagnosis, but only when it comes to ADHD and autism.

Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups.

They gave the example of children aged six to 17 â more than 4% have been diagnosed with autism. That's well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level.

But this comes with a big caveat. There are weaknesses in the data. Evidence about the true level of autism relies on surveys that have not been done for nine years, so the review team have had to estimate what has happened since.

And there are some age groups where these conditions are still being under-diagnosed, and that should not be overlooked.

It is why the review team said it could not yet conclude over-diagnosis was happening "at scale". But there is certainly evidence to suggest we are moving from an era of under-diagnosis to one of over-diagnosis, the experts said.

They warn not every difficulty requires a medical response and there is a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the "normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour".

News.title: Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
News.content:
But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election â and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.

Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And he repeatedly declined to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.

But this morning he did speak to journalists.

He told BBC Breakfast that if he had he been there for the vote he "would have voted for the amendments".

Asked if he would have voted against the motion in the hall on that day, Polanski said: "the motion as amended I would have voted for, the motion unamended I wouldn't have voted for."

He added: "I think it's an imperfect motion, there's parts I disagree with and parts I agree with."

Some in the party are furious about what has happened in recent days, with one figure telling me: "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control."

Green Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.

Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.

And â significantly â the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.

Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".

He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people".

"I believe that is clearly racist," he added.

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

And asked if he believed in a two-state solution â an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other â he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".

He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together".

"No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.

But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.

The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.

News.title: New evidence gives family hope after death in Spain
News.content:
Four years after watching his brother die in his arms, Maximilian White believes new evidence could help him get answers.

Tobias White-Sansom, a father-of-two from Nottingham, died in a Spanish hospital in July 2022, five days after a night out in Magaluf, and his family believes the way security and police officers handled him that night led to his death.

A blood spatter report and a court order received by the family this month have reignited their hopes that criminal proceedings could commence in the Spanish courts.

White told the BBC: "I won't stop until we get justice for Toby."

The 46-year-old medical cannabis entrepreneur said he found it difficult to talk about the way he lost his younger sibling, who was on a family holiday at the time.

White-Sansom was pinned down at a nightclub following a row over him removing his T-shirt because he was too hot, his family said.

They told the BBC the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was called and he was handcuffed, Tasered and injected with tranquilisers before going into cardiac arrest.

News.title: Teen's life transformed by gene editing
News.content:
A teenager has revealed how her life has been transformed thanks to pioneering gene editing, which reversed symptoms of a crippling blood disorder.

Vian, 16, was born with thalassemia, a condition that affects haemoglobin - used by red blood cells to transport oxygen around the body. It left her short of breath and with no appetite.

Her own stem cells were edited and she no longer needs the monthly blood transfusions she endured for most of her life.

"My whole life's different now. It's changed so much," she said.

The treatment, for patients with thalassaemia or sickle cell disease, is offered to young people at three children's hospitals in the country.

Vian, from Coventry, was one of the first to have it.

News.title: Abusive ex admits murdering woman after she began new relationship
News.content:
A man with a history of domestic abuse has admitted murdering his former partner a day after learning she had begun another relationship.

Lee Inglis pled guilty at the High Court in Edinburgh to stabbing Stacey Hogg to death in her home in Hawick earlier this year.

BBC Scotland News has learned that the 39-year-old had twice avoided prison for previous knife attacks on the mother of three.

He was still serving a home curfew and an unpaid work order when he killed the 35-year-old in June.

He waited until his curfew ended at 07:00 before making the three-minute journey from his parents' home to Stacey's house.

Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting

The court heard that he slipped in through the back door and attacked Stacey as she came down the stairs.

She suffered "catastrophic wounds" to her neck and head. Police found her in a pool of blood on a downstairs bathroom floor.

The court heard that when he was arrested by police he told them: "I intended to cut off her head."

"If I couldn't have her, nobody would," he added.

Inglis will be sentenced at the High Court in Edinburgh on 5 November.

News.title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
News.content:
Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.

The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of Â£400m.

In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter".

"The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said.

"When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters.

"With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton."

TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window.

In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025.

Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.

Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a Â£40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong.

Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after.

The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry.

TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward".

"Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued.

News.title: Drought declared in Yorkshire after dry weather
News.content:
Drought has been declared across Yorkshire following months of unusually dry weather.

The Environment Agency (EA) said low water levels in reservoirs and rivers had triggered the move despite recent rainfall across parts of the region.

Yorkshire officially entered drought status on Friday after a lack of spring and summer rainfall, having previously been classified as in a period of prolonged dry weather.

Yorkshire Water said it was not planning to introduce water restrictions for customers at this stage despite the drought declaration.

Andy Shaw, head of water production, treatment and energy at Yorkshire Water, said the EA's decision reflected dry conditions across the region but "does not mean water restrictions are currently needed".

EA manager Vicki Townend said Yorkshire had seen its fifth driest period on record between April and September.

Townend said: "The ongoing lack of rainfall means the flow in rivers and groundwater levels in certain parts of our area are very low and have now reached our trigger for declaring a drought.

"Even if we receive a few weeks of rain, we cannot quickly reverse the effects of the lack of rainfall during a very dry spring and summer."

News.title: Teenager who lost mum says she no longer feels alone in her grief
News.content:
Until recently 17-year-old Niamh says she would often feel alone while dealing with the loss of her mother who died a few years ago.

But now she says creating art and talking to other young people has helped her process that grief.

She is one of about 100 teenagers who have taken part in a project to help them deal with bereavement and loss.

Through storytelling and art, young people are encouraged to think about signs of grief with fellow pupils and are offered ways to cope with their feelings.

Niamh said: "The whole experience just made me more comfortable to talk to others about grief and I built a lot of strong friendships from it.

"I think it has just helped make me a more resilient person overall and more comfortable with expressing my feelings."

News.title: Man who stabbed ex in 'rage of anger' as she walked her dog jailed for 24 years
News.content:
He said the attack was interrupted after Sidaway told him to stop and screamed, and a neighbour shouted.

Neighbour Susan Edwards heard "high-pitched screaming" and the "bushes shaking" before McKenna ran away.

Sidaway phoned for an ambulance and said: "I've been stabbed by my ex-partner... he's been stalking me."

McKenna dumped his rucksack and knife at an allotment near the park after eating yoghurt.

He then walked three miles (4km) to Bronwydd village along the River Gwili.

"I found some shelter, a quiet woodland away from the road," he said.

"I was devastated and kept having flashbacks."

He was there for three nights before getting a taxi and bus to Bronglais Hospital in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion.

Police bodycam footage showed Sidaway sitting on her doorstep with paramedics, covered in blood.

There were 17 areas of damage to her coat and her clothing was extensively blood-stained. She received injuries to her chest, arm and hand.

Sentencing McKenna, Thomas said: "You had been in a relationship with a woman of whose vulnerabilities you would have been fully aware.

"When she decided, as was entirely her prerogative, that she no longer wanted to be in a relationship with you, you reacted, as you had done in the past, immaturely, and more significantly with violence.

"You stalked her in the park in Carmarthen that morning, then you returned in the afternoon with exactly the same intention. It was planned, and it was wholly calculated.

"You stabbed her no fewer than 11 times. Three of those being to the chest and therefore heart area.

"That lady only survived because it was a cold day and she was wearing five layers under a thick coat. But after you did that, you left her to die in bushes in a park.

"You only handed yourself in when you developed frostbite from sleeping rough."

He said McKenna was "full of self-pity".

News.title: Harry says he 'slipped into depression' after leaving UK
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said he "slipped into depression for about two weeks" after relocating to Canada in 2019 ahead of his move to the US.

Prince Harry, who recently returned to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children, said he had originally left the country to "get some space."

The duke also discussed feeling "emotionally numb" after the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales, because he felt "disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her".

He opened up about his mental health with a neuroscientist in a session for a video learning platform.

He and his brother, the Prince of Wales, have previously been candid about their mental health struggles, including over their mother's death, and both are involved in mental health charities.

Prince Harry, who stepped back from royal duties to move to California with Meghan, made the latest comments as part of a paid-for online masterclass on dealing with grief.

"Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I'd never experienced before," he recalled.

"It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house.

"I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks and I felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline."

News.title: F1 Singapore GP LIVE: George Russell eyes sprint pole ahead of Kimi Antonelli
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

George Russell went fastest in first practice in Singapore ( Reuters )

Formula 1 returns to the Marina Bay Street Circuit this weekend for the Singapore Grand Prix - and the final sprint race of the 2026 season.

Kimi Antonelli took another giant step towards his first world championship at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. His accomplished second-place finish came with the unfortunate late retirement of George Russell. The Italian’s lead over his Mercedes teammate is now 84 points with seven rounds remaining.

Max Verstappen claimed his first victory of the season - and Red Bull’s first as a power-unit supplier - in Sepang while Lewis Hamilton fought back from a dreadful start to claim a memorable podium for Ferrari.

Singapore represents the final sprint weekend of the season, with Russell claiming three short-format victories this season. However, the Briton will start from the back of the grid for this Sunday’s grand prix after taking a new power unit.

Follow live updates from the Singapore Grand Prix with The Independent

News.title: My covert SAS life: I was hiding in a hedge as an Irish farmer covered me in petrol
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The two SAS soldiers had been peed on before. But petrol being poured onto the hedge they were hiding in and now running down their faces was a new and dangerous low.

For days they had barely moved. Now the farmer they had been secretly watching had an inkling that someone was watching. He was systematically soaking the vegetation around them with fuel.

John, then a young SAS soldier serving in South Armagh, remembers sitting absolutely still as the liquid soaked through his camouflage uniform.

“We’re sitting there and his petrol was running down our faces,” he recalls. “It’s all over us and we’re thinking, this is going to get quite ugly.”

Listen to the full third episode of SAS: The Shadow War here, or become an Independent Member for exclusive access to all eight episodes:

For much of the SAS’s secret war in Northern Ireland, this was what soldiering looked like. Not black-clad men abseiling through windows or dramatic gun battles, but two exhausted men, buried inside a wet hedge, staring through binoculars at a farmhouse and trying desperately not to be discovered.

They called it an OP, an observation post. The job was simple to describe, difficult to do.

“You’d have a place that you were watching,” John says. In South Armagh, it was often a farm. The soldiers recorded who arrived, who left, which vehicles appeared and who spoke to whom.

They were building up profiles of suspects, looking for “patterns of life” that might indicate militant activity – and sources of finance for violent groups like the Irish Republican Army.

Telling the inside story of a routine operation for the special forces on SAS: The Shadow War, an eight-part audio podcast series from Aurra and Independent Studios – John reveals the everyday reality of what serving in Northern Ireland is like.

Their equipment was basic. Binoculars, notebook and radio. The radio was barely used. A couple of clicks at predetermined intervals, “proof of life”, to the operations room. Otherwise – silence.

OPs could take days and stretch to weeks of sleep deprivation and indignity. Discovery, known as “compromise”, could be fatal – or worse.

open image in gallery Members of the SAS on training exercises in the Brecon Beacons in the 1970s ( Popperfoto/Getty )

Winter brought cold, mud and water. Sleep came in fragments. Men got trench foot.

“Once you've got yourself in somewhere, you can't very well wander off,” John says. “You might get found, you might get shot, you might give away your position.”

So the men urinated into lemonade bottles and defecated into plastic bags while sitting shoulder-to-shoulder.

“It wasn't for the shy and retiring,” he adds.

But discomfort was incidental. The real danger was a single movement, sound or piece of bad luck that told somebody the hedge was occupied.

A dog could end an operation.

“If the dogs found you, then it was game over,” John says. If locals suspected surveillance, he says, they might begin deliberately searching hedgerows, sometimes thrusting a stick through the vegetation in the hope of hitting a hidden soldier and forcing a reaction.

On one operation, John and his partner were concealed near the door of a farmhouse when the owner returned from the pub. The man stopped at precisely their hiding place to pee.

open image in gallery Sam Kiley speaks to SAS soldier John as he describes the grim reality of surveillance ( The Independent )

“You're just sitting there,” John remembers, “with wee running down your face and over your clothes.”

“This isn't very glamorous,” he thought.

The comedy could slide to tragedy in a heartbeat.

“Paranoia was them opening up on you from somewhere around you,” he says.

But death in a bomb blast or a blizzard of bullets was preferable to what all SAS and other special forces operators most feared - capture.

“You knew you could live with being shot and blown up,” he says. But if you were abducted, “there was no good ending coming to you”.

The image that haunted him was brutally simple: several men suddenly appearing, a bag pulled over the soldier's head, then being shoved into the boot of a car. Days, perhaps weeks of torture and interrogation would be followed by murder and an unknown grave.

The SAS team didn’t know if the farmer they were watching was in the IRA or not. But he was deeply suspicious of being watched.

For a couple of days the farmer walked around the three hedges in the field where John and his partner were hiding.

On the third day, he emerged from an outbuilding carrying half a dozen jerry cans.

Then he took two cans to the hedge and began splashing their contents over it. He then fetched two more. This time he came towards John.

“He just walked along in front of us and covered the hedgerow in what was now obviously petrol.”

open image in gallery A soldier patrols in the republican district of Belfast, on 23 March 1988, Northern Ireland ( AFP/Getty )

The soldiers radioed a warning. They might have to break cover. Backup might be needed.

But how to escape?

If the farmer knew where they were, perhaps others did too. And the obvious escape route — backwards through the hedge — was exactly where John imagined an IRA gun team would be waiting.

“You're in a sort of gambling situation,” he recalls. “What are your options now?”

The farmer went indoors. John assumed he was waiting to see whether the soldiers would panic and run.

The two men stayed where they were, soaked in petrol, discussing their choices in whispers.

Then the farmer emerged from his house. He had a boy with him, a young teenager - maybe even just 10 years old. John watched the two talk.

Then the youngster struck a match and threw it into the hedge.

“Bang! The whole thing literally is exploding in a matter of a few seconds,” says John.

The hidden OP had become an inferno. The OP team could not run to the rear for fear of an IRA ambush.

The two heavily armed, smoke-blackened men suddenly erupted from a hedge that had appeared empty seconds earlier, “shouting and hollering like a couple of banshees,” John says.

open image in gallery Members of the Provisional Irish Republican Army (IRA) hold a banner reading "Elizabeth Regina, Queen of Death, 69-77-1,800 dead" march 10 August 1977 in the streets of Belfast ( AFP/Getty )

The farmer and boy were terrified. The soldiers ran straight past them. Then they kept running down the farm track until a vehicle reached them farther along the road.

Nobody fired.

“Everything out there is a gamble,” he says. “On that day, we called it correctly, but equally, we could have called it another way.”

“The margin,” he says, was desperately small.
