31m ago 07.27 EDT A reminder of the Premier League table before it all kicks off again Share

32m ago 07.25 EDT Liverpool v Man City (Sunday, 4.30pm) “Is there any truth to the rumour,” begins Krishnamoorthy V, “that Liverpool have printed a pennant with the slogan You Will Walk Alone for Sunday’s game?” Share

49m ago 07.09 EDT World Cup qualifier: Greece v England (5.30pm) The Lionesses are in Crete for the first leg of their World Cup qualification playoff against Greece. This is what you get when you mess with us you’re drawn in the same qualification as Spain. This clown will be on liveblog duty for the game. For now, here’s Tom Garry’s preview. Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff Read more Share Updated at 07.09 EDT

1h ago 06.59 EDT Rob Smyth is here to guide you the next little while, with the likes of Andoni Iraola, Mikel Arteta, Michael Carrick, Xabi Alonso and Roberto De Zerbi all due to speak soon. Share

1h ago 06.43 EDT All the Premier League managers are being asked about Manchester City, including Brighton’s Fabian Hürzeler who said “hopefully it will be dealt with”. Brighton go to Sunderland tomorrow looking to pick up where they left off in the Premier League, with that 3-0 win over Arsenal. They are third in the league going into the weekend – Harry Paterson assesses how high they can finish this season … Are Brighton genuine contenders to qualify for the Champions League? Read more Share

1h ago 06.34 EDT Staying in Spain, Sid Lowe has been speaking to Rayo Vallecano striker Sergio Camello, who has scored seven goals in seven games in La Liga this season. The interview is accompanied by some wonderful pictures of Camello in Vallecas, the working-class Madrid neighbourhood that is home to Rayo and its wonderfully old-fashioned ground. double quotation mark Rayo is the last team standing from football from another time, that’s what I like. Even just parking here on the street right in front changes things. The same faces, every time. The least important thing about the football here is the football; it’s what they stand for every weekend, what they believe in, the connection. View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello at Vallecas’ dressing room entrance. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian Sergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’ Read more Share

2h ago 06.26 EDT Mourinho hits out at 'ridiculous' Mbappé criticism José Mourinho joked this week that he’ll be “lucky to still be around” when the Manchester City case is put to bed. “I think we will eventually get an ending, but we [Mourinho and the journalist] are both in our 60s and we’ll need ​to be lucky ​enough to still ⁠be around when the final verdict arrives,” Mourinho told the Italian newspaper Corriere dello Sport. During his press conference in Spain today, Mourinho has defended Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé after the striker was pictured at a nightclub in Paris and riding a bike in Switzerland while he recovers from a knee injury. “Are these criticisms over the top? They are ridiculous,” Mourinho said today. “All the players who were obliged to be present every day for their recovery were here. “Mbappé came, like the others, to undergo scans in order to be diagnosed. He then went to see a specialist in France, because he has history with his knee which we cannot ignore. “Problems involving football are not sufficient for you [the media]. “Therefore you have raised the issue of the nightclub, which in fact was not one, because it was used for a private event for Fashion Week. “As for the bicycle in Switzerland. It was in a hotel, made up of small houses, which makes them available so guests can ride to the communal areas, and you would have us believe he was competing in the Tour of Switzerland.” Real Madrid host Villarreal at the Bernabéu tomorrow night and are six points off the leaders Barcelona in La Liga. View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé trains at Real Madrid on Thursday. Photograph: Maria Jimenez/Real Madrid/Getty Images Share Updated at 06.39 EDT

2h ago 06.16 EDT Tim gets in touch on email: double quotation mark As a Liverpool fan, I don’t think the Man City players cheated or weren’t a great team. But the point is that they cheated to have such a great team. There were times during our title battles where we had a better team (just) but their squad was ridiculous. Regarding injuries, tiredness, fatigue etc they had a huge - unfair - advantage.



And on this idea of a Premier League glass ceiling that they so nobly broke, Liverpool went nearly 25 years without winning it, often finishing mid table. See also Arsenal and Man Utd. Being a big club with lots of fans is obviously an advantage, but one built over the course of a century, rather than being bestowed on the whims of a foreign state.



Anyway, whatever their punishment, City fans will think it’s too harsh and everyone else too lenient. May as well just get it all over and done with. Share

2h ago 06.11 EDT Another little tidbit from Maresca was his quip about possibly having to coach City in lower leagues. Guardiola had previously said (joked?) he would stay with City if they were relegated to League One. “I won the Championship with Leicester, so in case we’re in League One, we’ll see,” Maresca said with a smile. “But we are thinking about something we don’t know.” View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca wins the Championship with Leicester. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters Share

2h ago 06.03 EDT One of the more interesting things Maresca admitted was that the topic of City’s 115 charges (114 of which they are now guilty of) did not come up in conversation during his talks about succeeding Guardiola in the summer. Share

2h ago 05.59 EDT Well, that was a grilling. Maresca fielded questions for about 20 minutes from some of the British sports media’s top journalists. He acknowledged that perhaps he was not giving the answers they were hoping for as he repeated the club’s official lines on sticking together and the confidence they will win an appeal. I think City will be relatively pleased with his performance. Share

2h ago 05.53 EDT Maresca: I trust Manchester City completely, there is nowhere I would rather be Jamie Jackson at Etihad Campus Enzo Maresca has stated he “trusts completely” Manchester City and repeatedly said “when we win the appeal” in the manager’s first media conference since the club were found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules. “I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club,” said the Italian. “There is not another club in the world where I would like to be. I’m very happy to be [here] I’m very proud.” Maresca was also asked if City’s honours won since the Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008 have been tainted. “Absolutely not,” he insisted. “The last time I was here was in the treble season [2022-23, as assistant manager] and I know the effort from the players, the club, the manager. I know the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target so I don’t have any doubt about that.” City strenuously deny any wrongdoing and have lodged an appeal against the verdict of an independent commission. One sanction the club could face should thee appeal fail is expulsion from the Premier League. City travel to Anfield on Sunday to face Liverpool. View image in fullscreen All eyes on Maresca. Photograph: Andy Hampson/PA Share Updated at 06.18 EDT

2h ago 05.51 EDT And with that, Maresca takes his leave. Just the one slip-up against a barrage of probing questions from the media – saying he trusts the club “at the moment”, which he later clarified to say he trusts them “always”. Another thing to note: Maresca said he spoke to Pep Guardiola after the derby win over Manchester United last month but seemingly not since the guilty verdict. Share

2h ago 05.48 EDT “Finally,” Maresca smiles when a Norwegian journalist asks him about Erling Haaland’s fitness. “He’s ready for Anfield,” he adds. Share Updated at 05.49 EDT

2h ago 05.47 EDT Maresca is asked whether he would have accepted the City job had he known about the charges. “100%,” he replies. “I know the organisation from years ago. I know how serious they are. They do the right things. I would like to speak about this when we win the appeal. “To be honest. We didn’t speak about that,” he says of whether he spoke to City about the charges before taking the job. “That wasn’t a problem for the club at the time because they are speaking in an honest way. They are convinced in the end that they are going to win the appeal.” Share

2h ago 05.44 EDT “I understand that probably you want to hear different words from me,” Maresca admits. “But the real words is that, the players … yes, the noise is there … they are 20-25 years old. They come, they enjoy their training sessions. They go home happy. They are top of the league. “So the players are relaxed. They are just thinking of how we can beat Liverpool.” Share

2h ago 05.41 EDT “They can face the pressure, absolutely,” Maresca says of the test facing his players at Anfield on Sunday. “They already experience a similar a situation. I don’t know … Enzo Fernandez is playing in Argentina. In Argentina, it’s almost every game to go to Anfield.” Share

2h ago 05.39 EDT Maresca is asked about what might happen if City lose the appeal against the guilty verdict. “What happens if we win the appeal? We are predicting the future,” he replies. Asked again about whether he would stay if City are relegated, he reminds the media that he won the Championship with Leicester. Share

2h ago 05.36 EDT Maresca is quizzed about his comments just now about trusting the club completely “at the moment” and whether that trust could change. “Sorry that was the wrong answer,” he replies. “I completely trust the club in this moment, in the future, always. “Thank you, I can modify the answer,” he laughs. Share Updated at 05.36 EDT

2h ago 05.33 EDT Maresca says City achievements ‘absolutely not’ tainted Maresca is asked whether his achievements as Pep Guardiola’s assistant feel tainted by the guilty verdict. His response? “Absolutely not.” He slightly dodges a question about whether, as Guardiola had said previously, he would stay on as head coach if City are relegated. “There is not another club in the world where I want to be,” Maresca says. View image in fullscreen Maresca meets the media. Photograph: Andy Hampson/PA Share Updated at 06.17 EDT

2h ago 05.31 EDT Enzo Maresca faces the media Maresca bats away the first question from the BBC about the guilty verdict. “I understand the reason why most of you are here,” he says to the journalists present, “but the only thing I can say is that something I already said: there is a process ongoing and in this moment I completely trust the club. This is what I can say about that.” Share

3h ago 05.27 EDT The seats are filling up in the media theatre at Manchester City’s training ground. We shall see how much Enzo Maresca is willing or able to talk about the club’s guilty verdict. As usual, it is the head coach who must front up to the press about club issues instead of those higher up. Maresca has arrived … Share

3h ago 05.23 EDT European FAs pushing for three-week international break to be abandoned Nick Ames Europe’s football associations have raised serious concerns about the impact of the extended international break and will ask Uefa to push for a reversion to the previous scheduling. The new three-week break left European countries tasked with four Nations League games, which typically took place within 11 days. It has brought deep misgivings about player workload, injuries and financial viability, with one FA president telling the Guardian it was “a disaster” and numerous others saying the schedule is unworkable. European FAs pushing for three-week international break to be abandoned Read more Share

3h ago 05.17 EDT Football Weekly: You can watch/listen to the pod squad discuss Sunday’s clash between Liverpool and Manchester City, plus much more, in the latest episode. 51:36 Manchester City go to Anfield and is Eckert’s Spygate ban too lenient? | Football Weekly video Share

3h ago 05.10 EDT A reminder that Enzo Maresca will face the media in 20 minutes’ time at the Etihad Campus in Manchester. You can follow the press conference live here. Share

3h ago 05.04 EDT Big interview: Oliver Glasner has told Ben Fisher he has “two hearts” beating inside his chest as he prepares to take his Nottingham Forest team to face former club Crystal Palace on Sunday. When Glasner left Palace at the end of last season, he raised a few eyebrows by turning up at Forest. Relations between the two clubs have been tense since Forest took Palace’s place in the Europa League last season after they complained to Uefa about a breach of its multi-ownership rules. double quotation mark It was not a decision against Crystal Palace, because I decided last October, one year ago, not to sign a new contract. It was then, in the summer, a decision for Nottingham Forest, due to different reasons. Sometimes unexpected things happen in life … there was no plan for me to be Forest manager. Oliver Glasner: ‘There was no plan for me to be Nottingham Forest manager’ Read more Share

3h ago 04.55 EDT What do Man City fans actually think? The Guardian has spoken to a handful on either side of the Atlantic. double quotation mark Whatever happens, nobody can take the last 15 years away from us. We lived every moment: Agüero in 2012, the centurions, the treble, Istanbul. Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that. Right now I just feel confused – Ben, season ticket holder double quotation mark I can’t give those memories back. But I do know that the richest people in the world thinking that the rules don’t apply to them, that they can cheat and then arrogantly chuck endless money at the situation, has nothing to do with what I love about football, nothing to do with what I love about Manchester, nothing to do with what I love about my club … I’m really sad – James, fan for more than 40 years double quotation mark The severity and duration of City’s offences warrant significant punishment, but the verdict that it took this much sustained rule-breaking and money to prevent United, Arsenal and Liverpool adding to their own trophy cabinets is an indictment on the Premier League – Jon, fan in Washington DC ‘Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that’: Manchester City fans’ views Read more Share

3h ago 04.46 EDT “I have titles but I don’t have them hanging on my wall. I have them in my head,” said Coventry manager Frank Lampard, who spent one season at Manchester City in 2014-15, during his press conference yesterday. “Most players that have played and competed against the best players have worked very hard to win. I think it would be very hard to take someone’s title away as a player individually as I think they should be in your head as opposed to in this beautiful glass cabinet or whatever. “I’m not inside the story, I’m outside it completely – I played for Man City a long time ago, for one year – so we’ll wait and see what the result of the appeal is.” Lampard’s Coventry, who picked up their first win of the season against Nottingham Forest three weeks ago, host Newcastle on Monday night. Share

Sports.title: Everton owner The Friedkin Group exploring sale of club after two years
Sports.content:
Everton’s owner, The Friedkin Group, is looking to sell the club less than two years after taking over from Farhad Moshiri.

The Houston-based company confirmed in a statement on Friday that it was seeking fresh investment in Everton but was also open to relinquishing control should a suitable buyer be found. No timescale has been placed on a sale but TFG is confident of attracting a buyer quickly and potentially concluding a deal this season.

“The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest,” it said. Moelis & Company, an investment bank, will handle any sale.

Quick Guide How do I 

TFG’s announcement follows a calamitous end to the summer transfer window that raised scrutiny over its long-term commitment to the Premier League club. The group’s decision is understood to be based on the amount of funding needed to further Everton’s ambitions and restrictions surrounding multi-club ownership. Roma, another high-profile asset requiring serious investment, and Cannes are also in TFG’s stable. The company is preparing to launch an NHL franchise in Houston worth about $3.5bn (£2.6bn).

TFG’s move is also an opportunity to make a quick profit on a club it bought as a distressed asset from Moshiri in December 2024. TFG spent about £400m to take over Everton and the club’s considerable debt – Moshiri walked away with an initial £25m – and has stabilised the finances while securing funding for Hill Dickinson Stadium on more favourable terms. An asking price of about £800m, including long-term debt of about £380m, would represent a healthy return in the event of a full sale, although all levels of investment are being considered.

The statement said: “When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club’s future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters.

“With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton. We will only entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward and build on the momentum that has been established. Throughout this process, TFG’s focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves.”

TFG’s financial and personal commitment to Everton has been questioned in recent months. The club’s transfer strategy changed midway through the summer window to a sell-to-buy policy, with the owner’s decision to accept a £40m offer from Nottingham Forest for Harrison Armstrong the first sign of that shift. Armstrong’s sale was halted after a backlash among Evertonians but the team’s most creative asset, Iliman Ndiaye, was then sold to Manchester City for £65m. David Moyes, whose long-term future at Everton is also uncertain, then revealed he had never spoken to Dan Friedkin, TFG’s founder and the club’s chair, since returning as manager in January 2025.

Moyes’s squad was left short on numbers and a centre-forward on deadline day after Beto’s sale to Fiorentina and the collapse of Folarin Balogun’s mooted £40m move from Monaco. Everton have plans to address those weaknesses in January but they could be affected by a potential takeover.

TFG believed they could work around Uefa regulations on multi-club ownership should Everton and Roma qualify for the same European competition. That is not the case and, with Uefa enforcing rules on such ownership structures strictly, TFG faces having to put one club in a blind trust to avoid any sanctions.

With the stadium move complete and finances stabilised, Everton are a more attractive proposition than when TFG bought the club.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
Sports.content:
1 Rice rested and refreshed?

Declan Rice’s future role in England’s midfield was questioned by Gary Lineker after Alex Scott’s impressive first senior international start in the 7-0 thrashing of Croatia. But the decision to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel’s squad in an attempt to manage his workload made sense after Rice had only three weeks off post-World Cup before returning to pre-season training. The 27-year-old has struggled with persistent back problems after suffering a hamstring injury last December and Mikel Arteta will hope that the rest has done Rice – who is thought to be close to agreeing a lucrative new contract at the Emirates – the world of good as they prepare to resume the defence of their Premier League title against Leeds on Saturday. Ed Aarons

Arsenal v Leeds, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)

2 Ready? Garnacho’s time to shine

Several Aston Villa players shone for their countries during the international window but one of those who stayed with the club may have made the biggest impression on Unai Emery. Villa’s remaining squad went to Spain for a mid-season training camp, including Alejandro Garnacho, whose last cap for Argentina was almost two years ago. Garnacho has been lesser-spotted in a Villa shirt, playing just 31 minutes as a substitute, but scored in both of Villa’s friendlies during the break, against Southampton and Sevilla. The 22-year-old, who joined Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer with a conditional obligation, was an unused substitute for their past four matches but is he now primed to affect games? Villa are hopeful Emery has unlocked Garnacho, who has struggled for form since leaving Manchester United. “Ready now!” Garnacho posted on social media last weekend and Villa will hope that is the case. Ben Fisher

Aston Villa v Brentford, Saturday 3pm

3 Toth can soothe pain of Scott’s injury

With Eli Junior Kroupi, Amine Adli, Veljko Milosavljevic and Julián Araujo yet to feature this season due to injury, Marco Rose must have been tearing his remaining hair out upon learning Alex Scott got hurt on England duty and will be out of action for two months. Sitting 17th and still searching for their first league win, the German’s side squandered nine points from winning positions in four of their first five games – and it was the 23-year-old who was central in ensuring Bournemouth had those leads in the first place. With just 55 minutes of football behind him this season, it seems unlikely Alex Toth will get the nod to replace Scott when Bournemouth travel to Chelsea with the older, more experienced Ryan Christie available and in good form. But having forced his way into the Hungary starting lineup during the international break it would be no surprise to see the 20-year-old get more minutes with a view to being used far more often given his side’s gruelling schedule of nine matches in the next month. Barry Glendenning

Chelsea v Bournemouth, Saturday 3pm

View image in fullscreen Alex Toth impressed for Hungary during the international break and will look to make his mark for Bournemouth. Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP

4 Ipswich’s calm an obstacle for Fulham

Ipswich’s place in mid-table, their total of six points, came via victories over Sunderland and Crystal Palace. Gary O’Neil’s team were presented with a tough opening schedule, and while defeated by Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, their manager has not allowed those reverses to dilute team spirit. Speaking to the media following the home defeat by Liverpool, O’Neil painted an ultra-positive picture that defied most observers’ view of a game beyond his team’s reach from the early stages. Thus far, a successful strategy, certainly by comparison to early season at winless Fulham. Like O’Neil, Álvaro Arbeloa is new to his job. An improved performance in the draw against United did not result in a victory Fulham deserved, though there were signs of the progressive, attacking football the arrival of the former Real Madrid interim promised. Much of the burden has fallen on Josh King, the teenager building on last year’s breakthrough season. John Brewin

Ipswich v Fulham, Saturday 3pm

5 Ballard’s absence a boon for Brighton

Still in the Carabao Cup, with a Europa League campaign to negotiate and just four points acquired from their opening five Premier League excursions, the games are about to start coming thick and fast for a Sunderland side whose ability to cope with such a hectic schedule remains to be seen. Having lost Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey to hamstring injuries during the international break, Régis Le Bris will have to reshuffle his pack against a free-scoring Brighton side who make the 700-mile round trip to Wearside for their first game since embarrassing Arsenal three weeks ago. While Wilson Isidor will almost certainly deputise for Brobbey, Ballard’s centre-back berth will be filled by either Omar Alderete or Nordi Mukiele. Having shipped five last time out against Manchester City, a Sunderland defence that had looked conspicuously porous in the early stages of this season will need all their focus if they are to stop the gallop of a team that have already scored 16 goals. BG.

Sunderland v Brighton, Saturday 3pm

6 Crisis talk lingers in air at Old Trafford

If “Dr Tottenham” is a thing, Manchester United possess their own healing powers for opponents. Self-harm is a factor too. They rolled out the welcome mat to Premier League newcomers Hull on opening day and Brighton were ushered back into a Carabao Cup tie. In United’s final game before the international break flagging Fulham were able to restore some faith, their goal via slapstick defending from Lisandro Martínez and Senne Lammens. Can Old Trafford, where fans will have regulatory matters at City to celebrate, lift the gloom for Tottenham? This season, like last season and the one before that, Spurs have assumed the mantle of crisis club, a status Michael Carrick’s January arrival temporarily removed from United. Lose to Tottenham, and the crisis prefix is likely to be reattached. Tottenham have done damage before. In September 2024, a 3-0 Spurs win at Old Trafford began Erik ten Hag’s hurtle towards the exit. Losing the Europa League final started Ruben Amorim’s downward spiral. Carrick beware? JB

Manchester United v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm

7 Fiery reception for Glasner at Palace

All eyes will be on Oliver Glasner as he returns to Selhurst Park with Nottingham Forest on an afternoon that will be emotionally charged for both sets of supporters and in the boardroom. The Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, sought to defuse tensions last week when he urged fans to “buck the trend” by welcoming the manager who led the south London club to the first three major trophies in their history in the space of 12 months. “I would be mortified if he gets anything other than the roof blown off,” said Parish. But given the strength of feeling towards Forest and their owner, Evangelos Marinakis – who is still blamed by some for Palace’s demotion to the Conference League at the expense of Forest last season – many have still not forgiven Glasner for joining their rivals and could still make their feelings known when the Austrian takes his seat in the dugout before kick-off. EA

Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest, Sunday 2pm

View image in fullscreen Was this the calm before the storm for Oliver Glasner? Photograph: Ritchie Sumpter/Nottingham Forest FC/Getty Images

8 Aerial battle of the dead-ball bosses

In Sergej Jakirovic and David Moyes, Hull City and Everton boast two of the more “pragmatic” managers in the Premier League. Renowned for their safety-first defensive styles, both teams are happy to surrender possession, rank among the top flight’s lowest sides in pass completion rates, and rely on rapid transitions and set pieces for a major share of their total expected goals. A game featuring two defences that pride themselves on their obduracy may well be settled by a well-delivered dead ball into a packed penalty area. While it may not be aesthetically pleasing, expect to see the massed ranks of defenders on both sides spending much of Sunday afternoon bracing themselves for rearguard action while peering towards the sky. The last time these sides met in the Premier League, Everton ran out easy 4-0 winners. A decade on, the aerial traffic is unlikely to be quite so one-way. BG

Hull City v Everton, Sunday 2pm

9 Anfield to turn up heat on besieged City

Manchester City resume playing under the darkest of clouds, with a visit to their greatest rivals of a golden period now shrouded by a guilty verdict. Five Premier League wins from five under Enzo Maresca had offered hopes of success in a post-Pep Guardiola era. The dial has since moved on what constitutes success for a club where minds are consumed by legal issues but the band must play on. Can Maresca summon a siege mentality? City lifted a treble, including the Champions League, when the 100-plus charges first came to public light in 2023. The Anfield crowd will readily remind City of the infamy their club faces down. That Guardiola’s now-disputed dominance came at the cost of Jürgen Klopp’s great team will add to the ire, and very probably the pyro greeting to Anfield. Cool heads may be required in the policing and on the field, to which a return to focusing on football may offer welcome relief. JB

Liverpool v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm

10 Will Coventry build on first win?

International football’s incursions have curbed the adrenaline rush of Coventry’s win at Nottingham Forest and Jay Dasilva’s brilliant goal, his club’s first in the top division since 2001. That gave Frank Lampard foundations to build on, a blueprint, where Forest were allowed to blow themselves out before Dasilva’s strike came on the counter. It was Stephen Mfuni, 18, on loan from Manchester City, who starred in that rearguard effort on his Premier League debut. Coventry now seek a first Premier League goal at a stadium opened in 2005, after the club’s long decline had set in. Newcastle this week passed five years of the ownership of a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. There have been two seasons of Champions League football, a trophy lifted and yet a sense of unfulfilled promise. Matthias Jaissle is leading the second phase of a jagged development process, this season’s positive signs tempered by reverses such as the 4-1 defeat by Leeds, shows how far Coventry must travel. JB

Sports.title: Oliver Glasner: ‘There was no plan for me to be Nottingham Forest manager’
Sports.content:
Oliver Glasner puffs his cheeks and starts the search for the right words to explain his emotions as he prepares to return to Crystal Palace for the first time since leaving. There is the small matter of heading back on Sunday with Nottingham Forest to Selhurst Park, where bitterness runs deep over the club seizing Palace’s place in the Europa League last season. Forest’s owner, Evangelos Marinakis, is suing Palace for defamation relating to a banner unfurled by their supporters and the rivalry heightened when Glasner joined Forest in the summer, 40 days after winning the Conference League with Palace.

“I know I will be, but I don’t want to be in the middle of all the comments and the stories about this game,” he says in the boardroom at Forest’s training base. By which point Glasner, a charismatic and intelligent individual who studied for an economics degree while a player in Austria, has turned to Faust, by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, to explain how he feels about facing his previous club. “Two hearts are beating in my chest,” he says, tapping his torso, alluding to a line in the classic play. “Here is a little bit similar, because we had a little bit more than two great years [at Palace].”

Glasner led the Eagles to their first major trophies, backing up an FA Cup win at Wembley last year by clinching the Conference League in Leipzig in May, the competition to which Palace were demoted after Forest complained to Uefa about a breach of its multi-club ownership rules. Palace also won the Community Shield for the first time under Glasner. It is owing to that unprecedented success that the Palace chair, Steve Parish, has said he would be mortified if Glasner receives anything but a hero’s welcome.

Glasner hopes the Palace supporters recall fond memories. “They should look back at the emotions they had when they attended the final at Wembley, when they attended the final in Leipzig, when they watched the Community Shield; how much joy they had, how much they enjoyed being a Crystal Palace fan,” he says, keen to stress the timeline of events that led to him joining Forest. “It was not a decision against Crystal Palace, because I decided last October, one year ago, not to sign a new contract. It was then, in the summer, a decision for Nottingham Forest, due to different reasons. Sometimes unexpected things happen in life … there was no plan for me to be Forest manager.”

Glasner, who remains in touch with Parish and has visited him in London, will not apologise for being outspoken. He refers to the February episode when he told Palace supporters to “stay humble” after some had chanted for him to be sacked while on a run of one win in 15 matches, during which they were knocked out of the FA Cup by the part-timers Macclesfield.

View image in fullscreen Oliver Glasner (second right in a Palace shirt) and his players celebrate after their 2025 FA Cup triumph ended the Eagles’ wait for a major trophy. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

“I will never say what everybody wants to hear, I will say it if I think it’s right. And then I have to accept the booing, I have to accept that not everybody is aligned with what I’m doing in my life. I’m now 52, I don’t need to ask everyone if it’s fine what I’m doing … as long as it’s aligned with the law.”

Supremely comfortable in his own skin, Glasner is on good form across more than an hour of conversation, whether discussing working with Marinakis, experimenting with a four-man defence in last weekend’s friendly win over Swansea, or providing the lowdown on some hotly contested recovery sessions: an in-house padel tournament. Nikola Milenkovic and Nicolás Domínguez were champions, beating Glasner and his assistant, Michael Angerschmid, in the final. “I was disappointed that I lost,” Glasner says, smiling. “But Milenkovic and especially Domínguez, an Argentinian, were too good.”

The international break offered Forest breathing space after a disappointing start, time to evaluate. A week on from victory at Aston Villa, Forest crashed to defeat at home to a previously pointless Coventry.

“It’s always in these situations [that] the season is decided,” Glasner says. “In these situations, after losing against Coventry, it’s important how you react. Not on the pitch, but how you react in the club, in the team, all together. Do you stay together? Do you blame each other? Do you look for: ‘Well, it’s [because of] you, it’s [because of] you. It’s always the other ones, it’s never me.’ Then, things don’t change.”

Forest fans can take heart from the fact Glasner also made a slow start to life at Palace, winning none of his opening eight league games. At Eintracht Frankfurt, he won none of his first eight matches but finished the season by hoisting the Europa League trophy in Seville. When Glasner met Marinakis in Athens, discussing the job over a seafood platter in Vouliagmeni, on the outskirts of the city, he advised the Greek owner that there was no quick fix for a team that cycled through four managers and finished 16th last season. “I said: ‘If you expect everything to work within one month, I’m the wrong one, take another one.’ I see things going in the right direction. I feel the messages we are delivering to the players, the things we are demanding are getting more and more natural.”

View image in fullscreen Nottingham Forest go into the game at Palace with with one win and two draws in their five league games. Photograph: Action Plus Sports Images/Alamy

Three months in, it is still easy to wonder how Glasner ended up here. Externally, joining Forest on a three-year contract was viewed as a surprise, if not a sideways move. He glances at a glossy image on a wall of the City Ground and talks about a similar-sized picture he has in his home office, of him on the balcony of the Frankfurt Römer town hall, 50,000 fans celebrating behind him. “I get goosebumps,” he says. “When I’m considering a club, it’s not just about winning the Premier League. For me, it’s: what is the potential? Is there a real chance to do better with the team? And, at the end, is there potential where I can help to get all this potential to the surface and do better? Is it possible together – because I can’t do anything alone – with the players, with the staff and with the ownership that we can write a chapter that stays in the history books of the club?”

Glasner was on holiday in the serene Austrian lakes with his wife, Bettina, the sun beating down on the water, when the interest from Forest ramped up. “She said: ‘Why are you always looking at your phone?’ [I said:] ‘I’m going to Athens tomorrow.’ She said: ‘Are you crazy? We are here on vacation.’ There were many, many different options in the summer. The one I thought I would do is staying at home, which is why my family was not really pleased with my early decision to leave again … but in that moment when I looked in detail, into the [Forest] squad, and [gathered] my thoughts, I started to get butterflies.”

His enthusiasm for the job is discernible in his voice. Last week, he welcomed grassroots coaches and schoolchildren to training, taking part in a Q&A and putting on a 45-minute session for the kids. “The biggest difference compared to London is that everybody seems to know me,” Glasner says. “Whereas in London you can be quite anonymous; I always took the tube and then maybe there were two or three [supporters who recognised me], and maybe I’d do 10 selfies. But here everybody recognises me and they want to have a few photos.” On Sunday afternoon at Selhurst Park, it is fair to say that there will also be no such invisibility cloak.

Sports.title: Will Carlos Baleba fix Manchester United? Three big questions ahead of potential debut
Sports.content:
Carlos Baleba cost Manchester United $88.7m (£65m) plus $6.8m (£5m) in add-ons when they signed him from Brighton in August. He may be worth even more now despite the fact that the Cameroonian has yet to debut for his new club. Many United fans are counting on Baleba to be a one-man solution to their early-season problems. No pressure.

An ankle injury kept Baleba on the sidelines as Michael Carrick’s side struggled against Everton, Manchester City and Fulham. The 22-year-old joined United just a few days after the opening-weekend defeat to Hull City, so he’d already had a preview of his new team’s troubles to come. The scale of Baleba’s task has grown since then.

United will return to action against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday and Baleba could feature. What sort of impact can fans expect? Will everything click into place with him finally in the lineup? Or could Baleba’s introduction confuse things further?

What’s wrong with United’s midfield?

United spent the best part of $200m (£150m) revamping their midfield in the summer transfer window. Andrey Santos joined from Chelsea before Youri Tielemans left Aston Villa to make the move north. Baleba’s capture from Brighton represented the final component of a long-overdue rebuild.

Carrick has used Kobbie Mainoo and Tielemans as a double pivot in United’s last four Premier League outings with mixed results. While Mainoo has impressed, proving to Thomas Tuchel why he might have been wrong to deny him an opportunity at the World Cup for England, Tielemans’s performances have been trickier to analyze.

Statistically, the Belgian’s numbers are strong. Only Noussair Mazraoui and Mainoo are averaging more accurate passes per 90 minutes for United this season than Tielemans, who is also covering the most distance per 90 minutes of any United player. And yet the Old Trafford outfit have been far too open in the center of the pitch.

Whether that’s due to Bruno Fernandes’s positioning and the freedom he is given as a No 10, Tielemans’s weakness in defensive transition or something else, Carrick has yet to find the right balance. This is reflected in the sheer chaos of United’s first five league games: they have won just one and conceded eight.

How will Baleba fit in?

Baleba has presumably been signed by United to give their midfield some legs. He is known for his defensive ability and athleticism as well as his press resistance in possession. “You need the courage to come out with the ball in difficult and risky areas,” Baleba said in a Sky Sports interview.

This instinct should encourage United supporters. The club has lacked a true two-way midfielder for years, stretching all the way back to the latter stage of the Alex Ferguson era. Paul Pogba was signed to be that player, but was largely misunderstood by a string of different managers who failed to recognise his attacking instincts.

It’s not clear how Carrick will fit Baleba into his new-look midfield considering Mainoo is in the best form of his career and Santos and Tielemans surely joined United on the promise they would be key figures. Dropping Tielemans in particular could further weaken United’s ability on the ball.

Last season, Baleba ranked seventh among his Brighton teammates for accurate passes per 90 minutes. He ranked 16th for big chances created. Some of this was linked to Baleba’s general struggle for form and fitness, but United haven’t exactly signed a natural creator.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When will Baleba feature?

Baleba was included in a matchday squad for the first time away to Fulham on 20 September before the international break and played his first minutes in a behind-closed-doors friendly match last week. He could feature against Spurs this weekend, most likely from the bench given his lack of match sharpness.

Spurs have suffered their own midfield issues this season. Roberto De Zerbi is grappling with many of the same problems Carrick is experiencing and so there could be scope for United to control the center of the pitch, especially with Saturday’s match being at Old Trafford.

On the flip side, if Carrick gets the balance of his midfield wrong or introduces Baleba to the lineup before he’s ready it could prove costly. The United manager is under pressure to prove he can point his team in the right direction again. Another underwhelming result could have Carrick fighting for his job.

If United fans expect Baleba to single-handedly fix their team, they could be disappointed by what the Cameroonian is able to offer. There’s only so much one player can do when Carrick is fighting against years of poor recruitment and boardroom mismanagement. At long last, though, United may finally get to see exactly what they paid all that money for.

Sports.title: Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff
Sports.content:
Sarina Wiegman heaped praise on Ella Toone for her positive reaction to being left out of England’s initial squad for their Women’s World Cup playoff against Greece, after recalling the Manchester United midfielder for Friday’s first leg in Heraklion, Crete.

An injury sustained by Lucy Bronze, described by Wiegman as “really small”, prompted the England right-back to return to Chelsea and Wiegman called up Toone, who travelled to Greece from Spain, where she had organised a training routine during the international window.

Toone has 69 caps and has scored 24 goals, including in the Euro 2022 final and 2023 World Cup semi-final, but Wiegman said when naming her squad that she had left out Toone and Chloe Kelly because “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch”. On Saturday, after starting Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, Toone took ownership of things, telling the BBC: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

Wiegman, asked whether she had been impressed with Toone’s response, said: “Yes, very much. I think when I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call. But she took that straight away. Of course [she was] very disappointed, but the first thing she did [was say]: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’ She has the support around her too.”

The head coach referenced Toone’s post-match comments when she said: “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good. And then getting everything ready to go to Spain instead, but go for training there, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

That will be music to the ears of Toone, whose experience is also understood to have been a factor in Wiegman picking her rather than a replacement right-back. She could feature on Friday, when the European champions will hope to build a strong first-leg lead before Tuesday’s reverse fixture in Leicester.

To qualify for next summer’s finals in Brazil, England must overcome Greece and win another two-leg playoff, against Slovakia or Ukraine, in December.

Quick Guide Greece v England: Wiegman's probable team for visitors Show (4-2-3-1) Hampton; Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood; Stanway, Walsh; Mead, James, Hemp; Russo Greece v England, Pankritio Stadium, Friday, 5.30pm BST Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The draw for the World Cup will follow on 11 December and it would feel inconceivable for the 2023 runners-up to miss out. They are in the playoffs despite winning five of their six qualifiers in a group with Spain, the defending champions, who pipped England to top spot by virtue of their stronger head-to-head goal difference.
