View image in fullscreen Sarina Wiegman (centre), speaks to the players during a training session in Heraklion, Greece. Photograph: Naomi Baker/The FA/Getty Images

Greece have never qualified for a major tournament and, major underdogs against England, will probably set up in a low, defensive shape. The England defender Esme Morgan said she and her teammates would remain calm even if it takes time to break through: “It’s just [about] persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. I think a really good example of it was the away game we played against Ukraine [in qualifying].

“We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half – the keeper was making saves, I think we struck the woodwork a couple of times – but the messaging at half-time among the players and when Sarina came in to speak to us was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities. Not to start snatching or taking hot shots from distance, just trusting in the style of play that we have and in our ability to keep finding gaps in and around the defence. We came out for the second half after that and scored really, really quickly. So it’s just sticking to the gameplan, trusting in what we do and being patient”

Sports.title: Sergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’
Sports.content:
An 11-year-old, second-hand VW Beetle with more than 300,000km on the clock pulls over on Fofó the Clown Street in the heart of Vallecas. The music goes off, the Smiths silenced and out gets Sergio Camello: movie aficionado with 156 films reviewed, part-time photographer, sometime drummer, Olympic gold medallist and the second-top goalscorer in Europe’s biggest five leagues. Engulfed in graffiti, stickers covering the glass between metal bars in red, a single step up from the street, the small door into Rayo Vallecano’s ground is locked, but in 64 hours it will open for the first time this season. “It’s my home, it’s Vallecas,” Camello says.

Forced to abandon their place, on Saturday at 2pm the tenants return. With the Madrid council declaring Estadio de Vallecas unsafe, unfit for purpose, Rayo’s home matches have instead been played in Leganés, out of the city to the south and boycotted by fans. Walking the neighbourhood that is proud of its social conscience, its community and its team, Camello can’t wait to be back again. And not just for the football; maybe not even for the football. “It’s the pre-game, the post-game, the people,” he says, passing the bar where they’ll be waiting for him after, same as always.

View image in fullscreen ‘I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team’ – Sergio Camello at the door to Rayo Vallecano’s Vallecas ground. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Yet the football is good too, good as it’s ever been. Across the continent’s major leagues only Raphinha has more goals than his seven in seven games and Camello himself has never had so many either. “I try not to think about it but my teammates keep reminding me,” he says. “They’re all calling me Pichichi or ‘the Film Guy’. ‘Pichichi! Pichichi!’ It’s not Sergio any more.” Pichichi was the great Athletic Club striker whose name adorns the top-scorer award. No pressure, then. “None, I love it,” Camello replies, “and I love that they’re enjoying it.”

Two months into the season, this is already his best campaign in primera where the previous totals were five, three and three. And although there’s a tactical element, the new coach Beñat San José altering his movement, Camello looks deeper for an explanation. Above all he looks inside, which is where, from the beginning, another conversation starts: a simple question prompts a complex, nuanced and human discussion, the striker talking calmly, thoughtfully and with startling unexpected honesty.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello celebrates after scoring against Barcelona in August. Photograph: Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty Images

Camello is that most unusual of footballers – prepared to speak on materialism, racism, or homophobia, social media “poison” or the housing crisis, that rare player prepared to use his platform, which he says was born of his upbringing but also learned being here in the barrio. This though is personal, but at once universal too, something in his experience that is about everyone. Who knows, maybe there is something in what he has lived that can help, some reason to share it, the goals scored offering tangible proof of an intangible process.

So what has changed? “How I go on to the pitch,” he says. “I thought it would be much harder to change my mindset but I’m seeing that I can be myself: be free, connect with the Sergio I can offer Rayo. To feel liberated, to enjoy it – and it’s been a long time since I enjoyed all this like this.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello has been outscored only by Barcelona’s Raphinha so far this season. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“The first thing was to have many conversations with friends, people who truly know me. Especially my twin brother Gonzalo; there’s a connection that goes beyond the human. He could see I wasn’t enjoying it much, wasn’t myself. We talked and I tried to take that on to the pitch. Above all, to play without the pressure. Because pressure is horrendous. It makes it so that you don’t enjoy absolutely anything, puts you in a position where if things don’t work, that leads to frustration, frustration leads to pity, and suddenly everything is negative. There’s a point in the conversations where it’s: ‘That’s it; it’s done’.

“This is a sport you chose before it was your job, because it’s what made you happiest. It’s about connecting to that kid again. I’d discussed this in therapy too; the idea of getting back to that kid.”

Somewhere that can be lost – not just failure you have to live with but also success. “The pressure can come from everywhere,” Camello says. “We’re young, the change happens so fast, no one prepares you for it. If you can’t manage that it can do a lot of damage and that happened to me. [Early on], I would even get a bit paranoid, have fixations. ‘They’re looking at me.’ The first day in primera, when I scored, the journey there had been normal – scooter, bus, metro, bus – but on the same journey home some kids followed me shouting: ‘Camello! Camello!’ It was a shock. The night we returned from the Olympics I was in the usual bar, people crowded and I had a kind of anxiety attack and had to go. And, look, I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team. I can’t imagine what it is like for someone at Lamine Yamal’s level. I don’t envy that.”

“But it’s about seeing the balance, understanding,” Camello continues, “and football has given me so, so much. There are so many people who can’t enjoy their job, who don’t have the [financial] freedom. When you have bad moments, when the clouds come, when you feel that cycle of negativity, you talk.”

Camello looks across the room: it’s quiet, 25 chairs sitting empty. “One of my friends [Dani Fernández] is a musician about to do four sellouts at the Wizink [Centre]; when I met him, he wouldn’t have sold out this room,” he says. “We both got ‘caught’ in this about the same time and we talked a lot. When he had doubts, I was there; when I did, he was. A torch in the darkness. You think: ‘I’d love to be a rock star’, and then someone you admire who is tells you how bloody shit it can be behind the scenes. You understand each other, you think: ‘Bloody hell, maybe I don’t have to analyse things so deeply.’ If in even those places you idealise, there is darkness, solitude, maybe I’m not so bad.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello says he his thriving by playing without pressure. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Otherwise you could go into a very dark place where you feel you have to escape this [football]. Even then the world wouldn’t end. And fortunately, the positive in football has always weighed much more heavily. And that’s been shown to be right. Those conversations give me perspective, make me conscious of how fortunate I am.”

Although Camello says doubts about the game itself are rarely shared in such depth in the dressing room – “football might be the most important thing in the entire world to your teammate” – something about this place helps. The club’s problems are significant, debilitating and should not be romanticised, he insists, and yet somehow they have made a success of it, built through solidarity. Besides, he says, “we’re also here because we want to be” and there is something about Rayo, something about breaking out of the bubble, that has been good for him, for all of them, as people as well as players. There’s a moment when he talks about everything that comes with being a footballer and says “it’s easy to be a dickhead”, but that’s diminished at a club not just in the barrio but of the barrio, one that’s “totally different” to anywhere else he knows, where “your feet are that bit more on the ground and you realise you’re not stars”.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello says the club and players have a unique connection with the Vallecas neighbourhood. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Rayo is the last team standing from football from another time, that’s what I like,” Camello says. “Even just parking here on the street right in front changes things. The same faces, every time. The least important thing about the football here is the football; it’s what they stand for every weekend, what they believe in, the connection. It’s Isi in the bar on the corner. Unai and his mates in the one down the bottom there. The bar we’ve taken over. That doesn’t exist anywhere else. To have those guys you were watching half an hour ago in the same bars, doesn’t happen. I’ve built relationships that are very sincere that I never expected. I’m a normal bloke who fulfilled mine and many kids’ dream. Like a superhero when they pull on the mask; I come here, I put on the kit, I’m the most competitive, most professional person you can be. But when I leave I take it off and forget about it.”

There is a release, refuge in something else. In the camera. In the drum lessons Camello admits have been slow and the guitar he’s abandoned, the ability God gave his feet denied to his fingers. In the indie rock music first heard in the family carand encouraged by the musician mates he has made. The music discouraged by reggaeton-loving teammates who control the stereo blaring out each morning– and, he says laughing, they wonder why he’s not so keen on the gym.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello with the Action for Music charity. Photograph: Action for Music

The music that can make a difference, too; if there is anything that moves people, reaches them like football, it may only be that. “There’s something I’ve wanted to do for a long time and it’s really fun,” Camello says. “I joined a charity, Action for Music, which gives opportunities to kids to play music in humble neighbourhoods. They go to four hours of classes a week: percussion, strings, wind. The kids don’t pay a euro, everything’s free: the space, the teachers, the instruments. They have schools in Tetuán and Carabanchel. I’m getting involved, learning, and I want to set up a school in Vallecas next year.” He stops, grins. “Only I’m going to do it my way … with rock.

“I did a session with them the other day, me trying to play the drums after six months. There was a kid on sax: wow, what a vibe he had, he was just loving it. When you don’t know where to go, there’s a place, someone who believes in you, gives you an opportunity. Forty kids: put some drum sticks in their hand, a guitar, a sax, something that will give them so much. Tell them they can be good at something, feel good about themselves. Have fun, maybe find something inside they didn’t know was there. It’s a way of giving back to Vallecas everything it gives me. I’m so excited.”

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello stops to take a selfie with a fan while walking through the Vallecas neighbourhood. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Imagine them playing the Wizink. “I can be their manager,” Camello laughs. “The idea is to do concerts at the end of each year. Imagine those kids, coming into their first class … then going on stage. It’s good to see yourself up there, with an instrument. Their family there, people who have bought tickets to see them play, the applause. That feeling: ‘I’m worth it.’”

Sounds like scoring a goal. Camello’s eyes light up. “Yes, it is,” he says. “I’m still the same guy as I was when I didn’t score, eh. But at that moment when you’re standing there, there’s nothing else in your head, just a feeling that all this makes sense. When the ball hits the net, when you get a ground on its feet, all together, when they’re celebrating, it’s like it’s all worth it. You feel important, you’re good at something.”

Sports.title: Zavier Gozo: ‘You have to be uncomfortable to get to the highest levels’
Sports.content:
Much has changed in Zavier Gozo’s life since May.

Back then, Gozo was a day removed from learning that he wasn’t among Mauricio Pochettino’s 26 selections for the World Cup, having just made what proved to be his third-to-last appearance with boyhood club Real Salt Lake.

Gozo had only ever lived in Utah at that point. He would watch the World Cup from home, where he lived with his mother.

Today, less than five months later, he lives half a world away, is getting Premier League minutes and, as of a week ago, his first cap with the senior US men’s national team.

“It’s a big change to go from Utah to London,” said this master of understatement, stationed on a sofa in the lobby of the team’s downtown Minneapolis hotel in shorts, slippers, and a pristine white hoodie.

He has joined a familiar face there, at least, in his new international teammate – Chris Richards. The center-back has become a stalwart for club and country since joining Palace in 2022. He’s an every-minute option along the back, arguably their lead defender following the recent exits of Marc Guehi and Maxence Lacroix. Gozo has evidently endeared himself to Richards’ young daughter, too..

Then again, landing alongside a compatriot was far from the biggest hook that helped Gozo opt for Palace.

“I think I knew more [about them] than maybe the average [club],” Gozo says before listing their recent triumphs in the FA Cup (in 2025), the Conference League, and the Community Shield (both in 2026). “They were in a good run of form, and they have been for the last couple years, and have been showing it on the European stage.

“I’ve known them from [Wilfried] Zaha, and being a very good club that develops wingers and forwards in general. It seems like they always have a player that’s coming through their system that’s either sold for a lot or just becomes a very good player. And obviously, when Chris was there, I was just following them, and him, and their success. I feel like I knew a fair amount.”

Given Gozo’s ambitions, Palace’s track record of developing players from both their own academy and players brought in from other clubs was a significant reassurance. Their trophy cabinet and its rapidly waning open shelving was another boost, and their place in the Europa League offered even more games for Gozo to make his mark.

By the end of his time in MLS, Gozo hardly showed a flicker of fear. On one occasion, against Atlanta, he collected a ball at the edge of the final third near the right touchline with minimal attacking support. Rather than wait for support, he swiftly put the defender marking him through the spin cycle, cleverly dribbling infield and uncorking a curler to the far post. Four weeks later, against Kansas City, a split-second at the edge of the box was all he needed to execute a bombastic self-volley.

Rather than taking an incremental step up in difficulty, he’s now contending to make the bench in the world’s most competitive league.

“I think the coaching staff believes in me and is bought into developing me and the talent that I have,” Gozo said. “I think it’s a perfect environment for me to learn, but also be thrown into the fire a little bit. When you’re at RSL and you’re starting to become their best player, or one of their best players, and you go to Crystal Palace, sometimes you can lose confidence. Because it’s like, ‘oh wow, I can’t do the things I used to be able to do.’

“You just kind of have to figure out how you can become effective again, and yeah, obviously it can be hard at times, but also it’s what you want. You have to be uncomfortable to get to the highest levels.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Beyond the sheer culture shock of switching from Salt Lake City to South London, Gozo has also seen his status on the roster switch. Gone are the days of being the boy wonder, the homegrown hero that fans have watched develop into a leading forward in MLS. Now he bears the pressure that comes with arriving on an eight-figure transfer fee, one of many promising American upstarts determined to thrive at the sport’s highest levels.

“It’s very different. Obviously, you don’t feel the connection with the fans as much. But also, you want to be able to do something for the fans, for them to be able to connect with you,” Gozo said. “[You want to] bring them happiness and bring them joy with what you do on the field. It’s more trying to prove yourself to the fans; I feel like with the fans of RSL, it’s kind of like they’re bringing you up, like giving you confidence while you’re coming up.”

He’s made three appearances from the bench for Palace in all competitions thus far, giving him a sense of the newly raised bar. The rate of play has increased considerably. Those defenders meeting him on the wing, like the aforementioned poor soul in Atlanta, are better supported by their teammates. Those spaces at the edge of the box, like the plot of grass afforded to him by Kansas City, are in far shorter supply.

For now, anyway.

View image in fullscreen Zavier Gozo made his international debut in the last international window. Photograph: Mark Thorstenson/ISI Photos/Getty Images

Asked what he aims to improve after his Premier League introduction, Gozo said “physicality and not even being necessarily strong, but using your body in a way to either win a foul or protect the ball, and knowing when to take two touches, or take one touch, or turn and go dribble. Those are all things that you just have to have kind of perfect.”

Further refining those skills should also help him stick around Pochettino’s rejuvenated United States project. This past international window saw Gozo debut along with 11 rising upstarts, including fellow wingers Cavan Sullivan and Mathis Albert. Gozo appeared in just one of the four friendlies, logging nearly half an hour against Peru.

Gozo may be new to the senior team, but past camps and tournaments at the youth international levels are especially relevant given the program’s young sea change. He’s one of five members from the 2025 U-20 World Cup squad to debut in this window, having played with some since his first call-up to the U-15 level in 2022.

“I feel like the vibe at the national team has changed, especially since Pochettino has come here,” Gozo said, “Even just since the World Cup, I think a lot of people are more involved and paying attention.…It’s just an elevated energy, almost. It feels good to walk in and to be a part of this group.”

Sports.title: Liverpool fans urged to deploy unusual tactic and throw Man City off at Anfield
Sports.content:
Liverpool fans urged to deploy unusual tactic and throw Man City off at Anfield

Liverpool fans should kill Manchester City with kindness when the two sides meet on Sunday - it could be more effective than booing.

That's the advice of talkSPORT's Alex Crook, who has given the Reds a unique way to target their visitors in their huge Anfield showdown following City's seismic guilty verdict from the Premier League.

5 Manchester City's players will now compete this season with a huge question mark over their heads Credit: Getty

An international break like no other unfolded as City were found guilty of all serious Premier League financial breaches.

An independent commission adjudged them to have inflated their revenue by more than £900million by disguising owner funding as sponsorship over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018.

During this period, City won eight trophies including three top-flight titles.

The Citizens insist they are innocent and have submitted an appeal against the verdict.

While they await the outcome of this, they now return to Premier League under a huge microscope as the legitimacy of all their achievements in recent history has been called into question.

And they could hardly have asked for a tougher first game back, with a trip to rivals Liverpool likely to reach boiling point on Sunday.

For many years, the Reds under Jurgen Klopp were the closest challengers to City and could have claimed a lot more titles if the guilty verdict is to stand, with this set to make an already hostile atmosphere even more volatile at the weekend.

Reverse psychology could stun Man City

Ahead of what promises to be a spicy affair at Anfield, talkSPORT's Crook has suggested an alternative way for Liverpool's fans to rile the Man City players.

Speaking on Fiery Fridays as part of talkSPORT's Daily podcast, he began: “The focus this weekend is going to be on the reception those Man City players get.

"There's a history of the Man City team coach being targeted on recent visits to Anfield when these two have met."

5 Anfield promises to be an absolute cauldron when Man City's players walk out on Sunday afternoon Credit: Getty

5 City's players have been receiving hostile greetings on Merseyside for years as they battled it out with Liverpool for titles Credit: Getty

He continued: “I’m sure Liverpool fans have got plenty of imaginative and witty banners ready to greet those Man City players - 'cheats'.

"As they sit here now, until the unlikely eventuality that they prove themselves innocent, there’s going to be lots of chants aimed in their direction as well."

Sharing his suggestion, Crook claimed the best way for the Anfield crowd to rattle City is, rather than jeering them, to sarcastically applaud.

A huge Manchester United fan, he pointed to similar tactics being used by the Old Trafford faithful in a 2009 meeting between the Red Devils and Chelsea.

Crook said: “The Liverpool fans should go the other way, I wonder if they should be applauding these Man City players rather than booing them

“Hear me out, I’ll go back to 2008, Man United won the Champions League in Moscow [against Chelsea] - John Terry famously fell over and missed the decisive penalty in the shootout.

5 John Terry missed the chance to win Chelsea their first-ever European Cup in 2008 Credit: Getty

“I was at the game as a fan a few months later - January 2009 - the first time the two had met at Old Trafford since that final in Moscow.

“Rather than jeering John Terry as you may normally expect, every time he touched the ball he got a standing ovation from the United fans and he could not handle it - he had an absolute stinker, United won 3-0. He couldn’t get his head around it."

Crook insisted that City's players will only be given more motivation by a hostile reception, while applause could totally throw them off.

He explained: “Football is littered with people who use those boos as motivation to silence their critics.

“I know Enzo Maresca is going to be speaking to those Man City players before the weekend, underlining the fact that the club is still confident of proving their innocence.

“And I'm sure he's going to do what the club has done so far - try and create this siege mentality - ‘It’s us against the world, we're going to get dogs abuse from these Liverpool fans, let’s ram those taunts back down their throats’.

5 Could Liverpool stop the Premier League's top scorer in Erling Haaland by applauding him rather than jeering? Credit: Getty

“So again, just say Anfield stands and applauds Man City for all their previous achievements when they come onto the pitch, I think their heads will absolutely fall off and you can see a really comfortable Liverpool victory."

But with City the only side with a 100 per cent record in the Premier League this term, Crook warned taunting their players could end badly for Liverpool.

He concluded “If they boo them, you’re going to get a wounded animal and that may just work against Liverpool this weekend.”

Sports.title: Chelsea monitoring international star as possible late replacement for Enzo Fernandez
Sports.content:
Chelsea monitoring international star as possible late replacement for Enzo Fernandez

Barcelona midfielder Frenkie de Jong is attracting interest from Chelsea, according to reports.

The 29-year-old has been at Barcelona since 2019 after he joined from Ajax for €86million (£72m).



3 De Jong is currently on the road to recovery from a serious medial collateral ligament (MCL) tear Credit: Getty

During the last seven years, he has accumulated 297 appearances and earned the captain's armband.

The Dutch international suffered a knee injury during the World Cup in North America with Barca wanting to operate on the player, while De Jong opted for conservative treatment.

He has now returned to training on the pitch; however, it will be a long time until the midfielder plays another match.



During his time out injured, Rodri has made an immediate impact in the middle of the pitch after he moved from Manchester City for £65m in the summer.

Additionally, Hansi Flick also has Pedri, Fermín López, Marc Bernal, Gavi and Dani Olmo competing for the position.



Reports in Spain now claim Chelsea are monitoring De Jong's situation.

The Blues are understood to view the Dutchman as an ideal successor to Enzo Fernandez, who replaced Rodri at the Etihad.



Flick has remained clear that De Jong still plays an important role at the club and recently said: "Frenkie is a great player and we need him."

Valentin Barco and Jordan Henderson were two midfield arrivals at Stamford Bridge during the summer.

Lamine Camara looked set to be a third from AS Monaco on deadline day, but a move fell through.

3 Fernandez has enjoyed a good start to life in Manchester Credit: Getty



Liverpool are understood to have impacted the move by instructing him to stay at Monaco ahead of a potential switch next summer.

Despite failing to sign Camara, Chelsea still allowed Fernandez to join Man City for £125m.

Man City sniffed about

Additionally, De Jong had the opportunity to leave Barcelona during the summer as City considered a move.

Barca reportedly did not oppose a potential transfer if they received a suitable offer and made it clear the Dutch international was not an untouchable player.



Manchester City eventually opted for younger midfield profiles and spent heavily on Fernandez, Elliot Anderson, and Ayyoub Bouaddi for a combined total of €375million (£318million).

The 29-year-old is under contract with Barcelona until 2029, and still has time to prove his worth in LaLiga.

3 Man City pulled out after reviewing the medical reports regarding his knee Credit: AFP

Under new manager Xabi Alonso, Chelsea have had an entertaining but highly inconsistent start to the Premier League season.



The Blues currently sit tenth with seven points, recording two wins, one draw, and two defeats.

Chelsea are currently on a three-match winless streak in the league, most recently suffering a heavy 3-0 defeat away at Brentford.

Sports.title: Two managers ready to pounce with Man United vs Tottenham set for huge ramifications
Sports.content:
Two managers ready to pounce with Man United vs Tottenham set for huge ramifications

Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur face a crunch clash in their respective seasons this weekend.

The result could even see Michael Carrick or Roberto De Zerbi fighting for their job, according to Gabby Agbonlahor.



5 Both Spurs and United will be desperate for a win this weekend Credit: Getty

United welcome Spurs to Old Trafford on Saturday, with kick-off at 5:30pm to mark both sides' return to action after the international break.

However, neither team found themselves in form prior to the Premier League's three-week hiatus.

Instead, they mustered a combined one win between them across the opening five matchdays.



Spurs sit bottom of the table with just two points to their name as pressure mounts on manager De Zerbi.

Meanwhile, the Red Devils are just three points better off in 13th amid a three-match winless run.



Their slow start has also seen questions asked of Carrick, who was only named as permanent boss in May.

As a result, Agbonlahor believes this weekend's meeting could lead to the first Premier League managerial change of the season.



The talkSPORT co-host has also revealed the two managers who could be waiting in the wings to takeover.

Speaking on Breakfast, he explained: "Michael Carrick was getting a lot of people coming out saying that he is under pressure, especially after that Fulham performance.

"It was a late equaliser against Fulham. Own goal by Lisandro Martinez.

5 Carrick has been warned two former Premier League bosses are waiting to take his job Credit: Getty



"He needs a performance from his players because you've got Antonio Conte saying that he's ready to come back into management now.

"You've got Eddie Howe, who's probably waiting now thinking, 'maybe I'm ready to come back into management now.'

"So Michael Carrick needs a performance, but Spurs need to start getting points because the longer you leave it, if they lose Saturday, they'll have two points from six games.

"I think Manchester United win this at home. I feel like Bruno Fernandes would be the difference in this sort of game."



The fixture was also a topic for debate on talkSPORT's Premier League All Access podcast this week.

Debating who is more in need of a win out of Carrick and De Zerbi, Troy Deeney admitted: "I think Carrick will be coming at it from very level point of view of 'let's worry about our job, get everyone back playing in the right position.'

5 De Zerbi is still chasing his first Premier League win of the season Credit: Getty

"I'm not sure Amad (Diallo) is back yet, but I saw rumours those boys could be really close to being back fit so he'll have a lot more of a positive step.



"I've looked at a lot of the Spurs stuff and it is still a lot of the same messaging, '(Dejan) Kulusevski's going to be great when comes back.' How do we know? We haven't seen.

"It's hopeful from a Spurs point of view as opposed to Man United, where it's like 'we're looking ahead.'

"I think from a dressing room point of view, Spurs are getting more and more nervous, but you'd want a big game and Man United just want to get back to playing football and shutting people up. They're used to the noise."

O'Hara's United vs Spurs prediction

Despite Tottenham's ongoing woes, Jamie O'Hara has a positive feeling about his former side this weekend.



The talkSPORT co-host admits he can never be too certain with Spurs, though.

5 O'Hara is confident despite Spurs' winless start to the season Credit: Getty

Discussing the fixture on The Sports Bar, he said: "I’m quietly confident we can get a result, but I also know what I’ve been watching."

In response, Cundy explained: "Both sets of fans are going to go to that game feeling the same way.



"Man United are a giant, Spurs are a massive football club. You are both at the wrong end of the table. It’s like two bald men fighting over a comb."

Sticking with the hair-related analogies, O'Hara added: "I feel like Spurs are a bit like your hairline when you first had it (hair transplant) done.

"There were encouraging signs. You’re going, ‘you know what? Yes, it’s going to come, it’s going to happen.’

"I can see it, it’s going to happen, then it didn’t. Then it’s like you’ve been scammed. Now look at you."



5 United head into the match without a win in their last three league outings Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Man United and Spurs head-to-head

Despite their lowly league position, Spurs could leapfrog United in the table with a sizeable win on Saturday.

A four-goal away victory would be enough to overcome the current six between them on goal difference.

However, this fixture last season saw United take all three points in February thanks to a 2-0 triumph.



It saw them end the campaign unbeaten against Spurs in the Premier League following a 2-2 draw in north London.

The previous season did see Tottenham complete a league double over the Red Devils, though.

Their last three Premier League meetings at Old Trafford have seen a win apiece as well as a 2-2 stalemate in January 2024.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca grilled over commitment to Man City if they get relegated in tense press conference
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca grilled over commitment to Man City if they get relegated in tense press conference

Enzo Maresca was quizzed over his long-term dedication to Manchester City during an intense media scrum on Friday.

The Manchester City boss fronted up for his first press conference since the club were found guilty of 115 financial breaches by an independent commission.



4 Enzo Maresca was peppered with media questions over the charges Credit: Getty

The Italian faced a barrage of questions following the bombshell verdict that dropped during the international break.

Maresca remained coy on the intricate details of the charges with the appeal currently ongoing.

He did, however, respond to questions regarding his commitment to the club, should City fail in their appeal.



Asked if would stay at the club if they are relegated, he replied: "I won the Championship with Leicester. League One? We will see."

But despite the tumultuous situation City find themselves in, Maresca reiterated his trust in the club and his colleagues.



"I understand the reason why most of you are here, but the only thing I can say is something that I already said," he added.

"There is a process ongoing and at this moment I completely trust the club.



"I trust the club and I trust the people, that is why I joined the club. There is no other club where I would like to be, so this is what I can say about that."

Maresca was asked whether or not the charges against the club have tarnished their achievements over the time in question.

"Absolutely not," he said. "I know the effort from the players and the club so I know what they did for that target.

4 Maresca only received a couple of questions unrelated to the Man City verdict Credit: Getty



"For me and the players, we can control the pitch side, we can focus on that. We cannot control something different."

What next for City?

City are awaiting the outcome of the appeal with potential punishments ranging from a fine to a points deduction or expulsion from the Premier League.

There could be further legal matters for City to deal with in that rival clubs may seek compensation from them in a saga that could drag on for months.

However, City insist they are innocent, describing the verdict against them as 'opinion' and 'conspiracy'.



City's trip to Liverpool this Sunday, normally a newsworthy fixture in itself, took a back seat as Maresca withstood the media onslaught over the saga.

The breaches relate specifically to a nine-year period between 2009-2018.

4 Manchester City chiefs have once again pleaded their innocence ahead of the appeal outcome Credit: Getty

The commission found that City inflated revenues amounting to £830million via 'sham' agreements.



Manchester City won three Premier League titles, one FA Cup, three League Cups and one Community Shield between the during the time of the breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Despite that, Maresca maintains that City's achievements have not been tarnished.

"Absolutely not," he said. "I know the effort from the players and the club so I know what they did for that target.

"Absolutely not [tainted]. For me and the players, we can control the pitch side, we can focus on that. We cannot control something different."



Stepping into the cauldron

Ironically, City travel to Anfield on Sunday to face a Liverpool team that were pipped to multiple Premier League titles by Pep Guardiola's side.

4 Man City step into the lions den at Anfield on Sunday

A hostile atmosphere is expected at Anfield when City's players take to the pitch but Marecsa says all focus will be on the match rather than off-field issues.

"It will be a tough game, tough test," the Italian said. "We need to be ready. The focus has to be about the team, it may be even worse because of the situation.



"They can absolutely face the pressure, we have players who have faced similar. We have Enzo Fernandez, in Argentina it is like this every game.

"It is a matter of being together, stick together. In this moment, this is the situation, the noise.

"We are on the same page. As I said yesterday, we need our fans and hopefully we can celebrate a win.

"Ruben [Diaz]and Erling [Haaland] need to handle the pressure. Yes the noise is there, they go home happy and are top of the league."

Sports.title: Vincent Kompany makes first statement on Manchester City saga since guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Vincent Kompany makes first statement on Manchester City saga since guilty verdict

Vincent Kompany has admitted he is 'not too occupied' by the verdict in Manchester City's Financial Fair Play (FFP) case.

His former club have been found guilty of all charges against them, the Premier League announced last week.

3 Kompany played for City throughout the period when their FFP breaches took place Credit: AFP or licensors

City were first charged in February 2023, with the alleged offences taking place between 2009 and 2018.

Kompany was at the Etihad Stadium throughout the period in question having joined the club in 2008 before spending 11 years with City.

He was also named captain in 2011, a role he held until he departed in 2019.

The 40-year-old's links to City were highlighted during his latest Bayern Munich press conference.

Kompany addresses City verdict

Kompany spoke to reporters this week ahead of his side's trip to face Augsburg on Saturday.

It marked the first time he had addressed the media since City's guilty verdict.

When asked, Kompany admitted: "I'm only thinking about my work at FC Bayern.

"We have important games coming up, and that takes a lot of time. There's not much time to think about other stuff.

"For me it's simple, I played 11 years for the club and I've loved all the years I've played for the club.

"Everything we've achieved and done on the pitch I'm really proud of. Everything else, as a player you're not a part of that.

3 Kompany is adamant his focus remains solely on Bayern Credit: Getty

"And right now as a coach of Bayern Munich I'm not too occupied with that topic as much as preparing for the game next week and the game we have to win tomorrow and everything I have as a coach."

Kompany at City

Kompany won 12 trophies with City including four Premier League titles.

However, the first three of those came during the period in which their FFP offences took place.

City have since launched an appeal against the independent commission's ruling in the case.

Following his arrival from Hamburg, Kompany made 360 appearances for the club.

The former Belgium defender also scored 20 goals for City from centre-back before returning to boyhood club Anderlecht in 2019.

3 Kompany captained City to four Premier League title triumphs Credit: Getty

Having moved into management since he ended his playing career, Kompany is into his third season in charge of Bayern.

He has already won back-to-back Bundesliga titles as well as a domestic double last term.

Sports.title: Scott McTominay linked with blockbuster signing next summer in reunion with ex-manager
Sports.content:
Scott McTominay linked with blockbuster signing next summer in reunion with ex-manager

Scott McTominay is being eyed up by Real Madrid after his impressive performances in Serie A.

The Scotland international was sold to Napoli in the summer of 2024 after being told he would not be a part of Manchester United's future plans.

2 McTominay has become a big fan favourite at Napoli Credit: Getty

The midfielder scored 13 goals and provided six assists in his first season in Italy as he guided the club to Scudetto glory.

He received the 2024/25 Serie A MVP for his performances, and followed it up the following season bagging 14 goals and four assists.

According to Il Mattino, Madrid boss Jose Mourinho is interested in McTominay after previously working with the player at Old Trafford and handing him his senior professional debut.

The 29-year-old has two years remaining on his current deal and is reportedly seeking a lucrative new contract with Napoli, though negotiations remain ongoing.

McTominay returned to training with the rest of his Napoli teammates on Wednesday, only 30 days after undergoing heart surgery.

He had an ablation procedure – a minimally invasive operation to correct irregular heart rhythms on September 8.

The 29-year-old missed all four of Scotland’s international games during the international break.

Napoli released a statement that read: "On Wednesday, Scott McTominay underwent further diagnostic tests, which showed that he is fit to play. He therefore resumed training with the rest of the team after the period spent training separately."

Before the midfielder's return, teammate Billy Gilmour said: "We’re missing Scott right now.

"Hopefully everything went well, we can’t wait to have him back.

2 McTominay won the Serie A title in 2024/25 alongside his Scotland teammate Credit: Getty

Additionally, there is reportedly interest from Premier League clubs including Man United and Aston Villa.

Italian journalist Giovanni Scotto insisted that McTominay is not in any rush to confirm his future and has decided to 'wait' amid interest from other clubs.

Scotto said: "He hasn’t renewed with Napoli and wants to think things through. Manchester United and Aston Villa have shown some interest, but McTominay intends to wait.

"Napoli don’t want to lose McTominay and will offer him a contract renewal with the possibility of leaving through a gentlemen’s agreement, a sort of handshake.

"I’m not aware of any clauses. If the midfielder receives a significant offer, Napoli could let him leave in two or three years.

"If the player wants to leave as early as June, his valuation for next summer is €25-30m (£21.7-26m), no less."

Sports.title: What are Man City’s next five games? Upcoming schedule for Maresca and co amid chaos at Etihad
Sports.content:
What are Man City’s next five games? Upcoming schedule for Maresca and co amid chaos at Etihad

Enzo Maresca and his squad are returning to chaos at the Etihad after Manchester City were found guilty of all charges by the Premier League.

The Premier League recently released a 40-page statement confirming that City have won none of their charges while inflating their financial position by over £900million between the period of 2009 to 2018.



2 Maresca has walked into a firestorm at City Credit: Getty

City are protesting their innocence and have stressed they will be taking the necessary legal requirements.

Pep Guardiola left the Etihad at the end of last season after ten years in charge, with the former Chelsea manager replacing him in the role.

The Premier League giants won three titles during the period when the offences took place, including their first under Guardiola.



Now, Maresca will have the job of trying to continue City's unbeaten run in the league while dealing with the noise about the charges surrounding the club.

Now the international break is over, City are set for a busy run of fixtures, starting with one of the biggest games of the season.

Sports.title: The £13,128 ticket: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua is sport's most expensive standard seat EVER as fans complain they are half a million places back in online queues
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua tickets have reached £13,128 at the top end of the scale, as more than half a million fans joined an online queue for one of the most eagerly anticipated fights in boxing history.

The most expensive seats for the December 11 showdown in Cardiff cost more than those for some of the world's biggest sporting events, eclipsing the top face-value price of £6,300 for the 2026 Super Bowl and World Cup ticket prices of £8,333.

Tickets for Fury vs Joshua went on sale at midday on Friday, with Saudi Arabia's Turki Alalshikh keen to ensure fans had an accessible entry point, reflected in the starting price of £88.50 including fees. However, prices at the top end of the scale climb to a staggering £13,128.

The figures do not include VIP packages, hotel and travel packages, group bookings or concession prices, and all tickets remain subject to availability.

Demand for the fight was immediately apparent, with more than half a million people waiting in the online queue as fans raced to secure seats for the long-awaited clash.

The fight will take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on December 11, bringing an end to years of speculation over a meeting between the two former world heavyweight champions.

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua tickets have been priced from £88.50 to a staggering £13,128, as fans prepare to snap up seats for the long-awaited heavyweight showdown

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 1am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury and Joshua have been linked with a blockbuster contest for more than a decade, with negotiations repeatedly failing to produce the long-awaited clash.

Now, the British rivals are finally set to share a professional ring in a contest that could prove defining for both men's careers.

Fury, 38, returned to the ring in April after another retirement announcement, beating Arslanbek Makhmudov on points. The former WBC heavyweight champion has won 36 of his 39 professional contests, with two defeats and one draw.

Joshua, 36, won Olympic gold at London 2012 before becoming a two-time unified heavyweight world champion. He has recorded 30 victories, including 27 knockouts, alongside four defeats.

Joshua's most recent high-profile outing came in December 2025, when he stopped Jake Paul, before returning to the ring in July 2026 to defeat Kristian Prenga by second-round knockout.

The December showdown will give both men the chance to settle their long-running rivalry and claim a defining victory in front of a huge crowd.

The Principality Stadium can accommodate up to 80,000 spectators for major events, while Netflix is set to stream the contest globally.

Main-event ring walks are expected at approximately 1am local time on Saturday, December 12, although the final schedule remains subject to confirmation.

The December showdown will give both men the chance to settle their long-running rivalry and claim a defining victory in front of a huge crowd

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

As for those in attendance, Turki Alalshikh had been keen to ensure there was an accessible entry point for fans, with tickets starting at £88.50 including fees.

At the top end of the scale, tickets cost a staggering £13,128, putting them among the most expensive publicly listed prices for a major boxing event.

The figure is not without precedent in a sport where premium seats can command eye-watering sums.

When Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao met in 2015, official tickets cost up to $10,000 (£6,700), while resale listings subsequently reached around £94,000 after the initial allocation sold out in less than a minute.

Meanwhile, a premium hospitality package for Mike Tyson's 2024 bout with Jake Paul was advertised at $2million (£1.57m) for 10 tickets and an exclusive ringside experience.

Some individual ringside seats were also listed on the secondary market at $50,000 (£39,000).

The highest-priced ticket previously listed for a British boxing event was a VIP ringside seat for Anthony Joshua's 2017 showdown with Wladimir Klitschko at Wembley, which was advertised for £202,400 on resale platform Viagogo.

However, that figure was an asking price rather than a confirmed sale. Around 90,000 fans attended the fight, which saw Joshua stop Klitschko in the 11th round.

Meanwhile, face-value prices for inner-ringside seats at Tyson Fury's 2022 fight against Dillian Whyte at Wembley reached £2,250.

Sports.title: Defiant Enzo Maresca insists he would have taken Man City job had club already had guilty verdict - and vows to speak 'when we win the appeal'
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca insisted that Manchester City would still have been his dream job had the club been found guilty of serious financial breaches before offering him the role. The Italian presented defiantly after the bombshell guilty verdict handed down by an independent commission last week, confidently claiming that he will talk openly once City win an appeal. Club chiefs held discussions with Maresca about their case and the manager threw full trust behind the ownership and chief executive, Ferran Soriano. ‘I completely trust the club,’ Maresca said. ‘I trust the people and it’s one of the reasons I joined the club. There isn’t another club in the world where I would like to be.’ Asked if he would have accepted the job had he known what would transpire in the bitter case with the Premier League, Maresca added: ‘One hundred per cent. I know the organisation from years ago. ‘I know how serious they are and they do the right things. I want to speak about this when we win the appeal.’ Enzo Maresca insisted he would have still joined Man City had they been found guilty of financial breaches prior to him being offered the role Maresca threw his backing behind the club's ownership and chief executive Ferran Soriano, right, and vowed to speak openly 'when we win the appeal' The Man City boss rejected the notion that previous titles won – including the Treble campaign for which he was Pep Guardiola’s assistant – have been tarnished Maresca rejected the notion that previous titles won – including the Treble campaign for which he was Pep Guardiola’s assistant – were tarnished. If City lose their appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion. And the 46-year-old suggested that he would have no issue dropping down the divisions given his past experience. ‘I won the Championship with Leicester City,’ Maresca smirked. ‘So in case we are in League One we will see. But we are thinking about something we don't know. ‘What happens if the appeal is won? I don’t know. We’re predicting the future. I’m worried about tomorrow, two days. It’s fair from my point of view to respect the process.’ Maresca and Soriano both addressed the City squad on their return to training on Thursday afternoon, with the coach stressing the importance of remaining focused on the games ahead. That starts at Liverpool on Sunday in one of the most anticipated match-ups between the rivals in years, with City set for a hostile reception at Anfield. ‘Anfield is a nice pitch,’ he said. ‘Probably even more warm in terms of environment but the reason why I decided to be a manager is for this kind of game. ‘It will be a tough test. We need to be ready. The focus has to be about the game but we know the environment is nice, probably even worse because of the situation. ‘The players can face the pressure, absolutely. They already experienced similar situations. Enzo Fernandez played in Argentina, where almost every game is like going to Anfield. So it’s not a problem. ‘It’s a matter of being together, sticking together as Erling (Haaland) said. This is the situation, the noise, but the most important thing is we keep doing the right things. We’re on the same page with the players and CEO. ‘We completely understand the seriousness of the situation. We understand it but it’s our duty to control the noise. You cannot avoid it. ‘Viewing the environment inside the building the last two days, I’m not worried at all. It’s nice. We’re top of the league at the moment. The players have all the reason to be happy and excited.’
