Those numbers highlight the attacking confidence Comoros have carried into the competition. They have shown that they can take their chances and turn territorial dominance into goals.

However, the context is important.

The Sudan tie provided Comoros with a successful opening to their campaign, but facing Nigeria represents a substantial increase in the level of opposition. The Super Falcons possess greater experience in major international tournaments, a deeper history of competing against elite African teams and players accustomed to high-pressure fixtures.

Friday’s contest will therefore provide a more meaningful measure of how far Comoros have progressed and whether their first-round scoring form can translate against a more experienced opponent.

Eguavoen faces squad reshuffle

Nigeria’s preparations have not been entirely straightforward, with several players withdrawing from the original squad.

Asisat Oshoala, Ashley Plumptre and Oluwatosin Demehin are among those who became unavailable. Eguavoen also released Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Favour Nkwocha to rejoin the Flamingos ahead of the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco.

The changes forced the coaching staff to adjust their plans and bring in replacements before the opening fixture.

Nevertheless, Eguavoen has expressed confidence in the players available to him, insisting that the squad has sufficient quality and experience to handle the challenge.

The immediate task will be to establish control, maintain defensive concentration and ensure Nigeria’s attacking play produces a clear advantage before the return leg.

With both matches taking place in Ikenne, the conventional home-and-away advantage is largely removed. The Falcons must therefore approach the tie with the same seriousness they would bring to a difficult away fixture, while also making the most of their familiarity with the venue.

For Eguavoen, the key is to ensure that the squad changes do not disrupt the team’s organisation or its understanding of what is required over the two legs.

Nigeria’s experience should count for something, but that advantage must be reflected in their performance rather than simply assumed because of their history.

Ajibade wants Nigeria to take it one game at a time

Super Falcons captain Rasheedat Ajibade has also stressed the importance of starting the campaign positively.

With only two African teams set to qualify for the Olympics, every round carries significant consequences. A strong first-leg result would give Nigeria greater control over the tie and reduce the pressure heading into Tuesday’s return fixture.

Ajibade, however, has urged her teammates to remain focused on the immediate task rather than become distracted by the prospect of reaching Los Angeles.

“We’ll take it one step at a time, one game at a time,” she said.

That approach will be particularly important in a competition where one poor performance can bring an otherwise promising campaign to an abrupt end.

For Nigeria, the priority is to take control of the Comoros tie before turning attention to the increasingly difficult challenges that lie ahead.

Comoros coach embraces the challenge

Comoros head coach Yusuf Abdullah has acknowledged the difficulty of facing Nigeria but insists his team will approach the match with belief and a clear plan.

Abdullah described the opportunity to compete against the 10-time African champions as a significant honour and an important experience for his players.

He also emphasised the wider importance of the fixture to the development of women’s football in Comoros, viewing the tie as an opportunity for his team to test itself against one of Africa’s most established sides.

Rather than focusing on the possibility of defeat, the coach has encouraged his players to concentrate on their performance and compete according to their style of play.

Captain Assimina Maoulida has adopted a similarly composed approach, playing down the pressure surrounding the encounter and saying the players intend to enjoy the occasion while giving their best.

Comoros may enter the fixture as underdogs, but their 30-goal first-round performance suggests they will not lack confidence in the final third.

The question is whether they can reproduce that attacking effectiveness against a Nigerian side with considerably more experience of this level of competition.

Nigeria vs Comoros: The numbers

The contrast between the two teams is clear in their recent Olympic qualifying records and international achievements.

Nigeria

Previous Olympic appearance: Paris 2024

Women’s Africa Cup of Nations titles: 10

Current Olympic qualifying campaign: Bye into the second round

Goals scored in this qualifying campaign: Yet to play

Goals conceded in this qualifying campaign: Yet to play

Comoros

Previous Olympic appearance: None

Women’s Africa Cup of Nations titles: 0

First-round qualifying record: Two wins

Goals scored in this qualifying campaign: 30

Goals conceded in this qualifying campaign: 0

The statistics underline Nigeria’s greater experience and Comoros’ impressive start to the current campaign. However, neither set of numbers will decide Friday’s contest.

Nigeria must demonstrate that their pedigree can translate into an effective performance, while Comoros will look to show that their first-round scoring exploits were more than a product of the opposition they faced.

What is at stake?

The immediate prize is a place in the third round of African Olympic qualifying, where the winner of the two-legged tie will face Morocco.

Morocco have already progressed after Congo withdrew from their scheduled second-round tie, while Cameroon also advanced following Guinea’s withdrawal.

The qualification route remains a demanding one, with further knockout rounds separating Nigeria from a place at Los Angeles 2028.

For the Super Falcons, qualification would mean a second consecutive Olympic appearance and further evidence that their return to the Games at Paris 2024 was the beginning of a more consistent presence at the Olympics.

For Comoros, advancing would represent a landmark achievement and bring them closer to their first-ever appearance at the Women’s Olympic Football Tournament.

The unusual arrangement of playing both legs in Ikenne also means Nigeria will have to manage the tie carefully, knowing that there will be no conventional home fixture in Comoros to navigate.

A convincing first-leg victory would place the Falcons in a strong position before Tuesday’s return encounter. Anything less would leave more work to do in a qualifying campaign where the margin for error is slim.

For Eguavoen and his players, the mission is clear: respect Comoros, impose their quality and begin the journey to Los Angeles with a result that reflects Nigeria’s ambition.

World.title: ADC vows to publish independently collated 2027 election results
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) says it will independently collate and publish polling-unit results during the 2027 general elections, insisting that doing so is within its constitutional rights.

The opposition party was responding to a warning attributed to the Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Joash Amupitan, against sharing privately collated election results.

In a statement on Thursday, the ADC National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, said the party would document results through its polling agents and make verified figures available to the public.

“The ADC will share our collated results with the public. Our agents will document results, our structures will collate them, and we will communicate verified figures to the public, clearly identifying their source and status,” the statement said.

The party argued that its proposed action was protected by the constitutional right to freedom of expression.

“We are aware of our rights to freedom of expression under the Constitution. We are also aware of the limitations associated with those rights. And we hold that our rights to collate and share election results are not abrogated by any of the limitation clauses,” it said.

The ADC acknowledged that INEC has the statutory authority to announce official election results and declare winners but maintained that this did not prevent political parties and citizens from gathering and sharing election information.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

What the law says

Section 39 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, guarantees freedom of expression, including the right to receive and impart information.

The Electoral Act also provides procedures for counting, recording, collating and declaring election results.

Under the electoral framework, polling agents are entitled to receive copies of polling-unit results in accordance with the law.

Political parties can use these records to monitor the collation process and compare figures with those announced by electoral officials.

However, independently compiled results do not replace the official collation and declaration procedures prescribed by law.

The ADC did not explain how it would verify the figures before publication or address discrepancies between its records and those released by INEC.

World.title: NNPC filling stations to sell petrol at landing cost to cushion global oil price shocks — Presidency
World.content:
The Federal Government has announced that the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has agreed to forgo its petrol retail profit margin and sell the product at cost as part of broader efforts to cushion the impact of global oil price shocks on Nigerians, particularly vulnerable households.

In a statement issued on Thursday by Bayo Onanuga, spokesperson to President Bola Tinubu, the government said NNPC Retail would implement the arrangement for the next 30 days.

“This means if NNPC’s landing cost is N1,300, it will sell fuel to Nigerians, especially commercial vehicles, at the same price,” the statement said.

The Presidency said the discount, backed by President Tinubu, was among several measures earlier announced by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, to mitigate the effects of rising international crude oil and refined petroleum product prices.

It added that NNPC Retail, which the government described as already selling petrol at the lowest price in the market, was expected to provide temporary relief to consumers through the arrangement.

PREMIUM TIMES had earlier reported that Mr Oyedele said the Federal Government was negotiating a ceiling of ₦1,350 per litre on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol to limit price volatility.

The minister also rejected calls for the reinstatement of petrol subsidy, warning that restoring petrol prices to pre-reform levels could cost the government more than ₦20 trillion annually.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, such a move could exert further pressure on the naira, potentially pushing the exchange rate towards ₦3,000 to the dollar and petrol prices to at least ₦2,000 per litre.

Global oil price shocks

The proposed interventions come amid a sharp increase in global crude oil and refined petroleum product prices following the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran.

Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz have heightened concerns about global energy security and contributed to higher crude oil prices, with Brent crude rising above $100 per barrel.

The impact has been felt in Nigeria despite its status as a major oil producer, as international crude prices, shipping costs and refined-product prices influence domestic fuel prices.

Although higher crude oil prices could boost government revenue, increases in petrol, diesel and aviation fuel prices have raised transportation, production and logistics costs for households and businesses.

The pressure has compounded the cost-of-living crisis following the removal of petrol subsidy in 2023 and renewed calls for the government to introduce measures to protect consumers from further price increases.

Opposition parties have repeatedly criticised the Tinubu administration over the hardship associated with subsidy removal and the absence of adequate measures to cushion its immediate impact when the policy was announced during the president’s inauguration in May 2023.

The latest decision to have NNPC Retail sell petrol at landing cost has also generated debate over whether the arrangement amounts to a return to fuel subsidy.

The Presidency has rejected that interpretation, maintaining that the measure is a temporary intervention intended to moderate the effects of global price volatility rather than reverse the deregulation of the downstream petroleum sector.

The move has also attracted political scrutiny amid public dissatisfaction over the cost of living and preparations for the 2027 general elections, with some observers questioning whether the intervention could serve as a strategy to improve the administration’s standing with voters.

The Presidency said it hoped other petroleum marketers would follow NNPC’s example, noting that the sharp increase in crude oil and petrol prices was not expected to persist indefinitely.

It reiterated that the temporary discount should not be interpreted as a restoration of petrol subsidy, which the government says ended on 29 May 2023.

Forward crude sales to local refineries

The government also announced plans to sell crude oil to domestic refineries through forward-sale arrangements as part of efforts to reduce the impact of international market fluctuations on domestic fuel prices.

“As production rises and previously committed crude is freed up, this is expected to shield pump prices from global market volatility,” the statement said.

Mr Oyedele said the government was negotiating a ceiling of ₦1,350 per litre on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol to moderate price increases.

Under the proposed arrangement, where costs exceed the ceiling, refiners and importers would initially bear the shortfall and recover it later when crude oil prices or the exchange rate improve, without exceeding the stipulated ceiling.

“This is neither a subsidy nor a price control: it is designed to smooth prices over time rather than suppressing them,” the minister said.

He explained that maintaining relatively stable prices would provide greater certainty for consumers and businesses than allowing sharp increases followed by subsequent reductions.

The proposed ceiling would be reviewed monthly and adjusted according to prevailing costs, with the government publishing the relevant figures to promote transparency, he added.

Other measures

The government outlined additional interventions aimed at reducing transportation costs, supporting vulnerable households and limiting the effects of higher energy prices on businesses.

Under the 2025 tax reform laws, Mr Oyedele said the Federal Government was working with state governments and security agencies to curb the collection of road taxes and levies that increase transport fares and logistics costs.

The government also plans to increase funding for cash transfers to vulnerable households and expand access to subsidised credit for small businesses and consumers.

Faster CNG rollout

The government said it was accelerating the deployment of compressed natural gas (CNG) in collaboration with state governments.

It expects transport operators to pass on the savings from cheaper fuel to passengers through lower fares.

According to the statement, CNG is between 60 and 70 per cent cheaper than petrol.

Excess profit tax

The government said it would consider an excess profit tax for operators found to be taking undue advantage of consumers across the energy value chain.

Proceeds from taxes imposed on price gouging would be used exclusively to cushion the impact of higher fuel prices, including through transport support or vouchers for urban minimum-wage earners.

The government also plans to work with the National Assembly to consider additional tax relief for low-income earners under the 2027 Finance Bill.

Reduced regulatory costs

The Federal Government said it was cutting regulatory costs that contribute to the cost of doing business and, indirectly, increase the prices of goods and services.

It said the measure was intended to ease cost pressures on businesses and consumers.

National Strategic Fuel Reserve

The government also announced plans to establish a National Strategic Fuel Reserve to protect households and businesses against future energy supply disruptions.

Under the proposed framework, refined petroleum products would be released into the market under clearly defined and publicly available rules whenever global disruptions or hoarding threaten supply and price stability.

The Presidency said the reserve was not intended to subsidise fuel or fix prices but to secure supplies, discourage artificial scarcity and reduce market volatility.

It added that the initiative would help prevent market manipulation and strengthen Nigeria’s long-term energy security.

Traffic and logistics management

The government said traffic management agencies would improve traffic flow, particularly in major urban centres, to reduce fuel consumption.

It also cited the newly launched address codes by the Nigerian Postal Service (NIPOST) as a measure expected to improve logistics efficiency and lower delivery costs.

The Presidency stressed that the measures would not restore a blanket fuel subsidy, arguing that such a policy could expose the economy to renewed fiscal pressure.

Acknowledging the hardship Nigerians have faced since subsidy removal, the government said reversing the reform would risk repeating past economic difficulties.

“Removing the fuel subsidy came at a price. But the alternative has been tried. Nigeria has already lived through that cycle: scarcity, smuggling, a collapsing currency and a fiscal crisis,” the statement said.

The Presidency added that the government was not seeking to reverse the reform but to ensure that its benefits reached more Nigerians more quickly and tangibly.

It also disclosed that the Federal Government was working on a comprehensive package of fiscal measures aimed at sustainably reducing inflation to single digits in the near term.

World.title: INEC to display voter register, distribute PVCs in 168 Taraba wards
World.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) will begin displaying the National Register of Voters and distributing Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) across 168 registration areas in Taraba State on Friday.

The one-week exercise, which will run until 16 October, will allow registered voters to verify their details, collect available PVCs and raise claims or objections over entries in the register.

In a statement issued in Jalingo on Thursday, Ngunan Iyongo, INEC’s Head of Voter Education and Publicity, said the exercise would take place daily from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.

Ms Iyongo issued the statement on behalf of the Resident Electoral Commissioner in the state.

According to the commission, the exercise covers people who registered as voters, transferred their registration or requested replacement of lost PVCs between August and December 2025 under Phase One of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise.

INEC urged affected voters to visit their designated registration areas to confirm that their names and other details had been correctly captured in the register.

The commission said voters could also raise claims or objections where they discovered errors or discrepancies in their records.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, not all PVCs may be available during the exercise. INEC said additional cards would be made available for collection after they were received by its Taraba office from the commission’s headquarters in Abuja.

The display of the voters’ register will end on 16 October, but PVC collection will continue afterwards at INEC offices in the respective local government areas.

The commission urged eligible voters, community leaders, political parties and civil society organisations to encourage residents to verify their registration details and collect their cards ahead of forthcoming elections.

World.title: 2027: Okowa remains Anioma favourite for Delta North Senate — Chiazor
World.content:
By Jimoh Babatunde

Media consultant and veteran journalist, Dr Norbert Chiazor, has described former Delta State Governor, Dr Ifeanyi Okowa, as the favourite to win the 2027 Delta North senatorial election, citing his grassroots appeal, political experience, organisational strength and enduring relationships across Anioma.

Chiazor, a former chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Delta State Council, made the assessment while analysing the emerging political contest in Delta North, where Okowa, of the All Progressives Congress (APC), is expected to face Engineer Victor Ochei of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), whom he identified as his major challenger.

The journalist argued that Okowa’s political profile, built over several years in public service and party politics, placed him ahead of other contenders in the race for the Senate seat.

According to him, the former governor’s influence in Anioma politics goes beyond party affiliation, drawing strength from his grassroots connections, personal relationships and historical significance in the political development of Delta State.

Chiazor, who holds a PhD in Mass Communication from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN), traced Okowa’s political standing in Anioma to a screening exercise organised by the Anioma Congress in 2014, ahead of the 2015 governorship election.

He recalled that the organisation, then led by the late Asagba of Asaba, Obi Professor Chike Edozien, constituted a committee headed by respected technocrat, Chief Philip Asiodu, to assess several aspirants from Delta North seeking to become governor.

According to Chiazor, the committee identified Okowa’s personality, intelligence, depth and political experience as outstanding qualities during the exercise.

He said the process was significant because it reflected an effort by Anioma stakeholders to assess the aspirants beyond partisan considerations at a crucial period in the region’s quest to produce a governor.

Chiazor maintained that Okowa’s eventual emergence as governor and his completion of two terms in office further strengthened his place in the political history of Delta State.

He described the former governor’s emergence as the first person of Anioma origin to occupy the office as a defining milestone that continued to shape perceptions of his political relevance in the area.

Assessing the likely contest between Okowa and Ochei, Chiazor described the 2027 election as a contest of political hierarchy between two prominent sons of Anioma, insisting that the former governor possessed a greater political advantage.

“Ochei is good. Okowa is better, by far,” he declared.

He argued that Okowa’s name recognition, established political network and experience in electoral contests would be significant factors as the candidates seek the support of voters across the senatorial district.

Chiazor also identified the former governor’s grassroots connections and enduring interpersonal relationships as key elements of his political strength, saying his influence extended beyond the immediate boundaries of Delta North.

He dismissed suggestions that negative narratives or social media campaigns could substantially diminish Okowa’s political standing, maintaining that his record and established relationships remained important considerations in assessing his electoral prospects.

“No spurious stereotyping can sully his stature. No social media stunt or screaming headline can erase his standing. Okowa is the political mascot of Delta North. He leads. We listen,” Chiazor said.

He further expressed confidence in Okowa’s capacity to represent Delta North in the Senate, arguing that his experience in governance would enable him to contribute to legislative deliberations and advance the interests of his constituents.

On the contest with Ochei, Chiazor said the former governor remained his preferred choice, while acknowledging the latter as a worthy challenger.

“On the 2027 Senate seat, it is safe to bet: Okowa the winner, Ochei the fitting challenger. For Anioma people, Okowa is the reason; Ochei is the racer. One reigns; the other runs. No Victor, no vanquished. Hopefully,” he declared.

Chiazor expressed the hope that Okowa would bring his political experience, competence and temperament to bear if elected, representing Delta North with dignity while promoting the interests of Anioma people and contributing to national development.

The 2027 Delta North senatorial contest is expected to attract considerable political attention as aspirants and parties seek to consolidate their support across the district. Chiazor’s assessment, however, represents his personal political judgement of the contenders, with the eventual outcome to be determined by voters at the polls.

World.title: 2027: AAC sets up campaign council, targets voters across 36 states
World.content:
By Dickson Omobola

African Action Congress, AAC, has said the 2027 general election is about changing Nigeria’s political direction rather than merely changing the occupant of Aso Rock.

The party, which lamented the failure of the existing political order to meet Nigerians’ expectations, announced the inauguration of the Sowore–Magashi 2027 Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, as part of efforts to strengthen its preparations for the presidential election.

AAC’s Acting National Chairman, Samuel Ajeigbe, and National Secretary, Oshiokhue Ikpeminoghena, in a statement, said the council would comprise political strategists, organisers, policy advocates, media professionals, digital campaigners, election specialists, legal practitioners, finance personnel and grassroots mobilisers.

It said the team would coordinate campaign activities across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

According to the statement, the council would be led by its Director-General, Abdullahi Usman, supported by deputies in charge of Strategy and Political Affairs, and Diaspora and Resource Mobilisation. Juwon Sanyaolu would serve as the Campaign Council Secretary.

The party said 10 national directorates had also been established to oversee key campaign functions, including strategy and policy, grassroots mobilisation, labour and civil society engagement, publicity and communications, digital media, data and technology, election operations, finance, legal and compliance, and administration and field operations.

At the grassroots level, the campaign structure would link state, local government area, ward and polling-unit coordinators to build a nationwide network of volunteers, canvassers, polling agents and supporters.

The AAC acknowledged the role of the SOWORENOW app in coordinating support for the campaign, describing it as an important digital platform for organising supporters and managing campaign activities.

It, however, said the newly inaugurated council was not intended to replace the existing digital mobilisation structure but to expand and strengthen it through physical grassroots organisation, political coordination and community-level engagement.

The statement said: “The Presidential Campaign Council is not a replacement for this digital mobilisation infrastructure; rather, it is designed to upscale, deepen and expand it. The Council will combine the power of technology with physical grassroots organisation, political coordination and community-level mobilisation to ensure that the Sowore–Magashi campaign reaches Nigerians in every part of the country.

“The election is a defining moment for Nigeria, and the campaign would take its message to urban centres and rural communities, as well as state capitals and polling units. The 2027 election is not merely about changing the occupant of Aso Rock; it is about changing the political direction of Nigeria.

“We call on Nigerians who desire a different direction for the country to join the campaign because national change requires active public participation beyond the activities of politicians.”

World.title: Anambra: Police probe video showing operatives, court bailiff rift
World.content:
The Anambra Police Command says it is assessing a social media video concerning an encounter between a Court bailiff and police operatives attached to “B” Division, Awka.

The Police Public Relations Officer (PPRO) in the state, SP Tochukwu Ikenga, made this known in a statement on Wednesday in Awka.

Ikenga said that the investigation into the matter would assist the police in establishing the facts.

“The Anambra Police Command is aware of a video currently circulating on social media, concerning an encounter between a Court Bailiff and police operatives attached to “B” Division, in connection with the enforcement of a court order.

“The command notes that the circulating video captures only part of the incident and does not, in itself, provide the full circumstances or events preceding the encounter.

“The command has therefore commenced an assessment of the incident with a view to establishing the facts,” he said.

According to him, preliminary information indicates that the police operatives were responding to a distress call concerning the presence of unidentified persons and a reported disturbance at one premises within the jurisdiction of the division.

He said that upon arrival at the scene, the operatives met some individuals engaged in the eviction of persons and removal of properties from the premises.

The police spokesman said that in the course of establishing the identities of the persons involved and their mission, the officers approached them and requested appropriate identification.

“During the interaction, there was a disagreement between the police operatives and some of the persons present.

“The persons subsequently identified themselves as Court Bailiffs carrying out an enforcement exercise pursuant to a court order,” he said.

He said that the preliminary information available revealed that the Police Division was not previously approached for security assistance before the commencement of the enforcement exercise.

He also said upon being informed that the persons were Court Bailiffs acting pursuant to a court order, the police operatives advised them on appropriate procedure for requesting police security support during such exercises.

He said that after the advice the police subsequently withdrew from the scene.

The command reiterated its respect for the authority and independence of the courts, vowing its commitment to providing lawful security support for the enforcement of valid court orders.

According to him, where such support is duly requested and required, the police will ensure that all enforcement processes are conducted peacefully and in accordance with the law.

Ikenga said the command has noted the concerns arising from the incident and has engaged the relevant parties.

He said that was part of efforts to establish the complete facts and ensure that the matter was handled professionally, impartially and in accordance with the law.

He urged members of the public to exercise restraint and avoid reaching conclusions based solely on isolated video clips circulating on social media.

According to him, this is particularly true where such footage does not capture the complete circumstances surrounding an incident.

He said that the command would communicate further developments as necessary upon conclusion of the ongoing assessment.

(NAN)

World.title: NDLEA rehabilitates 53,843 drug users in five years — Marwa
World.content:
NDLEA boss, Mohammed Marwa

By Efe Onodjae

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA, has said it counselled, treated and rehabilitated 53,843 persons struggling with drug use across its 31 rehabilitation centres nationwide in the last five years.

The agency also disclosed that it conducted 17,213 outreaches under its War Against Drug Abuse (WADA) campaign within the period as part of efforts to prevent substance abuse and promote public awareness.

The Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of NDLEA, Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (retd.), disclosed this in his remarks delivered by the Assistant Comptroller-General, Archie-Abia Ibinabo, Director of Seaport Operations, at the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit held in Lagos on Friday.

Marwa, who was the Special Guest of Honour at the summit, said mental health challenges and substance abuse were closely connected, stressing that addressing one without considering the other would undermine efforts to support affected young people.

He said the agency encountered cases in which drug use was linked to underlying emotional and psychological struggles, including anxiety, depression and trauma.

“At the NDLEA, we meet this reality every day. Behind almost every case of drug abuse is a story of pain: anxiety nobody noticed, depression nobody named, trauma nobody treated,” he said.

According to him, some young people turn to drugs to cope with emotional distress, making it necessary to strengthen mental health support alongside efforts to combat drug trafficking and abuse.

Marwa said although the NDLEA would sustain its operations against drug traffickers and cartels, enforcement remained only one aspect of its responsibilities.

He explained that the agency’s balanced intervention strategy also prioritised drug demand reduction through prevention, counselling, treatment and rehabilitation.

The NDLEA boss said the approach informed the WADA campaign, which has taken anti-drug messages to schools, campuses, markets, places of worship, workplaces and communities.

On the impact of technology and social media, Marwa warned that young Nigerians were increasingly exposed to cyberbullying, unrealistic social comparisons, excessive screen use and online content that glamorised drug consumption.

He added that drug traffickers had also learnt to exploit digital platforms to reach potential users.

He, therefore, called for more effective social media campaigns to counter harmful narratives and for parents and schools to encourage open conversations about technology use and substance abuse.

Speaking on the summit’s theme, “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria through Access, Action and Advocacy,” Marwa said affordable mental healthcare and addiction treatment should be available to ordinary Nigerians, irrespective of their income or location.

He called for more trained professionals, better integration of mental health services into primary healthcare and treatment systems that would not turn away young people seeking assistance.

On early intervention, the NDLEA chairman said identifying and supporting students experiencing difficulties could prevent their problems from escalating to the point where rehabilitation became necessary.

He also identified stigma as a major obstacle to seeking mental health support, urging parents, teachers, religious leaders and the media to create an environment where young people could speak openly about their struggles.

Marwa called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, healthcare professionals, educators, civil society organisations, the private sector and the media to expand prevention programmes, referral systems, treatment and public education.

Addressing young people, he urged them to seek help early, support one another and avoid drug use, assuring them that their challenges did not diminish their potential.

“Your struggles are real, but so is your potential. Seek help early, speak up, look out for one another, and say no to drugs. Your life is worth more than any substance,” he said.

World.title: NNPC Ltd extends fuel discount promotion by one week
World.content:
The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC Ltd) has extended its N66 discount promotion on Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) by one week, with Automotive Gas Oil (AGO) now included in the offer at its retail outlets.

The company announced the extension in a promotional notice on X, urging customers to visit participating stations to benefit from the discount.

Recall that the company had unveiled on X a nationwide N66 fuel discount promotion to run from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7 as part of activities marking the 66th independence.

According to the notice, the promotion will now run at all NNPC retail outlets until Oct. 14, 2026, with terms and conditions applying.

It also encouraged customers to download the NNPC Fuel App by scanning the QR code provided or visiting onelink.to/nnpcfuelapp.

“One more week. More ways to save.

“The N66 discount promo on PMS has been extended by another week, and AGO is now included. Visit any participating station to take advantage.

“If you missed it earlier, you have another chance to enjoy the discount till Oct. 14, 2026,” it said.

The discount announcement comes as NNPC retail outlets sell fuel at different prices across Nigeria, reflecting variations in distribution and transportation costs.

Lagos and Rivers have the lowest listed price at N1,355 per litre, while motorists in Abuja pay N1,370 per litre. (NAN)

World.title: Everton’s US owners mull sale of club two years after takeover
World.content:
Everton’s American owners are considering selling the Premier League club less than two years after they took control.

The Texas-based Friedkin Group said in a statement on Friday it was exploring new investment options for the Liverpool-based club, “including the potential sale of a controlling interest”.

The Friedkin Group, which also owns Serie A club Roma, paid a reported £400 million ($529 million) to purchase Farhad Moshiri’s 94.1 percent stake in December 2024 and oversaw the move from Goodison Park to the new 53,000-capacity Hill Dickinson Stadium.

“When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch,” Everton’s statement said.

“With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton.

“We will only entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward and build on the momentum that has been established.”

Everton, ever-present in the English top flight since 1954, have finished 13th in the past two Premier League seasons under manager David Moyes after some rocky campaigns.

But the club’s owners came under fire after a poor summer transfer window. The late collapse of a deal to sign US striker Folarin Balogun left Everton with just one recognised striker in Thierno Barry.

In September, Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Dan Friedkin, CEO of the Friedkin Group, who is yet to attend a home game.

Everton, with nine titles, are fifth on the all-time list of English top-flight winners, behind only Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City.

But the last of those came in 1987 and the Toffees have not won a trophy since the 1995 FA Cup.

World.title: Nigeria lacks mental health specialists – Lagos govt
World.content:
Professor Akin Abayomi

By Cynthia Alo

Nigeria lacks adequate specialists and facilities to manage mental illnesses, the Lagos State Government has said, calling for a shift towards preventive mental healthcare to address growing mental health challenges, particularly among young people.

The State’s Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, made the remarks at the 4th edition of Vanguard Media Limited Mental Health Summit held in Lagos on Friday, with the theme, “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria.”

Abayomi, who was represented by the Director , Special Projects and Mental Health at the state Ministry of Health, said the growing willingness of young people to speak openly about their mental health struggles had created an opportunity to address the challenges.

He, however, stressed that awareness must be matched with adequate support, preventive measures and locally relevant information.

“We don’t have enough beds to manage mental illnesses. We don’t have enough specialists to manage mental illnesses. Even when you expand the number of providers, it will still not be enough to match the bodies,” he said.

The commissioner noted that young Nigerians were increasingly discussing anxiety, emotional distress and other personal struggles, including on social media, but warned that the information they consumed online could expose them to ideas and expectations that might not reflect their local realities.

He said the expansion of digital access had connected young Nigerians to the wider world but had also increased their exposure to foreign lifestyles, values and social expectations.

Abayomi illustrated the challenge with the example of a 10-year-old child in Yaba, Lagos, comparing their life with that of a child of the same age in California, United States, despite the differences in their social and cultural environments.

He said excessive screen time and exposure to online content could influence young people’s perceptions of themselves and their circumstances.

The commissioner also expressed concern that some children were growing up without sufficient knowledge of their immediate environment, arguing that parents, schools and other institutions needed to provide guidance that reflected the realities of Nigerian society.

“Our children are lacking social intelligence and local intelligence. The people who are supposed to teach them are no longer teaching them. And so they will get teachings from those who are available to them,” he said.

He stressed that young people needed support to develop the resilience and skills required to navigate life’s challenges, noting that difficulties were an inevitable part of human existence.

The commissioner urged stakeholders to focus on translating information about mental health into language young people could understand, while providing the context needed to help them cope with challenges.

He also called for a clearer understanding of the distinction between mental health and mental illness, explaining that poor mental health did not necessarily mean a person had a mental illness but could increase vulnerability to one.

“Our goal is to promote good mental health,” he said, adding that young people needed access to support, mentorship and appropriate services to help them navigate difficult periods in their lives.

Abayomi said the Lagos State Ministry of Health remained committed to promoting mental health under the leadership of Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, adding that stakeholders should be able to hold public institutions accountable for their interventions.

World.title: Lagos Corrections Command seeks affordable mental healthcare for youths
World.content:
By Efe Onodjae

The Nigerian Correctional Service, Lagos State Command, has called for affordable, quality and confidential mental healthcare for young Nigerians, urging stakeholders to strengthen access to services and tackle the stigma associated with mental illness.

The Controller of Corrections, Lagos State Command, Daramola George, made the call in a goodwill message delivered by the Deputy Controller of Corrections, Ajayi Francis, at the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit held in Lagos.

The summit, organised by Vanguard Media Limited, had the theme, “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria through Access, Action and Advocacy,” with discussions focusing on the impact of social media, technology and digital wellbeing.

George described mental health as fundamental to human wellbeing, productivity and national development, noting that young people needed adequate support to learn, work, innovate and contribute meaningfully to society.

He said neglecting mental health challenges could have far-reaching consequences for individuals, families, communities and the country.

The controller stressed the need for collective action involving government, healthcare professionals, parents, schools, religious institutions, businesses, civil society organisations, technology companies and the media.

He called for stronger mental health services at the primary healthcare level, expanded community-based support and the responsible use of digital platforms to provide counselling and other mental health services.

According to him, access to care should not be determined by a person’s income or geographical location, adding that young Nigerians needed affordable and confidential services that met appropriate professional standards.

On the impact of social media, George said digital platforms offered opportunities for learning, creativity, peer support and mental health awareness but could also expose young people to cyberbullying, online harassment, misinformation and harmful content.

He, therefore, advocated digital literacy and healthy online habits, alongside efforts to create safer online spaces where young people could share their experiences without fear of discrimination or judgment.

The controller also called for an end to stigma and misconceptions surrounding mental illness, stressing that seeking professional help should be recognised as a responsible step rather than a sign of weakness.

He urged media organisations, influencers, content creators, technology companies and public institutions to promote accurate and sensitive mental health information.

George further called for young people to be actively involved in developing policies and programmes designed to address their challenges, noting that their experiences with social media, education, employment and relationships should inform interventions aimed at improving their wellbeing.

He urged participants at the summit to translate discussions into concrete policies and measurable actions, stressing that sustained collaboration was necessary to build a society where young Nigerians could access mental healthcare and receive the support needed to fulfil their potential.

World.title: Chinese Embassy Explains One-China Principle to Nigerian Media Executives
World.content:
The Chinese Embassy has explained its One-China Principle, urging the Nigerian media to distinguish between reporting on Taiwan and descriptions that suggest the island is a sovereign country separate from China.

Speaking during a meeting with media executives in Lagos, Mr. Xu Fan, Director of Bilateral Relations and Commerce at the Chinese Consulate General in Lagos,

said China’s position on Taiwan was rooted in historical records, international agreements and the diplomatic framework established after the Second World War.

He cited United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758 of 1971 and Nigeria’s diplomatic recognition of the People’s Republic of China, while maintaining that the One-China Principle remained the political foundation of diplomatic relations between Beijing and Abuja.

Fan noted that Nigeria reaffirmed its commitment to the principle during President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s state visit to China in September 2024.

He clarified that China did not object to Nigerian media reporting on Taiwan but was concerned about terminology that could be interpreted as recognising the island as a sovereign state.

The explanation prompted a robust exchange with Nigerian media executives, who stressed the importance of editorial independence and the need to preserve the freedom of journalists to report issues in the public interest.

The discussion, which also examined Nigeria-China relations, trade, investment and media cooperation, underscored the importance of dialogue between Chinese diplomatic institutions and Nigerian media organisations.

The session was convened by Hon. Peter Ogbonna Eze, representative of Buffalo and Bay Media, and featured Ambassador Anderson Madubike, a former Nigerian High Commissioner to Australia, former Consul General in Shanghai, China, and former Chargé d’Affaires to South Africa.

Earlier, Eze described Nigeria-China relations as a partnership that had expanded beyond traditional diplomatic engagement to encompass infrastructure, trade, education, technology, agriculture, investment and people-to-people exchanges.

He urged media organisations to report the relationship with accuracy, balance and context, stressing that informed public discourse was essential to maximising the benefits of bilateral cooperation.

“The media does not merely report events. It shapes how societies understand countries, people, policies and opportunities,” Eze said.

Madubike, on his part, drawing on his diplomatic experience, described Nigeria-China relations as robust, citing the extensive diplomatic, commercial and infrastructure ties between the two countries.

He said the media had a critical role in sustaining diplomatic relations by shaping public perceptions, providing reliable information and promoting mutual understanding.

“Diplomacy opens doors, but the media helps to keep those doors open,” he said.

According to him, treaties and government agreements alone cannot sustain long-term relationships between nations without public understanding and engagement.

The diplomat also stressed the importance of reporting the human dimension of Nigeria-China relations, including the experiences of Nigerian students, entrepreneurs and traders in China, as well as Chinese investors, engineers and business operators in Nigeria.

He noted that credible information about markets, regulations, infrastructure, incentives and investment opportunities could encourage business partnerships and strengthen economic ties.

The interaction also featured concerns about the trade imbalance between Nigeria and China, import dependence and complaints by Nigerian traders that some Chinese businesses were competing with them in the retail market.

Responding, Xu acknowledged the concerns but argued that the solution should involve establishing clearer regulatory boundaries between wholesale and retail operations rather than excluding Chinese businesses from Nigeria.

He said the Chinese Embassy had engaged Chinese traders, market authorities and other stakeholders to explore practical solutions.

Xu also advocated a shift from a relationship dominated by trade in finished products towards greater Chinese investment in local manufacturing.

He said Chinese companies could establish more factories and production facilities in Nigeria to create jobs, transfer skills and contribute to the country’s industrial development.

The Chinese diplomat disclosed that bilateral trade reached approximately $28 billion in 2025, describing the figure as evidence of the growing economic relationship between both countries.

He also said China had become Nigeria’s largest market for engineering contractors, its second-largest export market and China’s third-largest trading partner in Africa.

Xu further highlighted China’s decision to extend zero-tariff treatment to 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations, including Nigeria.

He said the policy presented opportunities for Nigerian agricultural products, including sesame, cashew nuts and cocoa, to gain greater access to the Chinese market, subject to applicable rules of origin, inspection and quarantine requirements.

He urged Nigerian businesses to improve product quality, strengthen branding and take advantage of opportunities in the Chinese market.

The issue of illegal mining involving some Chinese nationals in Nigeria also featured prominently in the discussions.

Xu distinguished between law-abiding Chinese businesses and individuals involved in illegal activities, insisting that violations of Nigerian law were unacceptable to the Chinese government and diplomatic authorities.

He said the Chinese Embassy and relevant authorities were cooperating with Nigerian institutions by providing information and supporting efforts to identify Chinese nationals involved in illegal mining.

According to him, the Chinese government would not shield individuals found to have violated Nigerian laws.

Participants also called for deeper Chinese investment in manufacturing, technology transfer, industrial development and local value addition, arguing that bilateral cooperation should deliver more benefits to Nigeria beyond infrastructure development and the importation of finished goods.

The discussion highlighted the need for a partnership that promotes local production, employment, skills development and technological advancement.

On media freedom, Nigerian executives reiterated that editorial independence remained a fundamental principle of journalism and that disagreements over sensitive diplomatic issues should be addressed through dialogue, clarification and the right of reply.

In his concluding remarks, Xu described Nigerian media organisations as “partners and friends, not enemies.”

He offered to strengthen cooperation with Nigerian media through professional exchanges, training programmes, seminars, media delegations and other institutional initiatives.

He said Chinese authorities would continue to facilitate opportunities for Nigerian journalists to visit China, experience its development and gain a deeper understanding of its society, culture, economy and political system.

Xu also invited participating media organisations to propose practical joint initiatives, including media programmes, publications and professional exchange projects.

The engagement highlighted the opportunities and challenges in Nigeria-China relations, particularly the need to reconcile diplomatic sensitivities with the principles of editorial independence and responsible journalism.

Participants agreed that sustained dialogue, accurate reporting and stronger people-to-people engagement were essential to building mutual trust and ensuring that the bilateral relationship delivered greater benefits to both countries.

World.title: UNICEF Launches ‘Neem Tree Dialogue’ to Protect Children
World.content:
John Shiklam in Kaduna

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has launched ‘The Neem Tree Dialogue’, an initiative aimed at preventing violence against children and promoting positive parenting in five communities in Zaria, Kaduna State.

Speaking at the launch yesterday in Zaria, UNICEF’s Chief of Field Office, Kaduna, Dr. Gerida Birukila, said the initiative would strengthen families and mobilise communities to protect children from abuse, neglect and exploitation.

“We cannot build peaceful, prosperous and resilient communities while children continue to experience violence, neglect, exploitation, and deprivation,” she said.

Birukila said positive parenting requires families to recognise children as individuals with rights, dignity, potential, and voices.

“Positive parenting is not simply about changing how parents discipline their children. It is about transforming the way families understand children, as individuals with rights, dignity, potential, and voices that deserve to be heard,” she said.

She also called on traditional institutions to use their influence to challenge harmful practices and promote child protection.

Birukila maintained that the protection of children is not the responsibility of government or development organisations alone, but a shared responsibility of families, communities, traditional and religious institutions, government and society as a whole.

She described the ‘Neem Tree Dialogue’ as a platform for communities to discuss harmful practices and agree on practical actions to protect children.

“Let this Dialogue similarly become a space where communities come together, listen to one another, challenge harmful practices, and agree on practical actions to protect their children.

“When we invest in positive parenting, we invest in children. When we protect children, we strengthen families. And when we strengthen families, we build peaceful and resilient communities,” she said.

Also speaking on the initiative, the UNICEF Child Protection Specialist, Dr Willy Mamah, said the project is expected to engage at least 1,000 parents in Gelesu, Tudun Wada, Zaria City, Samaru and Kongo communities through storytelling, dialogue, parenting sessions and other creative approaches.

Mamah said the initiative was inspired by a book written by a grassroots lawyer and advocate, Maryam Marwa Abdu.

He explained that the project was designed to take the issues raised in the book beyond fiction and into communities where parents, traditional and religious leaders, young people and other stakeholders could discuss practical solutions to challenges affecting children.

“The Neem Tree Dialogue is a community action initiative using storytelling and dialogue to promote positive parenting, prevent violence against children, including child marriage, and strengthen the agency of girls and boys,” he said.

According to Mamah, the initiative was a collaboration involving the Kaduna State Ministry of Justice, Women and Children Rights Empowerment Foundation, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA), the National Orientation Agency (NOA), and UNICEF.

He said parenting remained an important component of UNICEF’s programme of cooperation with government, adding that preventing violence against children required strengthening families and the wider community systems surrounding them.

“Our approach recognises something fundamental: if we want to prevent violence against children, we must strengthen the family and the community systems that surround the child,” he said.

Mamah said the parenting component would focus on positive communication, quality time with children, emotional literacy, constructive conflict resolution, and knowing when and where to seek help.

He stressed that the initiative was not intended to tell communities what to think, but to create a safe space for them to examine harmful practices, reaffirm positive values, and develop solutions they could own.

Mamah urged stakeholders to support the initiative, stressing that child protection was a responsibility shared by the entire community.

World.title: Sensational Reporting Worsens Voter Apathy, Amupitan Warns Online Publishers
World.content:
The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Joash Amupitan, has warned online publishers against sensational reporting, saying fake news, unverified claims and exaggerated reports could destroy public confidence in elections and worsen voter apathy.

The warning was contained in a press statement e-signed by Adedayo Oketola, Chief Press Secretary and Media Adviser to the INEC Chairman, on Thursday, October 8.

Amupitan gave the warning in Lagos while speaking at the 10th Annual Conference of the Guild of Corporate Online Publishers (GOCOP), with the theme, “2027 Elections: Trust, Transparency and Shared Responsibilities.”

The INEC Chairman was represented by Prof. Ayobami Salami, the Resident Electoral Commissioner, Lagos.

The conference brought together publishers, editors, media professionals, election stakeholders, civil society organisations, academics and other critical stakeholders to discuss the role of trust, transparency and shared responsibility in strengthening Nigeria’s democratic process.

Amupitan said the media had a critical responsibility in shaping public perception of the electoral process, stressing that inaccurate reports could have consequences beyond the immediate news cycle.

The INEC chairman added that unverified allegations of electoral fraud could inflict lasting damage on confidence in the electoral process, even when subsequently corrected.

He said, “While INEC carries the legal mandate to conduct elections, the wider democratic health of Nigeria and indeed West Africa depends on the information infrastructure maintained by the media, particularly online publishers. This is where the core concept of Shared Responsibility becomes operational.

“We live in an era where the velocity of digital information frequently outpaces the verification of truth. Across our sub-region, election windows are increasingly targeted by coordinated information warfare, political violence narratives, synthetic media, and AI-generated deepfakes designed to inflame ethnic divides or passion and undermine institutional legitimacy.

“Fake news, unverified leaks, and sensationalised reports directly destroy public trust, incite civil unrest, and induce voter apathy. When an unverified claim regarding electoral fraud is published, the damage to public confidence is immediate and enduring; subsequent retractions or fact-checks rarely repair the injury.”

Amupitan urged online publishers to place accuracy above the pressure to break stories ahead of competitors, warning against the use of clickbait headlines and unverified information in election reporting.

He also urged publishers to provide proper context when reporting operational challenges during elections, rather than presenting isolated incidents as evidence of systemic failure.

The INEC chairman said responsible journalism would require media organisations to verify claims with the commission and other credible sources, particularly when reporting polling-unit results, electoral irregularities and allegations of manipulation.

He said the commission was proposing a three-point partnership with GOCOP, including dedicated digital fact-verification, stronger editorial self-regulation against the publication of unverified election results and altered result sheets, as well as a national voter education partnership.

Amupitan said the partnership was necessary because online publishers had become “primary storytellers and narrative custodians” of Nigeria’s democracy.

He urged them to use their platforms to strengthen public understanding of the electoral process, including voter education and the collection of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), rather than contributing to distrust and voter disengagement.

The INEC chairman said the commission would continue to strengthen its systems ahead of the 2027 elections, including the deployment of artificial intelligence for data auditing and cyber defence in partnership with Google and Microsoft.

“In strategic partnership with global technological leaders, including Google and Microsoft, we have embedded automated AI data-auditing tools and multi-layered firewalls to shield our databases against cyber intrusions, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and unauthorised data injection,” he said.

Amupitan said the technological measures were part of efforts to ensure that public confidence in the 2027 elections was based on verifiable processes rather than assurances.

He disclosed that the national register had risen to about 103 million registered voters following the conclusion of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise, while nationwide PVC collection was scheduled to begin on Friday.

He said INEC remained committed to delivering transparent elections and called on all stakeholders, including the media, to recognise their shared responsibility for building public trust in the process.

Amupitan added that INEC leadership was directly engaging Resident Electoral Commissioners, Administrative Secretaries, Heads of Department, Electoral Officers and Assistant Electoral Officers to identify operational gaps and implement corrective measures before Election Day.

He said comprehensive training programmes were also underway for election personnel, focusing on electoral administration, technology handling, conflict mitigation and legal compliance.

The INEC chairman said the commission had also commenced early procurement and distribution of non-sensitive electoral materials to its 36 state offices and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

He said the early procurement would provide sufficient time for batching, inventory auditing and distribution to the 774 local government areas ahead of the polls.

The commission, he added, had procured and commenced distribution of new operational pick-up vehicles to state offices and LGAs to address transportation challenges in difficult terrains, riverine communities and remote border settlements.

Amupitan said, “The procurement and physical delivery of non-sensitive electoral materials to all 36 State Offices and the FCT have already commenced. Commencing procurement months in advance provides adequate lead time for batching, inventory auditing, and downstream distribution to the 774 Local Government Areas well ahead of Election Day.

“To resolve field transportation bottlenecks —especially in difficult terrains, riverine areas, and remote border settlements—the Commission has procured and commenced the distribution of brand-new operational pick-up vehicles to State Offices and LGAs nationwide.”

He said INEC had also introduced a centralised Operational Activity Schedule to track material movement, storage security and vehicle deployment in real time across state command centres.

On election result declaration, the Lagos State Resident Electoral Commissioner, Prof. Ayobami Salami, explained that the Constitution specifically vests the authority to return an election result in the Returning Officer.

Salami clarified that being an INEC official does not automatically confer the constitutional authority to return election results.

He noted that even as a Resident Electoral Commissioner, he does not have the constitutional power to announce or return an election result.

He further explained that Returning Officers are appointed by the commission and are the officials constitutionally empowered to return the results of the elections assigned to them.

In his opening remarks, the Conference Chairman, Dr. Olisa Agbakoba, SAN, underscored the people’s constitutional right to vote, urging INEC to ensure that the 2027 elections are free, fair and credible.

Agbakoba raised key issues expected to shape political discourse ahead of the elections, particularly the future of fuel subsidy. He challenged presidential candidates to explain their positions on the subsidy regime and what they would do differently if elected.

The former NBA president also questioned who has the constitutional authority to declare election results, amid the growing influence of opinion polls, election projections and unofficial results circulated across traditional and digital media.

He queried whether opinion polls and other electoral projections should not be subjected to the same standards of verification and fact-checking required of other election-related information.

World.title: Lawyer Urges Tinubu to Prioritise Rail Expansion to Ease Road Congestion
World.content:
Amby Uneze in Owerri

Abuja-based constitutional lawyer and human rights advocate, Ikenna Ahumibe, has urged President Bola Tinubu to make the expansion and modernisation of Nigeria’s railway(rail transport system) a national priority, saying the country can no longer depend on roads to move most of its passengers and freight.

In an open letter dated October 7, Ahumibe said the federal government has rightly focused on rehabilitating and building roads, but rail deserves equal, if not greater, attention. He described roads and rail as complementary parts of a modern transport system, not competitors.

“Nigeria cannot realistically continue to move the overwhelming volume of passengers and heavy cargo exclusively by road.

“The consequences are already before us: incessant traffic congestion, rapid deterioration of roads, increased transportation costs, road accidents, and an enormous burden on the national economy,” he said.

He cited the recent gridlock on the Benin-Agbor-Asaba road, which left motorists stranded for several days, saying that in his view, a functional rail network would have spared many of them the ordeal.

“At least 70 per cent of those motorists could have been spared,” he said.

Ahumibe said cement, agricultural produce, petroleum products, minerals and containerised cargo could be moved by rail, easing pressure on roads, protecting public investment in them and lowering the cost of goods.

He pointed to China’s investment in high-speed and freight rail; India’s dedicated freight corridors, and Japan’s continued rail modernisation.

He also argued that rail would offer a safer, cheaper alternative to road and air travel at a time of rising airfares.

“Rail transportation can become an important instrument for reducing the cost of living and easing the economic hardship currently experienced by millions of Nigerians,” he said.

Commuter and inter-city lines, he added, would let people live in neighbouring towns and travel to work by train, easing congestion, overcrowding and housing pressure in major cities.

The lawyer urged a review of rail projects stalled by contractual, commercial and legal disputes, including the Warri-Itakpe-Ajaokuta line and the Calabar-Maiduguri corridor. He called for transparent negotiated settlement, mediation or other forms of alternative dispute resolution, where legally available, without compromising public accountability.

He also called for a substantial increase in the annual rail allocation, covering not only new track but also expansion of existing corridors and new regional lines; electrification of strategic routes; modern signalling and communications; dedicated freight corridors and cargo terminals; modernised stations; and protection of rail assets against vandalism and attack.

World.title: Alli Condemns Attacks on Oyo APC Candidates
World.content:
The Senator Sharafadeen Alli Campaign Organisation (SSACO) has condemned the attacks on Alhaja Tawakalitu Alli, wife of the Oyo State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Sen. Sharafadeen Alli, and two candidates of the party in Ibadan on Wednesday.

Mrs Alli was attacked during a medical outreach she organised at Ibikunle House, Ayeye, Ibadan while the Oyo South APC senatorial candidate, Aderemi Oseni, and Ibadan North West/Ibadan South-west Federal Constituency candidate, Folake Olunloyo-Oshinowo’s campaign trains were attacked during separate campaign events at Agbaje Market, Orita-Merin, and Idi-Arere, Ibadan on Wednesday.

The campaign organisation, in a statement by its Director of Media and Publicity Bisi Oladele, described the attacks as unwarranted, barbaric, and deliberate efforts to drag Oyo State back to the dark days of violence.

The statement read in part: “The Senator Sharafadeen Alli Campaign Organisation (SSACO) is at the least miffed by the unwarranted and barbaric attacks by Allied People’s Movement (APM) hoodlums on Alhaja Tawakalitu Alli during a medical outreach she organised at Ibikunle House, Ayeye, Ibadan, on Wednesday. Sponsored hoodlums also attacked the APC candidate for Oyo South Senatorial District, Hon. Aderemi Oseni; and the party’s candidate for Ibadan North-West/Ibadan South-West Federal Constituency, Hon. Folake Olunloyo-Oshinowo, during separate campaign events at Agbaje Market, Orita-Merin, and Idi-Arere, Ibadan on the same Wednesday.

“The SSACO calls on Governor Seyi Makinde who is the APM promoter in Oyo State, and the party’s governorship candidate, Hon. Bimbo Adekanmbi, to rein in on their hoodlums. APC candidates and supporters in Oyo State will not surrender our inalienable rights to freely associate, gather and campaign within the ambits of the law. And no amount of threats will deter the party from campaigning across Oyo State.

“Needless to stress that this ugly development which endangers the lives of political actors and innocent residents of Oyo State is a deliberate attempt by Governor Seyi Makinde and Hon. Adekanmbi to drag the peaceful Oyo State they inherited in 2019 back to the days of notorious violence which the state has already forgotten.

“As the chief security officer of the state, Governor Makinde carries the responsibility to protect all residents irrespective of their political leanings. This is the oath he swore to in 2019 and 2023. A governor and governorship candidate who sponsor violence against the opposition and the good people of Oyo State are nothing but enemies of the people and enemies of democracy.

“The SSACO calls on security agencies to fish out these perpetrators of violence and bring them to book in order to serve justice to the victims and also serve as a deterrence to violence in our dear state.

“It is obvious that Governor Makinde and Adekanmbi are sponsoring these attacks because of the imminent loss in the 2027 elections that is staring at them. But no ambition of any man or woman is worth the blood of others. They should stop this violence forthwith and allow peaceful campaign by all political parties in Oyo State. We are assuring Governor Makinde and Hon. Adekanmbi that APC candidates in Oyo State will continue to take their messages to the people. No threat against APC candidates will stop the imminent defeat of Adekanmbi and other APM candidates in the 2027 general elections.

“The good people of Oyo State deserve

issue-based campaigns, not violence. We advise Governor Makinde, Adekanmbi and other political parties to focus on presenting their programmes and policies to the electorate not visiting violence on the people.

“We advise Governor Makinde and Hon. Adekanmbi to call their APM thugs to order. APC candidates will not be intimidated by the violent APM machinery.

World.title: Yinka Babalola Convenes All Nigeria Rotary Peace Summit in Lagos
World.content:
Rotary International President Olayinka Hakeem Babalola will convene the All Nigeria Rotary Peace Summit 2026 in Lagos on Saturday, 7 November 2026. According to a statement, the summit will bring together Rotarians, leaders, peace advocates and key stakeholders for what is expected to be an important national conversation on building sustainable peace in Nigeria.

With the theme, “Good Governance, Justice and Equity: Foundations for Sustainable Peace,” the summit will hold in Lagos, beginning at 9:00 a.m.

The message behind the gathering is simple but urgent: peace cannot be separated from the conditions in which people live.

For President Yinka Babalola, the summit reflects Rotary’s conviction that peace is not merely the absence of conflict. It must be built deliberately; through dialogue, understanding, stronger communities and institutions that give people confidence in the future.

Commenting, Babalola said: “Peace must become more than something we wish for. It must be something we deliberately build in our communities, through our institutions and in the way we treat one another.”

The summit therefore moves beyond speeches to a deeper question: What must Nigeria do differently to create the conditions in which sustainable peace can flourish?

Participants will explore the relationship between good governance, justice, equity, economic opportunity and community development, while seeking practical pathways for collaboration and action.

Rotary’s involvement is significant.

Across Nigeria and around the world, Rotarians work at community level in areas including peacebuilding, education, maternal and child health, disease prevention, economic empowerment, water and sanitation, and community development. The peace ssummit brings those experiences into a wider national conversation, and it is coming at a perfect time as Nigeria prepares to head to the polls.

Rotarians, professionals, traditional and community leaders, civil society actors, young people, policymakers, the private sector, development partners and other stakeholders are invited to be part of the conversation.

“This is more than a gathering. It is a call to reflection, dialogue and action especially because building peace is everybody’s business,” the organisers said.
