He continued: “We did not want to reach this stage,” explaining that 20 diplomats, including the Consul General, will leave Israel, while a task force of 7 members will be permitted to remain inside the building with a “very limited operational scope.”

UK temporarily withdraws staff for security reasons

In response, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband stated that the United Kingdom has “temporarily withdrawn some staff” for security reasons, emphasizing that the mission “will continue to work with the Palestinian people.”

Miliband added that the UK government does not accept that Israel has the right to close the consulate, reiterating London’s position that “East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”

Miliband noted that following discussions with the Israeli government, the building “will not close” and will be known as the “UK Mission in Jerusalem.”

He further explained that the discussions did not yield an understanding regarding “the necessary guarantees for the security and protection of our staff and premises.”

He added: “Accordingly, the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and their families to ensure their security and safety.”

British sanctions on settlements

Israel had announced last September that it would close the British Consulate in retaliation for revised UK sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law.

The British government made last-minute efforts to persuade Israel not to close the consulate ahead of the deadline, after Tel Aviv announced it would close the consulate within 30 days of the sanctions’ announcement.

Israeli media had reported that the United Kingdom threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London, raising the prospect of further damage to bilateral ties between the two countries.

The British Consulate, originally established in 1838, manages UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem, as well as in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

According to the BBC, the consulate operates separately from the British Embassy in Tel Aviv, which serves as the UK’s primary diplomatic hub in Israel.

World.title: Israel issues high-level travel warning for Egypt and regional nations
World.content:
Israel’s National Security Council (NSC) has issued a renewed travel advisory urging Israeli citizens to avoid all travel to several regional countries, explicitly highlighting Egypt, including the Sinai Peninsula, under a Level 4 (High Threat) warning.

In an official public advisory, the NSC warned of heightened security risks, potential terror threats, and anti-Israel demonstrations targeting Israelis and Jewish communities abroad. The agency noted that regional threat groups and global jihad factions view this period as a key milestone to mobilize actions against Israeli targets.

Alongside Egypt, the Level 4 travel warning applies to destinations including Jordan, Qatar, and Somaliland.

Key recommendations from the NSC statement:

Avoid travel and depart promptly: Israeli nationals are advised to avoid traveling to Level 4 countries and to leave these areas if currently present.

Maintain low public profile: For citizens in regions under elevated threat levels, the council recommends minimizing the use of spoken Hebrew in crowded public spaces, avoiding public gatherings or protests, and refraining from displaying identifying symbols.

Digital and operational security: The advisory instructs citizens not to post advance travel itineraries or personal location details on social media, nor share content reflecting active or past service in Israeli security forces.

The NSC emphasized that citizens abroad experiencing immediate security threats should first contact local law enforcement authorities before notifying Israeli diplomatic hotlines.

World.title: Fitch affirms Egypt’s credit rating at “B” with a stable outlook
World.content:
Fitch Ratings has affirmed Egypt’s long-term foreign-currency sovereign credit rating at “B” with a Stable Outlook.

The agency noted that the rating is supported by expectations of relatively high economic growth for the Egyptian economy, continued strong support from international and regional partners, as well as the economy’s large scale compared to other peer countries in the same rating category.

Fitch stated that since the beginning of this year, the Egyptian economy has demonstrated improved resilience against external pressures. Total international reserves increased by approximately $5.5 billion over the first eight months of the year, reaching around $54.4 billion.

Additionally, the Central Bank of Egypt’s (CBE) net foreign assets surplus rose to nearly $19 billion in August, marking an increase of $5.6 billion during the first eight months of the year.

Fitch added that Egypt’s flexible exchange rate policy faced a real test with the outbreak of the war involving Iran, which led to an outflow of over $6 billion in foreign portfolio investments from government debt securities (around 1.4 percent of GDP).

This caused the Egyptian Pound to depreciate by more than 14 percent against the US Dollar. Despite these pressures, the CBE maintained currency convertibility without imposing foreign exchange restrictions or supporting the exchange rate, thereby enhancing the credibility of the flexible exchange rate regime.

The rating agency highlighted that “hot money” inflows returned quickly to the Egyptian market after weathering the initial war shock, helping the Egyptian Pound gradually recover.

Fitch expects that following the conclusion of Egypt’s IMF program in November 2026, the CBE will continue to maintain positive real interest rates alongside flexible exchange rate management.

Despite ongoing challenges, Fitch projects continued economic resilience, estimating GDP growth at approximately 5.1 percent in 2026, driven by improved performance across the tourism, manufacturing, and consumer sectors. While the agency expects growth to slow slightly to around 4.7 percent in 2027, it noted that this pace remains relatively high compared to many peer economies.

On the other hand, Fitch warned of persistent vulnerability factors, primarily weak public finances, exceptionally high interest-to-revenue ratios, significant external financing needs, inflation, and ongoing geopolitical risks.

World.title: Total closure on the 26th of July Axis and Ring Road in Giza for 5 days
World.content:
Giza Governorate has announced a total closure on the 26th of July Axis and the Ring Road (Western Arc) heading toward 15th of May Bridge for a period of 5 days.

In an official statement released today, the governorate explained that as part of the construction works for the Monorail project (Wadi El Nile – 6th of October Line) and to complete structural works at the Wadi El Nile Monorail Station on the 26th of July Axis, a total closure will be implemented for traffic coming from above the 26th of July Axis and the Western Arc Ring Road heading toward 15th of May Bridge.

The governorate clarified that the closure will initially begin on a trial basis without construction activity for 5 days, starting at 12:05 AM on Thursday, October 8, 2026, until the morning of Monday, October 12, 2026. This trial period aims to assess the impact of the closure on traffic flow prior to commencing actual construction once smooth traffic movement is ensured. Following the trial, the full closure will remain in place for 6 months starting Monday morning, October 12, 2026, until the completion of the project works.

Giza Governorate outlined the suggested alternative routes as follows:

First Alternative Route: Vehicles coming from the Ring Road (Western Arc) above the 26th of July Axis bound for 15th of May Bridge will take the off-ramp leading to Sudan Street, continue along Sudan Street until its intersection with Gamet El Dewal Al Arabeya Street, and then turn left onto Gamet El Dewal Al Arabeya Street heading toward 15th of May Bridge.

Second Alternative Route: Vehicles coming from the Ring Road (Western Arc) above the 26th of July Axis bound for 15th of May Bridge will take the off-ramp leading to Lebanon Square, enter Lebanon Street, turn left onto Shehab Street, and then turn left onto the surface road of the Wadi El Nile Tunnel to reach 26th of July Street toward 15th of May Bridge after bypassing the work zone.

The General Directorate of Giza Traffic, in coordination with the executing company, has placed all necessary traffic guidance and warning signs, floodlights, and flashing beacons around the entire work area to ensure public safety, alongside deploying traffic personnel to facilitate vehicle movement.

World.title: Who is Zack Polanski, the ‘eco-populist’ rattling the UK’s establishment?
World.content:
London — The leader of the UK’s Green Party, Zack Polanski, will on Thursday challenge the political establishment by taking on the ruling Labour Party in a special election for the seat held by former prime minister Keir Starmer.

Polanski, with his deep reserve of progressive policies and an active presence on TikTok cuts a markedly different figure to Starmer, who consistently alienated his Labour Party’s left-wing and developed a reputation as a stilted, ineffective communicator.

That contrast helped Polanski and the Greens gain traction as a popular left-wing alternative to the governing, center-left Labour Party, which has been bleeding voters in recent years over its stance on issues like welfare spending, trans rights and the war in Gaza. Polanski even said on more than one occasion that his party “is here to replace Labour.”

But that momentum has largely stalled since Starmer resigned as prime minister in the summer following enormous pressure from his party. He stepped down as a member of parliament (MP) last month, triggering the by-election.

In Starmer’s place, a more formidable opponent has emerged. Andy Burnham, the current prime minister, is widely seen as a better political operator and more capable of appealing to a broad spectrum of voters, including the progressives Polanski has been targeting.

Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham took office in July. Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

So the outcome of this by-election – in the central London constituency of Holborn and St. Pancras – represents more than just Polanski potentially becoming an MP.

It pits the Greens and Labour directly against each other for the first time since Burnham took office, acting as the first major electoral test for the new government as well as a barometer of the Greens’ ability to compete with a rejuvenated Labour.

If Polanski wins on Thursday, it will be a stern warning for the new prime minister and could be an early indicator that Britain’s left flank has irrevocably split. But if he loses and Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali holds the party’s seat, it will serve as a sign that Burnham has managed to pull progressives back into the Labour Party and slow its electoral decline.

Differing stances over the war in Gaza and antisemitism are central to that split, and to this by-election. Many Muslim voters have said they will not vote Labour because they think the government has not acted strongly enough over Gaza.

This weekend, the Greens adopted a controversial motion classifying Zionism, which Jewish groups sometimes define as a right to Jewish self-determination, as a form of racism, calling it an “ethnonationalist political project.”

Polanski, who is Jewish and changed his name from David Paulden when he was 18 to honor that heritage, did not vote on the motion nor mention it in his speech to the conference. He describes himself as an “anti-Zionist.” Israel responded by banning Polanski from visiting the country.

On Wednesday, a fresh storm broke out in British media over a reported friendship between the Green Party member who proposed the motion and a man convicted in the United States on al Qaeda terrorism charges.

Any split in the left comes at a critical moment in British politics, with Labour (and the Greens) also focused on containing a rising right-wing wave, most clearly signaled by the rapid ascent of the hard-right populist party, Reform UK.

Who is Polanski?

A self-described “eco-populist,” Polanski, 43, was catapulted onto the national stage last fall when he secured a surprise victory in the Greens’ leadership election, beating two of the party’s four MPs to claim the top job. Before that, he was still a little-known local politician, representing the Greens in the London Assembly.

The broad brushstrokes of Polanski’s image go something like this: to his admirers, he is an antidote to the stiff technocratic tendencies of more mainstream politicians; a gifted communicator willing to adopt the bold left-wing policies Labour has largely shied away from.

To his detractors, he is vague and unable to pin down the details of his own policies.

More recently, his social media use sparked controversy after he criticized the police’s response to an antisemitic attack in north London and, in a separate incident, reposted a photo that some interpreted as threatening Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK.

Zack Polanski is running to become an MP for the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras. Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty Images

Still, under his leadership, the party has commanded national attention, building on its best general election performance when it secured four parliamentary seats in 2024. By May, the Greens’ rise seemed astronomic – they briefly polled as high as Labour and the center-right Conservatives, the two parties which have dominated British politics for decades, and enjoyed historic gains in spring local elections.

While Polanski has tried to link the climate crisis to other issues, he has largely prioritized immediate everyday concerns, such as the cost of living and suggestions of public ownership of water and other utilities, alongside other progressive initiatives like championing a wealth tax and rent controls, while also adopting a pro-Palestinian stance.

Polanski has claimed credit for pushing Labour further to the left, most recently saying his party was responsible for influencing Labour’s shifting stance on the Middle East, including the government’s recently announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Actor turned politician

A former actor, Polanski’s strength lies in his communication. He hosts his own nightclub nights and holds weekly conversations with academics, activists and journalists on his podcast “Bold Politics” on ideas like an extreme wealth line (a proposed globally agreed limit for an individual’s net worth), re-nationalizing water companies and rejoining the European Union.

But he is prone to slip-ups too – in one disastrous interview shortly after becoming leader he seemed to confuse the national debt and deficit. Months later, he more carefully laid out his economic policy at a left-wing think tank event, though it remains “vague,” said Laura Serra, a political scientist at the London School of Economics.

“People don’t really know what they (the Greens) stand for, what they’re going to do,” she added.

While Polanski’s almost constant media presence has given him a far higher profile than previous Green leaders, analysts argue that the party’s increasing popularity has less to do with him and more to do with the shifting political climate in the UK.

A Green Party sign displayed outside a house. Carl Court/Getty Images

And at the same time, Green parties across Europe have become more influential, propelled by growing support among recent graduates and benefiting from “changing societal cleavages,” said James Dennison, a political scientist at the European University in Florence, who has studied the Greens for more than a decade. “The change is more rapid in the UK, and it’s exaggerated partially because of the electoral system, so it takes them longer to break through, and when they do, they go faster.”

Polanski self-consciously forms part of a wider populist trend too; he describes his approach to messaging as “substance with clickbait” and an alternative designed directly to confront the right-wing populism of Reform, and its Trump-supporting leader Nigel Farage.

“Populism is about the 99%, the vast majority… against the very, very wealthy… Trump and Farage come from the 1% and want to protect the interests of the elite,” Polanski told Bloomberg earlier this year.

This simultaneous rise of the Greens and Reform could fracture Britain’s political landscape, in which the first-past-the-post electoral system typically favors two or three major parties.

So, regardless of who wins on Thursday, the Greens even being competitive in a traditional Labour stronghold like this is indicative of how the smaller, more radical parties are increasingly challenging the mainstream.

World.title: What is pneumonic plague and how dangerous is it?
World.content:
A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.

The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.

The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.

“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.

What is pneumonic plague?

Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.

There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.

The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.

Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.

Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.

The bacteria Yersinia pestis causes plague, including the most common, bubonic plague, which typically results from the bite of an infected flea. Pneumonic plague is the most serious form of the illness. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Getty Images

How is pneumonic plague transmitted?

Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.

The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles.

What are pneumonic plague symptoms?

With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.

Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.

Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.

How is pneumonic plague treated?

Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.

Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.

Is there a vaccine for plague?

Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.

The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination, except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.

Why does plague still happen today?

Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.

Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.

Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.

The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.

Evans, who wrote “Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”

Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”

Soldiers monitored a hospital in India, on September 27, 1994, during an outbreak of pneumonic plague. The soldiers were posted after more than 50 people escaped quarantine. John Moore/AP/File

Globally, how concerned do people need to be about getting sick?

WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.

People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.

“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.

There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.

“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”

For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.

Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.

In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

World.title: Liberia Between Continuity and Change: Reassessing Former President Sirleaf’s Call for Sovereignty
World.content:
Former President Sirleaf: Liberia has been doing the same thing over and over, same structures, same type of policies, same type of attitudes, and mindset. It is time for change; Africa is changing, the world is changing, and Liberia can not be left behind. It will not happen until we agree to change our country. We have to stop following the United States of America. Let’s join the new area of sovereignty and respectability that Africa is pushing.” Source: Facebook, Voice of Liberia. https://www.facebook.com/share/v/18DEF7UL35/

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf: China’s Economic Agenda: In discussions regarding China’s role in Africa, such as in interviews with the Council on Foreign Relations, former President Sirleaf noted that China’s primary motivation was gaining rapid access to raw materials to sustain its domestic growth.



Former President Sirleaf: Credited Chinese investors and government programs with moving quickly and flexibly to address critical infrastructure needs, such as roads and public buildings, when traditional Western partners were more cautious.

Relations with the United States: Former President Sirleaf consistently maintained that Liberia’s partnership with Beijing did not conflict with its historic and strategic relationship with Washington.

The Inquirer Monrovia: February 26, 2008. By: Patrick K. Wrokpoh: www.allafrica.com/Liberia:

“America Has No Problem With China-Liberia’s Relations”

“The office of President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf says Liberia’s traditional friend, the United States of America, has no problem with the existing ties between Liberia and the People’s Republic of China.

President Sirleaf’s Press Secretary, Cyrus Wleh Badio, who briefed Executive Mansion reporters yesterday on details of President Sirleaf’s meeting with George W. Bush last Thursday, quoted President Bush as making it clear that his country has no problem with Liberia’s relations with China.”

“Liberia is a country with a rich history, but it has been slow to progress.” — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Independence Day Address, 2024.

“Reversal of multilateralism is not an option for a just and peaceful world.” — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, UN General Assembly Address, 2025.

“We call for greater inclusion, effectiveness, and respect for international law.” — President Boakai, UN General Assembly, 2025.

“Liberia remains positively engaged with its partners and friends at the bilateral and multilateral levels…with keen focus on national interest.” —Former President George Weah, 2021 State of the Nation.

Former President Weah: Identified Liberia’s foreign-policy objectives as including: “The preservation of the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the country “

Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s 2006 Inaugural Address: “Good neighborliness, non-interference, peaceful co-existence, regional cooperation and integration.”

Hon. Alexander B. Cummings, ANC Political Opposition Leader: In his 2020 address, Cummings recalled Liberia’s founding declaration in these terms: “We were free, equal to all nations, and not the subject of any nation.”

Hon. Benoni Urey — Opposition Political Leader: Discussing investment, he argued, “Foreign investment must also be prioritized.”

Former President Julius Nyerere — Tanzania, 1968: “No nation has the right to make decisions for another nation; no people for another people.”

“Mutually beneficial co-operation among the nations of the world.” — Former President Nelson Mandela, Non-Aligned Movement Address, 1998.

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o — Kenyan Novelist: “Africa actually enriches Europe.”

Ngũgĩ argued that:

“Economic and political control of a people can never be complete without cultural control.”

Former Liberian President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s statement that Liberia must stop repeating “the same thing over and over”, the same structures, policies, attitudes, and mindsets, raises an important question about the country’s political and economic direction.

Her argument that Liberia should not merely follow the United States but should instead join Africa’s emerging “era of sovereignty and respectability” reflects a powerful appeal for national self-determination.

At the same time, this appeal must be compared with the position expressed by her office in 2008, when it stated that the United States had no problem with Liberia’s relationship with the People’s Republic of China.

The two statements are not necessarily contradictory.

Both recognize that Liberia can maintain relations with multiple global powers.

However, they differ significantly in tone, political urgency, and implied criticism of Liberia’s historical dependence on the United States.

The central issue is whether Liberians should now heed Sirleaf’s call for change, even though she served as president from 2006 to 2018 and had considerable opportunity to advance the reforms she later described as necessary.

The answer should be neither an unquestioning yes nor a dismissive no.

Liberians should take the substance of her message seriously because Liberia still faces structural challenges that require a new national mindset.

Yet they should also evaluate her words critically, because leadership is measured not only by speeches after office but also by decisions made while holding power.

Former President Sirleaf’s legacy demonstrates both the possibilities and limitations of reform within a deeply dependent political and economic system.

Former President Sirleaf’s later statement is fundamentally a critique of repetition.

She argues that Liberia has continued with the same structures, policies, attitudes, and mentality despite changes occurring across Africa and the wider world.

This observation has strong historical relevance.

Liberia’s political history has often followed recurring patterns: centralized authority, elite control over resources, weak public institutions, dependence on foreign capital, inadequate investment in rural communities, and a tendency to expect external partners to solve domestic problems.

The country’s civil wars, public health crises, youth unemployment, poor infrastructure, and persistent corruption have all exposed the consequences of weak institutions and uneven development.

When former President Sirleaf says that Liberia must change, she is therefore not merely speaking about foreign policy.

She is speaking about national political culture.

A country can not become sovereign simply by announcing independence from foreign influence.

Sovereignty requires functioning institutions, accountable leadership, economic productivity, social cohesion, and citizens who believe that public office exists to serve the nation rather than private interests.

Liberia’s problem has never been only its relationships with powerful countries.

Every small country needs external partnerships.

The deeper problem is whether those relationships are managed from a position of national strategy or from a position of dependency and political vulnerability.

This distinction matters especially when comparing former President Sirleaf’s call to move away from “following the United States” with the 2008 statement on China-Liberia relations.

According to a report in The Inquirer Newspaper, published on www.allafrica.com/Liberia, former President Sirleaf’s office said the United States had no problem with Liberia’s existing ties to China.

The 2008 statement was diplomatic and reassuring.

It suggested that Liberia did not need to treat relations with Washington and Beijing as mutually exclusive.

Rather than framing China as a threat to Liberia’s traditional friendship with the United States, the statement presented the two relationships as compatible.

In practical terms, that position made sense. Liberia emerged from years of conflict with enormous reconstruction needs.

Roads, electricity, schools, hospitals, water systems, ports, and public institutions required major investment.

The United States remained an important historic partner, especially in areas such as governance, education, security, humanitarian assistance, and public health.

China, meanwhile, was becoming an increasingly significant actor across Africa through infrastructure projects, trade, loans, technical assistance, and diplomatic engagement.

For Liberia, cultivating relationships with both countries was not necessarily ideological inconsistency; it was a matter of national necessity.

The major difference between the 2008 position and the later statement lies in emphasis.

In 2008, former President Sirleaf’s administration appeared focused on assuring both the United States and China that Liberia’s diplomacy would remain balanced.

This cautious approach suited a postwar government seeking international legitimacy and investment.

Liberia could not afford to alienate the United States, which had played a major role in supporting the country’s recovery. Nor could it ignore China’s growing economic influence.

The message was essentially one of diplomatic inclusion: Liberia could work with China without abandoning its historic relationship with the United States of America.

By contrast, the latter statement has a more forceful and transformational tone.

It suggests that Liberia’s long habit of looking to the United States for direction may have become an obstacle to independent national development.

The phrase “We have to stop following the United States of America” should not necessarily be interpreted as a demand to end diplomatic relations with America.

Such an interpretation would be unrealistic and potentially harmful.

Instead, the statement can be read as a warning against psychological, political, and economic dependence.

Former President Sirleaf appears to be challenging Liberians to stop treating U.S. approval as the primary measure of national success.

This is an important distinction. A sovereign Liberia can maintain strong relations with the United States while refusing to be defined by those relations.

It can cooperate with China while demanding transparency, fair contracts, local employment, environmental protections, and long-term benefits for Liberian citizens.

It can partner with the European Union, ECOWAS, the African Union, India, Brazil, the Gulf states, and multilateral institutions without surrendering its national priorities.

Genuine sovereignty is not isolation. It is the capacity to choose partnerships based on the interests of the Liberian people.

Nevertheless, former President Sirleaf’s critics have reason to ask why this call for a new mindset was not more fully implemented during her presidency.

She inherited a country devastated by civil war, and it would be unfair to ignore the difficult conditions under which she governed.

Her administration helped restore international confidence in Liberia, secured debt relief, attracted donor support, rebuilt elements of state administration, and guided the country through major crises, including the Ebola epidemic.

Her election itself was historically significant, both for Liberia and Africa, as she became Africa’s first elected female head of state.

These accomplishments should not be minimized.

Yet her administration also faced serious criticism for failing to transform the very structures she later condemned.

Corruption remained a persistent concern. Economic growth did not sufficiently improve the lives of many ordinary Liberians.

Youth unemployment and underemployment remained widespread. Public services, especially outside Monrovia, continued to be weak.

The management of natural resources and concession agreements often raised questions about transparency, community benefits, and the distribution of national wealth.

Many citizens believed that political and economic power remained concentrated among a relatively small group of elites.

These criticisms do not mean that Sirleaf did nothing. Rather, they illustrate how difficult it is to reform a state where institutions are fragile and expectations of government are high.

They also show that political will alone is not enough.

A president may introduce reforms, but lasting change requires a civil service capable of enforcing laws, a legislature willing to exercise oversight, courts able to act independently, journalists free to investigate wrongdoing, and citizens prepared to demand accountability.

In Liberia, the problem of “same structures” cannot be blamed on one leader alone, even though every president bears responsibility for the choices made during his or her administration.

The question, then, is whether Sirleaf’s statement should be rejected because she did not fully achieve the change she now advocates.

That would be too simplistic. Political leaders can recognize unfinished work, and former leaders can still make valid observations about national problems.

A message should be judged by its truth as well as by the messenger’s record.

Liberia does need institutional reform, a stronger national identity, economic diversification, and a foreign policy based on self-respect.

If Sirleaf’s statement encourages citizens to think more critically about dependency, it has value.

However, Liberians should not simply “heed” the message in a passive sense.

They should convert it into concrete demands.

Calls for sovereignty must be matched by specific policies. For example, Liberia should develop a long-term national development strategy that is not rewritten every time a new administration takes office.

Such a strategy should prioritize education, agriculture, energy, health care, technology, transportation, and industrial development.

Liberia can not claim economic independence while importing basic food products that could be grown locally, exporting raw materials without processing them, and relying heavily on foreign aid to fund essential public services.

Liberia also needs greater transparency in its international agreements.

Whether a contract involves an American, Chinese, European, African, or Liberian company, citizens should be able to know the terms.

How much revenue will the government receive? How many Liberians will be employed? What protections exist for communities affected by mining, logging, agriculture, or infrastructure projects?

What environmental standards will be enforced? How will the agreement contribute to local capacity rather than merely extract resources?

Sovereignty is weakened when foreign agreements are negotiated in secrecy or when national leaders cannot explain how those agreements benefit the public.

The United States-China dimension should therefore not become a distracting ideological contest.

Liberia should avoid being pressured into choosing one global power over another.

The country’s leaders must reject the false choice that partnership with China automatically means hostility toward the United States, or that cooperation with the United States requires suspicion of China.

The 2008 statement from Sirleaf’s office correctly recognized this point. Liberia has the right to maintain constructive relations with both countries.

What matters is whether these relationships are balanced, transparent, and aligned with Liberian interests.

At the same time, Sirleaf’s later warning about “following” the United States deserves attention because historical relationships can create habits of dependence.

Liberia and the United States share unusually deep ties rooted in Liberia’s founding and in generations of political, cultural, religious, and economic interaction.

These ties can be beneficial, but they can also encourage the belief that Liberia’s future must always be validated from outside.

A mature relationship with the United States should be based on mutual respect, not paternalism.

Liberia should welcome American investment, educational exchange, trade, and support for democratic institutions, while retaining the confidence to disagree when national interests require it.

Similarly, Liberia must engage China with clear-eyed realism.

Chinese investment and infrastructure support can contribute to development, but such engagement should not be romanticized.

Liberia must guard against unsustainable debt, opaque contracts, weak labor protections, environmental damage, and projects that do not build domestic capacity.

The same standard should apply to every foreign partner. The issue is not whether a partner is American, Chinese, European, or African; the issue is whether Liberia’s leaders negotiate responsibly and whether Liberians receive durable benefits.

Ultimately, former President Sirleaf’s two statements can be understood as parts of a larger argument for diplomatic flexibility.

The 2008 statement defended Liberia’s right to cooperate with China without fear of U.S. opposition.

Her later statement calls for Liberia to become more independent in its thinking and more committed to African sovereignty.

Together, they suggest that Liberia should not be trapped by old alliances or new rivalries.

Instead, it should build relationships that serve a national development agenda.

Liberians should therefore listen to Sirleaf’s call for change, but they should also insist on accountability from all leaders, including former leaders who now speak about reform.

The country can not afford another cycle in which politicians condemn failed structures after benefiting from them while in office.

Change must become more than rhetoric. It must mean stronger institutions, transparent governance, productive investment, civic participation, and a foreign policy guided by Liberia’s own priorities.

Liberia does not need to abandon the United States in order to be sovereign, nor does it need to embrace China uncritically in order to be modern.

What it needs is the confidence to engage every nation on equal terms. That is the “respectability” former President Sirleaf invokes: not dependence on one power, not submission to another, but a Liberia capable of deciding its future for itself.

World.title: Liberia: The Mark Quiah PUzzle: Named in Drug Indictment, Missing From All 11 Counts
World.content:
MONROVIA – For months, Mark Egon Kuiah’s name has hovered over Liberia’s cocaine scandal without ever quite landing.

By Rodney D Sieh

He ran operations at Roberts International Airport, the country’s main gateway, where 198 plates of cocaine were found in June hidden in cargo declared as Maggi cubes and lappas. That seizure, valued at more than US$19 million, opened the first of this year’s drug cases. Weeks later, President Joseph Boakai dismissed Kuiah “with immediate effect” in a July 30 purge of security officials.



Now, the State has named him a defendant in its 55-page indictment in the far larger US$317 million case. But a FrontPageAfrica review of the document shows an unusual gap. Each of the 11 counts opens by listing the defendants it accuses. Kuiah’s name is in none of those lists, even though eight counts describe what he allegedly did.

What the indictment says he did

The State’s account of Kuiah is short and repeated almost word for word across eight counts. Caycee Nelson, the man prosecutors say managed the cartel’s front airline, “Afri-Connect Airlines,” recruited him. Kuiah allegedly asked for US$250,000 to help the operation through the airport and received US$50,000 up front. He was given two phones “for communication.”

He is also said to have recruited two aviation colleagues: F. Augustine Claudius Tamba, Deputy Director General of the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority, and Abner Wanah Yonly, Sr., manager of James Spriggs Payne Airfield. The indictment adds, in one paragraph, that the two “did not provide any support.” Neither is charged.

The State says Kuiah “knew and had reasons to know” the cartel planned to move cocaine through Liberia to Europe, and “accepted to provide the required assistance.”

What it does not say

The indictment never describes a single thing Kuiah did at the airport for the cartel. The cartel’s aircraft, bought in August 2025, landed at Spriggs Payne, not at Roberts International. The indictment does not allege it ever carried drugs. The cocaine seized at Cement Road, by the State’s own account, came in by sea and canoe up the Po River.

The sums are muddled too. One paragraph says Nelson handed Kuiah the US$50,000. The money-laundering count says it was paid by Jammel V. Jallah, through Christian L. Nyantee.

Even his job shifts. The caption calls him a former Deputy Director of Operations at the Civil Aviation Authority. Other paragraphs place him at Roberts International Airport. One calls him “Deputy Manager for Operations.” His name is spelled both Quiah and Kuiah. Government statements at the time of his dismissal described him as Deputy Director for Operations at RIA.

Then there is the charging language itself. Each count opens with a list of the defendants the grand jury finds probable cause against. Nikola Ivancic, Jewel Howard Taylor, Gerald Folley Smith, and others appear there, count after count. Kuiah’s name does not appear in any of those lists.

A defendant the counts leave out

Kuiah is a defendant. The caption names him, General Allegation 18 calls him “The Defendant Mark Quiah,” and the October 7 writ from Criminal Court “C” orders his arrest. The indictment’s closing clause applies to all the “hereinabove named defendants.”

But each count is meant to tell a defendant exactly what he is accused of. Here, eight counts describe Kuiah’s conduct while leaving him off the list of those the grand jury finds committed the offence. Defense lawyers can be expected to argue that he was indicted without being clearly charged in any count, and to seek to quash on that ground. Prosecutors are likely to answer that the caption, the general allegations and the closing clause are enough to put him on notice.

Whether the omission is a drafting slip, like the other errors FrontPageAfrica has documented in the indictment, or something more deliberate is an open question. It comes after weeks of talk that Kuiah has been helping investigators. In August, FrontPageAfrica reported that he had been giving investigators a considerable amount of information since his dismissal, and that he had not been arrested.

The Ministry of Justice has not said publicly whether Kuiah is a cooperating witness. He is not among the witnesses listed in the indictment, which names only three police officers and “documentary evidence.” FrontPageAfrica could not confirm whether he has been taken into custody since the writ was issued.

Kuiah’s July 29 appearance on an earlier police charge sheet followed a similar pattern. That document described a “Mark Quiah” as a friend brought in to help with aircraft operations in 2024. It did not list him among its 12 defendants.

The letter not in the file

One episode is absent from the indictment altogether. On July 13, while still at the airport, Kuiah signed a letter to the Liberia Maritime Authority as “registered agent” for Madris Group of Companies Incorporated. It asked that a cargo ship, the Comoros-flagged IB Atlantic IV, be allowed into the Freeport of Monrovia because it was “in distress at sea due to loss of engine performance.”

The Maritime Authority declined. The ship was later pursued by Liberian forces off Rivercess, amid unconfirmed reports that a smaller boat had approached it at sea. No link between the letter and any crime has been established, and Kuiah has not been charged over it.

The indictment makes no mention of the letter, the ship or Madris Group.

Kuiah has not commented publicly. He is presumed innocent, as are all those named in the indictment.

The bar owner who disappeared from the case

If Kuiah is a defendant, the counts leave out George Wah Harris, a man the government charged who is missing altogether.

Harris, also known as Leroy Harris, owns Private Bar Entertainment Center in Paynesville. In early August, the government announced at a Ministry of Information briefing that he had been charged in the US$317 million cocaine probe. The listed offences were possession, importation, trafficking, economic sabotage, money laundering, conspiracy, facilitation and solicitation.

Security forces searched his bar three times. Management said they found nothing illegal on any occasion. Harris was arraigned at the Monrovia City Court and sent to Monrovia Central Prison. On August 13, the Bureau of Corrections said he was still there and had been granted no judicial relief.

Yet the October 7 indictment in the US$317 million case does not mention Harris anywhere. Not in the caption, not in the counts, not in the narrative.

Instead, Harris turned up in the other case. On August 27, Criminal Court “C” issued a writ in the June airport seizure, the 198 plates found at Roberts International Airport. That indictment accuses Harris of offering US$100,000 to two Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency officers at the airport to recover the seized cocaine. It says he handed US$5,000 to one of them, Moses Jallah, at his bar.

The shift raises a question the government has not answered. Did investigators drop their claim that Harris was tied to the US$317 million haul, or is a separate charge still to come?

Readers should not confuse two other names in the new indictment. “Harris Ward” is a community in Royesville Township where prosecutors say the cocaine was stored, not a person. And the bar the indictment does mention is Private Bar in Paynesville, where the cartel allegedly held an introductory meeting for its airline. A man named there as the airline’s “Ground Handler,” Franklin Harberg (also spelled Herbert and Harbert), is not charged either.

One airport, two gaps

The two names point to the same weakness. Roberts International Airport sits at the center of Liberia’s drug crisis this year. It was the site of the June seizure, and it is the airport the cartel allegedly paid an insider to smooth its path through.

Yet in the case that names the airport’s own operations chief as a defendant, the counts themselves leave him out. And in that same case, a man the government publicly charged in August does not appear at all.

World.title: Liberia: Former Vice President Howard-Taylor among 19 indicted, six Defendants currently held at Monrovia Central Prison
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s most prominent drug trafficking and money laundering prosecution entered a new phase this week as several defendants, including a former senior security official, were arrested and sent to the Monrovia Central Prison to await trial.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The arrests followed a writ issued on October 7, 2026, by Criminal Court “C” at the Temple of Justice, ordering Montserrado County Sheriff Major Austine Seinavula, or his deputy, to arrest the 19 defendants named in a grand jury indictment and bring them “forthwith” before the court. Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor is among those defendants.



Who is in custody

The first arrest came late Wednesday, October 7, when Mark Quiah, former Deputy Director for Operations at the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), was taken into custody and sent to the Monrovia Central Prison.

Others followed, including Gerald Foley Smith, former Deputy Director for Administration at the National Security Agency (NSA), along with Jammel V. Jallah, Christian L. Nyantee, Cayce L. Nelson, Albenigo Janior and a defendant identified only as Sekou. They were brought before Criminal Court “C” before being jailed.

None of the defendants has been arraigned. They are being held pending further proceedings. The writ also requires the sheriff to file an official return showing how each defendant was served.

The scale of the charges

The indictment, handed up by the Grand Jury of Montserrado County, lists 11 offenses. Five relate directly to controlled drugs: unlicensed possession, importation, exportation, and sale, distribution and transportation, as well as illicit trafficking. Three are inchoate offenses: criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation and criminal solicitation. The remaining charges are money laundering and two counts involving physical objects for lethal use, covering both possession and sale.

Taken together, the charges allege far more than simple possession. They describe an organized operation that moved drugs into and out of Liberia, laundered the proceeds and had access to lethal weapons.

Why the defendants matter

The names on the indictment give the case its weight. The NSA is among the agencies charged with protecting the state from organized crime. The LCAA oversees the airports through which drugs can cross borders. Allegations that former senior officials from both institutions took part in a trafficking network raise uncomfortable questions about whether state institutions were compromised, regardless of what the courts ultimately decide.

The inclusion of Howard-Taylor adds a political dimension. She served as Vice President from 2018 to 2024 and was former President George Weah’s running mate in the 2023 election. The prosecution of a former vice president on charges of this kind has little precedent in Liberia, and supporters and critics alike will watch closely for signs of either political motive or political protection.

A test for the justice system

For the government, the arrests signal that the indictment will be enforced rather than left to stall. Making the case stick will be harder. Drug and money laundering prosecutions depend on financial records, seized evidence, intercepted communications and often cooperating witnesses. They are complex, and in Liberia such cases have frequently been slowed by delays, adjournments and disputes over evidence. How the prosecution handles disclosure, how quickly arraignment follows and whether bail is contested will offer early signs of the case’s strength.

The courts will also be judged on fairness. With high-profile defendants and intense public interest, the pressure for a swift conviction will be considerable. So will the demand that the process be seen as impartial.

What comes next

The defendants are expected to be arraigned before Criminal Court “C,” where they will enter pleas. Defense lawyers are likely to seek bail and may challenge the indictment. Attention will also turn to the remaining defendants, including the former vice president, and whether they will be taken into custody.

The indictment contains allegations only. All 19 defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction, and they are entitled to legal representation and a fair trial under the Liberian Constitution.

World.title: Liberia: MCSS Teachers Defy Return-to-Class Call, Vow to Sustain Go-Slow Until Demands Are Met
World.content:
Teachers at a mass meeting

Public school teachers across Monrovia and its environs under the banner of the Monrovia Consolidated School System Teachers Association (MCSS-TA) are embarking on a strike action until their four-count demands are met by the system.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Members of the Association say their demands have been overdue without tangible response from the authorities of MCSS headed by Dr. Augurie E. Stevens.



The Four-count Demand

In count one of their demands, the Monrovia-based public-school teachers are calling on the Ministry of Education to immediately replace missing instructional staff and place all active volunteer teachers onto the official government payroll.

They are also demanding salary upgrades, wanting compensation structures to be adjusted to reflect higher academic qualifications earned by teachers, with payments processed prior to verification delays.

Furthermore, MCSS-TA is craving payroll reinstatement and welfare, urging the Civil Service Agency (CSA) and the Ministry of Education to unconditionally reinstate omitted employees, increase salaries for all educators and support personnel – including janitors, security officers, and administrative staff—and provide adequate operational funding for schools.

The Teachers Association, at the same time, called for leadership accountability, with a call on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to immediately dismiss the MCSS Superintendent, Dr. Augurie E. Stevens, and introduce structural reforms to restore operational oversight.

‘Don’t Be Deterred’

As they remained steadfast with a united front, the Teachers Association held a mass meeting on Wednesday morning, October 7, 2026, at the Williams V.S. Tubman High School with the President of the Association, Mr. Augustine N. Nyormui, re-echoing the position of the group to each member.

At the well-attended meeting, President Nyormui called on members to remain unbending and stick to the mandate.

“We caused the problems in the past because we have not been rising against them. But from today, the mandate is simple: please, let’s stick to the go slow. Don’t be intimidated, don’t be deterred. President Boakai is a human being, and he will listen to us,” Nyormui ordered.

“Our main goal is that we are not teaching now. Go and sit down until you hear from us. You can go to your school of assignment and just sign in the log, but don’t teach.”

Action Starts Now

Asked by a member, Madam Rebecca Krubo Korward, an instructor at A. Glen Tubman Memorial as to when the action begins and ends, he responded: “This takes effect now and no one should betray us. Don’t be afraid; no one will dismiss you. Go and sign in daily and sit down. The go slow will continue as long as government does not attend to our demand.”

No Political Undertone

Nyormui told members that the entire process is germane and ill-political, as such, it should not be misconstrued by the public.

“I am a born Liberty Party child, a party that is collaborating with this government, but this is not about party issue; it’s void of politics. Let’s stick together. This is not about political issue.”

Nyormui also clarified that this is not in any way an attempt to thwart the pending electoral process of the Association slated for December, announcing that he would not, in fact, re-contest the position.

“Don’t let no one lie to you that we are doing this to stall the pending electoral process. Election will hold, and it will hold on the date announced. In the first place, I am stepping down and will not contest. So, this is not about delaying so that issue won’t be held. Anyone saying this is just another lazy propaganda,” he, among other things, added amid cheers in the Tubman High Cafeteria meeting hall.

MCSS Rejects Report of Widespread School Closures, But Acknowledges Teachers’ Go-Slow

When contacted, authorities of the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS) rejected claims that 20 of its 26 schools have been shut down as a result of a go-slow action by teachers.

In an exclusive interview with this paper while the meeting of the Teachers Association was ongoing, MCSS Communications Director Samuel Nyenuh explained that several schools have not yet fully resumed regular academic activities, and that they are shut down.

He said the reason is based on the fact that there are ongoing renovation works at some of the institutions, while at the same time student orientation is ongoing this week.

“We don’t have 20 out of 26 schools that are shut down as a result of the MCSS Teachers Association’s announced go-slow action. This is not true,” Nyenuh told this writer.

He named the institutions that are carrying renovations as G. W. Gibson High School, Botswein Junior and Senior High School, and Matilda Newport Junior and Senior High School.

This, he indicated, is being implemented by the MCSS administration in collaboration with the Ministries of Public Works and Finance and Development Planning.

Teachers’ Go-Slow Confirmed

In what stemmed out to be a sharp contradiction, the MCSS official acknowledged that teachers have raised concerns and that the leadership of the teachers’ association has confirmed a go-slow action.

He stated that the MCSS’ leadership is aware of the teachers’ grievances and is working to address them.

He, however, urged teachers to return to their classrooms while the issues are being resolved through the appropriate government channels.

“We don’t want to go that route. We are expecting our teachers in the various classrooms,” he further referring to possible disciplinary measures under the Civil Service Standing Orders.

Nyenuh narrated that MCSS teachers, as civil servants, are guided by the Civil Service Standing Orders, which provide procedures for addressing neglect of duty.

Salary Adjustments Remain a Major Concern

Among the major concerns raised by teachers is salary adjustment based on academic qualifications.

Nyenuh noted that the MCSS administration is fully aware of the issue, including concerns from teachers who have obtained additional qualifications but continue to receive salaries based on their previous credentials.

But maintained that the administration is working with the relevant government institutions to address the matter.

The MCSS Communications Director referenced provisions of the Education Reform Act of 2011, which he interpreted as providing for teachers to be compensated in accordance with their qualifications.

He acknowledged that teachers who were initially employed with lower-level qualifications may have subsequently obtained university degrees or master’s degrees without receiving corresponding salary adjustments.

Despite the acknowledgement, Nyenuh stated that resolving the issue requires government funding and must be reflected in the national budget.

Communications Chief Defends Superintendent

Accordingly, Director Nyenuh defended his boss, Dr. Augurie E. Stevens, saying she inherited several longstanding challenges when she assumed office in July 2025.

“This would be very unrealistic to expect the superintendent to resolve all of the school system’s problems within approximately one year and two months. One of the challenges she inherited was a large number of volunteer workers, and this is being addressed step by step.”

“More than 600 volunteers were initially identified, but a reverification exercise involving the Civil Service Agency, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning and other relevant institutions reduced the number to 459. Government resources had to be identified to accommodate the volunteers, which affected the availability of funding for other salary-related adjustments.”

2027 Budget Expected to Address Salary Concerns

In the pending budget, Nyenuh is hopeful for a better outcome as he revealed that MCSS has been lobbying the government for funding to address salary adjustments based on teachers’ qualifications.

He emphasized that MCSS is not an income-generating institution and cannot independently increase salaries unless it is done by the central government.

“General salary increases come from the national government based on available resources. MCSS depends on the national government for salary adjustments for its employees.”

Call For Teachers to Return To Classrooms

Meanwhile, MCSS through its communications chief has sounded a passionate appeal for teachers to resume teaching while the government works through the budgetary process.

“The way forward is for our teachers to be in the classroom. Teachers belong in the classroom.”

Admitting that while the teachers have legitimate concerns about compensation, Nyenuh added that they also have a responsibility to perform their duties.

World.title: Liberia: Inflation Eases to 4.5% as Central Bank Moves to Tighten Grip on Dollarized Economy
World.content:
Monrovia – The Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) has kept its benchmark Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) unchanged at 16.0 percent but has raised the share of US dollar deposits commercial banks must keep in reserve, a move aimed at chipping away at the country’s heavy reliance on the greenback.

Rodney D. Sieh

The decision came out of the bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting held on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, and was announced in Communiqué No. 28, signed by Executive Governor and MPC Chairman Henry F. Saamoi.



Dollar reserves go up

The committee increased the reserve requirement ratio on US dollar deposits by two percentage points, from 10 percent to 12 percent. The requirement on Liberian dollar deposits stays at 25 percent.

The CBL also narrowed its interest-rate corridor. The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), the rate banks earn when they park money with the CBL, moves from 6.5 to 6.0 percentage points below the policy rate. The Standing Credit Facility (SCF), the rate at which banks borrow from the CBL, moves from 1 to 0.5 percentage points above it. At the current 16 percent policy rate, that puts the deposit rate at 10 percent and the lending rate at 16.5 percent.

The bank said the changes are meant to strengthen how its policy decisions pass through to the economy, improve liquidity management and gradually reduce what it called the structural vulnerabilities tied to Liberia’s high level of financial dollarization.

Inflation falls, growth picks up

Headline inflation dropped to an estimated 4.5 percent in the third quarter, down from 5.4 percent in the previous quarter. The committee credited a more stable exchange rate, prudent monetary management and favorable domestic prices. Inflation is projected at about 4.6 percent in the fourth quarter, within the bank’s medium-term tolerance range.

Real GDP growth is projected at 5.5 percent for 2026, up from 5.1 percent in 2025, driven mainly by mining, manufacturing and services. The CBL’s Composite Index of Economic Activity gap widened from 0.8 percent to 2.7 percent, which the bank said points to greater use of productive capacity.

Broad money supply (M2) declined modestly during the quarter, which the CBL linked to the appreciation of the Liberian dollar.

Banks strong, but bad loans persist

The committee described the banking sector as stable and highly liquid. The Capital Adequacy Ratio stood at 38.64 percent, far above the 10 percent regulatory minimum, while the liquidity ratio rose to 58.71 percent against a 15 percent minimum.

But non-performing loans remain a worry at 13.38 percent, above the 10 percent prudential benchmark. The CBL warned that bad loans pose a significant medium-term risk to financial stability and limit banks’ ability to lend to productive sectors. It reaffirmed support for the National Strategy for Non-Performing Loan Resolution and related legal and judicial reforms.

The committee also noted that bank credit remains concentrated in trade, services and personal lending, and called for more financing for agriculture and manufacturing.

Debt, trade and reserves

Public debt fell from 49.6 percent to 43.3 percent of GDP, according to the communiqué. The external sector, however, showed strain: export earnings improved, but higher import payments widened the trade deficit.

Gross international reserves stood at 3.3 months of import cover, down from the previous quarter but still above the ECOWAS benchmark of three months.

Risks ahead

The CBL said risks are broadly balanced but tilted toward higher inflation. External risks include geopolitical tensions, rising global energy prices — Brent crude rose significantly during the quarter — commodity price swings and tighter global financing. At home, the bank pointed to bad loans, high dollarization, possible fiscal slippages and structural constraints on domestic production.

The committee said it stands ready to take further action if needed. Its next meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, January 20, 2027.

World.title: Liberian Envoy Invited to Opening of Barbados Slavery Memorial
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberia’s special envoy for cultural and heritage diplomacy has been invited to the opening of a national memorial in Barbados honoring 570 enslaved West Africans buried at a former sugar plantation.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Ambassador Lorenzo Llewellyn Witherspoon received the invitation from the office of Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley for the Nov. 28 opening of the Ancestral Memorial to the Enslaved at Newton, outside the capital, Bridgetown. Guests must confirm attendance by Oct. 23.



“Being personally invited by Prime Minister Mottley to witness this historic event is an important honor for Liberia and me personally,” Witherspoon said.

The ceremony falls two days before Barbados marks 60 years of independence and five years as a republic.

The memorial stands beside the Newton Enslaved Burial Ground, believed to be the largest communal burial site of enslaved people in the Western Hemisphere. The remains were identified using LIDAR, a laser-mapping technology.

Designed by British-Ghanaian architect David Adjaye, the memorial draws on traditional African tombs, prayer sites and pyramids. Visitors enter through a dome of red earth housing exhibits on the slave trade, then climb a sugarcane-lined ramp to a mound holding 570 teak poles from Ghana, one for each person buried there. Each pole is topped with a brass plate angled toward the sun.

Adjaye’s firm says the design seeks to balance “the ancestors and the living, this world and the next.”

The memorial is the first phase of the Barbados Heritage District, announced in 2021 after the island removed the British monarch as head of state. The district is also planned to include a national museum, archives and a genealogical research institute.

Liberia’s ties to Barbados date to 1865, when Barbadian families sailed aboard the brig Cora and settled in Crozierville, outside Monrovia, at the invitation of the Liberian government. Their descendants became prominent in Liberian law, politics and media.

Witherspoon said research into his own Caribbean ancestry, which he began in 2019, led to a meeting with Mottley at her official residence, Ilaro Court, in 2020. She tasked him with organizing the 2024 Sankofa Pilgrimage, which brought more than 500 descendants of the Barbadian emigrants back to the island.

He also helped facilitate diplomatic relations between the two countries and a 2025 state visit to Liberia by Barbados President Sandra Mason.

The two countries signed visa waiver and political consultation agreements in March.

“Thanks to the visionary leadership of President Boakai, a 160-year hiatus in the relationship between Barbados and Liberia has been broken,” Witherspoon said.
