World.title: Liberia: Witness Protection Agency Seeks to Build Trust as Push for War Crimes Court Gathers Momentum, but Funding and Capacity Remain Key Challenges
World.content:
Government militia fighters advance during fighting for control of a key bridge in Monrovia in 2003, as forces loyal to President Charles Taylor battled rebels of the Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy (LURD). Photo: Chris Hondros.

Summary:

· Liberia’s Witness Protection Agency is stepping up operations as the country pushes to establish war and economic crimes and anti-corruption courts.

· The Agency faces major challenges, including limited funding, a shortage of trained protection officers, no safe house of its own and the need to build public trust.



· The Agency plans to expand protection services nationwide, including safe facilities for witnesses and victims who may testify before a future war crimes court.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

As efforts build to establish war and economic crimes and anti-corruption courts in Liberia, the government agency responsible for protecting witnesses, victims and whistleblowers is confronting a fundamental challenge: persuading people that it can keep them safe.

The Witness Protection Agency, established by law in 2022 but operationalized only within the past nine months, has begun holding consultations, developing protection policies and working to build public confidence in a country where witnesses, whistleblowers and human rights investigators have faced threats and retaliation, and some have fled for their safety.

“If Liberian citizens continue to believe in panic and fear and cannot see that the government can be trusted to protect them, then this whole effort will be in vain,” said Teklo Maxwell Grigsby II, the Agency’s director, in an interview. “The more we invest in people, the more people can trust us, the more accurately we can push to get what the country deserves.”

The Agency’s ability to deliver on those promises could be critical to Liberia’s broader justice push. The proposed courts will depend on witnesses willing to provide evidence, including in cases involving powerful people and crimes committed decades ago. But getting people to testify may depend on whether they believe the government can protect them from retaliation — a difficult task for an Agency still struggling with limited funding, a shortage of trained protection officers, no safe house of its own and public mistrust shaped by past experiences.

Some Liberian institutions, including the Liberia National Police, Liberia Immigration Service, National Security Agency, Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission, Ministry of Justice and Office of the Ombudsman, have mechanisms or procedures that can provide protection, confidentiality or other safeguards for witnesses, victims and whistleblowers. But the Witness Protection Agency is the first institution established specifically to administer and coordinate a national program for their protection.

By operationalizing the Agency, Liberia joins a relatively small group of African countries, including Kenya and Ghana, that have enacted laws establishing dedicated agencies to protect witnesses and others who may face threats or retaliation for cooperating with investigations and prosecutions. Other countries, including South Africa and Uganda, operate witness-protection programs within existing justice or prosecution institutions.

Liberia’s Witness Protection Agency is headed by Grigsby, a lawyer, with Varney Ali Sherif serving as deputy director and Frank S. Suku, also a lawyer, as coordinator and head of its secretariat. Its mandate covers protection during investigations and pre-hearing proceedings, trials and the post-trial period.

Its services include identity and physical protection, psychosocial counseling and welfare support, legal assistance, safe housing, temporary or permanent relocation and reintegration. Confidentiality is one of its stated core values.

At a recent program to validate the Agency’s 5-year plan in Monrovia, Grigsby acknowledged that convincing Liberians to entrust sensitive information — and potentially their lives — to a government institution will not be easy. Past experiences with institutions responsible for handling sensitive cases, he said, have contributed to fears about whether people can safely disclose wrongdoing. Some have instead sought safety outside Liberia.

Few people understand those concerns better than Hassan Bility, director of the Global Justice and Research Project, Liberia’s leading war-crimes investigation group.

His organization and its Swiss partner, Civitas Maxima, have worked with authorities in foreign jurisdictions to help build cases against more than a dozen people accused of crimes connected to Liberia’s civil wars in the United States and Europe. Bility said he, members of his staff and witnesses involved in those cases have faced harassment and intimidation.

“One reason why witnesses don’t trust Liberians, don’t trust us Liberians generally, is that they think that we, in the Liberian English, ‘talk too much,’” said Bility, also at that event. “So there has got to be a system.”

He also stressed the need for experienced specialists to help develop Liberia’s protection system, something Grigsby acknowledged.

“You need people with the technical expertise who have worked in this area for many years to help us in setting the pace for legal and institutional framework,” Grigsby said in an interview. “We need the international dimension, global best practice for witness protection in Liberia.”

Grigbsy admitted they still face capacity challenges. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

With funding from the European Union, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights is providing financial and other support to the Agency. The Office has also brought in an international expert to help the Agency strengthen its strategic five-year plan and align it with international standards.

The Boakai administration has repeatedly pledged to strengthen protections for victims, witnesses and whistleblowers. In June, as President Boakai launched Liberia’s National Security Strategy 2026–2036 , promising to strengthen public confidence in the country’s security institutions.

His administration has also moved to strengthen incentives for people who disclose wrongdoing. According to the Witness Protection Agency, Boakai called on relevant government institutions at a March Cabinet meeting to review the Whistleblower Act of 2021 and propose amendments. The president directed then-Justice Minister Oswald Tweh to pursue stronger incentives for witnesses, victims and whistleblowers who provide information in high-profile corruption cases, mineral and natural-resource smuggling and other major crimes.

Among the proposed changes, the Agency is pushing to increase rewards for whistleblowers from 5 percent to 10 percent and introduce bounties intended to encourage reporting of corruption, organized crime and smuggling.

The Agency has consulted government ministries and agencies involved in anti-corruption efforts, lawmakers, the media and civil society about the proposed amendment. Grigsby said the proposal received overwhelming support.

But persuading witnesses and whistleblowers to come forward is only part of the problem. Keeping them safe can be expensive. Under its plan, the Agency is proposing more than US$6 million for protection operations as part of projected spending of US$20.54 million. Its financing proposal includes a one-cent levy on every gallon of petroleum imported into Liberia to help finance a proposed Victim, Witness and Whistleblower Trust Fund, alongside international donor support.

Current government allocations are far below those ambitions.

The 2026 national budget national budget allocated US$700,000 to the Witness Protection Unit, with projections of US$390,000 for fiscal year 2027 and US$401,000 for 2028.

Money is not its only constraint. The Agency currently employs 65 people, but Grigsby acknowledged that it does not yet have enough professionally trained protection officers. Many newly recruited employees are undergoing specialized training, requiring the Agency to rely on personnel from the Liberia National Police, National Security Agency and other security institutions.

Grigsby said 20 officers were being sent for basic police training to strengthen their capacity to provide physical protection. The Agency has also begun international training for personnel working in areas including internal control, finance and human resources. It plans to recruit about 45 additional protection officers and psychosocial counselors in 2027 as it expands its capacity.

The Agency is also trying to establish strict rules governing the information entrusted to its employees. Grigsby said staff members had signed confidentiality undertakings barring them from disclosing information about potential witnesses and victims, including their identities. Breaches, he said, could carry penalties of up to 10 years in prison.

Those safeguards will operate against a history in which some people who disclosed wrongdoing have reported retaliation. In 2023, New Narratives Narratives documented 12 cases of government whistleblowers who allegedly faced retaliation over the previous 14 years. Seven died in circumstances their families linked to efforts to silence them, four lost their jobs, and three fled the country or went into hiding.

The Agency, meanwhile, has no safe house of its own, limited vehicles and protection personnel, and operations largely concentrated in Montserrado. Its ambitious strategy proposes five safe houses — two in Montserrado and three elsewhere — where threatened witnesses and their families could be temporarily relocated.

The need could grow if Liberia establishes its proposed War and Economic Crimes Court. Grigsby said the Agency plans to coordinate with the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court over its proposed witness-protection unit. He said the Agency also wants existing and future safe homes used for witness protection brought under common national standards and coordination.

Grigsby said the Agency intends to take a more central role in overseeing facilities used to shelter witnesses and victims. “All safe homes across the Republic of Liberia will have a minimum standard, guided by our policy and coordinated by our office,” he said.

Grigsby said the Agency’s priority will be building enough public confidence for witnesses, victims and whistleblowers to trust the government with their safety. Without that trust, he said, the country’s efforts to finally address war time justice and combat corruption will fail.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: NHA Bets Big on 20,000 Homes by 2030 Amid Unresolved Controversy
World.content:
Monrovia-Liberia’s housing ambitions are entering a potentially transformative phase, with the National Housing Authority projecting the construction of 15,000 to 20,000 housing units by 2030, even as questions surrounding the Authority’s administration continue to linger.

By Willie N. Tokpah

National Housing Authority Managing Director Florence K. Geegbae made the projection Tuesday, October 6, at the Ministry of Information’s regular press briefing in Monrovia, outlining plans that include partnerships with foreign investors, prefabricated housing manufacturers and several public-private partners.



Her announcement has placed the NHA at the center of one of the Boakai Administration’s most consequential development promises, on addressing Liberia’s housing shortage while confronting the rapid expansion and increasingly congested urban landscape of Monrovia.

But as Geegbae unveiled the scale of the Authority’s proposed housing drive, she offered little new detail on allegations previously raised against her administration, including calls for audits and investigations.

Asked whether she had submitted to an investigation and whether the allegations had been addressed, Geegbae declined to discuss the matter in detail.

She said the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs, which she identified as her employer, had already inquired into the allegations and that a detailed report had been submitted.

“The Ministry of State, which is my employer, has inquired and we have done a detailed report to the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs,” she told journalists.

She then indicated that she preferred to move beyond the issue.

A Housing Push With Foreign Backing

Geegbae said the Authority’s long-term projection is no longer limited to government-funded construction.

According to her, discussions are underway with several investors, including potential partners from Turkey and Italy, while another group involved in prefabricated metal housing construction is being considered for projects in Liberia.

She said she recently visited factories, housing estates and construction sites associated with one of the potential foreign partners.

The NHA chief said some investors could contribute thousands of housing units to Liberia’s housing stock, pushing the Authority’s overall projection to between 15,000 and 20,000 units by 2030.

“We should be having close to 15, 20,000 housing units constructed by 2030,” she said.

The scale of the projection is significant for a country where affordable housing remains one of the most persistent challenges confronting low- and middle-income families.

But the larger question now is whether the NHA can convert its growing list of investment discussions into completed, affordable homes.

From 600 Units to Thousands

Geegbae also provided a more immediate timeline.

She said the NHA expects to conclude projects involving 482 housing units and another 600 units as part of its short-term program. According to her, the projects have already passed several preparatory stages, including design, permitting, implementation planning, site planning and soil testing.

The 600-unit component is particularly important because it formed part of the government’s previously announced social housing agenda.

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai announced in his January 2026 Annual Message that the NHA would begin construction of 600 social housing units across six counties.

Geegbae’s latest comments suggest the Authority considers the projects to be moving through the implementation process. The challenge, however, will be translating plans, permits and site preparation into visible houses that Liberians can occupy.

Monrovia’s Housing Crisis

Geegbae also acknowledged the severity of Monrovia’s urban development problems, attributing much of the pressure to continued rural-to-urban migration. She described the capital’s urban environment as increasingly difficult to manage and said the government would have to strengthen zoning and urban planning.

The NHA is working with development partners, including the United Nations Development Programme, on urban development initiatives, she said. Geegbae disclosed that the Authority has also established a portal intended to improve zoning and planning. But she acknowledged that correcting Monrovia’s longstanding planning problems will not be simple.

In some areas, she suggested, correcting existing development patterns could require the removal of structures that do not conform to future urban plans.

That prospect highlights the delicate balance facing the government, expanding housing while simultaneously attempting to bring order to an urban environment that has developed rapidly and, in many areas, without effective planning.

Questions She Did Not Answer

While Geegbae spent much of Tuesday’s briefing detailing what the NHA intends to build, she declined to reopen the controversy surrounding allegations previously reported by local media.

Reports have raised allegations concerning procurement practices, administrative conduct and other issues within the Authority. Those allegations have been disputed and have not, by themselves, established wrongdoing.

Some reports have also called for comprehensive financial and performance audits of the NHA. Geegbae’s response was that the matter had already been addressed through a report submitted to the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs.

That response, however, leaves the public with a distinction worth watching as the housing program expands: an internal response to allegations is different from independently verified evidence of how public resources, contracts and housing projects are being managed.

That distinction could become increasingly important as the NHA moves from planning to implementation and begins engaging more foreign investors and private-sector partners.

Bigger Promises, Bigger Scrutiny

The NHA’s proposed housing expansion represents an opportunity to address a genuine national need.

But a 20,000-unit projection also means a substantial expansion in the volume of land transactions, contracts, construction activities, partnerships and potentially public resources passing through the Authority.

That will inevitably require strong procurement systems, transparent contracting, measurable construction milestones and credible oversight.

Geegbae insisted that the NHA has the expertise and plans to move Liberia’s housing sector forward.

For now, the strongest test of that claim will not be the number of investors visiting Liberia, the number of factories toured or the number of housing units projected on paper. It will be the number of completed and occupied homes.

And as the NHA moves toward its 2030 target, the public will be watching whether the Authority can turn its ambitious housing blueprint into a measurable national housing legacy, while providing sufficient documentation and transparency to answer legitimate questions surrounding its operations.

For Geegbae, Tuesday’s message was clear: Liberia should prepare for a major expansion of housing construction. The next chapter will be whether the houses, and the evidence of how they were delivered, match the promise.

World.title: Kasama stakeholders anticipate policy direction from parliament opening
World.content:
Stakeholders in Kasama District in Northern Province have expressed optimism that the official opening of parliament by President Hakainde Hichilema today will give key policy direction to the country.

Speaking in separate interviews, the stakeholders say they are eager to hear how the government intends to advance the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda and accelerate national development.

Kasama District Civil Society Organisation Hub Chairperson, Peter Mumba said the President’s address presents an opportunity for the government to update citizens on progress being made and outline key priorities for the coming year.

“We expect to hear more on the economic development of the country and the plans the government has put in place under the Grow Zambia Agenda to improve the lives of citizens,” Mr Mumba said.

He noted that citizens are particularly interested in measures aimed at easing the cost of living through interventions in sectors such as energy and transport.

On energy, Mr Mumba said stakeholders are keen to hear the government’s plans for strengthening the sector and addressing the challenges associated with electricity tariffs.

He further called for increased support towards artisanal and small-scale mining, describing the sector as a potential source of employment and empowerment for young people.

And on agriculture, he urged the government to consider increasing the number of beneficiaries under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

“We are looking at how the government will increase the number of FISP beneficiaries so that we can achieve the objectives of the Grow Zambia Agenda,” he said.

And an educationist George Mumbi said the government has recorded notable progress in stabilising the economy and expressed hope that the gains will be consolidated.

“As regards to the stabilisation of the economy, a lot has been achieved by the government and we would like to see those gains sustained,” Mr Mumbi said.

He, however, called for enhanced efforts to restore order in the mining sector, particularly in addressing illegal mining activities.

Mr Mumbi has since appealed for greater accountability in youth empowerment programmes funded through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

“We would like to see the enforcement of loan repayments under youth empowerment programmes so that more young people can benefit from these initiatives,” he said.

He further described the Grow Zambia Agenda as a positive development framework capable of transforming lives if fully implemented.

“The Grow Zambia Agenda is a welcome move and we want to see it actualised for the benefit of all citizens,” Mr Mumbi said.

He further called for the continued preservation of peace, saying Zambia’s stable environment remains critical to national development.

Meanwhile, Victory Bible Church Pastor Chati Kasengele urged Zambians to unite behind national development efforts and support the country’s growth agenda.

“The election season is over and people have to move on. We are now under the auspices of the Grow Zambia Agenda, which is very significant for the country,” Pastor Kasengele said.

He said achieving the aspirations of the agenda will require collective efforts from the government, the private sector, the church and citizens.

“The President has already highlighted the direction the country needs to take. What is important is for all of us to support the vision and work together to achieve it,” he said.

President Hakainde Hichilema is expected to officially open the First Session of the Fourteenth National Assembly today.

World.title: Zambia/Zimbabwe JPC enhance country relations
World.content:
Ministry of Defence Permanent Secretary Maambo Haamaundu says the elevation of the relationship from the Joint Permanent Commissions on Defence and Security to a Bi-National Commission has created a broader framework for Zambia and Zimbabwe to deepen cooperation on matters of mutual interest.

The Permanent Secretary says the Technical Experts Meeting has therefore set the tone for future Zambia-Zimbabwe engagements aimed at strengthening peace and security in support of broader developmental objectives, saying peace and security are critical foundations for advancing Zambia’s economic and social development agenda.

Mr Haamaundu said security cooperation with neighbouring countries, including Zimbabwe, is important in creating a stable environment necessary for the country to pursue its development aspirations under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He was speaking after the close of the three day Technical Experts meeting for the Zambia-Zimbabwe Bi-National Commission held at Sandy’s Creation Resort in Lusaka.

Mr Haamaundu said the meeting has provided an opportunity for the two countries to establish a framework for future engagements on peace and security matters.

“Peace and security are very key because they are the foundation of economic and social development,” he said.

Mr Haamaundu noted that peace and security remain critical to Zambia’s economic and social development agenda, as they provide the foundation for sustainable development.

World.title: Chambeshi water fixes Mbala leaking tanks
World.content:
Chambeshi Water Supply and Sanitation Company Limited (ChWSSC) has commenced emergency rehabilitation works on five leaking elevated water storage steel tanks in Mbala District.

The company says the works are aimed at improving the reliability of water supply services to customers in the area.

In a press statement issued by Company Public Relations Officer, Tisa Banda and made available to the media Mbala today, Ms Banda said the rehabilitation works are intended to address leakages, structural defects and corrosion affecting the tanks.

Ms Banda disclosed that the water utility company has engaged Kenval Construction and General Dealers Limited to undertake the works at a contract value of 58,000 Kwacha, funded through operational funds.

“The rehabilitation works are aimed at ensuring that the tanks are safe and fit for operation, this will improve the reliability of water supply services to our customers,” Ms Banda said.

She has explained that the rehabilitation works are expected to be completed within four weeks.

Ms Banda added that the rehabilitated tanks will subsequently undergo testing and commissioning to confirm their suitability for operation.

The Public Relations Officer said the rehabilitation forms part of the company’s efforts to maintain and improve water supply infrastructure and provide reliable and quality water supply services to its customers.

World.title: LWSC, Chilanga Council tackle water losses
World.content:
Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company (LWSC) has engaged Chilanga Town Council to strengthen Non-Revenue Water (NRW) management through improved water accountability, particularly the recording of authorised water used for firefighting.

LWSC Manager for Non-Revenue Water, Engineer Mununga Mungalu, emphasised the importance of maintaining accurate records of firefighting water consumption to support effective NRW monitoring and reporting.

Mr Mungalu explained that the engagement focused on establishing systematic mechanisms for recording water drawn from fire hydrants and other authorised points.

He noted that accurate documentation will strengthen water balance, NRW monitoring and accountability for water supplied through the utility firm’s distribution network.

Chilanga Town Council, Director of Engineering, Chilufya Mukuka reaffirmed the council’s commitment to properly account for water used for firefighting and other authorised purposes.

He said the local authority has pledged to support efforts to reduce local NRW levels through improved water accountability and responsible water management.

Mr Mukuka said LWSC and Chilanga Town Council will strengthen record-keeping and reporting mechanisms for firefighting water consumption.

He added that the initiative forms part of ongoing efforts to improve water measurement, reduce water losses and promote efficient management of water resources.

World.title: Hichilema opens largest Parliament in Zambia’s history today
World.content:
Hichilema faces a 280-seat House, and a nation waiting to hear the word “unity”

President Hakainde Hichilema walks into Parliament Buildings in Lusaka today to open the First Session of the 14th National Assembly. He will set out the Government’s policy direction for 2026 and 2027 before the largest and most varied House the country has ever assembled. He arrives with a comfortable majority and an ambitious economic blueprint, while churches, business and the opposition all ask him to answer a different question first: how to bring a divided country back together.

The chamber he addresses has changed beyond recognition. Constitutional and electoral reforms, enacted through the Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025, have expanded the National Assembly from 167 members to 280. They have also introduced mixed-member proportional representation for the first time.

There are now 226 elected constituency members, up from 156 after 70 new constituencies were created. Forty more MPs entered through proportional representation: 20 women, 15 young people and five persons with disabilities. The rest of the House is made up of nominated members, the Speaker, the Vice-President and the First Deputy Speaker.

For a legislature that held just 25 women among 167 members before the August vote, the reserved seats alone mark a sharp break with the past.

A building stretched to fit

The physical Parliament has had to grow with its membership. Clerk of the National Assembly Loveness Mayaka said seating in the chamber had been expanded and committee rooms refurbished, and 70 new constituency offices had been opened. Multimedia conference systems now run in the chamber and committee rooms.

Accessibility has received equal attention. Ramps and handrails have been installed and two lifts are being fitted. Braille facilities, tactile signage and wider sign language interpretation have been introduced so that members with disabilities can take a full part in proceedings.

Ms Mayaka said the work went beyond simply finding chairs for new faces.

“These interventions are not only intended to accommodate the increased number of members, but also, and most importantly, to strengthen the capacity of Parliament to operate as a modern, inclusive, accessible and effective institution,” she said.

The arithmetic of power

The governing United Party for National Development holds 169 seats, a clear working majority. The main opposition, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), holds 67. Independents hold 20 and smaller parties share the rest.

That majority comes with a ceiling. Two-thirds of a 280-member House is 187 votes, the threshold for constitutional amendments, leaving the ruling party 18 votes short on its own.

The House has already given a first glimpse of how votes may fall. Speaker Nelly Mutti and First Deputy Speaker Malungo Chisangano were returned unopposed last week. In the only contested ballot, Mufumbwe Independent MP Nshamba Muzungu beat Vincent Mwale 166 votes to 58 for the post of Second Deputy Speaker. Mwale’s 58 fell nine short of NRPUP’s 67 seats.

On her return to the chair, Ms Mutti tied the new Parliament directly to the Government’s economic programme. She said legislative oversight must turn growth targets into jobs.

Grow Zambia meets the dinner table

That programme is the Grow Zambia Agenda, built on the targets the President has made his second-term signature. By 2031 it aims for:

10 million tonnes of maize

10,000 megawatts of electricity

five million tourist arrivals

three million tonnes each of copper and soya beans

one million tonnes each of wheat and sugar

a US$1 billion beef export industry

Business wants to hear how those numbers will be reached. Private Sector Development Association chairperson Yusuf Dodia said the President should spell out measures on electricity, fuel and regulation, and then hand the challenge to industry.

“We expect the President to talk about policies that support the private sector to be efficient, and then challenge the private sector and say, look, everything has been set up for you. Can you now come and perform and achieve these goals?” Mr Dodia said.

Families, for their part, will be listening for the cost of living. The Media Network on Child Rights and Development says free education has pushed enrolment to 2.5 million learners, putting heavy pressure on classrooms, teachers and school feeding. Its executive director, Henry Kabwe, has asked for more money for teacher recruitment and stronger child protection.

The healing question

For all the talk of tonnes and megawatts, the loudest appeal ahead of today’s address is about the country’s mood after a bruising election.

The Council of Churches in Zambia wants what its general secretary, Reverend Canon James Phiri, called a clear and people-centred speech. He said it should be honest about hardship rather than a list of achievements.

“National development must ultimately be measured not only by economic indicators and policy pronouncements, but also by tangible improvements in the living conditions of ordinary citizens,” Rev Phiri said.

He also warned about the tone of national politics. “We are particularly concerned about the potential of inflammatory political language to deepen divisions and weaken national cohesion,” he said.

That concern is sharpest on the opposition benches. NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 16 others remain in custody in Kabwe on treason charges. Leadership Movement president Richard Silumbe has called for an inclusive round table on the country’s future.

“The current political atmosphere in the country has crossed a red line,” Dr Silumbe said.

The President has signalled that he has heard the appeals. Responding recently to the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia, which asked him to make unity central to his address, Mr Hichilema committed to reaching across party lines.

“I heard your message loud and clear on unity to continue uniting the country. We will do our part to reach out to our colleagues… so that we can talk to each other,” he said.

What comes after the speech

The ceremony will follow its familiar choreography, but today’s address carries a heavier load than most. It must translate an economic plan into household terms, reassure investors and speak to a country still sore from the polls.

Once the President leaves the chamber, MPs will take up the policy pronouncements in his address on the floor of the House. This 280-member Parliament’s first real test begins there.

World.title: Zambia signs US$2.49bn US health pact after holding firm on data and minerals
World.content:
Zambia signs US$2.49bn US health pact after holding firm on data and minerals

Zambia and the United States yesterday signed a five-year health agreement worth about US$2.49 billion in Lusaka. The deal ends months of hard bargaining in which Zambian negotiators struck out a specimen-sharing clause, narrowed Washington’s demands for health data and kept the country’s copper and cobalt out of the deal. The memorandum of understanding will finance the recruitment of 40,000 health workers and secure an uninterrupted supply of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria medicines.

The United States will commit more than US$1.5 billion over the five years to priority health programmes. Zambia has pledged an extra US$975 million of its own money to the sector over the same period. The arrangement is therefore a co-investment, a clear break from the donor-and-recipient model that shaped American health support in Zambia for two decades.

The signing comes five months after the talks very nearly collapsed. In May, Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Mulambo Haimbe halted negotiations. He described the American demand for sensitive health data as unconscionable and rejected any attempt to tie health support to a separate agreement on critical minerals.

Mr Haimbe returned to the table with a very different message. Speaking at the ceremony, he said Zambia had successfully “decoupled” critical minerals from the health agreement. That matter, he explained, is being handled in separate talks with the United States and has no place in the signed document.

The minister said the negotiations had removed several conditions and clauses that Lusaka found unacceptable. He added that the final text was shaped through wide consultation across Government.

“I am also pleased to note that the development of this Memorandum of Understanding has been undertaken through an extensive consultative process involving Government institutions,” Mr Haimbe said.

A workforce dividend

For Health Minister Roma Chilengi, the headline is the people the money will put on hospital wards and in villages. He called the agreement a monumental and landmark decision for Zambia’s health system, and set out how the 40,000 jobs would be shared.

“Forty thousand healthcare workers will be employed, 15,000 being front-liners like nurses, medical doctors, midwives, pharmacists, clinical officers and laboratory scientists. While 25,000 will be community health workers,” Professor Chilengi said.

He said the partnership would also protect the country’s medicines supply chain, particularly for drugs used against malaria, HIV and tuberculosis. Disease surveillance will be strengthened and electronic health systems expanded.

The funded programmes cover HIV and AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance, and preparedness for infectious disease outbreaks. Together they make up the backbone of public health in a country where a single missed delivery of antiretrovirals can be felt in every district clinic.

The data fight, settled

The negotiations turned largely on information. Earlier drafts would have required Zambia to share health data for a period far longer than the five years of funding, along with requirements touching on personally identifiable information. Professor Chilengi said those provisions had been reviewed in the final agreement.

Zambia’s Ambassador to the United States, Chibamba Kanyama, went further. He said the requirement to share biological specimens had been removed entirely, and that data sharing was now restricted to monitoring and evaluating the programmes being funded.

Dr Kanyama said the public objections raised at home had shaped Zambia’s position at the table.

“In a true partnership, we cannot simply brush aside these public anxieties. They represent our cultural values, our sovereignty, and our right to protect our people’s data and resources,” he said.

Washington’s view

United States Embassy chargé d’affaires Mich Coker said American support to Zambia’s health sector since 2004 had exceeded US$5 billion, and that the new framework was designed to protect and build on those gains through Zambian institutions.

“This $2.49 billion MoU tells a powerful story of mutual commitment. Over the next five years, the United States, working with Congress, plans to provide more than $1.5 billion in Zambia’s priority health programmes,” Mr Coker said.

He said the agreement marked a shift towards a partnership based on Zambian leadership, ownership and shared accountability. The text, he added, carries clear protocols to protect personal health information, because data privacy is essential to keeping public trust. He repeated that critical minerals were not part of the deal.

Relief for the Treasury

Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane framed the agreement in fiscal terms. He said American support would ease the burden on a Government that would otherwise have to carry the full weight of the country’s health spending.

“The agreement that we have just signed provides relief in the sense that if we are to be 100 per cent responsible for our health expenditure, then life can be much harder,” Dr Musokotwane said.

World Bank data show that health spending reached 5.98 percent of gross domestic product in 2023, up from 5.21 percent the year before. That rising bill is the backdrop to the minister’s remarks.

A harder bargain than most

The agreement falls under the America First Global Health Strategy, which Washington launched in September 2025. It replaced traditional grants through USAID and the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief with five-year bilateral compacts.

Several African governments have struggled with the terms. Kenya’s agreement was stopped by its High Court amid challenges over patient data and pathogen information. Zimbabwe walked away from a deal worth about US$350 million, and Ghana turned down the American conditions over data sharing.

Zambia chose a third path: it stayed at the table, refused the clauses it could not accept and signed only once they had been rewritten. That outcome gives the Government a ready answer to those who warned that health aid would be traded for mineral concessions.

The recruitment drive and the Treasury’s US$975 million pledge now move from paper to practice over the next five years. The talks on critical minerals continue on their own, separate track.

World.title: Zambia, USA seal health deal
World.content:
Zambia and the United States of America have signed a Memorandum of Understanding and a Data Sharing Agreement to implement a five‑year Health Sector Cooperation Agreement.

Under the deal, the United States will provide more than US$1.5 billion over five years to Zambia’s priority health programmes, while Zambia will increase domestic health expenditure by US$975 million.

Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane signed the MoU, while his Health counterpart, Roma Chilengi signed the Data Sharing Agreement, in collaboration with United States Chargé d’Affaires at the US Embassy in Lusaka, Mich Coker, who signed the agreements on behalf of his government.

Witnessing the signing ceremony, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe said the agreement renews and redefines the Zambia-US partnership that will continue to shape and transform the lives of many people positively.

Mr Haimbe expressed gratitude to the government and people of the United States for their unwavering support and friendship.

He reiterated the need to continue building a resilient, sustainable and people-centred health system that delivers better health outcomes for every Zambian.

“I wish to commend the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Finance and National Planning, the Ministry of Justice, Cabinet Office, and other government institutions for the hard work and dedication that culminated in today’s signing ceremony,” the Minister indicated.

He acknowledged the longstanding relations between the two countries as evidenced in various areas of cooperation, including democracy and governance, economic growth, health and education.

Mr Haimbe noted that the partnership with the United States has greatly assisted in stimulating the growth of various sectors in the country.

Professor Chilengi, noted that the signed MoU will serve as a catalyst for Zambia’s journey towards greater self-sustainability and enhanced domestic resource mobilisation.

Professor Chilengi revealed that the agreement will enable the recruitment of more health workers, strengthen medicine supply and enhance disease surveillance.

He also clarified that the only data that the Zambian government will be required to share with the United States during the agreement period is that which speaks directly to the operations of the program.

Meanwhile, Dr Musokotwane said the support comes at a time of financial pressures arising from global economic factors, including the anticipated severe drought next year.

He noted that the partnership will provide the much-needed relief to enable the Government channel additional resources towards other critical sectors of the economy, in line with the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

For the Chargé d’Affaires, Mr Coker described the MoU as a transformative partnership, shifting from a donor‑recipient model to a true partnership, grounded in Zambian Leadership, Zambian ownership and shared accountability

Mr Coker affirmed that the signed MoU is focused on improving health outcomes, strengthening health financing, and enhancing systems within Zambia’s health sector.

World.title: Parliament expansion preps advance
World.content:
The National Assembly of Zambia is undergoing major rehabilitation and expansion works to accommodate the increased number of Members of Parliament (MPs) and ensure that the members operate in a conducive environment.

Clerk of the National Assembly Loveness Mayaka says the works are part of preparations for the commencement of the First Session of the 14th National Assembly.

Ms Mayaka said this in Lusaka today during a media briefing on the preparedness of the National Assembly for the new parliament.

She said the reforms, provided for under the Constitution of Zambia Amendment Act No. 13 of 2025, have resulted in changes to the electoral system and increased representation of women, youth and persons with disabilities.

She explained that the National Assembly has undertaken extensive preparations in infrastructure, systems and processes to accommodate the increased membership and effectively support 280 MPs in discharging their constitutional mandate.

She said the preparations have focused on four key areas, namely infrastructure, physical accessibility, sensory and communication facilities, and administrative support and staff awareness.

She explained that the interventions are aimed not only at accommodating the increased number of MPs from 167 to 280, but also at strengthening parliament’s capacity to operate as a modern, inclusive, accessible and effective institution.

She said the Chamber has been expanded to provide an additional 113 seats, while Information and Communication Technology (ICT) equipment has also been installed and upgraded.

The Clerk stated that the National Assembly has also established facilities to support the 70 newly created constituencies, with most of the facilities already operational.

Ms Mayaka said the transition comes at an important time in the development of Zambia’s democracy, following constitutional and electoral reforms undertaken during the 13th National Assembly.

She said the Assembly has further installed and commissioned conference systems in the chamber and committee rooms to enhance the performance of parliamentary functions.

She said renovations are also underway at the Members’ Motel, including expansion of the restaurant and kitchen, renovation of the laundry and refurbishment of rooms to improve accessibility for members with disabilities.

Ms Mayaka further said additional offices have been constructed on the eastern side of the Chamber to address the shortage of office space, additionally new water tank has also been installed to strengthen water security at the institution to make them accessible to persons with disabilities.

She said the institution is further strengthening sensory and communication facilities to ensure that members with visual, hearing and speech impairments can participate fully in parliamentary proceedings.

Ms Mayaka said the National Assembly has strengthened the provision of sign language interpretation and introduced braille facilities and signage to improve access to information.

She said the procurement of a braille machine, which will facilitate the production of reading materials in Braille, is at an advanced stage.

And Ms Mayaka disclosed that plans are underway for the construction of a new parliament building in the near future to accommodate up to 500 parliamentarians.

Meanwhile, National Assembly Director Public and International Relations Anthony Mpolokoso led the media personnel touring some newly constructed works, disclosing that a local contractor was engaged to do the renovation and expansion works at the National Assembly of Zambia.

World.title: South Africa: Zuma Remains in Hospital as Conflicting Reports Emerge Over His Health
World.content:
Former South African president Jacob Zuma has remained at a private hospital in Pietermaritzburg. However, there have been conflicting accounts about his health following his admission.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party said Zuma had attended a routine medical check-up, a procedure he undergoes twice a year, and reassured supporters that he was "healthy and in good spirits".

According to News24, his brother Khanya said that Zuma was unwell and remained in hospital. He said the situation was concerning and that the family was praying for Zuma's recovery.

The 84-year-old former president is set to testify before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) cases inquiry in two weeks.

Zuma was president from 2009 to 2018.

He now leads the uMkhonto weSizwe Party. His hospitalisation comes as his party continues its campaign activities for the local government elections on 4 November.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Home Affairs Withdraws Asylum Directive After Soweto, Durban Unrest

The Department of Home Affairs has withdrawn a directive on the intake of asylum applications following violent anti-immigration protests in Soweto and Durban, where at least 24 vehicles were torched and foreign-owned businesses were looted. The directive was introduced after a July Constitutional Court ruling that allowed asylum seekers to apply for protection regardless of how they entered South Africa or whether they missed immigration deadlines. However, mounting pressure on refugee reception offices, concerns over staff safety and threats to public order prompted the department to reconsider its approach. Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi welcomed the withdrawal, saying it creates an opportunity for further consultation without undermining the court judgment. The ruling remains in force, and asylum applications must still be assessed individually. Police are investigating cases of vandalism, assault and public violence as authorities remain on alert for further unrest.

Yemen Conflict Escalating, Endangering African Economies, Regional Stability



Fears are mounting over Africa's economic stability, maritime trade and humanitarian situation due to the conflict involving Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. Fears of further disruption to world trade have been raised by the alleged seizure of Yemen's Perim Island by the Houthis. The island lies near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. If the strait becomes impassable, shipping companies may be forced to divert vessels around the southern tip of Africa, increasing transport costs, insurance premiums and consumer prices. African economies are already grappling with fuel and fertiliser shortages linked to disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also triggered a humanitarian crisis, with at least 3,700 refugees reportedly crossing from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10, mostly women and children. Djibouti faces additional pressure because of limited water resources, while neighbouring Ethiopia is particularly vulnerable because it relies on Djibouti's ports for about 95% of its imports and exports. Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region and escalating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea could further destabilise the Horn of Africa and threaten shipping through the strait. African countries have called for a United Nations-led diplomatic solution. Ports in Kenya and Tanzania could benefit from increased shipping activity if vessels continue to avoid the Red Sea.

Ethiopia's Humanitarian and Food Crisis Worsens as Tigray Conflict Flairs

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis that has seen millions of people face food shortages after years of conflict, displacement and drought. Four years after a peace deal was signed in 2022, communities are still struggling to recover from the effects of the unresolved territorial disputes, limited reconstruction and reduced international aid. About 44% of Tigray's prime agricultural land remains inaccessible to displaced residents, and erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells have wiped out crops and grazed away livestock grazing areas. Regional assessments have reported the destruction of over 252,500 hectares of planted crops, dire conditions in 140 districts, and the threat of starvation and disease to over 3.5 million livestock. Some 3.9 million people require urgent food assistance, with millions more still in need of adequate support. Renewed hostilities since late September have further disrupted humanitarian operations through air strikes, damage to infrastructure, telecommunications blackouts, and closure or seizure of regional airports. Aid deliveries are either suspended or delayed, and the looting in Mekelle has destroyed the critical supplies, vehicles and medical equipment of humanitarian organizations. These losses have disrupted services for healthcare and support for displaced people and vulnerable children, including children living with HIV. Humanitarian workers are calling for an immediate pause in fighting and safe access for food, medicine, fuel and cash to reach affected communities, warning that continued disruption could push the region towards famine.

At Least 84 Kenyans Killed or Missing in Russia-Ukraine War

At least 84 Kenyans have been killed or remain missing in connection with the Russia-Ukraine war, according to figures released by Kenya's Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs. The government has identified 354 Kenyan nationals as having become involved in the conflict, including 77 reportedly on the front lines, 38 in military camps and 52 whose locations remain unknown or unclassified. Another 34 are hospitalised, 62 have been repatriated, and five are being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine. One Kenyan is in detention, while another has completed their military contract. Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said Ukrainian authorities confirmed the five prisoners of war on September 3, adding that Kenya is seeking to have them recognised as potential victims of human trafficking because some reportedly enlisted after receiving misleading employment offers. The government is pursuing their release and repatriation while investigating the deaths and disappearances of other nationals, including four whose remains are reportedly in Ukrainian custody. Kenya also says it secured Russia's inclusion of Kenyan nationals on a "Stop List" during a diplomatic visit in March, a measure intended to prevent further recruitment. Mudavadi has urged families to report missing relatives promptly to help authorities verify cases, trace their whereabouts and provide assistance. The government says it will continue diplomatic efforts and strengthen preventive measures against deceptive recruitment.

Guinea-Bissau Elections Face Delay

Guinea-Bissau's planned presidential and legislative elections, scheduled for December 6, could be delayed after Prime Minister Ilídio Vieira Té said the conditions necessary to hold the polls had not been met. Following a meeting with transitional President and junta leader General Horta N'Tam, Té said political parties were not adequately prepared to contest the elections and that several needed to renew their leadership structures. The National Electoral Commission also warned that organising the polls on the scheduled date would not be technically feasible, although no formal postponement has been announced. The elections form part of a 12-month transition programme introduced after the military seized power on November 26, 2025, just days after presidential and legislative elections were held but before their results were declared. The takeover halted the electoral process and led the junta to schedule new elections for December 2026. Political tensions have since intensified, particularly after the authorities barred former president Umaro Sissoco Embaló from returning from exile earlier this month, citing national security and public order concerns. Embaló had intended to contest the presidential election. The junta has also faced opposition over constitutional changes approved in an August 30 referendum that strengthen presidential powers and alter the country's political and electoral framework. With no new election date announced, uncertainty remains over the country's political transition and the restoration of civilian democratic rule.

Close 

Wajir Patient Tests Negative for Ebola, Positive for Malaria

Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has confirmed that a patient in Wajir County who was being assessed for a possible Ebola infection has tested negative for the virus and positive for malaria. The patient, who was receiving treatment at Habaswein Sub-County Hospital in Wajir South, was started on antimalarial medication after laboratory results confirmed the diagnosis. The findings have eased concerns about a possible second Ebola case as Kenya strengthens surveillance following its first confirmed imported case, involving a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of Congo for seven years and died in Nairobi on October 6. The deceased patient travelled from the DRC through Uganda before boarding Jambojet flight JM8523 to Nairobi on October 3, and laboratory tests confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease. Health authorities are tracing family members, healthcare workers and passengers who may have been exposed, while strengthening screening at points of entry and preparedness at designated treatment facilities. Wajir Governor Ahmed Abdullahi has called on residents to stay calm and not circulate unverified information. The Ministry of Health says Kenya is not experiencing an outbreak of Ebola on a large scale. Authorities continue to encourage good hygiene, prompt medical attention for concerning symptoms, and strict infection prevention measures among healthcare workers. Members of the public can access official health information through the Ministry's toll-free line, 719. The Wajir patient's negative result is separate from the confirmed imported case in Nairobi, and surveillance efforts remain ongoing.

World.title: South Africa: Home Affairs Withdraws Asylum Directive After Violent Anti-Immigration Protests
World.content:
Chaos erupted in Durban city centre during a march by hundreds of anti-immigrant protesters.

The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) has withdrawn a directive on the intake of asylum applications following violent anti-immigration protests in Durban and Soweto, as the government seeks to find a way to implement a Constitutional Court ruling without further escalating tensions.

The directive, issued on 28 September, followed a July judgment by the Constitutional Court in the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town case. The ruling struck down provisions of the Refugees Act that prevented some asylum seekers from accessing the application process on procedural grounds before their claims could be assessed on their merits.

The judgment allows asylum seekers to apply for protection regardless of how they entered South Africa. However, it does not automatically grant applicants refugee status or permanent residence, as each claim must still be assessed in accordance with the law.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Home Affairs said the directive was introduced as an operational measure to implement the court order but was issued by the department’s director-general without the knowledge of the minister or other political office-bearers.

The department said the implementation process had presented unforeseen challenges, with Refugee Reception Offices overwhelmed by the number of people seeking to submit asylum applications within days of the directive being issued.

It also raised concerns about the safety of departmental officials and the potential impact on public safety and order.

The department will now develop a revised operational approach to ensure compliance with the Constitutional Court’s judgment while addressing the challenges experienced at its offices.

The withdrawal of the directive does not overturn the court ruling, and Home Affairs has yet to announce details of its revised approach.

The development follows violent protests in Durban and Soweto during which vehicles were torched, and businesses vandalised amid growing opposition to immigration and the processing of asylum applications.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi has welcomed the department's decision, describing it as a relief that creates an opportunity for further consultation.

World.title: South Africa: Four Killed in Germiston Shack Fire - South African News Briefs - October 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Four Killed in Germiston Shack Fire

Four people, including three children aged two, five and seven, have died in a fire that destroyed 12 shacks at the Marathon informal settlement in Germiston, Gauteng, reports EWN. Ekurhuleni Emergency Management Services spokesperson William Ntladi said the victims' bodies were found beneath the rubble. Ntladi said the scene has been handed over to the South African Police Service (SAPS) for investigation, rehabilitation and the removal of the deceased. The cause of the fire remains unknown and is under investigation.

R10 Billion Bill Adopted to Help Stabilise Fuel Prices

The Standing Committee on Appropriations has adopted the Second Special Appropriations Bill, which proposes withdrawing R10 billion from the National Revenue Fund to help stabilise fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, reports SABC News. Committee chairperson Mmusi Maimane said that consumers should receive immediate relief from fuel price volatility. The Bill will soon be tabled in the National Assembly for consideration.

Govt Warns Against Asylum System Abuse

The government has warned foreign nationals that those who do not qualify for asylum or refugee status will be deported, following the Department of Home Affairs' resumption of asylum application processing, reports EWN. Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni said the process would help identify undocumented migrants and those attempting to misuse the system. The announcement comes amid heightened tensions over immigration, with protests turning violent in Durban’s CBD and Soweto, leaving about 20 vehicles torched.
