World.title: West Africa: Russia-Ukraine Conflict Finds New Battleground in Africa's Sahel
World.content:
Ukraine has vowed to counter Russia wherever it can, even "in the scorching sands" of the Sahelian desert, as evidence mounts that Kyiv is backing Tuareg separatists battling Mali's army and its Russian allies.

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso -- all led by military juntas that have turned their backs on former colonial ruler France and moved closer to Russia -- have reacted by severing diplomatic relations with Kyiv.

They accuse Ukraine of supplying weapons to the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) -- a predominantly Tuareg armed separatist group loosely allied to Al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM).

"In Africa and the Sahel, (Ukraine) is providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop alleged at the United Nations in September.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Niger's Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine singled out France and Ukraine, alleging they were directing "proxies" along his country's northeastern borders to attack military positions and oil facilities.

Ukraine's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment on the allegations.

The accusations followed posts on X by Kyrylo Budanov -- a former Ukrainian intelligence chief who became President Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff in January -- in which he hinted at the presence of Ukrainian agents in Africa's Sahel region.

"From Russia to Africa... the Main Intelligence Directorate protects Ukrainian interests across the globe by all means... in the scorching sands of deserts and the freezing snows of Antarctica," Budanov wrote on September 7.

The post was accompanied by a photo showing four white men, their faces blurred, alongside armed, turbaned men in pickup trucks in a desert.

Five days later, a CNN report said Ukrainian military intelligence officers had confirmed that drone operators in the Sahel had provided training and support to the FLA.

- Training -

Armed groups are increasingly using low-cost, remotely piloted technologies for reconnaissance and strikes -- tactics possibly inspired by the war in Ukraine.

Details of what the Ukrainians are doing in sub-Saharan Africa are disputed.

A source within the FLA told AFP the Malian separatists "maintain contact with the Ukrainians".

But the source stressed: "All the fighting over the past few months has been carried out by the FLA and JNIM."

He denied Kyiv had provided logistical, material or intelligence support and dismissed Budanov's photos as "just Ukrainian propaganda".

Kyiv had provided some instruction, though, he said.

In 2023, "three or four Ukrainians" travelled to northern Mali to train some FLA fighters and several combatants underwent "an intensive 30-day course in Ukraine on the use of FPV (first-person view) drones", he said.

The training course in northern Mali "took place near the Mauritanian border", a second source within the FLA said, adding the photos posted by Budanov were "either from that time or were taken in Syria".

- Mauritania -

A diplomat based in the region, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the Ukrainians had "a definite presence in northern Mali, where they move about and collaborate with Tuareg rebels".

They said the border with Mauritania was the main crossing point for exchanges between the Ukrainians and the FLA and the drones used by the separatists came from Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that Kyiv opened an embassy in Nouakchott in 2024, given that Mauritania serves as a rear base for FLA leaders," the diplomat said.

Close 

The diplomat said the FLA systematically denied or underplayed reports of Ukrainian assistance to avoid creating problems for Mauritanian authorities.

In November, a study by US think tank Carnegie Endowment for International Peace indicated that Kyiv had been supplying drones to the separatists since early 2024.

In July of that year, Ukrainian military intelligence official Andriy Yusov hinted that Kyiv had provided information to FLA and JNIM fighters, who carried out an attack in northern Mali which killed dozens of Russian mercenaries and Malian soldiers.

In recent years, Ukraine has opened several embassies across Africa as it seeks to boost its influence in a continent where Russia has a significant presence.

In March Ukraine laid out its first strategy for extending its reach in Africa and in August Zelensky asked his ambassadors to pay close attention to certain African regions, including the Sahel.

World.title: Somalia: Trump Urges Minnesotans to 'Fight Back' Against Somali Immigrants
World.content:
Washington — US President Donald Trump on Thursday continued his long-running attacks on Somalis by urging Minnesotans to "fight back" against the Somali community in the state.

"The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The people of Minnesota must fight back."

He added: "The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue."

The White House did not immediately respond to an inquiry about how Trump wanted Minnesotans to "fight back."

Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S.

During his time in office, Trump has repeatedly attacked Somalis, as well as Rep. Ilhan Omar, who was born in Somalia.

Trump's rhetoric against Somalis in Minnesota has intensified following reports last year about dozens of people of Somali descent being convicted in fraud schemes. Since then, Trump has referred to Somalis as "crooks" and called Somalia "filthy, dirty, disgusting, dirty."

World.title: South Africa: South Africa-Born Navanethem "Navi" Pillay Wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
press release

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.

This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time.

The first Nobel Peace Prize was awarded 125 years ago. Already then, the Norwegian Nobel Committee underscored the importance of resolving conflicts through international law – a theme that has remained prominent throughout the history of the peace prize. The reach of international law expanded after the Second World War, in particular with the creation of the UN institutions. The key insight was that lasting peace must be built on legal principles, not on the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power. Additional legal mechanisms were introduced in the post-war decades, and momentum picked up further after the end of the Cold War.

However, the rules-based international order has never been perfect. The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim.

Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms, rather than threats, violence and warfare. Leaders and populations alike have come to the same conclusion: international law is a foundation for a more peaceful world.

At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity.

And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence.

In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice.

History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench.

Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law. She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor. In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda.

Close 

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 springs directly from Alfred Nobel’s will. Navi Pillay strengthens fraternity between nations and – by systematically advancing the use of tribunals for peace and justice – she provides substance, direction and motivation for peace conferences in their modern form.

Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.

World.title: Ethiopia: Call for a Special Session to Prevent Further Atrocities
World.content:
Civil society joint letter to the United Nations Human Rights Council

To Permanent Representatives of Member and Observer States of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Council (Geneva, Switzerland)

8 October 2026

Ethiopia: The Human Rights Council should convene a special session to address the quickly deteriorating human rights situation and prevent further atrocity crimes



Excellencies,

As armed hostilities have resumed on a large scale in Ethiopia, with risks of repetition of the atrocity crimes documented during the 2020-2022 conflict, we, the undersigned civil society organisations, urge the Human Rights Council to urgently convene a special session on the human rights impact of the conflict. At the session, we urge the adoption of a resolution requesting the Council's President to appoint an advisory panel of experts, drawn from the pool of existing independent UN and African human rights experts, to undertake a swift assessment, compile a summary report, and make recommendations on steps the Council could take to address the human rights situation in Ethiopia.

The Council should stand ready to take further action, as appropriate, to address any developments in Ethiopia or the sub-region, send a message of deterrence to all actors, and indicate that those responsible for perpetrating, ordering or facilitating violations should be held accountable.

On 22 September 2026, after long-simmering tensions between the Ethiopian Federal Government led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated from sporadic clashes and airstrikes to open military confrontation, fighting resumed on a large scale and spread to the Afar and Amhara regions in northern Ethiopia.

Heavy fighting, involving the use of drone strikes, mortar strikes and artillery fire, including indiscriminate airstrikes in populated areas and on civilian infrastructure that may amount to war crimes, is pitting federal forces, the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), and allied forces against not only the TPLF's Tigray Defence Force (TDF) but other regional armed groups, including the Amhara Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), both of which formed an alliance with TPLF and other regional groupings to topple the federal government. Renewed hostilities are also occurring amid the backdrop of ongoing conflict in the Amhara and Oromia regions.

At the time of writing, fighting and airstrikes were ongoing in Tigray, including near camps for internally displaced persons in central Tigray, and northern Amhara. ENDF and pro-government forces also reportedly captured several towns, including the regional capital, Mekelle. On 1 October, blasts were reported in Addis Ababa after Ethiopia's National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) declared a ban on operating drones and other flying objects in the capital.

This significant escalation means that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (CoHA) signed in Pretoria in November 2022 between Ethiopia's Federal Government and the TPLF, has effectively collapsed. The escalation occurred against a backdrop of geopolitical tensions that led to the cutting of diplomatic ties between Eritrea and Ethiopia. Observers point to the role of external actors and the risk of a regional conflict threatening to destabilise the entire Horn of Africa sub-region, as well as the Red Sea area.

The conflict is exacerbating the already dire humanitarian situation in northern Ethiopia due to disruptions to essential services and supply routes, including access to health care, Internet and communication services, air travel, and banking services (including cash and mobile banking, as well as remittances, on which many depend for survival). During the 2020-2022 war, the Ethiopian Government deliberately obstructed commercial and humanitarian supplies, shut down banks, and imposed an effective siege on Tigray.

Communication disruptions and access restrictions in conflict-affected areas are occurring alongside severe civic space restrictions in Ethiopia, including government attacks against journalists, media workers, human rights defenders, and other independent actors who could report on the situation.

The previous conflict was marked by atrocity crimes, massacres of civilians and other unlawful killings, widespread conflict-related sexual and reproductive violence, attacks on health, forced displacement, and ethnic cleansing, with estimates of a death toll of up to several hundred thousand.

There has been no accountability for the grave crimes committed, including because the federal government has largely shelved its transitional justice process and the Human Rights Council terminated the mandate of the International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (ICHREE) it had established, despite warnings by the mechanism of acute risks of further atrocities. Impunity for these crimes points to grave risks for civilians, including of new atrocities.

The UN Secretary-General, the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and the African Union (AU) have all expressed alarm about the situation and urged restraint, de-escalation and civilian protection.

~ ~ ~

The situation in Ethiopia requires the international community's urgent attention and close scrutiny by regional and UN human rights bodies and mechanisms. In line with its prevention mandate and its responsibility to respond promptly to human rights emergencies and address gross and systematic violations, and given the sharp deterioration of the situation on the ground, the Human Rights Council should act before its next regular session, which is scheduled for February 2027.

The Human Rights Council should urgently convene a special session on the human rights impact of the conflict in Ethiopia and adopt a resolution that, among other things:

Condemns all violations and abuses of human rights and violations of international humanitarian law committed in Ethiopia;

Requests the President of the Human Rights Council, following consultations with relevant stakeholders, including the Coordination Committee of Special Procedures, to appoint on the most expeditious basis possible an advisory panel of three independent human rights experts, drawn from the pool of existing experts from the United Nations special procedures and African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights special mechanisms:

To swiftly undertake an assessment of violations and abuses of human rights and violations of international humanitarian law committed in Ethiopia by all parties to the conflict since August 2026, with a view to preventing a further deterioration of the human rights situation; To prepare a summary report outlining the human rights impact of the conflict in Ethiopia and setting out recommendations to the warring parties, relevant States, and the Human Rights Council, to be presented during an inter-sessional briefing convened by the President of the Council before 31 January 2027; To engage with the Ethiopian authorities and all other relevant stakeholders and to ensure the complementarity and coordination of this effort with other efforts of the United Nations, the African Union, and other regional and international entities; and To make recommendations on steps the Human Rights Council could take to address the human rights situation in Ethiopia, taking into consideration the findings and recommendations of the International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, including those outlined in report A/HRC/54/55, as well as the panel of experts' own findings, including on supporting further investigations, evidence collection and preservation, identification of those responsible for violations, ending impunity and addressing its root causes, and ensuring accountability for all violations and abuses.

Requests the advisory panel of experts to keep the Human Rights Council updated on the situation in Ethiopia by holding urgent inter-sessional briefings as necessary and advising the Council's President, Member and Observer States on the need for any additional urgent meetings or actions;

Decides to convene an enhanced interactive dialogue on the human rights situation in Ethiopia, to be held at its 64th regular session, with the participation of a representative of the advisory panel of experts, the High Commissioner for Human Rights, the Special Adviser of the Secretary-General for the Prevention of Genocide, representatives of the African Union or the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, and civil society;

Encourages the High Commissioner to resume public reporting on the human rights situation in Ethiopia, in accordance with his global mandate and the mandate of his office in Addis Ababa;

Requests that the advisory panel of experts be provided with all necessary resources to fulfil this mandate, including by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights;

Requests the Government of Ethiopia to facilitate access to the country for the experts; and

Makes clear that the Council will stand ready to take further action to prevent human rights violations and abuses and violations of international humanitarian law in Ethiopia, including the risk of atrocity crimes, and take steps to ensure accountability for past and ongoing violations.

Close 

We thank you for your attention to these pressing issues and stand ready to provide your delegation with further information as required.

Sincerely,

World.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: France's free speech crackdown shows what happens when politicians define truth
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

French President Emmanuel Macron went full Orwell recently. While long the darling of Western media, Macron has been one of the most anti-free-speech leaders in the world. On Sept. 29, he declared that "The so-called American ‘free speech’ today, which some people have promoted, is the opposite of free speech." Having Emmanuel Macron holding forth on free speech is akin to Joey Chestnut proselytizing on veganism.

France has been in a headlong plunge into censorship and speech criminalization. These laws criminalize speech under vague standards referring to "inciting" or "intimidating" others based on race or religion.

For example, fashion designer John Galliano was found guilty in a French court on charges of making antisemitic comments in a Paris bar in 2010 and 2011.

MACRON TRASHES AMERICAN FREE SPEECH AS RIOTS GRIP FRANCE — INTERNET UNLOADS: ‘ENORMOUS FOOL’

In another case, the father of French conservative presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was fined because he had called people from the Roma minority "smelly" in 2013. A French teenager was charged for criticizing Islam as a "religion of hate" in 2020.

Many of us were disgusted recently when Macron celebrated Brigitte Bardot's life as someone who "embodied a life of freedom." As I discussed, the French government repeatedly prosecuted Bardot for speaking about her views.

FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15

Macron’s praise for Bardot’s "life of freedom" is reminiscent of the reaction of French officials to the massacre of editors at Charlie Hebdo, a satirical magazine. After hounding the victims for years with criminal investigations, the French government organized a march for free speech. As predicted, it then used the killing by Islamic extremists to further crack down on free speech.

In my book "The Indispensable Right," I discuss how France has careened down the slippery slope of censorship for decades, and the desire to silence others has now become an insatiable appetite.

UK ‘IN FREE FALL’ ON FREE SPEECH, EXPERT WARNS AS BRITISH MP BRANDS TRUMP ADMIN GRANT 'MAGA MONEY MEDDLING'

Macron has supported figures like his anti-free-speech ally Thierry Breton in globalizing the reach of the infamous Digital Services Act (DSA) to curtail speech, including Americans and American companies.

In his latest pitch for censorship, Macron pulls out an old saw that if everyone can speak freely, no one can speak freely.

BIBLE VERSE LEADS TO TRIAL IN EUROPE. GROWING CRACKDOWN THREATENS OUR US-UK VALUES

Macron declared that: "There is no freedom if there is no limit to my freedom, which begins with the freedom of others and respect for a common framework. I know this when I walk down the street: my freedom cannot mean hitting you, insulting you or trashing the public space we all share."

That line is remarkably telling. It captures how even "insulting" language is treated as a crime in France.

UK LAWMAKER WARNS IT’S ‘OPEN SEASON’ ON CHRISTIANS AS HE SOUNDS ALARM OVER ‘TWO-TIER JUSTICE’

Since then, France has been a leader in the rollback of free speech in the West, with ever-widening laws curtailing free speech. France regularly charges people for political and religious speech, including comedians and those criticizing the police.

Many of us were disgusted recently when Macron celebrated Brigitte Bardot's life as someone who "embodied a life of freedom." As I discussed, the French government repeatedly prosecuted Bardot for speaking about her views.

Macron's visceral reaction to free speech is shared by many in the European Union.

ERDOGAN'S TURKEY CRACKS DOWN ON LGBT COMMUNITY IN NAME OF PRESERVING FAMILY VALUES

I spoke in Berlin at the World Forum, which boasted the slogan, "A New World Order with European Values." Former President Bill Clinton and his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and other Americans cheered on the European efforts.

The Digital Services Act bars speech that is viewed as "disinformation" or "incitement." When it was passed over the condemnations of many of us in the free speech community, European Commission Executive Vice President Margrethe Vestager celebrated by declaring that it is "not a slogan anymore — that what is illegal offline should also be seen and dealt with as illegal online. Now it is a real thing. Democracy’s back."

JONATHAN TURLEY: COMEY’S SHELL POST MAY BE CRASS, BUT CHARGING HIM IS A FREE SPEECH TRAP

Despite his unpopularity in France, Macron remains a favorite of the establishment and the media in the United States. I was appalled years ago when he came to Congress to spread his anti-free speech gospel. Macron called for a joint war against "fake news" and declared, "Democracy is about true choices and rational decisions. The corruption of information is an attempt to corrode the very spirit of our democracies."

Our representatives applauded like seals with little recognition that he was referencing censorship. Macron believes that he should be able to dictate which views are "corrosive" to the spirit of democracy.

LEGAL EXPERTS WARN COMEY ‘86 47’ INDICTMENT FACES FIRST AMENDMENT HURDLES

The claim that more speech means less speech is an oxymoronic talking point of the anti-free-speech movement. As I discussed in my book, there has not been a single censorship system in history that has worked to kill a single idea or movement. Instead, it has given more power to politicians like Macron to silence critics and intimidate opponents.

In the end, the only true solution to bad speech is better speech. The public can sort out its own values and weigh opposing views without the strict guidance of the government. Free speech serves as its own disinfectant.

Ultimately, allowing people not just free inquiry, but free expression bends the arc of humanity toward truth. Hate and prejudice are inherently flawed values that tend to collapse when exposed to full, robust debate.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That does not mean that it will eliminate racism, sexism or other forms of hate. Neither censorship nor free speech can make everyone better people. However, what Macron is peddling is the same tired, dishonest claim that free speech is harmful, and the government must control what people see and say in public discourse.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This is a nation that still echoes the cry of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity ("liberté, égalité, fraternité"). However, in today’s France, "liberté" remains a declining value. Individual rights of religion and speech are routinely sacrificed in the name of "equity" and "fraternity."

World.title: Aaron Judge's frustration with Yankees is understandable, but his 'all-in' criticism misses the mark
World.content:
I preface this by saying Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone have overstayed their welcome in the Bronx.

But Aaron Judge knows how the average New York Yankees fan operates, and quite frankly, he has played them like a fiddle over the last couple of weeks.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

When Boone confirmed that Judge had a "moderate" calf strain, Judge made it a point that night that he was not happy his manager, who has his players’ backs to a fault, had divulged that (obviously true) information. He made it known that if it were up to him, he’d be on the field in the postseason, arguably putting pressure on the team.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Then, minutes after the Yankees were swept by the Tampa Bay Rays, he all but threw the front office under the bus.

Judge said he wanted the organization to be "all-in," and when asked if he felt they had been, he said, "it’s tough to say."

"I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year, but I know that's not realistic. They give us a winning team every single year, but that's not good enough here in New York. We're the Yankees. You've got to go out there and expect championships and go all-in every year. I'm excited to see what they do," Judge said.

It goes without saying that the offseason of running back practically the same team, headlined by giving Trent Grisham the $22 million qualifying offer, was not exactly a decision made in a Mensa meeting.

But the Yankees have a payroll of over $308 million. The three teams remaining in the American League have a combined payroll of $273.4 million. Are the Rays, Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians "all-in"?

Look, guys like Grisham, Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm didn’t work here, whether it was the weight of New York or an organizational philosophy just not meshing.

Maybe Cashman should have made a harder push for, say, catcher Adley Rutschman – although Austin Wells’ bat was the least of the Yankees' concerns after the All-Star break and in October. Maybe there are a few prospects out there, like Jasson Dominguez, Clint Frazier and Miguel Andujar, that Cashman held on to for too long. Maybe gambling on the future of Anthony Volpe instead of bringing in the proven Corey Seager (who just hit a career-worst .227 at age 32 with six years left on his deal) was the wrong move. Maybe doing the same with George Lombard Jr. and passing on Tarik Skubal (as if they really needed him) is a mistake, too.



But before Judge even had his first arbitration case, the Yankees acquired reigning National League MVP Giancarlo Stanton, eventual MVP candidate DJ LeMahieu, and bona fide ace Gerrit Cole, fresh off a 326-strikeout, 2.50 ERA season.

Throughout his tenure, they have added players like Anthony Rizzo, Carlos Rodon, Cody Bellinger, Devin Williams, David Bednar, Luis Garcia and Max Fried, while turning almost anyone who walks into the bullpen into a threat. The Yankees have developed their next MVP candidate in Ben Rice, and Cam Schlittler is going to win the Cy Young Award next month in his first full MLB season.

Meanwhile, anyone reading this would be lucky to name a total of 10 people on this year’s notably all-in Rays, White Sox and Guardians.

To make a guess, the one "all-in" move that could have been made was keeping Juan Soto. The Yankees acquired him after missing the postseason in 2023, knowing he was going to free agency. Soto hit a career-high 41 home runs to help the Yankees to their first World Series appearance since 2009 , as Judge and Soto were the best 1-2 tandem in recent memory.

That only lasted for a year, though, as the New York Mets won the Soto sweepstakes with a 15-year, $765 million deal. The Yankees offered 16 years and $760 million, but the Mets offered Soto travel, suites and $40 million more if he does not opt out after his fifth season.

I mean, are we really going to be mad at the front office that Soto chose to take over $800 million with the Mets?

And if Soto were still in the Bronx, Bellinger and Fried would not be, so there would be something else to complain about.

Were the Yankees "all-in" when they acquired Scott Brosius to play third base ahead of the 1998 season instead of, say, Ken Caminiti, who won the NL MVP just one year prior?

Going all-in doesn’t mean having an All-Star everywhere, and Judge obviously knows that. Sometimes, "all-in" is simply masked as players playing well.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Speaking of which, here’s the ugly truth — Aaron Judge would have at least one title is he wasn’t a .205 hitter in the postseason from 2017 to 2024.

The Yankees’ title drought, tied for the longest since 1923, is the fault of many — players (including Judge) and decision-makers alike. Judge will be 35 in April, and if the impending lockout goes awry, he could be 36 by the time baseball is played again. He sees his mortality, and he’s probably desperate at this point.

But his desperation is clouding his perception of reality.

World.title: Divers uncover ancient treasures linked to Roman giant who helped shape American history
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A 2,100-year-old shipwreck off the coast of Turkey has revealed thousands of luxury dishes of a type once prized by Cicero, the famed Roman statesman whose writings later influenced America's Founding Fathers — with an expert calling the find "quite rare."

The recovery was recently announced by Turkish officials, the state-run Anadolu Agency (AA) reported Sept. 28.

Pictures show divers working among piles of ancient pottery, with ceramic plates and bowls scattered across the sandy seabed.

ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS SAYINGS ABOUT ROME MAY BE WRONG, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

The artifacts include 122 different forms and sizes of plates, bowls and trays, including dishes used for nuts, soup and fish.

Researchers believe the ship was traveling from Rhosus to Rome when it struck a shallow area during a storm and sank, according to AA. The wreck lies about 138 to 180 feet below the surface.

The discovery is particularly significant because the ceramics are believed to have originated in Rhosus, a production center mentioned in the writings of Cicero — though there's no evidence that the recovered dishes belonged to Cicero himself.

Cicero, one of ancient Rome's most celebrated orators and politicians, significantly influenced the U.S.'s Founding Fathers, especially Thomas Jefferson and John Adams.

DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS

In a letter to his friend Atticus in 50 B.C., the statesman wrote that he had ordered ceramic vessels from Rhosus for him, according to AA.

Taco Terpstra, a professor of classics and history at Northwestern University, told Fox News Digital that the discovery offers an unusual opportunity to connect ancient artifacts with historical writings.

"It's unusual that we have so much of this type of ceramic," Terpstra said.

DAMAGED FRAGMENT DEEMED 'UNREMARKABLE' TURNS OUT TO BE RARE PIECE OF HOMER'S 'ODYSSEY' HISTORY

He explained that coins found aboard the ship help researchers date the wreck, while the pottery can be traced to a production region in what is now southern Turkey and northern Syria.

"This is for a high-end market, which is one reason why Cicero talks about these."

The combination of archaeological evidence, ancient coins and historical writings makes the discovery especially rare, he said.

CLICK HERE TO 

Terpstra also described the ceramics as "the equivalent of fine china" today.

"This is not ordinary tableware," he said. "This is not the kind of stuff that ordinary Romans would have on their table."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"This is for a high-end market, which is one reason why Cicero talks about these."

Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the ceramics were remarkably well preserved because clay had been packed between them before they were placed in wooden crates — a detail that caught Terpstra's attention.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The historian suggested the material may have been unfired clay, although he noted that the report did not specify its exact form.

"I imagine they meant unfired soft clay, which, when the ship went down, preserved the ceramics to a very high degree," Terpstra said.

Terpstra added that, while Roman shipwrecks in the Mediterranean are "quite common," the convergence of historical evidence makes this find exceptional.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's quite rare for all of it … [all] the lines of evidence to come together, like monetary, archeological, literary," Terpstra said.

World.title: 16-year-old allegedly led ransomware gang behind hundreds of attacks
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

When you picture the person running an international ransomware operation, a 16-year-old probably does not come to mind. Yet investigators say a teenager was the suspected main operator behind KillSec, a cybercrime group linked to around 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide. About 500 of those attacks have so far been identified as successful.

Now, an international law enforcement operation has taken KillSec's leak site and key servers offline. Authorities also secured at least 110 terabytes of stolen data that could have been exposed or used to pressure victims. The takedown offers a remarkable look at how accessible cybercrime has become. More importantly, it shows how attackers continue to find their way into poorly protected systems and turn stolen files into leverage. What investigators uncovered about KillSec shows how the group operated, how AI reportedly played a role and what you can do to make ransomware attacks harder to pull off.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com

FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER

Police take down KillSec ransomware operation

The crackdown, known as Operation KillSwitch, took place on Sept. 30. Authorities from the United States and several European countries participated in the investigation. Europol and Eurojust also helped coordinate the effort.

Police carried out eight searches in Greece, Romania, Spain and the United Kingdom. Three suspects were provisionally arrested. Investigators also took control of five central servers connected with KillSec's operation. One of the biggest moves involved KillSec's dark web leak site. The group allegedly used the site to name victims and threaten to publish stolen files unless they paid. Authorities have now taken control of that infrastructure.

A 16-year-old is suspected of running the operation

Perhaps the most startling part of this case involves the age of the suspected operator. Investigators identified a 16-year-old as KillSec's suspected administrator and main operator. Another suspected member, described as a developer, turned 18 in August and was reportedly still a minor when some of the alleged crimes occurred.

Investigators also identified people suspected of serving as a negotiator and an affiliate. Authorities say the investigation remains ongoing. Age aside, the alleged operation was anything but small. KillSec has been active since around 2024. According to Europol, the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points to break into organizations. Attackers then copied sensitive internal files to systems they controlled.

How KillSec allegedly pressured its victims

Once attackers had the files, the pressure began. KillSec allegedly listed organizations on its dark web site and threatened to publish their stolen data if they refused to pay. In some cases, the stolen files were reportedly made available after victims declined to hand over a ransom.

Europol says the group received substantial ransom payments from some attacks. That strategy shows how ransomware has changed over the years. Criminals do not always need to lock every file on a computer to create leverage. Stolen information itself can become the threat. If an attacker gets employee records, customer information or confidential business documents, the victim can face serious consequences even when backups work perfectly.

KillSec reportedly used AI to support its attacks

Investigators also uncovered another detail that caught my attention. Europol says members of KillSec used artificial intelligence to help build and maintain ransomware infrastructure and identify potential victims.

That does not mean AI carried out the entire attack by itself. However, it shows how cybercriminals can use the same technology everyone else is experimenting with to speed up parts of their work. A teenager may no longer need to build every piece of an attack from scratch. Tools, stolen credentials, vulnerable systems and AI assistance can lower some of the barriers that once required deeper technical expertise. That should make all of us pay closer attention to basic security habits.

FBI'S FIRST CYBER FUGITIVE ON TEN MOST WANTED LIST RETURNS TO US AFTER CAPTURE IN VENEZUELA

What happens to KillSec now?

The investigation remains active. Authorities are examining computers, servers and other seized evidence. Investigators are also following cryptocurrency and other alleged criminal proceeds.

That evidence could uncover additional attacks, victims or people connected with the operation. Europol also cautions that the current number of successful attacks may change as investigators continue reviewing what they seized.

For now, KillSec's core infrastructure has taken a significant hit. However, ransomware groups have a long history of disappearing, reorganizing and resurfacing under different names. That makes prevention especially important even after a major takedown.

Why this ransomware takedown should get your attention

KillSec appears to have focused mainly on organizations rather than individual home computer users. Still, the methods behind the attacks offer lessons that apply to everyone. Europol says the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points. Those are the same types of weaknesses security experts have warned about for years.

An old router, forgotten account or unpatched computer can give attackers an opening. A compromised password can do the same. Once criminals gain access, they can steal information before anyone realizes something has gone wrong. So, while you probably cannot stop an international ransomware gang yourself, you can make your devices and accounts harder to break into.

7 ways to reduce your ransomware risk

A few simple security habits can close some of the openings attackers commonly look for.

1) Install software and security updates

Do not keep putting off updates on your computer, phone, browser and other connected devices. Security updates often fix vulnerabilities attackers already know how to exploit. CISA recommends regularly patching operating systems and software, especially on devices exposed to the internet. Turn on automatic updates when that option is available.

2) Use strong, unique passwords

Using the same password across several accounts gives an attacker more opportunities if one login is exposed. Create a different password for each important account. A password manager can help generate and store strong credentials without forcing you to remember every one. You should also check whether passwords you already use have appeared in known data leaks. Your iPhone or Android phone may already have tools that can flag compromised passwords.

HACKER CLAIMS 7.49M CUSTOMER RECORDS STOLEN FROM AMERICAN UTILITY COMPANY

3) Turn on two-factor authentication

A stolen password becomes much less useful when your account requires another form of verification. Enable two-factor ( 2FA ) or multifactor authentication on your email, financial accounts, cloud storage and other important services. When available, consider phishing-resistant options such as passkeys or security keys instead of relying only on text-message codes.

4) Keep an offline backup of important files

Ransomware becomes far more painful when your only copy of a photo, document or financial record lives on the compromised device. Back up important files regularly . Consider keeping one copy in the cloud and another on an external drive. If you use an external drive, disconnect it when the backup finishes. Some ransomware can also target drives that remain connected to an infected computer.

5) Be careful with unexpected downloads and attachments

A convincing email, fake update warning or malicious attachment can provide an attacker with a way into your computer. Avoid opening files you were not expecting. Instead of clicking an urgent update prompt from a webpage or email, open the app itself and check for updates there. If something feels unusual, stop before entering a password or running a downloaded file.

6) Use security software on your devices

Strong antivirus software can help detect ransomware, malicious downloads and other threats before they spread. Keep the protection updated and run a full scan if your computer suddenly behaves differently, redirects your browser or shows unfamiliar programs. Security software will never replace safe habits. However, it can provide another opportunity to catch a threat before the damage grows. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

7) Know what to do if ransomware hits

If you see a ransom message or suddenly lose access to important files, disconnect the affected device from your network. Avoid plugging backup drives into the compromised computer until you know the device is clean. The FBI says it does not support paying ransomware demands because payment does not guarantee that your information will be restored. The agency also encourages victims to report ransomware incidents. You can file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov or contact your local FBI field office. The FBI specifically directs ransomware victims to use those channels. One more thing: type IC3.gov directly into your browser. The FBI has warned that scammers have created fake IC3 websites, including lookalike pages that may appear in sponsored search results.

Kurt's key takeaways

The age of KillSec's suspected operator is going to grab the headlines, and I understand why. Sixteen is incredibly young to be accused of running an operation connected with this many attacks. What stays with me, though, is how familiar the alleged entry points sound. Vulnerable software and poorly protected access can still give criminals exactly the opening they need. That is why I keep coming back to the basics. Update your devices. Protect important accounts with more than a password. Keep a backup that an attacker cannot easily reach. You may never know which security step stopped an attack. That is far better than discovering which one you skipped after your files are already gone.

If a 16-year-old can allegedly help run a ransomware operation tied to hundreds of successful attacks, do you think powerful hacking tools and AI are making cybercrime too easy to enter at a young age? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

World.title: Woman says public was forced to leave California forum over her 'Save Girls Sports' shirt
World.content:
A California women’s sports advocate and candidate for office says organizers cleared the audience from a school board candidate forum after a dispute over her "Save Girls Sports" shirt.

Shannon Kessler, the Republican candidate for California’s 30th Assembly District and founder of Save Girls Sports Central Coast, told OutKick she was instructed to cover the shirt at a Sept. 21 forum for Lucia Mar Unified School District trustee candidates in Arroyo Grande.

The shirt also carried her name and Assembly campaign information on the back, Kessler acknowledged. She said she offered to cover that portion before eventually agreeing to conceal the front as well.

CALIFORNIA SUPERINTENDENT CANDIDATE EJECTED FROM SPORTS LEAGUE MEETING FOR BOISTEROUS TITLE IX DEFENSE

The League of Women Voters of San Luis Obispo County hosted the forum with the American Association of University Women’s 5 Cities Pismo Beach Branch. Footage shows the host of the forum announcing a "violation," before instructing everyone to leave.

"From this point on, this forum has been cancelled, because of that violation, we can not proceed," he said, as seen in footage provided by Kessler. "We will ask you to leave now, yes, due to the violation. The violation that there are not to be any slogans, no campaign slogans in the forum, we can not continue."

The candidate forum continued without an audience, with participants answering previously submitted written questions on camera. The event was held at Arroyo Grande High School, rather than being a regular school board meeting.

Kessler said the confrontation began when she entered wearing the shirt and was told its message violated the event’s rules.

"It’s just a women’s rights shirt," she said.

She said organizers suggested she turn the shirt inside out in a bathroom, but she initially refused. Kessler argued that the slogan reflected her advocacy against transgender athletes competing in girls’ sports and was not specific to her Assembly campaign.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Kessler said she then offered to borrow a jacket to cover the campaign information on the back.

"That wasn’t good enough for them. They said I had to cover Save Girls Sports, that message," she said.

According to Kessler, a woman she described as a League leader then told her the front needed to be covered because it carried an "anti-trans hateful message."

"I cannot control how you perceive it, but I don’t mean it that way," Kessler said she responded.

Kessler did not identify that organizer by name in the interview.

She also alleged that the rules were enforced differently against other attendees. Kessler said a person wearing a "Trans kids belong" shirt and attendees wearing other candidates’ campaign information were not asked to cover their clothing.

"I don’t have a problem with him wearing that shirt," she said of the attendee displaying the transgender advocacy message. "Once again, I feel that he has the right to carry that message."

The League’s published forum rules prohibit campaign signs, banners, buttons, clothing and literature inside the forum room. Its website allows campaign materials in a designated area outside the room and says organizers can refuse entry to attendees wearing clothing considered political or disruptive.

Kessler said companions wearing Save Girls Sports shirts were also instructed to cover them or turn them inside out. She said organizers threatened to call police if they did not comply.

Arroyo Grande police records list a disturbance-of-the-peace call at the high school’s address at 6:07 p.m. Sept. 21. The public log does not explain the underlying dispute or what action officers took.

Kessler said police never entered to remove her.

Instead, organizers dismissed the audience.

Footage provided by Kessler shows an exchange with a staffer about the shirt and audience members leaving the room.

Kessler said she ultimately covered the shirt with a borrowed jacket, had the signs taken away and put a campaign-branded water bottle in her purse after trustee Colleen Martin raised an objection to it.

"I had finally said, okay, look, if you’re going to eject everyone, I’ll cover the shirt. And they still canceled the meeting," she said.

CALIFORNIA GIRLS' TRACK AND FIELD STARS SPEAK OUT AS GAVIN NEWSOM'S TITLE IX CRISIS GROWS

Kessler described the episode as discriminatory.

"I feel like it was viewpoint discrimination and against my First Amendment rights," she said.

The dispute follows a prolonged local debate over transgender students’ participation in girls’ sports and access to locker rooms.

OutKick reached out to the League of Women Voters of San Luis Obispo County; AAUW Five Cities–Pismo Beach branch President Jean Burns Slater; Lucia Mar School District communications representative Amy Jacobs; school board Vice President Colleen Martin; and the Arroyo Grande Police Department for comment.

"The Lucia Mar School District said the forum "was not a school- or District-sponsored event," explaining that the League rented the high school facilities through its facilities-use process," the district said.

"The Sept. 21 candidate forum was not a school- or District-sponsored event. The event was sponsored and conducted by the League of Women Voters, which rented Arroyo Grande High School facilities through the District’s facilities use process."

Beyond processing the facilities-use application, neither the school nor the District had a role in planning or conducting the event, establishing or enforcing event rules, or making decisions regarding the audience. Questions regarding those matters are best directed to the event organizers.

Kessler has advocated before the Lucia Mar board for restrictions based on biological sex. Her organization’s website says Save Girls Sports Central Coast was founded in March 2025, before she launched her Assembly campaign.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In May 2025, the board voted 5-2 against placing a proposed resolution supporting Title IX and fairness in girls’ sports on a future agenda. District Superintendent Paul Fawcett said the proposal would have committed the district to advocacy directed at state and federal officials and the California Interscholastic Federation, rather than immediately changing district policies.

Kessler, who is challenging Democratic Assemblymember Dawn Addis, said her advocacy extends beyond the election and that she intends to continue pressing school officials on the issue.

"We’re not against any individuals," she said. "We’re against this state policy."

World.title: WWE's Michael Cole refuses to dip his toe into political waters, bucking trend among sports broadcasters
World.content:
Some sports broadcasters have inserted their opinions into societal issues more and more over the years.

Amazon Prime broadcaster Al Michaels took a jab at President Donald Trump renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America," former ESPN broadcaster Mark Jones had made a litany of controversial remarks during his time at the company and even NBC Sports’ Cris Collinsworth waded into political waters last year with a sly remark about the government shutdown.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Still, one of the places where broadcasters rarely – if ever – make a political comment, statement or take a quick jab is during a WWE show.

Legendary WWE broadcaster Michael Cole, who has worked for the company for three decades, has never been known to insert any type of political commentary into his calling of the matches one way or the other. Cole talked to OutKick’s Bobby Burack with OutKick Dropkick about staying out of those murky waters.

"Not at all. Again, when I started in the company 30 years ago, there was a total non-political stance. We’re out here to entertain everyone and that’s the case still today. I don’t go on social media, I just don’t," he said. "All I’m going to do is get myself in trouble if I tweet something out because someone is going to take it the wrong way, right? So, I don’t get involved in any type of social media. I don’t have Facebook. I don’t have Instagram. I don’t have any of that type of stuff.

"And when we’re on television, what I try to remember is that I’m not Sean Coulthard – my real name and my real life. I’m Michael Cole. Michael Cole is an actor. That’s my job. My job is to play a role in this weekly episodic television show that is scripted entertainment. There’s no reason for me to make a political statement on the air. None. My job is to be an actor and play by the rules of what the script tells us to do each and every week. If you follow that formula, you’ll never get yourself in trouble."

Cole being able to avoid politics is a feat in and of itself.

Everyone has an opinion, even pro wrestlers, about politics, world issues, etc. But for Cole, he believes the audience doesn’t care about the WWE figure's political point of view.

"Here’s the deal on that," he said. "No one cares what Michael Cole has to say about anything political. They don’t. Just like I don’t care about any other broadcaster and what they have to say about anything political. It doesn’t matter to me. I watch the NFL, not hear the broadcasters – they enhance the game – I watch it for the game. People don’t watch WWE for Michael Cole. They watch it for the superstars in the ring and then I hope I do my job, which is to enhance what these people are seeing on their screens.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"That’s it. No one cares who I voted for. Nobody cares what party I’m affiliated with. No one does. So, why would I go out there and put it out there. It’s silly."

Furthermore, Cole said he’s done a good job at being able to separate his WWE life and his life at home and shared a rather interesting fact about his family and their interests in pro wrestling.

"Listen, I have done a really good job separating my WWE life from my normal life," he said. "My family are not fans of the product. They don’t watch the product. In fact, today, I’m celebrating my 31st wedding anniversary. My wife has never watched one wrestling show for the 31 years we’ve been married with the exception of the match I had at WrestleMania. That’s it.

"I’m able to come home and spend my time at home, living a normal life and not talking about WWE and not talking about the company with my family and I think that has been so important to me. It’s kept me grounded and it just makes life so much better."

World.title: Man loses 15 stubborn pounds after age 50 without giving up pizza or donuts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Maintaining weight loss in midlife doesn’t necessarily require strict dietary bans or extreme fasting protocols.

Carl Daikeler, co-founder and CEO of the fitness and nutrition company BODi, says a simple routine earlier in the day has helped him manage his weight while allowing more freedom at dinner.

Los Angeles-based Daikeler, 63, who has led the health brand formerly known as Beachbody for 28 years, openly admits that he doesn't have an affinity for healthy foods.

10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG

"I eat like a third-grader, okay? Pizza's a food group," Daikeler joked in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"I'm just constantly trying to figure out how can I hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of those diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that."

When Daikeler turned 57, he found himself unable to lose 15 pounds he had gained around his waistline. Rather than adopting a strict diet, he adjusted two specific meals during the day while leaving his evening schedule unrestricted, he shared.

For breakfast, Daikeler replaced standard options with a nutrient-dense shake containing protein, fiber, prebiotics, probiotics and greens, totaling roughly 250 calories.

NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS

"I got rid of breakfast, or I changed my breakfast to this shake that we've got called Shakeology," Daikeler said. "I put some spinach in there and I put a banana in there."

For lunch, Daikeler prepares a large salad loaded with baby spinach, carrots and chicken, mixed with toppings that mask the taste of the greens.

"I hide it with some cheese, some nuts, some sliced strawberries, and it's delicious, and I put chicken in there ... I don't feel like I'm eating a bowl of vegetables, but I am."

By keeping breakfast and lunch relatively structured, Daikeler gives himself more flexibility at dinner.

BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK

"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."

He does, however, follow a single guideline regarding alcohol intake. "I'm careful not to drink too much," he said.

"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."

"Once I did that — Shakeology for breakfast, a big salad for lunch, total freedom for dinner, limited alcohol — the 15 pounds just got wiped out. And it stayed off."

Daikeler warns that overly restrictive nutrition plans are usually difficult to stick with long-term, leading many to abandon their health goals entirely.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If you're trying to be too restrictive, I don't think that's life," he said. "The whole point is living ... So if it's too restrictive, it's going to break."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Instead of completely banning indulgence foods, Daikeler recommends using portion control and mindfulness to enjoy without overeating.

"I love pizza. But I've learned that I can enjoy pizza without eating the whole pizza," he said. "I like doughnuts. I've learned that I can have literally a quarter of a doughnut and be like, that was delicious. But I get no additional satisfaction by eating the whole doughnut."

CLICK HERE TO 

For Daikeler, that balance is part of a broader focus on "health span" — prioritizing quality of life and the ability to stay active as he ages.

"Health span versus lifespan is all about quality of life," he said. "I'm all for longevity, but it's really about quality of life — a way to live and enjoy life that is balanced with maximizing your time on earth."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While Daikeler said this approach has worked for him, weight-loss strategies are not one-size-fits-all.

According to the National Institutes of Health, different eating plans can support weight loss, but the most effective approach depends on a person's individual health needs, preferences and ability to maintain the habits long-term. Individuals are generally advised to consult a doctor or registered dietitian for personalized guidance.

World.title: Food pantries overwhelmed by Trump cuts
World.content:
“There’s a decent chance we could run out,” said Likens, who runs the food pantry in Dunlow as director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, a small brick church he attended growing up.

“I don’t want them to sit in that line and not get anything,” he said. “But I don’t have a lot of extra food these days.”

Increasingly, the job of feeding the nation’s hungry is falling on the shoulders of everyday Americans like Likens, who have become the last bulwark against hunger in a land of plenty.

Likens and others on the front lines of feeding their neighbors say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. Food distribution programs are getting less food from federal programs to feed the hungry after cuts by the Trump administration. At the same time, restrictions on food stamps from the Republicans’ “big, beautiful bill” have driven up demand, while rising gas prices because of the Iran war have cut into the budgets of households and food banks alike.

Bill Likens, director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, grew up hungry in Dunlow. Now he works to make sure that doesn't happen to other kids. Mike Belleme for NBC News

The challenges extend far beyond Appalachia. An NBC News survey of 48 of the largest food banks across 35 states and Washington, D.C., found that nearly three-quarters said more people are showing up at their doors over the past year, from workers on their lunch breaks to older adults overwhelmed with medical expenses. At the same time, more than 80% said the food and funding they received through the U.S. Department of Agriculture had dropped and they were struggling with higher fuel costs for transporting food.

In Maine, Good Shepherd Food Bank said the USDA cut the amount of food it received from 13 million pounds to 9 million pounds in one year. A Michigan food bank, Forgotten Harvest, said it’s handing out less food to make sure there is enough to go around: one bag of potatoes instead of two, two tubs of yogurt as opposed to six.

“People are facing multiple hits to their budgets,” said Poonam Gupta, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a think tank that researches social and economic issues. “It is really difficult to find a way to continue affording a healthy and nutritious and balanced diet when you just have these constant hits.”

Food banks’ struggles started in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term when officials cut a $400 million Covid-era program to supply food banks with food from local farmers and paused an estimated $500 million in other planned food purchases by the USDA. Funding from Congress for a separate decades-old program to supply food banks with emergency food assistance has increased over the past several years, but many food bank leaders said they’re still getting less overall than during the Biden administration.

We want to hear from you Have you been affected by changes to the SNAP/food stamp program? Share your story here.

Trump also signed into law the new restrictions on who can receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, or food stamps, requiring nearly all able-bodied adults not caring for young children to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month. Since the law was enacted, more than 5 million people, including at least 1 million children, have lost their food benefits.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the administration’s policies, saying Trump is “uplifting every American’s financial situation” through tax cuts and efforts to increase jobs and business investments.

“President Trump is strengthening SNAP for the Americans who need it by ensuring these programs are sustainable for future generations,” Kelly said, including measures to “crack down on waste, fraud and abuse.”
