World.title: First Georgia Senate debate spotlights fight over Trump- and Biden-era policies
World.content:
It was debate night in Georgia, but President Donald Trump and former President Joe Biden seemed to be onstage.

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins squared off Thursday in the first debate in this nationally consequential Senate race, with both trying to hit the other for policies implemented by the current and former presidents.

Ossoff repeatedly asked why Collins supported tariffs that have been a key factor in the rise in the cost of consumer goods that has kept Trump’s approval ratings at historically low levels, a question Collins never directly answered.

“Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs,” Ossoff said after having already asked about Trump’s tariff regime several times.

Collins spent the hourlong debate, hosted by WANF-TV of Atlanta, not directly answering questions about the unpopular war in Iran or Trump’s economy but rather trying to saddle Ossoff with votes he took during the Biden administration to make the case that Biden is the reason for the current state of inflation and high prices.

“That Bidenomics, that Green New Deal my opponent voted for, that’s where this inflation came from,” Collins said.

The debate was broken up into four segments, but each was dominated in some form by the economy and consumer prices, topics that an NBC News poll showed are the most important issues on voters’ minds in the lead-up to Election Day.

Collins voted to support the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill, the biggest legislative achievement of Trump’s second term. The bill included provisions including no taxes on tips for hospitality workers and Social Security, which are regular midterm talking points for Republicans. But Democrats have consistently highlighted how the sweeping tax proposal disproportionately benefits the wealthy and increased the federal deficit by $1.4 trillion.

“Tax cuts are the answer to keeping more money in people’s pockets,” Collins said. “That creates ... more tax-paying people, and businesses grow.”

As Trump’s approval rating has tanked, helping Democrats overcome the GOP’s huge national financial advantage, Republican candidates across the country have distanced themselves from him on key policies ranging from tariffs to the war in Iran. Collins, however, has not been among them, keeping his place as one of Trump’s staunchest allies in key midterm Senate races.

Ossoff pressed Collins several times about why he supports Trump policies on the economy and foreign affairs.

He did say Trump’s tariffs make things “fair” in the context of trade with China and helping Georgia’s ports, which are key to the state’s economy.

“Savannah port and Brunswick port have been on my mind,” he said, without offering specifics about how the tariffs have helped them.

Pressed about the Iran war, which is increasingly unpopular, Collins defended Trump’s decision to begin bombing raids with Israel in February.

“The president had every right to make sure Iran does not get a nuclear weapon. Jon Ossoff knows this,” he said.

Ossoff has also regularly attacked Collins for continuing to support Trump’s insistence, without proof, that the 2020 presidential election was stolen, an issue that also took center stage during the debate.

“Mike Collins and Donald Trump, they are still obsessed with overturning the 2020 election,” Ossoff said.

Collins did not back down from the idea the 2020 election was stolen but focused on GOP election measures and saying Ossoff opposes the SAVE Act, a Trump-backed bill that, among other things, would require proof of citizenship to register to vote.

“Voters need confidence,” Collins said. “We live in the best country in the world, and no reason we should not have the most secure elections in the world.”

The bill has been passed in the House, but it has not had enough support in the GOP-led Senate.

Each candidate also tried to frame the other as scandal-plagued.

Ossoff hit Collins over a series of social media posts in which his son-in-law promoted white nationalist posts.

“Imagine running for the U.S. Senate while neo-Nazi propaganda is disseminated to an audience of millions from your house,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins is a bigot.”

Collins said he does not support racism or antisemitism, and he said he has told his family that.

“I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that,” Collins said of his son-in-law.

In contrast, Collins said billionaire Reid Hoffman, whose name appeared in the Epstein files, is an Ossoff donor.

“Billionaire Reid Hoffman, also one of Epstein’s buddies out there, has funneled money into his campaign,” Collins said.

Authorities have not accused Hoffman of wrongdoing in connection with Epstein. Hoffman has said he regrets having associated with Epstein.

Ossoff has been the subject of significant national speculation about whether he wants to run for president in 2028, which he has said he has “no interest” in, but that has not kept him off early shortlists.

That idea is bolstered by the fact that $50 million of the more than $100 million he has raised is from so-called small-dollar donors, which are relatively small contributions typically raised through email and other digital means from supporters across the country. An ability to digitally raise money at that clip is generally a sign of a candidate’s national name identification and support among the party’s most intense base voters, who often play an outsize role in helping choose presidential nominees.

Collins has raised more than $7 million for his campaign, according to the most recent campaign finance reports, and he has gotten his biggest boost, $25 million, from the Senate Leadership Fund, a national group that supports GOP Senate candidates.

At the beginning of the 2026 midterm cycle, the Georgia contest was seen as likely to be one of the closest in the country and a key component for Republicans as they try to hold on to their slim majority in the Senate.

The race, however, has slowly trended Ossoff’s way. Most public polling has him with a sizable lead, including a YouGov poll released last month that had him topping Collins by 10 percentage points. The poll, which has a margin of error of 2.7 percentage points, was conducted Sept. 15-18.

Georgia is still seen as a key midterm Senate battleground contest, but many Republicans see it slipping away and are focusing on other states, like Texas, Maine, North Carolina and Alaska, to try to maintain control of the Senate.

Each candidate used his finishing remarks to attack the other.

Ossoff said Collins, who runs a trucking company started by his father, a former congressman, misleads about his professional record.

“Mike has called himself a trucker,” Ossoff said. “This is a congressman’s son who inherited a seat in Congress.”

Collins got the final word, once again hitting Ossoff for voting on Biden-era policies.

“We still have not heard why Jon Ossoff votes the way he does,” Collins said. “Why he voted against our farmers ... why he voted against hardworking Georgians out there.”

World.title: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico off the trail with the flu
World.content:
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.

But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days.

His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend.

While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.

It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date.

“We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.”

While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation.

“He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event.

“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”

Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail.

“After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.”

Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him.

Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem.

“Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.”

Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election.

Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence.

“It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.”

To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention.

At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail.

“You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said Wednesday at a rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”

After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton.

“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social.

It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though he’s not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media:

“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX.”

World.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay
World.content:
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African legal pioneer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for defending international law and institutions in a world in which increasingly “might overtakes right.”

Pillay, 85, has a decadeslong career that spans defending Nelson Mandela and standing up against the racist apartheid regime in South Africa, to leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

01:21 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay 00:00 00:00

Using the award to make a wider point about geopolitics, Frydnes contrasted Pillay’s work with the wider international “shift towards power politics,” in which “international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”

Her “distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” he said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

Pillay learned of her prize at the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany. She told an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” prompting laughter.

That was a reference to President Donald Trump’s long-standing ambitions to win the Nobel Peace Prize, and the offer by last year’s winner, Maria Corina Machado, to share it with him as she sought support for her efforts in Venezuela.

“Everybody asks me: ‘When are you going to stop? When are you going to stop?’” Pillay said, adding that despite turning 85 last month, she had no intention of doing so.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza, namely what’s happening there is genocide,” she said to cheers.

“One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage,” she added. “But why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law and you look at all the facts.”

Having just been told the news, she added jokingly, “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”

Among her many positions, Pillay has been a judge on the International Criminal Court

Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, was in Germany and among the first people to tell Pillay she had won.

“This could not be a better choice at a time of attacks against international justice,” Callamard told NBC News. “She is a former ICC judge at a time when the U.S. administration is seeking to destroy the ICC” and she led the U.N. commission “which found that Israel committed the crime of genocide at a time when many states are trying to defend and protect Israel’s actions.”

Pillay was not among the front-runners, who included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, and Mykola Kuleba, who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly taken to Russia.

Trump was among the 287 candidates, according to the leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia, who said they nominated him. But Trump said this week he didn’t think he would win.

“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

World.title: Hurricane Isaias strengthening, heading for northern Gulf Coast. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, has been intensifying as it makes its way toward the northern Gulf Coast. It's forecast to reach land tonight or early Saturday, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle.

"Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today," the National Hurricane Center said.

Isaias is a Category 2 storm with maximum sustained winds of 110 miles per hour, but on the verge of becoming a Category 3, which would make it a major hurricane. Its winds only have to increase 1 mph for that to happen, and the hurricane center says that's likely to occur this morning.

Maps show hurricane's path

A hurricane warning is in effect for the coast from Ocean Springs, Mississippi to the Bay/Gulf County Line in Florida. Landfall is expected within the warning area, the hurricane center says.

The core of Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," was about 200 miles south-southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River, rushing north-northeast at 24 mph, according to the hurricane center's latest update early Friday. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 30 miles from the storm's center, and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 185 miles.

"Isaias is expected to approach the U.S. northern Gulf Coast this afternoon and make landfall within the warning area tonight or early Saturday," the Miami-based center says. "Slight weakening is expected before landfall, but it is expected to remain a dangerous hurricane."

Map shows the potential path of Hurricane Isaias as it heads toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued for the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish Line in Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi and east of the Bay/Gulf County Line to the Aucilla River in Florida. A storm surge warning was up for the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River and a storm surge watch was in effect for the Suwannee River to Yankeetown, Florida.

Map shows watches and warnings as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 4 to 8 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast from southern Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and Florida's Big Bend and southwest Georgia. Also, 2 to 5 inches are expected across much of the rest of the Southeast, with up to 10 inches possible, especially across the Southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.

Map shows the 3-day rain forecast for the Gulf Coast and Southeast from Hurricane Isaias. CBS News

What's more, the center said "a tornado risk will begin late this afternoon and continue tonight in coastal areas of Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, and far southwest Georgia. The tornado threat will continue Saturday across parts of eastern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, Georgia, and the Carolinas."

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a Thursday news conference that twisters can occur far from the center of the storm. "Please be on the lookout. Even if you're way outside the cone, you could still have tornado risks."

Evacuations underway

Evacuations have been ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which are both in the Panhandle.

Kelly Benzon, visiting the Panhandle from Illinois, said he was evacuating. "I don't want to be trying to get out of here in the pouring down rain and wind so we're gonna be smart and we're gonna move," he said.

Voluntary evacuations were in place for coastal spots in southeastern Alabama, with officials in the city of Gulf Shores urging non-residents to leave the area to "help reduce congestion, support emergency operations, and ensure the safety of those who may be most vulnerable during the storm."

Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News that his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community was whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.

"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."

DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in Florida, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties. Government buildings will close in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also declared a state of emergency.

The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay
World.content:
The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 was awarded Friday to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born former judge with the International Criminal Court who went on to become the United Nations human rights chief and is still serving with the U.N.'s other judicial body, the International Court of Justice. She also led a U.N. inquiry last year that accused Israel of genocide in the Gaza Strip, and Israel was quick to condemn her receiving the honor on Friday.

The Nobel Committee said it was honoring Pillay "for her efforts to promote peace and international law," and that awarding the prize to someone with her body of work on international justice was a message to those seeking to undermine international law institutions.

The South African-born former United Nations human rights chief, who is 85, was recognized for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

"This is definitely a message to those who are undermining the international system and institutions," Frydnes said.

"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack," he said, noting what the committee saw as a shift "towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice."

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has come under fire from Israel and the Trump administration in recent years, with the U.S. imposing sanctions against the U.N. court last year after it issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump accused the court of "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel."

The ICC condemned the U.S. sanctions against its staff and said they were intended to "harm (the Court's) independent and impartial judicial work."

Pillay served as an ICC judge from 2003 until 2008, when she resigned to take on the role of United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She was the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that said last year it had concluded Israel's actions in Gaza amounted to genocide. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous."

Then-United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay speaks during a press conference at the United Nations offices in Geneva, Dec. 2, 2013. Murat Unlu/Anadolu Agency/Getty

The Israeli Foreign Ministry blasted the Nobel committee for awarding the prize to Pillay on Friday, saying in a statement posted online that "if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."

It condemned the committee for awarding her as "the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice."

Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge for the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is separate to the ICC, in the case of Gambia v. Myanmar, in which Myanmar's ruling military junta stands accused of genocide over its treatment of the nation's Rohingya Muslim minority in the western state of Rakhine.

Frydnes said the committee wasn't immediately able to reach Pillay Friday to tell her she had been awarded the prize, adding from the podium that if she was watching and saw a call coming in from a Norwegian phone number, to "please pick up."

Pillay soon appeared in a video posted on social media by the head of Amnesty International, being applauded by well-wishers at the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, Germany.

"If you clap a little bit louder I may share this prize with Trump," she quipped, drawing laughs from the crowd. She said that when she was informed that she had been awarded the prize, she first thought "it must be a joke," and that as a "lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this thing."

South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief Navi Pillay speaks about being awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, Oct. 9, 2026, in Nuremburg, Germany, in an image from video posted online by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard. Agnes Callamard/X

She noted that she was lauded by the Nobel committee for her courage, which she questioned, saying: "You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's an impartial decision you make."

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness."

Machado gave President Trump, who has long said he deserves the prize, her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: The Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.

Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.

Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize Thursday for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).

Education activist Malala Yousafzai is the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate; she won at 17 in 2014.

The United States is the most-credited country, with 24 awards naming U.S. institutions or individuals, ahead of the United Kingdom (13) and Switzerland (11). No laureate listed as American has won since then-President Barack Obama was awarded in 2009.

The prize has gone unawarded on 19 occasions, most of them during the world wars. In 1948, the year Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, no prize was awarded; he had been nominated 12 times and never won.

In 1939, a Swedish member of parliament nominated Adolf Hitler, then withdrew the nomination, saying it was never meant seriously.

World.title: Chipotle shares jump after report that Starbucks has explored a takeover
World.content:
Chipotle Mexican Grill's stock jumped as much as 8% on Thursday after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks has explored a deal to buy the "fast-casual" restaurant chain.

A potential merger would represent one of the largest restaurant acquisitions in history, according to industry analysts. In 2014, Burger King acquired Canadian chain Tim Hortons in an $11.4 billion deal that remains one of the largest restaurant buyouts to date, according to Melius Research.

Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol was previously chief executive of Chipotle, whose stock price has dropped about 50% since he left the post in August 2024. Its stock has lost about 20% of its value over the past year. Starbucks shares slipped about 4.4% in earlier trading on Thursday before recovering to end the day largely flat.



Starbucks has recently sought counsel on a proposal to take over Chipotle, a $41 billion chain, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. It is unclear if Starbucks has made a formal offer to acquire the restaurant chain, the media outlet reported.

Neither company responded to CBS News' requests for comment on the report.

"Chipotle has struggled since Brian Niccol's departure and is pulling several levers to incentivize its customer base into visiting more often," analysts with Seaport Research Partners, an investor advisory firm, said in a report. "If synergies are not the primary motivation, then a key question for Brian Niccol would be what he would do differently than Chipotle's current management team."

Chipotle's same-store sales dropped 2.5% in the fourth quarter of 2025, but rebounded in early 2026. The company reported revenue of $3.3 billion for the second quarter of 2026, up 9.3% compared to the year-ago period. The increase was driven by 100 new restaurant openings and growth in same-store sales, Chipotle said.

On his second day as Starbucks CEO, in September 2024, Niccol launched a marketing campaign to return to what he described as the coffeehouse's roots: a "welcoming coffeehouse where people gather, and where we serve the finest coffee, handcrafted by our skilled baristas."

Last month, Niccol said the company has made "tremendous progress" in delivering on the promise to improve customer service and restore human connection in its cafes.

"Starbucks' turnaround initiatives are beginning to deliver positive traffic, but U.S. operating margins remain pressured," Melius Research analysts said in a report. They added that Niccol's time at the helm of Chipotle gives him "considerable familiarity with the business he is reportedly considering acquiring."

Still, Wall Street analysts said there are no obvious synergies between the two companies, while TD Cowen analysts said they view the deal "as a low-probability outcome at this stage."

"We argue Brian Niccol's priority at Starbucks has been executing the 'Back to Starbucks' U.S. turnaround," and pursuing a $40 billion acquisition would seem "inconsistent" with that goal, TD Cowen said.

World.title: 8 hospitalized after turbulence forces flight to divert to MIA, officials say
World.content:
Eight people were rushed to a Miami hospital early Friday morning after a flight to New York City was forced to divert to Miami International Airport due to severe turbulence, according to officials.

According to officials at Miami International Airport, Avianca Flight 042 was headed from Medellín, Colombia, to New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport when the severe turbulence was reported.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue told CBS News Miami that "multiple patients" were injured, and the flight landed safely at MIA around 3:30 a.m. Friday.

"When we arrived, when we landed, we saw that very close to where we were going to disembark, there were more than five or six ambulances. Seven of them with their lights on as if they were waiting for something," passenger Maria Paula Jimenez told CBS News Miami in Spanish. "When we arrived, well, you know, it wasn't normal."

Eight of the injured passengers were brought to the hospital after the plane landed, MDFR continued.

The extent of the injuries is unknown.

CBS News Miami has reached out for more information and will update this story as soon as new details are received.
