World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: US plans its first military execution since 1961, by firing squad and livestreamed
World.content:
US plans its first military execution since 1961, by firing squad and livestreamed

9th Friday, October 2026 - 07:48 UTC Full article

Hasan, then an Army major, opened fire with a semi-automatic pistol on November 5, 2009, at a medical centre on the base where soldiers were being prepared for deployment to Afghanistan

The Pentagon will livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the military psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, scheduled for December 3. It will be the first execution carried out by the US armed forces since 1961, the first by firing squad since 1945 and the first publicly broadcast in the country’s history.

“The secretary is right. It will be livestreamed. Details will be released later,” a senior Defense Department official confirmed. The secretary, Pete Hegseth, had announced the plan in an interview with the Human Events Daily programme on the conservative network Real America’s Voice. “We’ll make sure people can see it, that it’s public. Because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for this kind of thing,” he said. Asked about the condemned man’s last wishes, he replied: “I don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

The execution will take place at Fort Hood around 1pm, at the same site and close to the time of the shooting. Military law requires presidential approval for a firing-squad execution; the Pentagon said on Monday that President Donald Trump had given it on Hegseth’s recommendation.

Hasan, then an Army major, opened fire with a semi-automatic pistol on November 5, 2009, at a medical centre on the base where soldiers were being prepared for deployment to Afghanistan. He killed 13 people and wounded 32. A military jury sentenced him to death in August 2013. He represented himself, admitted the attack and said he had “switched sides” to defend the Taliban. He was left paraplegic by police gunfire and is held at the Fort Leavenworth military prison in Kansas. The Supreme Court declined to review his case in March 2025.

The last military execution was that of Private John Bennett, hanged in 1961. In 2008, President George W. Bush approved the execution of Ronald Gray, but a federal court stayed it. The last public execution in the United States took place in 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky.

Since 1976 only six civilians have been executed by firing squad in the country, three in Utah and three in South Carolina, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The Trump administration expanded the execution methods authorised for the most serious federal crimes, partly because of difficulties obtaining lethal injection drugs.

World.title: US charges Maduro and Cilia Flores with torture and repression in Venezuela
World.content:
US charges Maduro and Cilia Flores with torture and repression in Venezuela

9th Friday, October 2026 - 07:35 UTC Full article

Maduro and Flores, held since January 3 following a US operation in Caracas and detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, have pleaded not guilty to all charges

US federal prosecutors on Thursday brought new torture and repression charges against former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, adding to the drug trafficking and narco-terrorism case both face in a New York court. The same day, the judge denied a request by Flores for house arrest on health grounds.

According to the indictment, between 1999 and 2025 Maduro, Flores and senior officials around them “created and maintained a violent system of repression” in Venezuela, in which thousands of people were detained, tortured or killed by state agents. Prosecutors allege that Maduro “presided over this system”, “ordered the unlawful detention and torture of specific individuals” and received reports on particular prisoners, and that Flores helped develop it. The filing attributes a role to the so-called colectivos — armed civilian groups aligned with chavismo — the FARC guerrilla and the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence.

The new charges are based on testimony from at least three former senior officials of Maduro’s government, identified in the document by codes, who say they supervised or took part in torture, including of at least three US citizens. According to the indictment, victims suffered beatings, simulated drowning and electric shocks. Former military intelligence chief Hugo Carvajal, a co-defendant in the drug case, pleaded guilty in 2025 and has offered to testify.

Maduro and Flores, held since January 3 following a US operation in Caracas and detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, have pleaded not guilty to all charges. Their defence is seeking recognition of head-of-state immunity. Prosecutors respond that the United States never recognised Maduro as president and that acting president Delcy Rodríguez’s government has not sought, through diplomatic channels, either their release or their immunity. The issue will be addressed at a hearing on November 17; the trial is scheduled to begin on June 1, 2027.

Flores’s defence cited heart palpitations, epigastric pain and weight loss of around 11 kilograms, and proposed moving her to a private residence with guards and an electronic tag. Prosecutors opposed the request, citing an “extreme risk of flight” and saying she has refused some medical tests. The judge rejected the request but did not rule out revisiting it if her health deteriorates.

The UN Human Rights Council’s fact-finding mission has documented human rights violations in Venezuela committed since 2014.

World.title: Why Argentina's Falklands sanctions do not automatically reach Sea Lion's operator
World.content:
Why Argentina's Falklands sanctions do not automatically reach Sea Lion's operator

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:29 UTC Full article

Photo: Raphael WOLLMANN / Getty Images

The sanctions Argentina has imposed on companies involved in the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands target specific entities rather than entire corporate groups, so the subsidiary currently operating the field is not automatically covered, according to a legal analysis by specialist site Diplomacy & Law.

Argentina's Energy Secretariat declared Rockhopper Exploration plc's activities illegal in 2012 and barred it from operating in the country for 20 years in 2013. In 2022 it imposed a similar sanction on Navitas Petroleum LP. But the project's current operator is Navitas Petroleum Development and Production Ltd, a UK subsidiary of the Israeli group. “A sanction imposed on Navitas Petroleum LP does not automatically become an identical sanction against every affiliated company,” writes the author, Edmarverson A. Santos, unless the law expressly provides for it or a new measure is adopted.

Argentina's legal framework nonetheless reaches beyond licence holders. Law 26,659 of 2011 prohibits direct or indirect participation in hydrocarbon exploration or exploitation that the country regards as unauthorised on its continental shelf, with bans of five to 20 years. Subject to its conditions, it covers shareholders, service providers, financiers, logistics operators and technical advisers. Law 26,915 of 2013 added penalties for directors and companies.

The decree signed by President Javier Milei on September 3 designated the foreign ministry as the enforcing authority, set short deadlines for proceedings and required compliance declarations from those applying for the large-investment incentive regime or hydrocarbon permits in the country. That mechanism explains the effect on companies with business in Argentina: Halliburton, SLB and Baker Hughes have said they will not work on Sea Lion, and Halliburton said the authorities raised criminal and civil enforcement with it.

The analysis distinguishes between making rules and enforcing them. Argentina can deny permits and benefits and sanction those under its jurisdiction, but it cannot exercise coercive authority in the archipelago or another state without an independent legal basis or that country's cooperation. For companies with no ties to Argentina, the risk is mainly reputational or commercial.

None of these measures resolves the underlying question. “Falkland licences cannot establish British title to the islands, and Argentine administrative resolutions cannot establish Argentine title,” the author concludes. The United Kingdom maintains that the activity is legitimate and governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law; Argentina maintains its sovereignty claim and holds that the licences are invalid.

World.title: What could happen when Argentina's Sea Lion ultimatum to the UK expires
World.content:
What could happen when Argentina's Sea Lion ultimatum to the UK expires

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:18 UTC Full article

Milei ordered on September 28 the start of arbitration and said that, if London does not act, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea

The two-week deadline Argentina gave the United Kingdom to halt the Sea Lion oil project in the North Falklands basin expires around October 12. Its expiry will not in itself suspend the project or establish a British breach of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, according to a legal analysis published by specialist site Diplomacy & Law.

President Javier Milei ordered on September 28 the start of arbitration under Annex VII of the convention and said that, if London does not act, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The analysis's author, Edmarverson A. Santos, stresses that the deadline was set by Argentina and does not derive from the convention, and that the government's instruction and the formal start of proceedings are separate steps: arbitration begins with written notification to the other state, accompanied by the claim and its grounds. There is no record that this has been sent.

The Annex VII route reflects both countries' choices. Under Article 287 of the convention, Argentina chose the Hamburg tribunal as its first preference and the United Kingdom the International Court of Justice; where the parties do not coincide, the dispute goes to arbitration. Beforehand, Article 283 requires an exchange of views on how to settle the dispute, something a tribunal would have to assess.

If Argentina seeks provisional measures, the Hamburg tribunal could order them while the arbitral tribunal is being constituted, provided it considers that the latter would have prima facie jurisdiction and that the matter is urgent. Such measures would be provisional, not a ruling on sovereignty or the merits.

The main obstacle is jurisdiction. Convention tribunals can only rule on its interpretation or application, not on territorial title. In the 2015 arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands, the tribunal declined to rule on a claim whose real subject was sovereignty; in the 2020 case between Ukraine and Russia, it excluded claims requiring a decision on Crimea, though proceedings continued on the rest. In addition, both countries have made declarations under Article 298: Argentina excluded maritime delimitation disputes, among others, in 1995, and the United Kingdom made exclusions in 2003 and, according to the analysis, again in 2020.

“Argentina would need to formulate claims capable of adjudication under UNCLOS without requiring the tribunal to decide, expressly or implicitly, sovereignty over the Falkland Islands,” the author concludes.

The United Kingdom rejected the arbitration on September 30 and maintains that the activity is governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law. Sea Lion, developed by Navitas and Rockhopper, has had a final investment decision since December 2025.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro proposes constitutional reform to overhaul the courts and lower the criminal age
World.content:
Flávio Bolsonaro proposes constitutional reform to overhaul the courts and lower the criminal age

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:10 UTC Full article

The candidate said he intended to use his party's legislative weight to choose the presiding officers of both chambers and “amend the Constitution, to redemocratise the country”

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who will face Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil's presidential runoff on October 25, has said that if he wins he will use his Liberal Party's congressional bloc to push a constitutional reform that would change the judiciary, lower the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 and abolish presidential re-election.

On Tuesday, at an event in Goiânia, the candidate said he intended to use his party's legislative weight to choose the presiding officers of both chambers and “amend the Constitution, to redemocratise the country, so that institutions once again respect the Constitution”. Amid concern over the remark, he set out the scope of the reform in Brasília on Wednesday and responded to those fearing an authoritarian turn: “I've seen people saying that now, with a majority, Flávio will do what his father didn't. Stop that. Let's come back down to the real world.” His father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup.

A constitutional amendment in Brazil requires three fifths of each chamber in two votes: 308 of 513 deputies and 49 of 81 senators. According to the newspaper El País, the Liberal Party won 121 seats in the Chamber of Deputies on Sunday, 20% more than in 2022, and with its allies would hold around 50 in the Senate. Those elected include the former president's wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, and his son Carlos, as senators.

Bolsonaro this week won the backing of two first-round candidates. Ronaldo Caiado, a former governor of Goiás who won around 2.2% of the vote, endorsed him at the Goiânia event: “I'm here to defeat the PT.” Former Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema, with less than 1%, did so on Monday. São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas, re-elected on Sunday, also attended.

Bolsonaro, who won 47% of valid votes to Lula's 45%, had already announced on Monday plans to cut the number of ministries and appoint at least four Supreme Federal Court justices. Lula held no public events on Monday or Tuesday and met his campaign team in Brasília, which has said the president will seek direct confrontation in the runoff.

World.title: Stuart Lawrence, for three decades a captain of Britain's Antarctic ships, has died
World.content:
Stuart Lawrence, for three decades a captain of Britain's Antarctic ships, has died

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:07 UTC Full article

He was awarded the Polar Medal in 1983 and appointed MBE in 1998. He retired in 2003 after 33 Antarctic voyages and 42 years at sea, with a farewell from the Ernest Shackleton in Stanley

Captain Stuart Lawrence MBE, who for more than three decades commanded the British Antarctic Survey vessels RRS Bransfield and RRS Ernest Shackleton, has died suddenly, according to the National Coastwatch Institution in Gosport, southern England, where he served as a volunteer watchkeeper.

His calling began at the age of five in Grimsby, where he lived on the same street as a Cunard liner captain. He entered the HMS Conway training ship at 13 and spent his seventeenth birthday as a Canadian Pacific cadet. He was about to join the Royal National Lifeboat Institution when its head, Admiral Egg Irving, urged him instead to sail to the Antarctic. He joined the British Antarctic Survey in 1970 and remained until 2003.

After two voyages on the John Biscoe, he moved to the Bransfield, taking temporary command in 1972 and permanent command in 1974. He took her every year to Halley, the organisation's most southerly station, through the Weddell Sea. In 1984, the UK Antarctic Place-Names Committee named Lawrence Channel, on the Antarctic Peninsula, after him. From 1999 he commanded the Ernest Shackleton.

Days before the 1982 Argentine invasion, he hosted a reception on board in Stanley. He sailed on March 31 and, halfway to Tierra del Fuego, learned of the invasion from Patrick Watts' radio broadcasts and alerted the organisation's headquarters in Britain. By his own account, he later had to restrain part of the crew, who wanted to return and scuttle the ship at the entrance to Stanley Harbour.

Ships under his command were regular visitors to Montevideo on voyages to Stanley and Antarctica, according to those who sailed with him.

He was awarded the Polar Medal in 1983 and appointed MBE in 1998. He retired in 2003 after 33 Antarctic voyages and 42 years at sea, with a farewell from the Ernest Shackleton in Stanley. His wife, Sue, had died months earlier.

He later worked for the UK Hydrographic Office and as an ice master on cruise ships, and from 2017 volunteered at the Gosport coastwatch station. “A watch with Stuart would be one of professionally recording every detail and aspect of incidents at sea, interspersed with tales of the Antarctic and any number of anecdotes,” the institution wrote.

World.title: What was the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two thirds of its nests
World.content:
What was the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two thirds of its nests

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:54 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicole Richters

The chinstrap penguin population on Zavodovski Island, in the South Sandwich Islands, has fallen by almost two thirds since 2011, according to a study by the British Antarctic Survey. The island, described that year as the world's largest penguin colony, has lost that title.

Researchers recorded 63% fewer occupied nests in 2025 than in 2011. That year, the same organisation estimated that some 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nested on the island. For the new study, a team sailed for 15 days to Zavodovski, a volcanic island north of the Antarctic continent administered by the United Kingdom, and used drones, aerial photography, satellite imagery and tracking devices fitted to 20 birds.

According to the study's lead, Professor Norman Ratcliffe, the cause is ocean warming. “With waters warming, the krill the chinstrap penguins eat have moved southwards. Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food,” he said. The researchers believe the species may now qualify as officially endangered.

The team ruled out other explanations. The island's volcano, Mount Curry, last erupted significantly in 2016, while the decline has been steady since 2011. Nor do they attribute the fall to competition for krill from humpback whales, which in turn help boost krill production.

By contrast, the macaroni penguin population increased markedly. Tracking data show they forage in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where they are likely supplementing their diet with fish and other crustaceans. Ratcliffe described the shift as “the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica” and as “further evidence of how rapid warming is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems”.

The world's largest penguin colony is now at Cape Adare, in the Ross Sea, more than 5,000 kilometres away on the other side of the Antarctic continent.

The study comes days after Antarctic sea ice recorded its third-lowest winter maximum since satellite measurements began this year.

World.title: On the war's third anniversary, 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza
World.content:
On the war's third anniversary, 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:53 UTC Full article

Some 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza for medical treatment, according to the territory's Hamas-run Health Ministry, as three years pass since the group's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed around 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and triggered the war.

To leave the Strip, patients need a referral from the Health Ministry, acceptance by a host country and Israeli security clearance. Among those recently evacuated is Raseel, a six-year-old girl injured at the al-Mawasi displacement camp in July, who travelled to Egypt in late September with support from the World Health Organization. Witnesses attributed the strike to an Israeli helicopter; the Israeli military said it had no record of a strike at that time and place.

Doctors warn that antibiotic-resistant infections are complicating the recovery of the wounded. A study shared with the BBC World Service, based on almost 80,000 bacterial samples collected at 11 hospitals between 2015 and 2025, found widespread resistance to key antibiotics. It was carried out by Gaza-based researchers with support from Imperial College London and the American University of Beirut; it has not yet been peer-reviewed and its findings are preliminary. “We will see the number of amputations rise, even if the war stops,” said Awni al-Jaafarawi, a Médecins Sans Frontières doctor at Nasser hospital.

The researchers link the problem to the destruction of water and sanitation. According to the UN, almost 90% of that infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged, and more than 80% of families face water insecurity. Cogat, the Israeli body that manages access to Gaza, says the water supplied exceeds the UN humanitarian threshold and that medicines, including antibiotics, enter without restriction.

Gaza's Health Ministry puts the number of Palestinians killed since the war began at more than 74,000, and at 1,421 since the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025. Israel disputes the figures and says it acts to minimise harm to civilians.

World.title: Inflation rises to 3.45% in September as fruit and vegetable prices climb nearly 9%
World.content:
Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate increased for a second consecutive month in September, rising to 3.45%, the national statistics agency INEGI reported Thursday.

The headline rate rose 0.19 percentage points from a 3.26% reading in August.

The annual core inflation rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, fell to 3.75% in September from 3.88% in August. INEGI reported that month-over-month inflation was 0.42% in September.

The annual headline rate reached its highest level since May in September. However, the rate was still well below the 2026 peak, which was 4.59% in March.

The publication of the inflation data for September comes two weeks after the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) board voted in favor of maintaining the central bank’s benchmark interest rate at 6.50%. Banxico targets annual inflation of 3% but tolerates a 2%-4% range. The central bank’s board will hold its next monetary policy meeting on Nov. 5.

Fruit and vegetable prices rise almost 9% annually

Fruit and vegetable prices rose 8.78% in the 12 months to September, the largest increase among the categories of goods and services tracked by INEGI. In contrast, meat prices fell 4.46% annually.

World.title: Mexico’s auto parts output hit a record high in July, but assembled vehicle production and exports are declining
World.content:
Mexico’s auto parts production registered record figures in July, while the country’s automotive industry experienced double-digit declines in both vehicle production and exports in September.

The National Auto Parts Industry (INA) released the July figures this week, reporting that production grew 7.15% in July compared to a year earlier, reaching a value of US $10.85 billion.

As the main supplier of auto parts to the United States, Mexico accounted for 43.6% of total U.S. imports of parts and components in July.

INA’s monthly report for July 2026 showed that between January and July, cumulative auto parts production reached US $74.68 billion, an 8.8% increase compared to the first seven months of 2025.

The increase occurred even as the United States reduced purchases of auto parts from around the world this year (reflecting its own 1.5% drop in car production).

The auto parts sector recorded exports of US $64.96 billion and imports of US $43.315 billion during the first seven months of the year, generating a trade surplus of US $21.643 billion.

Meanwhile, Mexico’s auto production registered its worst drop in nearly five years as vehicle assembly fell 15.1% year-on-year in September. At the same time, shipments abroad decreased 11.8%, the biggest drop since December of last year.

According to national statistics agency INEGI, automakers based in Mexico manufactured 301,803 light vehicles last month, 15.1% less than the 355,589 units assembled in September 2025.

This decline is the steepest for a month since November 2021, when auto production contracted 17.3%, amidst the COVID-19 pandemic and a global shortage of semiconductors.

The decline also impacted the year-to-date balance, as production reached 2,946,943 vehicles through September, 2.42% less than the 3,020,006 assembled in the same period of 2025.

Meanwhile, exports totaled 277,369 units in September, a drop of 11.85%, the largest decrease since December 2025, when shipments fell 14.5%.

In terms of export volume, this represented the lowest level for a September since 2021 (during the pandemic), when shipments abroad registered a drop of 24%.

Despite this, Mexico maintains its position as the leading supplier of vehicles to the United States, even as its exports face a tariff disadvantage (Mexican vehicles pay a tariff of up to 25%, while those from Japan and South Korea face a rate of just 15%).

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Searching mothers help uncover alleged ‘extermination center’ in Nayarit
World.content:
State and federal authorities are examining a property in Nayarit that was described by the state attorney general as an “extermination center” and “another version of the Izaguirre Ranch” — a site in Jalisco where the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) allegedly killed and/or cremated a significant number of people.

The property in Nayarit, located in the municipality of Xalisco south of state capital Tepic, was located by the Nayarit Attorney General’s Office on Saturday. An anonymous tip-off led authorities to the site in the community of La Curva where a “makeshift burner” and a pit containing the remains of recently cremated bodies were found, according to Nayarit Attorney General Elvia Ludmila Heredia Verdugo.

“Since October 3, we have been processing an incineration-based extermination center,” Heredia told a press conference on Monday.

“On Saturday, [searching] mothers joined the work. We’ve already found clothing and a makeshift burner. A drum is … filled with diesel, gasoline and soap. … Bodies are burned, bones are reduced to ashes, and they’re thrown into a [nearby] stream,” she said.

“… We’re also processing a grave where we’re collecting charred bones. … It turns out that we now have another version of the Izaguirre Ranch,” Heredia said.

Authorities have not said how many people they believe were killed and/or cremated at the property, and have not linked any specific criminal group to the site. The El Universal newspaper reported that there are “unconfirmed” claims that the property was used by the CJNG.

The discovery of clandestine graves where criminal groups have dumped bodies is common in Mexico. Such discoveries underscore Mexico’s disappearance crisis, with more than 130,000 people registered as missing or unaccounted for nationwide.

CNB sends a ‘technical team’ to Nayarit to strengthen search efforts

The National Search Commission (CNB) announced on Wednesday that it had sent a “technical team” to Nayarit to “strengthen the search work” at the property and contribute to the “rigorous and expeditious processing” of the site, “in coordination with the appropriate authorities.”

In a statement, the CNB noted that the Nayarit Attorney General’s Office is in charge of the processing of the site, the collection of evidence and “expert work” aimed at identifying the number of victims and their identities.

The CNB expressed its commitment to “accompanying” the families of missing people and ensuring that they receive “verified, transparent and timely information” about the progress made in examining the site and the “results” obtained.

Félix Arturo Medina Padilla, deputy minister for human rights in the Interior Ministry, of which the CNB is part, shared the search commission’s statement on social media, writing in the same post that “the search for missing persons is a national priority for the Mexican government.”

https://t.co/5UGi1snxI9 — Comisión Nal. de Búsqueda Mx (@Busqueda_MX) October 7, 2026

‘We are still here, we are still searching,’ says Nayarit-based collective

In a Facebook post on Wednesday, the Families United for Nayarit Collective (Cofaunnay) said that its members remained at the “search area” in the community of La Curva.

It said they are “monitoring the forensic recovery work derived from the discovery of human remains … at the property called ‘El Dragón.'”

“… The families [of missing people] continue to work with responsibility, respect and sensitivity, striving at all times to preserve the evidence, respect the investigative processes, and protect the dignity of the individuals and their families,” Cofaunnay said.

“… We will continue to do what we know how to do: search, accompany [authorities], document, and demand truth and justice. We are still here, until we find them. WE ARE STILL HERE. WE ARE STILL SEARCHING,” the collective said.

Alma Ríos, a member of the collective, told the Associated Press that the discovery of the property in the municipality of Xalisco has given her hope that her husband, Alberto López, can be found. Ríos has been searching for him since he was abducted in September 2019.

A reminder of the Izaguirre Ranch case

As Heredia indicated, the recently-discovered property in Xalisco, Nayarit, has similarities to the Izaguirre Ranch, which was discovered in Teuchitlán, Jalisco, in early 2025 by a collective that searches for disappeared persons. In March 2025, the Warrior Searchers of Jalisco collective found more than 150 pairs of shoes and human remains at the ranch, leading various media outlets to dub the property an “extermination camp.”

However, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch subsequently said there was no evidence that the property was “an extermination camp.” Rather, it was “a training center” for the CJNG, he said in late March 2025.

Nevertheless, human remains — some of which showed signs of cremation — were found on the property. It is not yet been been determined how many people they correspond to.

Earlier this year, the Federal Attorney General’s Office reported that 47 people had been arrested in connection with the Izaguirre Ranch case. Ten men implicated in the case received lengthy prison sentences last year after they were convicted of kidnapping and murder

With reports from EFE, El Universal, La Jornada and El País

World.title: Puerto Vallarta, San Miguel de Allende rank among world’s 5 best small cities in Condé Nast Traveler readers’ poll
World.content:
Readers of the highly regarded magazine Condé Nast Traveler have named two Mexican towns — Puerto Vallarta and San Miguel de Allende — as the second- and fourth-best small cities in the world.

The port and resort city of Puerto Vallarta on the state of Jalisco’s Pacific coast finished a close second behind only Canada’s Victoria, which was voted No. 1 for the fourth year in a row. The historic colonial town of San Miguel de Allende, in the state of Guanajuato, was edged out for the No.3 spot by Florence, Italy.

Condé Nast Traveler is part of the Condé Nast media empire that includes such high-end magazines as The New Yorker and Vanity Fair. Nearly 800,000 of its famously discerning readers participated in its annual Readers’ Choice Awards, with the two Mexican destinations in the poll’s top 10, joining such favorite sites as Venice (No. 9), Porto (7) and Lucerne ( 5).

Why San Miguel is the world’s No. 4 small city

The UNESCO World Heritage Site of San Miguel de Allende has made Condé Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards list seven years in a row, thanks to the city’s blend of colonial charm, modern amenities and cultural offerings

“A hub for expat artists, this highland city is known for its Spanish Colonial architecture and colorful façades,” the magazine said.

Condé Nast Traveler referred to the city’s vibrant art scene with attractions such as Fábrica La Aurora, a former textile factory that is now home to galleries and pop-up shops. It also mentioned the Rosewood San Miguel de Allende hotel, “a hidden oasis” in the middle of the city.

Why Puerto Vallarta is the world’s No. 2 small city

Puerto Vallarta reinforced its position as the second-best small city in the world for a second consecutive year, despite a prevalent stereotype that Condé Nast debunked

“Puerto Vallarta is often associated with cruise ships, crowded beaches, and bars hosting rowdy groups of spring breakers — but there’s so much more to this Pacific coast getaway,” the magazine said.

Highlighting the Old Town’s charm and its “winding cobblestone streets lined with bougainvillea,” the magazine invited travelers to explore lesser-known spots like Ocean Grill, an open-air restaurant set in a rocky cove, and Yelapa, a secluded beach that can only be reached by boat.

6 Mexican destinations made the Best Beaches list

The magazine also asked readers to name their favorite beaches, dividing the results by regions. For the Americas, Tulum was named second-best (behind only Hawaii’s Hanauma Bay), joining two other Quintana Roo beaches — Playa del Carmen (No. 11) and Playa de Akumal (13).

Puerto Vallarta claimed the No. 15 spot to go with its second-best small city honor. The two other Mexican beaches selected were Playa Balandra, Baja California (5) and Playa del Amor, Marieta Islands (16).

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How Toluca is turning tree trunks and old tires into playgrounds
World.content:
Old tires and tree trunks are getting a second life in Toluca, where municipal workers are turning recovered materials into playground equipment, benches and tables for the city’s parks.

Workers and neighborhood residents installed the equipment at Vicente Guerrero Park last month, creating a test site for a program officials hope to expand to schools and other public spaces in the capital of México state.

The park’s new amenities were made by municipal public services employees using materials recovered through local waste collection and recycling efforts.

Public services director Gustavo Anaya Maya said the tires, discarded furniture and tree trunks were collected through events in Toluca’s 48 districts and at 12 collection centers.

From there, they went to a municipal workshop, where employees turn them into benches, tables and playground equipment.

The broader program began in the second quarter of 2026. By September, workers had produced 10 tables, 15 playground sets, 15 benches and a bamboo house, according to the news website Plana Mayor.

Materials include trunks, logs and trimmings from authorized tree pruning and removal; reclaimed wood; old tires; recycled plastics; and recovered metal.

Installation has begun in parks and gardens across Toluca, about 50 minutes west of Mexico City via a new passenger railway.

Anaya Maya said expansion would depend on public response. If schools embrace the initiative, parents could receive training to build furniture and playground equipment, with the city supplying materials.

He said the effort also aims to keep discarded materials out of rivers and canals and reduce tire burning.

Toluca is not alone.

In San Pedro Mixtepec, Oaxaca, the recently opened La Tortuga playground features equipment containing 80% recovered plastic — an amount equivalent to about 60,000 bottles.

Mexico City’s Cuitláhuac Park offers a larger precedent.

Built on a former landfill, Cuitláhuac Park’s redevelopment incorporated recycled construction debris and plastics into paths, ground stabilization and other infrastructure. The final phase opened in 2023, showing how recovered materials can support playground projects beyond equipment, benches and tables.

With reports from El Sol de Toluca, Plana Mayor and EJE Central

World.title: Isaias becomes first Atlantic hurricane of 2026, as Simon threatens Pacific coast
World.content:
Listen to this article

Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, is whipping past the Yucatán Peninsula on its approach to the U.S. Gulf Coast, while Tropical Storm Simon is poised to become a hurricane in the Pacific by Thursday night.

Hurricane Isaias, located 280 km northwest of Progreso in northwestern Yucatán is bringing heavy and intense rainfall to eastern and southeastern Mexico.

Actualización del #Huracán #Isaias sobre el #GolfoDeMéxico. Mantiene su desplazamiento hacia el este-noreste. Detalles ⬇️ https://t.co/KKkyat7qtd — CONAGUA Clima (@conagua_clima) October 8, 2026

After rapidly intensifying over the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico to the west of the peninsula, “Isaias” is heading on a trajectory directly towards the southern United States.

Upgraded to a hurricane on Wednesday night, Isaias — the ninth named storm of the season — is the latest first hurricane in the 60-year modern era.

The previous record-long wait for the first hurricane in the satellite era was until Sept. 11 (in both 2013 and 2002), although the pre-satellite era record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.

Isaias could become a Category 3 hurricane before it makes landfall anywhere from Mississippi to Florida on Friday evening.

Meanwhile, the storm’s intense circulation will dump heavy rains (from 80 to 150 mm) along Mexico’s Gulf coast, drenching Veracruz, Tabasco, Campeche and Yucatán.

Additionally, cloud bands will cause significant rainfall along the coastal strip of Tamaulipas and in northern Quintana Roo.

Sustained winds of up to 40 km/h with gusts of 50 to 70 km/h are expected in Veracruz, while on the coasts of Tamaulipas, Tabasco, Campeche and Yucatán gusts will range between 40 to 60 km/h.

In the Pacific, Simon is forecast to become a hurricane later today as it approaches Mexico’s west-central coast on Saturday.

A Hurricane Watch is in effect from Manzanillo, Colima, to Punta San Telmo, Michoacán. The U.S. National Hurricane Center warned of life-threatening wind and storm surge impacts as it becomes a major hurricane.

9 am CST – Tropical Storm #Simon is expected to become a hurricane later today and a very dangerous category 4 hurricane before it reaches the coast of Mexico. A Hurricane Watch has been issued for a portion of west-central Mexico. Visit https://t.co/NyUGSIFCuo for updates. https://t.co/nHqbATVHVq — NHC Pacific (@NHC_Pacific) October 8, 2026

Located 305 km south-southwest of Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán, Simon is moving west at about 11 km/h and is forecast to turn northward and approach the southwestern coast of Mexico on Saturday.

Heavy to torrential rains are forecast for areas of Guerrero, Oaxaca and Chiapas today, while winds with gusts of 50 to 70 km/h are expected along the coasts of Michoacán and Guerrero.

With reports from USA Today, Meteored, El Financiero and CNN en Español

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Craft beer, gourmet foodies and ‘Fallout’ fans unite
World.content:
A couple of weeks ago, we told you all about Día de Muertos and Halloween in Mexico City, so this week, it’s time for something a little different. Over the coming weeks, the capital will host a trio of events catering to beer lovers, foodies and “Fallout” fans alike, including a massive gathering of 170 brewers and distributors, a gourmet festival featuring more than 60 chefs, and a free fan fest celebrating the hit video game and TV franchise.

Let’s get into it.

170 brewers and distributors on tap for Expo México

Grab all your sudsy buds and head to the Expo Cerveza México. This celebration of all things beer will take place Oct. 23 to 25 at the World Trade Center convention hall in Mexico City’s Nápoles area, roughly a 30-minute drive from Centro Histórico, depending on traffic.

The event features a whopping 170 brewers and distributors, including local names like Beer Company, Falling Piano and Cervecería Chilango Banzai, as well as a handful of international brands such as Europe’s iconic Erdinger-Delirium, Vulcano Brewing from Argentina and Old Rasputin, which is making the trip down from California.

Also on tap is a special tasting room experience, organized by Catadoras y Cerveceras de México, which for the past 13 years has been working to uplift women in the country’s craft beer industry. Several tastings are planned for each of the expo’s three days, but space is limited and registration is required.

Dates: Oct. 23 and 24, 12 p.m. – 10 p.m.; Oct. 25, 12 p.m. – 7 p.m.

Location: Montecito 38, Nápoles, Benito Juárez, 03810 Ciudad de México

Cost: General admission on Oct. 23 and 24 is 380 pesos, while Sunday’s limited hours run 300 pesos. Both include a commemorative glass. There’s also a special “Friday Godin,” or “office worker,” price, which gets you into the expo for 200 pesos on Oct. 23, from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m.

For more information and to purchase tickets, visit Expo Cerveza México’s official website.

Latin American flavors, culinary talent take center stage at Food and Wine Festival

If you’re looking for something a little more refined, the 6th edition of Mexico City’s Food and Wine Festival will bring more than 60 chefs and “prestigious gourmet brands” to Jardines Campo de Marte in the capital’s swanky Polanco neighborhood on Nov. 7 and 8.

This year’s theme is Un Mundo de Sabores (“A World of Flavors”), paying tribute to the varied and rich cuisine of Latin America, including the regions’ raw ingredients and “exotic recipes,” according to the event’s website.

More than just a bunch of food stalls dishing out their signature fare, the Food and Wine Festival kicks off with a Best New Chefs 2026 series, featuring some of Latin and South America’s newest culinary talent offering tastings and “experiential master classes” for attendees.

However, the flagship event will see more than 20 chefs preparing meats, shellfish, fish and rice dishes over this year’s premier cooking method — fire.

Other activities include Pacific tuna cutting demonstrations, mixology classes, ceviche preparation, and the enigmatically described “magic shows” at different times of the day.

Dates: Nov. 7 and 8, 1 p.m. – 7 p.m.

Location: Av. Paseo de la Reforma, Floor G, Polanco, Chapultepec, Miguel Hidalgo, 11560 Ciudad de México

Cost: Tickets start at 800 pesos. Right now, there’s a special flash sale with three tickets for the price of two.

For more information, check out the official Food and Wine Festival website or visit Boletia to purchase tickets.

Explore the wasteland with fellow ‘Fallout’ fans

Immerse yourself in a retrofuturistic wasteland at the titular fan fest for the popular video game franchise turned TV series, “Fallout,” Nov. 7 at PARCUR Chapultepec.

Described as a “gathering created by and for the Fallout community,” this free event features cosplay, content creators, activities, contests, photo ops and “many surprises inspired by the post-apocalyptic universe” that has taken the gaming community by storm since it was first released nearly three decades ago.

“Fallout” is a post-apocalyptic story set more than two centuries in the future, following a nuclear war between the United States and China. To date, the franchise has spawned 10 games and related titles, the last of which was released in 2020, as well as a television series on Amazon Prime that wrapped up its second season earlier this year.

The franchise is critically acclaimed, having racked up numerous accolades, including four Emmys for the series’ costume and production design, an Art Directors Guild Award in 2025, and a Golden Joystick Award the year prior, among others.

Date: Nov. 7, noon

Location: Av. Ignacio Zaragoza 224, Bosque de Chapultepec III Secc, Miguel Hidalgo, 11100 Ciudad de México

Cost: Free

For more information and to register your space, visit Boletia.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How many foreigners live in Mexico?
World.content:
How many foreign-born residents does Mexico have? Where in Mexico do they live?

We answer those questions in this “Mexico in Numbers” article, which is based on the recently published results of INEGI’s 2025 Intercensal Survey.

Let’s delve into the data.

Mexico has almost 1.2 million foreign-born residents

INEGI reported that 1,170,030 (1.17 million) foreign-born residents lived in Mexico in 2025.

That figure represents an increase of just 147 people — or 0.01% — from 2020, when the most recent census was conducted in Mexico.

Mexico’s foreign-born population represents just 0.9% of Mexico’s total population, which was 130.91 million in 2025, according to the results of the Intercensal Survey.

By contrast, foreign-born residents of the United States accounted for about 14.8% of the U.S. national population in 2024, according to the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, a large-scale survey of American households.

Just over half of Mexico’s foreign-born residents — 50.7% — have Mexican citizenship, according to INEGI.

Almost 60% of Mexico’s foreign-born residents were born in the US

Of the 1.17 million foreign-born residents of Mexico, 668,658 were born in the United States, according to INEGI.

Thus, 57.1% of Mexico’s foreign-born population was born in the United States. INEGI reported that 66.5% of U.S.-born residents are Mexican nationals.

INEGI also reported that:

75,826 residents of Mexico were born in Venezuela, a figure that accounts for 6.5% of the foreign-born population.

61,663 residents of Mexico were born in Cuba, a figure that accounts for 5.3% of the foreign-born population.

54,680 residents of Mexico were born in Guatemala, a figure that accounts for 4.7% of the foreign-born population.

309,203 residents of Mexico were born in “other countries,” a figure that accounts for 26.4% of the foreign-born population.

Just over one-fifth of the Venezuelan-born residents (21.1%) and the Cuban-born residents (22.6%) are Mexican nationals, according to INEGI.

Just over one-third of the Guatemalan-born residents (34.3%) are Mexican nationals. Among the more than 300,000 residents of Mexico born in “other countries,” 32.2% are Mexican nationals.

Baja California and CDMX have the largest foreign-born populations

A graph published by INEGI in its Intercensal Survey results report shows that two federal entities have more than 100,000 foreign-born residents: Baja California (131,221) and Mexico City (114,273).

Seven states have more than 50,000 foreign-born residents. They are:

Chihuahua: 98,785

Jalisco: 76,441

Chiapas: 73,711

México state: 71,703

Tamaulipas: 63,691

Nuevo León: 56,532

Quintana Roo: 50,325

According to INEGI, Tlaxcala has the lowest foreign-born population among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, with 3,758 residents born abroad.

Three other states have fewer than 10,000 foreign-born residents: Tabasco (6,429), Colima (6,802) and Campeche (7,595).

* This article is based on Intercensal Survey data published by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) in September. MND acknowledges that there are various estimates of the number of U.S. citizens living in Mexico, including a 2024 U.S. State Department estimate of 1.6 million. The State Department estimate could include U.S. citizens born in Mexico, whom INEGI, for obvious reasons, does not classify as foreign-born. Mexican-born people who moved to the United States, obtained U.S. citizenship, and subsequently returned to Mexico fit into this category. The State Department estimate could also include part-time residents (who may or may not have a Mexican residency permit and who may or may not have been in Mexico when the Intercensal Survey was conducted) as well as temporary residents on tourist visas, including digital nomads.

World.title: Best Places to Live in Peru for Expats 2026
World.content:
Expats · Peru

For most American expats, Lima is the best place to live in Peru, followed by Arequipa and Cusco. The trade-off is money and safety: average asking rent in Barranco was about US$1,260 a month in April 2026, and extortion complaints rose 19% in 2025.

Key Facts —Who. US retirees, remote workers and families choosing a base in Peru. Dollar budgets matter more than sol budgets. —What. Three bases ranked on rent, safety, altitude and visas. Average asking rents in April 2026 ran from S/3,868 (about US$1,129) in Miraflores to S/4,317 (about US$1,260) in Barranco. —Why it matters. Peru’s homicide rate was a preliminary 10.7 per 100,000 people in 2025, against 10.1 in 2024, according to the statistics institute INEI. Extortion complaints rose to 26,585 from 22,361. —Watch. The central bank’s next rate decision is scheduled for 12 November. Lima held a mayoral election on 4 October; no winner has been proclaimed, and the electoral court has yet to rule whether Rafael López Aliaga, who ran as first councillor on the Renovación Popular list, may take the mayor’s post. —Prediction markets. Polymarket traders put about 91% on Rafael López Aliaga becoming the next Mayor of Lima and about 4% on Francis Allison (US$511,741 traded across the event). Bets, not polls. Read 9 October 2026, 07:07 ET.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Peru 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 3 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Free. The same address also receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing with an expat desk. We send a confirmation link first and nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves. Privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

The Short Answer: Lima First, Arequipa for Calm

Lima ranks first because it has the deepest choice of private clinics, the most international flights and the most neighbourhoods used to foreign residents. Arequipa ranks second as a calmer city with sunny weather. Cusco ranks third, because altitude and tourism shape life there.

This ranking is our editorial judgement, not a statistical index. We weighed rent and recorded crime, which can be measured. We also weighed how easy daily life is for a foreigner, which cannot.

Rank City Altitude and climate Average asking rent, three-bedroom apartment of about 100 m² Main drawback 1 Lima (Miraflores, Barranco, San Isidro) Sea level; mild, grey and humid in winter S/3,868 to S/4,317 (about US$1,129 to US$1,260); city average S/3,356 (about US$979) Crime, extortion and traffic 2 Arequipa About 2,300 m; dry, sunny days and cold nights Not confirmed from a primary source Misti volcano and earthquake zone; fewer international flights 3 Cusco and the Sacred Valley About 3,400 m in Cusco; temperate, rainy summers Not confirmed from a primary source Altitude sickness and tourist-driven prices

How We Ranked, and Which Dollar Rate We Use

Rents come from the property portal Urbania, which reported April 2026 asking-rent averages for three-bedroom apartments of about 100 square metres. We convert at S/3.4273 per dollar, the USD/PEN rate on 9 October 2026 (EODHD). Rents move with the exchange rate, so treat the dollar figures as a guide.

We did not find a primary source for current rents in Arequipa or Cusco, so we give none. Safety rankings by city are also missing, because the city-level homicide figures we found could not be confirmed. Where we lack a number, we say so.

1. Lima: Miraflores, Barranco and San Isidro

Lima is Peru’s capital, on a desert coast, and it is where most foreign residents land. Miraflores and Barranco face the Pacific from cliff-top parks. San Isidro is the business district, with offices and many of the city’s private clinics.

Rents are the entry price. Urbania’s April 2026 averages were S/4,317 in Barranco, S/4,213 in San Isidro and S/3,868 in Miraflores (about US$1,260, US$1,229 and US$1,129). The Lima-wide average was S/3,356 (about US$979). Cheaper districts exist: La Molina averaged S/2,583 (about US$754) and Lince S/2,690 (about US$785).

Rents are also rising. Urbania found year-on-year increases of 9.5% in San Isidro and 4.6% in Barranco. For a full monthly budget, see our cost of living in Lima and cost of living in Peru guides.

The drawback is security. The government has extended a state of emergency in Lima and Callao several times, and the national statistics institute counted 26,585 extortion complaints in 2025. Most expats live in the districts above and take taxis booked by app rather than hailing them on the street.

The Yanahuara lookout, built from white volcanic sillar stone, frames the Misti volcano above Arequipa. Photo: Karney Hatch / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0
