2. Arequipa: White Stone and a Volcano

Arequipa is Peru’s second city in the south, at about 2,300 metres. Its centre is built from pale volcanic stone, and the Misti volcano rises behind it. Days are usually dry and sunny, and nights are cold in winter.

Expats who choose Arequipa usually do so for the quieter pace and the lower altitude than Cusco. The cost is distance: Lima is the main international gateway, so most trips abroad start with a connection there. The city also lies in an earthquake and volcano zone, so check building standards before you rent.

3. Cusco and the Sacred Valley: Altitude Decides

Cusco sits at about 3,400 metres, and the Sacred Valley villages such as Pisac lie lower and are milder. Many foreigners live there for the culture, the markets and the hiking. Tourism lifts prices for restaurants and short-term rentals.

Textile stalls at the market in Pisac, in the Cusco region, pictured in 2022. Photo: Christoph Strässler / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

Altitude is the main practical test. Spend a week at height before you sign a long lease, and ask your doctor about heart and lung conditions. Rainy summers can disrupt travel by road.

Safety, Visas and Health Cover for Americans

The US State Department rates Peru at Level 2, “Exercise Increased Caution”, citing crime, unrest, kidnapping and terrorism. It advises against travel to the Colombia–Peru border area in the Loreto region. Peru’s national homicide rate was a preliminary 10.7 per 100,000 in 2025, according to INEI.

For long stays, the rentista resident status is the usual retirement route. Migraciones asks for proof of at least US$1,000 a month in pension or other permanent income. Remote work income does not usually qualify, so ask a Peruvian lawyer before you apply.

Medicare generally does not pay for care in Peru. Americans normally buy private plans or international insurance. For a broader view, read our Peru safety guide for expats and Peru versus Colombia for expats, or return to the Peru hub.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market, lists a market on who becomes the next Mayor of Lima. On 9 October 2026 at 07:07 ET, traders put López Aliaga at about 91% and Allison at about 4%. The event had US$511,741 traded, and the price carries the risk that the electoral court rules on López Aliaga’s eligibility.

Official counts showed Renovación Popular at 27.7% and Avanza País, Allison’s party, at 26.8% with 92.7% of tallies counted on 6 October. López Aliaga headed the list as first councillor, and no winner has been proclaimed. Whoever is proclaimed mayor takes office on 1 January 2027.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What to Watch

The central bank’s rate decision is scheduled for 12 November. It moves the sol, and so the dollar cost of your rent. The electoral court’s ruling on Lima’s mayoral post will decide who runs the city from 1 January 2027.

What It Means for You

If you earn in dollars, Lima’s rents are manageable but not cheap, and security costs time as well as money. Arequipa and Cusco suit people who want a smaller city and accept the practical trade-offs. Visit for a month before you commit to a lease.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm current average rents in Arequipa and Cusco, or city-level homicide rates, from primary sources. No winner of the Lima mayoral election had been proclaimed when we wrote this, and the electoral court had not ruled on López Aliaga’s eligibility. We will update the guide when those figures are published.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best place to live in Peru for expats?

For most American expats, Lima is the best base, because it has the deepest choice of private clinics, the most flights and the widest choice of apartments. Arequipa ranks second for a calmer, sunnier city. Cusco ranks third because altitude and tourism shape daily life.

How much does rent cost in Lima?

Urbania reported average asking rents of S/3,868 in Miraflores, S/4,213 in San Isidro and S/4,317 in Barranco in April 2026, for apartments of about 100 square metres. At S/3.4273 to the dollar, that is about US$1,129 to US$1,260 a month. The Lima-wide average was S/3,356 (about US$979).

Is Peru safe for American expats?

Peru is rated Level 2, “Exercise Increased Caution”, by the US State Department, which cites crime, unrest, kidnapping and terrorism. The national homicide rate was a preliminary 10.7 per 100,000 people in 2025, up from 10.1 in 2024, according to the national statistics institute INEI. Extortion complaints rose to 26,585 in 2025 from 22,361 in 2024.

Can Americans retire in Peru on a pension?

Peru has a rentista resident status for foreigners with a pension or other permanent income. The immigration agency Migraciones asks for proof of at least US$1,000 a month. Check the current requirements with Migraciones or a Peruvian lawyer before you apply.

Will Medicare pay for care in Peru?

No. Medicare generally does not cover health care outside the United States, according to Medicare.gov. Americans usually buy private Peruvian health plans or international insurance.

Is altitude a problem in Cusco?

It can be. Cusco sits at about 3,400 metres, so many newcomers feel headaches or breathlessness in the first days. Lima is at sea level, and Arequipa is about 2,300 metres, which most visitors find easier.

Sources

World.title: Wau Court Jails Soldier for Killing UN Worker
World.content:
A military court in Wau, South Sudan, has sentenced a soldier to 10 years in prison for killing a United Nations staff member, according to reports published on 9 October 2026. The soldier, from the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF), was convicted over the death of Bol Rhoch Mayol Kuot, a language assistant with the UN mission UNMISS.

US readers have a stake because UN missions and aid groups depend on local staff to work in South Sudan. Americans who work or travel there also rely on a secure environment for UN staff and aid workers.

Key Facts —Who. A soldier of the SSPDF, not named in reports, was convicted. The victim was Bol Rhoch Mayol Kuot, a South Sudanese language assistant with UNMISS. —What. A General Court Martial imposed 10 years in prison, demotion and dismissal from the army. It also awarded 51 head of cattle to the victim’s family. —Where. The court sat in Wau, in Western Bahr el Ghazal state. The victim was detained near Wau, in the Hai Masna area, according to court reports. —When. The sentence was reported on 9 October 2026. The victim was detained on 15 December 2025. As of 9 October 2026, 11:30 GMT

What We Know

The General Court Martial in Wau found the soldier guilty of killing the UNMISS staff member. It sentenced the soldier to 10 years in prison and ordered demotion and dismissal from the army.

The court also awarded 51 head of cattle to the victim’s family. Cattle are a traditional form of compensation in South Sudan.

Bol Rhoch Mayol Kuot was a South Sudanese national who worked as a language assistant with UNMISS, the UN peacekeeping mission. Security actors detained him near Wau on 15 December 2025, and he was killed in custody while on official duty.

Earlier reports, based on an Associated Press account, said he was taken from a UN vehicle after a flat tyre following a patrol to a displacement camp. Those reports added that an army lieutenant and two other soldiers were arrested after admitting the killing and disclosing the location of the body.

Anita Kiki Gbeho, the UN Special Representative and head of UNMISS, called the judgment “a milestone in efforts to ensure accountability for crimes against United Nations personnel in South Sudan.” In December 2025, UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the killing “in the strongest terms.” The UN also called for a swift and transparent investigation.

The court martial session heard 10 cases and delivered 8 judgments. Four ended in convictions and four in acquittals.

An aerial view of Juba, South Sudan’s capital. File photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on South Sudan Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Is Not Known

Reports do not give the soldier’s name or rank. They also do not say whether prosecutors or the defence will appeal.

The outcomes of the cases against the other suspects arrested earlier have not been reported. The soldier has the right to appeal, and the ruling remains subject to appeal.

The reports we reviewed do not state a motive for the killing. We do not speculate beyond what the court and officials have said.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The UN and aid groups rely on local staff, including language assistants, to work with communities. A conviction in a case like this matters to those staff and to the organisations that employ them.

Readers who follow UN work in South Sudan will watch how the country handles crimes against UN personnel. This case went before a military court, which also delivered four acquittals in the same session.

South Sudan hosts the UN mission UNMISS, and its security situation remains fragile. Americans who work or travel there should follow official government travel advice.

The verdict does not change the security situation by itself. It shows that a court can hold a soldier to account when a UN worker is killed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was sentenced, and for what?

A soldier of the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces was sentenced to 10 years in prison by a General Court Martial in Wau, according to reports on 9 October 2026. The soldier was convicted of killing a UNMISS staff member.

Who was the victim?

Bol Rhoch Mayol Kuot was a South Sudanese language assistant with UNMISS. He was detained near Wau on 15 December 2025 and killed in custody while on official duty.

What else did the court order?

The court ordered the soldier’s demotion and dismissal from the army. It also awarded 51 head of cattle to the victim’s family, a traditional form of compensation.

Can the verdict be appealed?

Yes, the soldier has the right to appeal, and the ruling is subject to appeal. Reports do not say whether prosecutors or the defence will do so.

World.title: Rwanda and Its Neighbours in East Africa
World.content:
RWANDA · EAST AFRICA

Key Facts — The country Landlocked Rwanda, 26,338 sq km, borders Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, DR Congo.

— The peace deal US-brokered Washington Accords signed 4 December 2025; fighting persisted into 2026.

— What happened Treasury sanctioned Rwanda’s army on 2 March 2026 over M23 support.

— The trade DR Congo took 88.1% of Rwanda’s re-exports, April–June 2026.

— What it means for you US advisory Level 3; avoid 10 km strip along Congo border.

— Still open No public statement yet from the September 2026 Geneva security talks.

A war next door, a US-brokered peace deal and a closed southern border shape how Rwanda deals with its region.

The Rwanda neighbourhood is small on the map but crowded with history. Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo border this landlocked Great Lakes state.

In October 2026 the key relationship is with Congo, where Washington brokered peace and then sanctioned Rwanda’s army. For US readers, the region tests whether minerals deals can end a war.

Mapping the Rwanda Neighbourhood, Four Borders and No Coast

Rwanda covers 26,338 square kilometres, about the size of Maryland, says the East African Community (EAC). Rwanda joined this regional bloc in July 2007, and has no coastline.

Kigali, the capital, sits roughly in the middle of the country. The western edge runs along Lake Kivu and the Rusizi River, which form much of the frontier with Congo.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Guinea-Bissau says its 6 December vote cannot go ahead” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

In the east, the Kagera River and the Rusumo Falls crossing mark the border with Tanzania. The volcanoes of the Virunga chain rise along the north-western corner, where Rwanda, Uganda and Congo meet.

Background is in the Rio Times guide Rwanda explained, with daily coverage on the Rio Times Rwanda page. Sibling explainers cover Congo’s neighbourhood, Tanzania’s and Kenya’s.

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. DR Congo, M23 and the Washington Accords

Congo is Rwanda’s largest neighbour and its most troubled relationship.

Kinshasa accuses Kigali of backing the March 23 Movement (M23). This rebel group fights the Congolese army in North and South Kivu.

The US Treasury agrees with Kinshasa on that point. On 2 March 2026 it sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF), Rwanda’s military, and four senior commanders.

Treasury said the RDF was “actively supporting, training, and fighting alongside” M23. It added that “thousands of RDF troops are deployed across eastern DRC.”

Rwanda’s Office of the Government Spokesperson replied the same day that the sanctions “unjustly” targeted one party. It blamed Congolese drone attacks and ground offensives for breaking ceasefires.

Kigali’s core security complaint is the FDLR, the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda. Rwanda’s government calls it a “genocidal militia” that fights alongside Congo’s army.

Rwanda says Congo committed to an “irreversible and verifiable end” to state support for the FDLR, but has not acted.

The diplomatic framework is the Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity. President Donald Trump hosted the signing on 4 December 2025, according to the State Department.

President Félix Tshisekedi signed for Congo and President Paul Kagame for Rwanda. The accords recommit both sides to a peace agreement first agreed in Washington on 27 June 2025.

They also include a Regional Economic Integration Framework, a bilateral economic plan for the Great Lakes. The State Department says it “creates opportunities for the U.S. private sector.”

On 25 June 2026 Treasury also sanctioned Gasabo Gold Refinery, a Rwandan refiner. It said at least 60 kilograms of eastern Congolese gold reached it in early 2026.

More on the militia question is in the Rio Times report on the FDLR disarmament protocol.

Where the Peace Deal Stands in October 2026

Implementation runs through two committees, attended by the United States, Qatar, the African Union and Togo as mediator. The Joint Oversight Committee (JOC) handles politics; the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) handles military steps.

On 17 and 18 March 2026 the two governments agreed in Washington on a schedule.

Rwanda would lift its “defensive measures” in defined areas. Congo would intensify efforts to neutralise the FDLR.

By June the tone had darkened. The sixth JOC, meeting in London on 24 June 2026, voiced “serious concern over the escalating fighting.”

It also cited drone strikes on civilians and the Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo. It urged support for separate Doha talks between Kinshasa and the AFC/M23 rebel coalition.

The latest published step came in Geneva on 12 and 13 August 2026, at the sixth JSCM. Congo presented a disarmament plan for the FDLR, and the parties agreed to advance two monitoring initiatives.

They also agreed to a planning conference in October 2026 to produce a revised operations order. A seventh JSCM was set for 16 and 17 September in Geneva, as The New Times, Kigali’s main daily, reported.

As of 9 October 2026, the State Department’s Congo page carried no joint statement from that September meeting. The accords remain in force on paper, but neither side has declared its main obligations met.

Burundi, the Closed Border to the South

Burundi, Rwanda’s southern neighbour, shares a similar language and a similar ethnic history. Relations under President Évariste Ndayishimiye remain hostile.

Burundi closed the land border with effect from 11 January 2024. Rwanda’s government called the decision unilateral and said it “violates the principles” of EAC cooperation, KT Press, a Kigali outlet, reported.

The Ghana News Agency reported at the time that Bujumbura accused Kigali of backing Burundian rebels.

Trade has not stopped, as Rio Times reported. The National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR) recorded US$13.39 million of exports to Burundi in April–June 2026, double the first quarter.

Neither government has explained how those goods travel. The wider picture of Burundi’s economy is in the Burundi explainer.

Uganda and Tanzania, the Roads to the Sea

Rwanda reaches the Indian Ocean along two routes. The Northern Corridor runs through Uganda to Kenya’s port of Mombasa, and the Central Corridor runs through Tanzania to Dar es Salaam.

Tanzania is the bigger supplier. NISR data show US$182.93 million of imports from Tanzania in April–June 2026, second only to China.

Kenya, which does not border Rwanda, supplied US$106.10 million in the same quarter. Uganda supplied US$90.16 million, while Rwanda sold Uganda only US$5.75 million, down from US$12.22 million in the first quarter.

Uganda is Rwanda’s northern gateway to Kenya’s port, and it shares the Virunga volcanoes with Rwanda. The Uganda explainer covers Kampala’s own politics.

Kampala sent Vice President Jessica Alupo to the Washington signing in December 2025.

Trade, the East African Community and Where Rwanda Leads

Rwanda’s total goods trade reached US$2.33 billion in April–June 2026, up 23.4% on the first quarter, NISR reported. Imports of US$1.61 billion far exceeded domestic exports of US$548.98 million.

China was the top export market at US$142.38 million, ahead of the United Arab Emirates. Congo came third at US$89.51 million, and the United States fifth at US$24.22 million.

Congo matters even more for re-exports, goods Rwanda imports and sells on. It took 88.1% of them, and 76.9% of Rwanda’s domestic exports to EAC states.

Rwanda’s surplus with Burundi and Congo combined reached US$239.77 million in the quarter, up from US$190.02 million a year earlier. In short, war or no war, Kigali is the trading hub for the eastern Congolese market.

The EAC, headquartered in Arusha, Tanzania, is the bloc that ties these economies together through a customs union and common market. Rwanda hosts one of its institutions, the East African Science and Technology Commission.

Rwanda leads where it can sell services and order: conferences, aviation, technology and security. It follows on geography, because its fuel and containers depend on Tanzanian and Kenyan ports.

NISR reports its trade figures in US dollars. For scale, US$1 bought about RWF 1,478 on 9 October 2026, per open.er-api.com.

Lake Kivu and the Shared Rivers

Lake Kivu is the clearest picture of how close the neighbours live. At the lake’s northern tip, the Rwandan town of Rubavu, once called Gisenyi, faces the Congolese city of Goma.

The lake drains south through the Rusizi River into Lake Tanganyika, past both Congo and Burundi. Any shared hydropower or fishing plan on these waters therefore needs at least two governments to agree.

In the east, the Kagera River flows from the Rwanda–Burundi–Tanzania borderlands into Lake Victoria. That places Rwanda in the upper catchment of the Nile.

For visitors, the Kivu shore is where the US travel advisory bites hardest. The Rio Times report on the Congo entry ban explains entry rules after a Congo visit.

What It Means for US Readers

Sanctions come first. The RDF, four commanders, Gasabo Gold Refinery and three linked mining firms are on the US Treasury sanctions list.

Anyone sourcing gold, tin, tantalum or tungsten from the region should expect tougher due diligence. The State Department, meanwhile, pitches the Washington Accords as an opening for US investors.

For travellers, the State Department rated Rwanda Level 3, “Reconsider travel,” in an advisory issued on 4 June 2026.

It says not to travel within 10 kilometres of the Congo border. That zone includes Rubavu and much of the Kivu shore.

Kigali lies well outside that strip. Entry rules for US citizens are in the Rio Times Rwanda visa guide.

What Is Not Known

The State Department had not published the outcome of the seventh JSCM in Geneva, set for 16 and 17 September. Whether the October planning conference has met is also unclear.

Independent verification of Rwanda’s troop disengagement and of Congo’s steps against the FDLR is still being set up. No public figure exists for Rwandan forces still in Congo in October 2026.

Neither Burundi nor Rwanda has given a date to reopen their land border, or explained how goods now cross it. Current output from Lake Kivu methane gas power plants was not confirmed for this guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries border Rwanda?

Four: Uganda to the north, Tanzania to the east, Burundi to the south and DR Congo to the west. Rwanda has no coastline, so its sea trade crosses Uganda and Kenya or Tanzania.

What are the Washington Accords?

A US-brokered peace package between Rwanda and DR Congo, signed in Washington on 4 December 2025 by Presidents Kagame and Tshisekedi. It builds on a peace agreement of 27 June 2025 and adds a regional economic integration framework.

Is the Rwanda and Congo peace deal working in October 2026?

Only partly. Talks continue in Geneva and Doha, but a June 2026 statement voiced serious concern over escalating fighting.

Is the border between Rwanda and Burundi open?

Burundi closed the land border from 11 January 2024, and no reopening date appears in official statements. Rwandan statistics still show exports to Burundi rising in 2026.

Is it safe for Americans to visit Lake Kivu?

The State Department rates Rwanda Level 3 and advises against travel within 10 kilometres of the Congo border. That zone covers much of the Rwandan shore of Lake Kivu, including Rubavu.

Is Rwanda part of the East African Community?

Yes. Rwanda joined the East African Community in July 2007, and Burundi, Uganda, Tanzania and DR Congo are members too.

World.title: Ghana Culture, the Key Figures to Know in 2026
World.content:
GHANA · CULTURE

Key Facts — The country About 34.4 million people (2026 projection), English-speaking, in West Africa.

— UNESCO heritage Kente weaving listed in 2024, highlife music and dance in 2025.

— Who Black Sherif, Stonebwoy, Kofi Kinaata, El Anatsui, the late Daddy Lumba.

— What happened in 2026 Black Sherif top artiste; Black Stars out in World Cup last 32.

— Coming up African arts festival AFESTACC in Ghana, 9–12 December 2026.

— Still open AFESTACC host venues have not yet been announced.

From highlife and kente to Black Sherif and El Anatsui, these are the people and traditions that define Ghana culture in 2026.

Ghana culture runs from highlife, the guitar-led dance music UNESCO recognised in 2025, to hand-woven kente cloth and young rappers. It matters to US readers because Ghana markets itself as a home for the African diaspora, and its artists reach American audiences.

This guide names the key figures in music, books and film, visual art, sport, media and festivals. It also explains what they say about a country of about 34.4 million people, the 2026 projection of the Ghana Statistical Service.

Ghana Culture at a Glance

Ghana sits on the Gulf of Guinea between Côte d’Ivoire and Togo. It won independence from Britain in 1957, and English remains the official language.

The country is home to many peoples, among them the Asante, Fante, Ga, Ewe and Dagomba. Each has its own language, chiefs and festival calendar, and that diversity is the raw material of its culture.

We never share your email.

Two recent decisions by UNESCO, the United Nations cultural agency, put this heritage on a global map. Kente, the strip-woven cloth worn at Asante and Ewe ceremonies, joined UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage in 2024.

Highlife music and dance followed in 2025. These are Ghana’s only two entries on that list as of October 2026, according to UNESCO.

The state’s culture portfolio sits with Abla Dzifa Gomashie, Minister for Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts. She is a performing artist and the member of parliament for Ketu South in the Volta Region.

She serves under President John Dramani Mahama, who took office in January 2025. The guide to who holds power in Ghana explains the wider government.

Music, From Highlife to Black Sherif

Highlife grew up in the coastal cities in the early 20th century, blending local rhythms with brass bands and guitars. It later spawned hiplife, a fusion with hip-hop, and fed into the Afrobeats sound now heard worldwide.

The genre lost one of its biggest stars in 2025. Daddy Lumba, born Charles Kwadwo Fosu, died on Saturday, 26 July 2025, aged 60, the Ghana News Agency reported.

President Mahama said his “unmatched musical genius provided the soundtrack to our lives.” In May 2026 the Ghana Music Awards gave him a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award.

Those awards, sponsored by the telecoms company Telecel, are the country’s main music prize. The 27th edition was held on Saturday, 9 May 2026, at the Accra International Conference Centre.

Black Sherif, a rapper and singer, dominated the night with five awards. He was Artiste of the Year, and Iron Boy won Album/EP of the Year, according to the official winners list.

Other winners show how wide the scene is. Kofi Kinaata won Highlife Artiste, Medikal took Hiplife/Hip-Hop Artiste and Stonebwoy won Reggae/Dancehall Artiste.

Wendy Shay was named Afrobeats/Afropop Artiste and Diana Hamilton won Gospel Artiste. Gospel matters because Ghana is a deeply churchgoing country, and church choirs are a training ground for many performers.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Writers and Film-Makers

Ghana’s modern literature began with the independence generation. Ayi Kwei Armah and Ama Ata Aidoo wrote novels, plays and stories about the hopes and disappointments of the post-colonial state.

Their themes still shape how Ghanaians write about corruption, migration and family. Aidoo died in 2023, but her work is still widely read.

The best-known Ghanaian voice in the United States today is Yaa Gyasi, a Ghana-born novelist raised in Alabama. Her debut novel Homegoing won the PEN/Hemingway Award, says her publisher Penguin Random House.

On screen, Ghana has two industries: Accra produces English-language films and television. Kumasi’s “Kumawood” makes low-budget comedies and dramas in the Twi language.

The National Theatre in Accra hosts drama, dance companies and concerts. It is a main stage for the performing arts that the minister herself came from.

Visual Artists, From El Anatsui to the Venice Pavilion

Ghana’s most celebrated living artist is El Anatsui. He was born in Anyako, Ghana, in 1944 and has mostly worked in Nigeria, says Tate, Britain’s national gallery group.

He is famous for vast, shimmering hangings stitched from thousands of liquor-bottle tops. They echo the patterns of kente while speaking about trade, waste and the history of the Atlantic.

He won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the 56th Venice Biennale in 2015. On 9 October 2023 Tate Modern in London unveiled Behind the Red Moon, which Tate called his largest work to date.

His work also featured in Ghana’s first national pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2019. That pavilion announced a confident contemporary scene, with artists working between Accra, Kumasi and Tamale.

Sport Icons and the Black Stars

Football is Ghana’s shared passion, and the national team, the Black Stars, is its most powerful symbol. The name comes from the black star on the national flag.

The team qualified for the 2026 World Cup in North America and reached the round of 32. It lost 1–0 to Colombia in Kansas City on Friday, 3 July 2026, the Ghana Football Association reported.

Jhon Arias scored the only goal in the 14th minute. Ghana’s coach, the Portuguese veteran Carlos Queiroz, had led the side through a group that included Croatia and Panama.

Forward Antoine Semenyo and veteran Jordan Ayew, who both played against Colombia, are household names at home. The preview of the Colombia tie and the report on the group game against England cover the campaign in detail.

Boxing is the second sporting tradition, rooted in the old Accra districts of Jamestown and Bukom. Their gyms still draw young fighters hoping to follow earlier champions.

Media, Festivals and the Black Star Experience

Ghana has one of West Africa’s liveliest media scenes. The state broadcaster GBC competes with private radio and television groups, and talk radio shapes debate on politics and culture.

The festival calendar is where most visitors meet Ghanaian culture. The government’s flagship programme for it is the Black Star Experience, launched by President Mahama on Thursday, 1 May 2025.

He called it “a 365-day celebration” of Ghanaian creativity, the Ghana News Agency reported. It packages festivals, concerts, fashion, food and heritage tours into one year-round calendar.

Mahama named three examples at the launch. They were the Chale Wote street art festival in Jamestown, Hogbetsotso in the Volta Region and Fetu Afahye in Cape Coast.

Chale Wote turns the old harbour district of Jamestown into an open-air gallery of murals, music and performance. The other two are traditional festivals led by chiefs, with drumming, processions and durbars.

For the diaspora, the key dates are PANAFEST and Emancipation Day, centred on the former slave forts of the Central Region. The 2025 edition ran in late July, according to the Ghana Tourism Authority.

Ghana will host the first African Festival of Arts, Culture and Creatives (AFESTACC) from 9 to 12 December 2026. Minister Gomashie announced it in August, the Ghanaian Times reported.

December is already Ghana’s peak party season, when diaspora visitors fly in for concerts and weddings. The guide to Ghana’s place in the world explains why this soft power matters to the government.

What the Key Figures Say About Ghana

Taken together, these names describe a country proud of tradition but restless to modernise it. Kente and highlife are protected as heritage, while Black Sherif and El Anatsui reinvent them for global audiences.

They also show how much of Ghana’s culture is made abroad. Writers, film-makers and footballers often build careers in the United States and Europe, then return to Accra as ambassadors.

Finally, the state now treats culture as an economic tool. The Black Star Experience aims to turn festivals into tourism revenue and jobs, competing with neighbours for visitors.

The guide to Nigeria’s culture covers the biggest rival, and the guide to Ghana and its neighbours explains the region. More coverage sits on the Ghana page.

What It Means for US Readers

For travellers, the festival calendar is the best way in. December and the PANAFEST season in July and August are the busiest periods, so flights and hotels in Accra fill early.

For students and universities, the links are deep: Ohio University says it enrols more Ghanaian students than any other US university. Minister Gomashie attended its Global Arts Festival in March 2026.

For music fans, Ghanaian artists are part of the Afrobeats wave on US streaming services and tour circuits. Highlife’s new UNESCO status is likely to bring more festival bookings and reissues.

For collectors and museums, Ghanaian contemporary art is now a serious field. El Anatsui’s work has filled the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern and won top honours in Venice.

What Is Not Known

The host venues and full programme for AFESTACC in December 2026 have not been announced. It is also unclear how much public money the festival will receive.

There are no published official figures yet on whether the Black Star Experience has raised visitor numbers since May 2025. Who coaches the Black Stars after the World Cup is also not settled in the sources checked.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Ghana culture best known for?

Abroad, Ghana is best known for kente cloth, highlife music, football and its festivals. UNESCO listed kente weaving in 2024 and highlife music and dance in 2025.

Who is the biggest Ghanaian music star right now?

Black Sherif was named Artiste of the Year at the Ghana Music Awards on 9 May 2026. He won five awards, including Album/EP of the Year for Iron Boy.

Who was Daddy Lumba?

Daddy Lumba, born Charles Kwadwo Fosu, was one of Ghana’s most popular highlife singers. He died on 26 July 2025, aged 60, and received a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award in May 2026.

Who is El Anatsui?

El Anatsui is a Ghanaian sculptor, born in 1944, known for huge hangings made from bottle tops. He won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the 2015 Venice Biennale.

What is the Black Star Experience?

It is the Ghanaian government’s year-round programme of festivals, concerts and heritage events, launched by President Mahama on 1 May 2025. It aims to make Ghana a cultural destination all year.

How did Ghana do at the 2026 World Cup?

The Black Stars reached the round of 32. They lost 1-0 to Colombia in Kansas City on 3 July 2026.

Sources: Ghana Statistical Service; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage; Ghana News Agency (music awards); Ghana News Agency (Daddy Lumba); Ghana News Agency (Black Star Experience); Ghana Football Association; Ghana Tourism Authority; Tate; Penguin Random House; Ohio University; Ghanaian Times (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Morocco Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
MOROCCO · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country North African kingdom of 36.8 million people (2024 census), close US ally.

— Who rules King Mohammed VI, on the throne since 1999, controls army, religion, diplomacy.

— What happened Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri named head of government on 29 September 2026.

— Still open No cabinet named as of 9 October 2026; majority needs 198 seats.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives El Mansouri 94.5% odds of taking office and winning investiture (9 October, 6:27 a.m. ET).

Morocco elects a parliament and names a head of government, but the King still holds the decisive levers of power.

Morocco politics in October 2026 is in a handover.

On Tuesday 29 September, King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as head of government. She leads the Authenticity and Modernity Party.

She is still assembling a coalition after the 23 September election, while Aziz Akhannouch’s outgoing cabinet handles current business. For investors and visitors, the key point is simple: elected politicians run the economy, and the palace runs everything strategic.

This guide explains who holds which lever, from the throne and the army to the parties, the courts and the provincial governors. It is written for readers with no prior knowledge of the country.

How Morocco Politics Works Under the 2011 Constitution

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, a system often described as executive monarchy. The rules come from the 2011 constitution, adopted by referendum after the Arab Spring protests of that year.

That text gave elected politicians more room than before. Article 47 obliges the King to pick the head of government from the party with the most seats in the lower house.

The King then appoints ministers on the head of government’s proposal. Under Article 88, the cabinet needs a confidence vote from an absolute majority of 395 members, or 198 votes.

Parliament has two chambers. The House of Representatives is directly elected for five years, while the 120-member House of Councillors is chosen indirectly.

The King opens the first parliamentary session each year on the second Friday of October. In 2026 that is Friday 9 October, and the Royal Household said the speech would be broadcast from 3:45 p.m.

The King and the Palace Circle

Mohammed VI has reigned since July 1999, when he succeeded his father, Hassan II. The constitution makes him head of state, supreme arbiter between institutions and supreme commander of the Royal Armed Forces.

He also holds the title Commander of the Faithful under Article 41, making him the highest religious authority. He chairs the Higher Council of Ulema, the only body allowed to issue official religious rulings.

The King chairs the Council of Ministers, which approves strategic policy, draft laws on the army and senior appointments. Ambassadors, walis and governors, the central bank governor and security chiefs are all named through this channel.

Around the King sits a circle of royal advisers, a group Moroccans often call the Makhzen, meaning the palace establishment. The best known is Fouad Ali El Himma, a former deputy interior minister who co-founded the Authenticity and Modernity Party in 2008.

Crown Prince Moulay El Hassan, born in 2003, increasingly represents his father at official events. His growing public role is watched closely, because the line of succession is fixed by the constitution.

In practice, the palace also keeps several so-called sovereign ministries out of party hands. These are interior, foreign affairs, Islamic affairs and the defence administration, usually led by technocrats close to the King.

The Head of Government and the Coalition Talks

Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri is the first woman to head a Moroccan government. A Marrakech lawyer and mayor, she was housing minister in the outgoing cabinet.

The Royal Household’s communiqué of 29 September cited Article 47 and asked her to form the new government. A full profile of her career is in the Rio Times profile of Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri.

Her predecessor, Aziz Akhannouch, has led the government since 2021. The guide to Morocco’s economic power players explains his business empire, built around the Akwa group.

Akhannouch’s cabinet continues to handle current affairs until the King appoints a new one. As of the morning of 9 October 2026, no new cabinet had been announced.

Le360, a Moroccan news site, reported on 7 October that El Mansouri is heading for a majority modelled on the Koutla. That was a 1990s reform bloc of Istiqlal, the Socialist Union and the Party of Progress and Socialism.

With her own party, those four groups would hold 207 of 395 seats, nine more than a majority. The Rio Times report on the coalition talks follows how each party has positioned itself.

The Parties in the New Parliament

Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit announced the provisional results on 24 September, and the ministry later confirmed them as final. National turnout was about 38 percent, against 50.35 percent in 2021.

The seat count, as published by the Interior Ministry through the government portal maroc.ma, was:

Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), 97 seats. A centrist, palace-friendly party founded in 2008, led by El Mansouri; up from 87 in 2021.

A centrist, palace-friendly party founded in 2008, led by El Mansouri; up from 87 in 2021. National Rally of Independents (RNI), 66 seats. A liberal, business-minded party that led the 2021–2026 government; Mohamed Chaouki replaced Akhannouch as its president in February 2026.

A liberal, business-minded party that led the 2021–2026 government; Mohamed Chaouki replaced Akhannouch as its president in February 2026. Istiqlal (Independence Party), 65 seats. Morocco’s oldest party, founded in 1943, conservative and nationalist, led by Nizar Baraka; its national council has voted to join the government.

Morocco’s oldest party, founded in 1943, conservative and nationalist, led by Nizar Baraka; its national council has voted to join the government. Justice and Development Party (PJD), 54 seats. An Islamist-rooted party that led governments from 2011 to 2021; under Abdelilah Benkirane it says it will sit in opposition.

An Islamist-rooted party that led governments from 2011 to 2021; under Abdelilah Benkirane it says it will sit in opposition. Popular Movement (MP), 29 seats. A rural, Amazigh-rooted conservative party whose council has let its leader decide on joining the government.

A rural, Amazigh-rooted conservative party whose council has let its leader decide on joining the government. Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP), 26 seats. A social-democratic party led by Driss Lachgar, in opposition since 2021.

A social-democratic party led by Driss Lachgar, in opposition since 2021. Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS), 19 seats. A left-wing party descended from the old Communist Party, led by Nabil Benabdallah.

A left-wing party descended from the old Communist Party, led by Nabil Benabdallah. Constitutional Union (UC), 17 seats. A centre-right, pro-business party whose leadership has authorised talks on joining the government.

A centre-right, pro-business party whose leadership has authorised talks on joining the government. Smaller groups, 22 seats. The Democratic and Social Movement and the Left Alliance won eight each; four micro-parties with six seats formed a joint caucus.

The biggest story of the vote was the RNI’s fall from 102 seats in 2021 and the PJD’s rebound from 13. The Rio Times election results report sets out the shifts in detail.

Parties matter for budgets, housing, jobs and subsidies, but far less for security and diplomacy. That is why low turnout is often read as a verdict on politicians rather than the monarchy.

The Army, Police and Intelligence Services

The Royal Armed Forces answer to the King, not to the head of government. There is no full defence minister; a minister-delegate attached to the head of government manages the defence administration.

The Royal Gendarmerie polices rural areas and highways, and it also reports through the military chain. The Auxiliary Forces, a paramilitary body, sit under the Interior Ministry.

Internal security is concentrated in one man, Abdellatif Hammouchi. He heads both the national police, the DGSN, and the domestic intelligence service, the DGST.

The DGST’s investigative arm leads counter-terrorism cases and works closely with US and European agencies. Foreign intelligence sits with a separate service, the DGED.

The Interior Ministry is the most powerful civilian ministry, organising elections and supervising governors and local councils. Its minister acts as a bridge between the palace and the parties.

Courts, Governors and the Regions

The constitution declares the judiciary independent and names the King its guarantor. He chairs the Supreme Council of Judicial Power, which appoints, promotes and disciplines judges.

The Constitutional Court has 12 members, six named by the King and three elected by each chamber. It rules on election disputes and on whether laws respect the constitution.

Since 2017 prosecutors have answered to an independent Public Prosecution Presidency rather than the justice minister. On 3 October 2026 it said the legislative elections had taken place under normal conditions.

Outside Rabat, power runs through walis and governors appointed by the King. They represent the central state in Morocco’s 12 regions and its provinces, alongside regional councils that voters elect.

This dual structure explains why a mayor or regional president can be popular yet limited. The governor, backed by the Interior Ministry, still controls permits, security and much of the local budget process.

Religion, Western Sahara and the Red Lines

Three subjects sit above party politics: the monarchy, Islam and the territorial claim over Western Sahara. Parties that challenge them are not allowed to compete, and journalists who cross them face prosecution.

Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony that Morocco controls largely and claims fully, is the core foreign-policy file. The United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in December 2020, and Washington has kept that position since.

On 31 October 2025 the UN Security Council backed Morocco’s autonomy plan as the basis for talks on the territory. The guide to Morocco’s geopolitics explains the dispute with Algeria and the Polisario Front.

Religious policy is run from the palace through the Ministry of Habous and Islamic Affairs. Morocco promotes a Maliki, Sufi-influenced Islam and trains imams from other African countries, a form of soft power.

The Rising Figures to Watch

Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri. Head of government-designate; her cabinet list and confidence vote will define her first months.

Head of government-designate; her cabinet list and confidence vote will define her first months. Nizar Baraka. Istiqlal secretary-general and outgoing minister of equipment and water; his party is the largest likely partner.

Istiqlal secretary-general and outgoing minister of equipment and water; his party is the largest likely partner. Mohamed Chaouki. RNI president since February 2026; whether his party joins the cabinet or leads the opposition is undecided.

RNI president since February 2026; whether his party joins the cabinet or leads the opposition is undecided. Abdelilah Benkirane. PJD leader and head of government from 2011 to 2017; he is set to lead the largest opposition bloc.

PJD leader and head of government from 2011 to 2017; he is set to lead the largest opposition bloc. Abdelouafi Laftit. Interior minister since 2017, who ran the 2026 election; whether he keeps the post is a signal of palace continuity.

Interior minister since 2017, who ran the 2026 election; whether he keeps the post is a signal of palace continuity. Nasser Bourita. Foreign minister since 2017 and the face of the Western Sahara campaign abroad.

Youth discontent is the wider force behind these names, and young voters’ anger over hospitals, schools and jobs shaped the campaign. The Rio Times election explainer describes that mood.

What It Means for US Readers

Morocco is a major non-NATO ally of the United States, a status granted in 2004. The US-Morocco Free Trade Agreement has been in force since 2006, according to the US Trade Representative.

The change of government does not alter that relationship, because foreign and security policy sit with the King. The annual African Lion military exercise and cooperation on counter-terrorism are palace-level matters.

What can change is economic policy: the 2027 budget, subsidies, housing programmes and the tempo of World Cup 2030 spending. US companies in Morocco, from aerospace suppliers to energy firms, should watch who takes the finance and industry portfolios.

For travellers, the political transition is orderly and has no visible security impact. Morocco co-hosts the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal, and the state treats stability as a national priority.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket’s “Next Prime Minister of Morocco?” market resolves only once a new head of government takes office and wins investiture. At 6:27 a.m. ET on 9 October 2026, El Mansouri traded at 94.5%, on about US$19,500 in bets.

A larger market, “Aziz Akhannouch out as Morocco Prime Minister by December 31, 2026?”, has drawn about US$171,600. Its rules say an announced removal resolves it to Yes, and its last trade was at 99%.

That market had not been formally resolved on the morning of 9 October. Its thin order book showed bids at 79% and offers at 89%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

The final make-up of the coalition is not known, nor whether the RNI will be inside or outside it. No date for the cabinet’s appointment had been announced by the morning of 9 October 2026.

It is not known who will be elected speaker of the House of Representatives. Le360 reported that the PAM wants the post, but that has not been officially confirmed.

The content of the King’s speech opening Parliament on 9 October was not public at the time of writing. It is also unclear whether a new cabinet can table the 2027 budget bill by the legal deadline of 20 October.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the head of state of Morocco?

King Mohammed VI, who has reigned since 1999. He commands the armed forces, leads religious affairs and sets foreign policy.

Who is Morocco’s prime minister in October 2026?

The King appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri head of government on 29 September 2026. Until her cabinet is named, Aziz Akhannouch’s outgoing team handles current affairs.

Who won Morocco’s 2026 election?

The Authenticity and Modernity Party won 97 of 395 seats on 23 September 2026. No party has a majority, so a coalition is needed.

Is Morocco an absolute monarchy?

No, it is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament and government. The King, however, keeps the army, religion, foreign policy and senior appointments.

Which parties are in Morocco’s opposition?

The Justice and Development Party has said it will sit in opposition. The RNI’s position depends on the final coalition deal.

Does the change of government affect US travellers or investors?

Security and foreign policy stay with the palace, so ties with the United States are unchanged. Economic policy, including the 2027 budget, is where the new cabinet can make a difference.

World.title: Egypt Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
EGYPT · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country About 118.4 million people in 2025, per the World Bank.

— Head of state President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, in office since 2014, term to 2030.

— Head of government Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly chaired the cabinet on 7 October 2026.

— Parliament Speaker Hisham Badawy leads a House dominated by pro-government parties.

— Security Lt Gen Ashraf Salem Zaher is defence and military production minister.

— Still open No named successor; Sisi’s current term is set to be his last.

A president in his final term, technocratic ministers, a loyal parliament and a powerful military decide who runs Egypt.

Egypt politics in October 2026 revolves around one man, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, and the security institutions around him. Parliament, the cabinet and the courts work inside limits the presidency sets.

For US readers, Egypt matters as a long-standing security partner that runs the Suez Canal and borders Israel and Gaza. This guide sets out who holds power as of October 2026 and how the pieces fit together.

How Egypt Politics Works Under the Constitution

Egypt is a presidential republic governed by its 2014 constitution. The president is head of state, names the prime minister and sets the direction of foreign and security policy.

Day-to-day government belongs to the cabinet, led by the prime minister. Parliament has two chambers: the House of Representatives, which passes laws, and a smaller Senate.

Elections are run by the National Election Authority, an independent body the 2014 constitution created in Article 208. Its ten-member judicial board is chaired by its most senior member from the Court of Cassation, the top appeals court.

On paper, power is spread across these bodies. In practice, the presidency and the armed forces sit at the centre, and the other institutions rarely challenge them.

For the wider picture of the country, see the Rio Times explainer on Egypt and the Egypt news hub.

President Sisi and the Presidency

Abdel Fattah el-Sisi rose to power after the 2013 removal of President Mohammed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood. He was first elected president in 2014.

He won a third term in a December 2023 election with more than 89 percent of the vote, Al-Monitor reported. He was sworn in on Tuesday, 2 April 2024.

That six-year term runs to 2030 and is set to be his last under the current constitution. Changing that would require another constitutional amendment.

The president is also supreme commander of the armed forces, the title the cabinet uses for him. On 6 October 2026, Sisi began an Asian tour in South Korea, followed by Malaysia and Indonesia, the presidency says.

Foreign policy, including ties with the Gulf states and Gaza diplomacy, is steered by the presidency. The Egypt geopolitics explainer covers those relationships in detail.

The Prime Minister and the Key Ministers

Mostafa Madbouly is prime minister. He chaired the weekly cabinet meeting at the government headquarters in the New Administrative Capital on 7 October 2026.

His cabinet is made up of technocrats and senior officers rather than party leaders. It carries out the president’s programme.

The ministers who matter most, according to the official cabinet list as of October 2026:

Defence and Military Production: Lt Gen Ashraf Salem Zaher, an air defence officer and former head of the Egyptian Military Academy.

Lt Gen Ashraf Salem Zaher, an air defence officer and former head of the Egyptian Military Academy. Interior: Maj Gen Mahmoud Tawfik, who rose through the National Security sector, the domestic intelligence arm.

Maj Gen Mahmoud Tawfik, who rose through the National Security sector, the domestic intelligence arm. Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptians Abroad: Badr Abdelatty, the country’s top diplomat.

Badr Abdelatty, the country’s top diplomat. Finance: Ahmed Kouchouk, who runs the budget and talks with the IMF, the International Monetary Fund.

Ahmed Kouchouk, who runs the budget and talks with the IMF, the International Monetary Fund. Planning and Economic Development: Ahmed Rostom, who presents the economic programme to lenders and rating agencies.

Ahmed Rostom, who presents the economic programme to lenders and rating agencies. Transport: Lt Gen Kamel al-Wazir, an army engineer who headed the Armed Forces Engineering Authority from 2015.

Lt Gen Kamel al-Wazir, an army engineer who headed the Armed Forces Engineering Authority from 2015. Water Resources and Irrigation: Hani Sewilam, a former negotiator on Ethiopia’s Nile dam.

Hani Sewilam, a former negotiator on Ethiopia’s Nile dam. Justice: Counsellor Mahmoud Helmy El-Sherif; “counsellor” is the title of senior judges.

Counsellor Mahmoud Helmy El-Sherif; “counsellor” is the title of senior judges. Information (minister of state): Diaa Rashwan, who handles government media policy.

A deputy prime minister for economic affairs, Dr Hussein Issa, coordinates the economic ministries. The guide to who runs Egypt’s economy profiles them and the central bank.

Parliament, the Parties and the Speaker

The House of Representatives began its 2026 to 2031 term in January 2026. On 12 January 2026, it elected Hisham Badawy, a former head of the Central Auditing Organization, as speaker.

Badawy won 521 of 570 valid ballots, Egypt Today reported. His only challenger, Mahmoud Sami El-Imam of the Egyptian Social Democratic Party, received 49.

The split of committee chairs shows who controls the chamber. Of 25 committees, Nation’s Future took 12, Homeland Defenders 6 and the National Front 4, Al Manassa reported on 14 January 2026.

The main parties in brief:

Nation’s Future (Mostaqbal Watan): the leading pro-government party, with the most committee chairs.

the leading pro-government party, with the most committee chairs. Homeland Defenders (Homat al-Watan): a pro-government party, second by committee chairs.

a pro-government party, second by committee chairs. National Front: a newer pro-government party that holds four committee chairs.

a newer pro-government party that holds four committee chairs. Republican People’s Party: a smaller party allied with the government; it holds one committee chair.

a smaller party allied with the government; it holds one committee chair. New Wafd and Reform and Development: smaller parties that hold deputy committee posts rather than chairs.

The Senate has 300 members, 100 of them appointed by the president, as Ahram Online reported in October 2025. Counsellor Essam Farid, a member of the Supreme Judicial Council, was elected Senate president for the 2025 to 2030 term.

The Military and Security Services

The armed forces are the most powerful institution outside the presidency. Generals also hold key civilian posts as of October 2026.

Two lieutenant generals sit in the cabinet: the defence minister and the transport minister. A minister of state for military production, Maj Gen Salah Soliman, also serves.

The army is an economic actor as well. The US State Department says state and military-owned companies compete directly with private firms, and notes resistance to selling state assets.

The interior ministry runs the police and the National Security sector. Its minister, Mahmoud Tawfik, rose through that service, whose work includes extremism cases.

Courts, Elections and Governors

The Supreme Constitutional Court decides whether laws comply with the constitution. The Court of Cassation is the highest court for criminal and civil appeals.

Judges also play a direct role in politics. They staff the National Election Authority, and the Supreme Administrative Court hears appeals against its decisions on national elections.

The 2025 House election was a drawn-out process. The authority was still issuing final re-run results in early 2026, under its decisions No. 1 and No. 2 of 2026.

Governors run Egypt’s provinces, but they are appointed rather than elected. The president swears them in, as Ahram Online reported of a 2015 reshuffle.

They work with the local development and environment minister, Manal Awad, and meet in a cabinet governors’ council.

Opposition and the Rising Figures

Organised opposition is weak. The Muslim Brotherhood, Morsi’s movement, holds no seats and is absent from parliament.

Smaller and opposition-leaning parties won no committee chairs in January 2026. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party fielded the only rival to Badawy for speaker.

Rising figures to watch come mainly from within the system. Speaker Badawy, Prime Minister Madbouly and Defence Minister Zaher all owe their posts to the president.

Former foreign minister Sameh Shoukry now chairs a House committee as an independent, Al Manassa reported. Former housing minister Assem El-Gazzar was among the nominees for deputy speaker, Egypt Today reported.

No one has been publicly positioned as Sisi’s successor as of October 2026. The question will grow louder as 2030 approaches.

What It Means for US Readers

Egypt is a major recipient of US aid. Since 1978, the United States has provided over US$50 billion in military and US$30 billion in economic assistance, the State Department says.

That aid ties Washington to a country that controls the Suez Canal, borders Gaza and hosts the Arab League. Decisions in Cairo affect shipping costs, Gaza diplomacy and the security of Israel.

For investors, the concentration of power means policy shifts come from the presidency, not parliament. The military’s business role matters for anyone weighing a partner or a tender.

For travellers, politics rarely touches daily life in tourist areas. Visitors should still keep away from political gatherings and demonstrations.

What Is Not Known

Total House seats by party were not confirmed at a primary source; the parliament and Senate websites could not be reached. Committee chairs are used here as a measure of strength.

It is not known who would succeed Sisi, or whether the constitution will be amended again before 2030. The names of the current army chief of staff and intelligence chief were not confirmed for this guide.

The cabinet list gives no date for the most recent reshuffle. Changes after 9 October 2026 are not reflected here.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the president of Egypt in 2026?

Abdel Fattah el-Sisi is president as of October 2026. He was sworn in for a third six-year term on 2 April 2024, which runs to 2030.

Who is the prime minister of Egypt?

Mostafa Madbouly is prime minister as of October 2026. He chaired the cabinet meeting on 7 October 2026, according to the cabinet office.

Which party controls Egypt’s parliament?

Pro-government parties dominate the House of Representatives. Nation’s Future leads them, taking 12 of the 25 committee chairs in January 2026.

Who is the speaker of Egypt’s parliament?

Hisham Badawy, a former head of the Central Auditing Organization, was elected speaker on 12 January 2026. The Senate is led by Counsellor Essam Farid.

How powerful is the military in Egypt?

The armed forces are the strongest institution after the presidency. Generals hold the defence and transport ministries, and military-owned firms are active across the economy.

When is Egypt’s next presidential election?

Sisi’s current term ends in 2030, so the next presidential vote is due before then. No date has been set as of October 2026.

Sources: Presidency of Egypt; Egyptian Cabinet, composition; Egyptian Cabinet, news; National Election Authority; US State Department; World Bank population data; Egypt Today; Al Manassa; Ahram Online (Senate); Ahram Online (governors); Enterprise; Al-Monitor (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Kenya Culture, the Key Figures to Know in 2026
World.content:
KENYA · CULTURE

Key Facts — The country About 47.6 million people (2019 census); eight UNESCO World Heritage sites.

— Who Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, Wangari Maathai, Lupita Nyong’o, Eliud Kipchoge, Faith Kipyegon.

— What happened Kenya’s 10 October holiday became Mazingira Day, an environment day, in 2024.

— Dates Holidays 10 and 20 October; Kenya co-hosts AFCON from 19 June 2027.

— For US visitors Level 2 State Department advisory as of July 2026; eTA required.

A Nobel laureate, an Oscar winner, Olympic champions and painted minibuses: the people and places that define Kenya abroad.

Kenya culture reaches far beyond the safari image, from a Nobel Peace Prize laureate to an Oscar winner and Olympic champions. This guide names the musicians, writers, film-makers, artists, athletes, media houses and festivals that matter as of October 2026.

For a US reader, the links are closer than they look. Several of these figures built their careers in American universities, museums and film studios.

How Kenya Culture Is Built: Languages, Peoples and Heritage

Kenya counted 47,564,296 people in its 2019 census, according to the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), the official statistics office. That is roughly the population of Spain.

No single group defines the national culture. Dozens of communities, from the Kikuyu and Luo to the Maasai and coastal Swahili, keep distinct languages and rites.

We never share your email.

Most urban Kenyans move between Kiswahili, English and a home language. In Nairobi, young people add Sheng, a fast-changing street slang that mixes Kiswahili and English.

UNESCO, the UN cultural agency, lists eight World Heritage sites in Kenya as of October 2026, five of them cultural. Gedi, a historic coastal town and archaeological site, was the latest addition in 2024.

The other four are Lamu Old Town (2001), the Mijikenda Kaya Forests (2008), Fort Jesus in Mombasa (2011) and Thimlich Ohinga (2018). The three natural sites include Mount Kenya and the Lake Turkana National Parks.

UNESCO’s intangible heritage register adds four Kenyan traditions in need of urgent safeguarding. They include the Isukuti dance of western Kenya and three Maasai rites of passage for young men.

Culture also sits on the calendar. Kenya’s Public Holidays Act, last amended 26 April 2024, sets Mazingira Day on 10 October and Mashujaa (Heroes’) Day on 20 October.

The 10 October date was gazetted as Utamaduni (Culture) Day in 2020, the Nation newspaper reports. The 2024 amendment renamed it Mazingira, the Kiswahili word for environment.

In 2026, Mazingira Day falls on Saturday 10 October and Mashujaa Day on Tuesday 20 October. Jamhuri Day, which marks independence in 1963, follows on 12 December.

Music From Benga to Gengetone

Kenyan popular music grew out of the guitar. Benga, a fast, guitar-led dance music rooted in Luo communities around Lake Victoria, became a defining sound after independence.

On the coast, taarab, a sung poetry tradition with Arab and Indian influences, still accompanies weddings in Mombasa and Lamu. Upcountry, church choirs and gospel singers fill radio playlists.

Modern Afro-pop is carried by names such as Sauti Sol, a four-man Nairobi band, and its singer Bien, who also records solo. Their harmony-led songs mix Kiswahili, English and Sheng.

In the late 2010s, gengetone, a rowdy rap style sung in Sheng, spread through Nairobi’s matatus, the privately run minibuses. Its loose, chant-like hooks were built for matatu sound systems and dance floors.

The capital’s hip-hop scene also trades on nostalgia, with reunions such as the Camp Mulla Funky Town night in Nairobi. Live music clusters in Nairobi venues, coastal resorts and year-end festivals.

Writers Who Shaped How Africa Is Read

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o is the central name in Kenyan letters. His novels include Weep Not, Child, Petals of Blood, Devil on the Cross and Wizard of the Crow.

He was Distinguished Professor of English and Comparative Literature at the University of California, Irvine, which he joined in 2002. UC Irvine announced his death, aged 87, on 29 May 2025.

Ngũgĩ became known for arguing that African writers should use African languages, and he wrote fiction in Gikuyu. That debate still shapes Kenyan publishing, schools and literary festivals.

Wangari Maathai, the environmentalist and memoirist, won the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it. The Nobel committee cited her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace.

Maathai was born in Nyeri in 1940 and died in Nairobi in 2011, according to the Nobel Foundation. The tree planting promoted on Mazingira Day echoes her legacy.

A younger generation includes the late essayist Binyavanga Wainaina and the novelist Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor. Their satire and lyrical prose pushed back against outsiders’ clichés about Africa.

Film, Television and the Fight Over Rafiki

The Kenyan actor Lupita Nyong’o won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for 12 Years a Slave. The award came at the 86th Academy Awards in 2014.

At home, the director Wanuri Kahiu made Rafiki, a love story between two young women in Nairobi. The Cannes Film Festival selected it for its Un Certain Regard section in 2018.

The Kenya Film Classification Board, the state film regulator, banned it for promoting lesbianism, the Nation newspaper reported. High Court judge Wilfrida Okwany lifted the ban for seven days in September 2018.

The short window let adults see the film and kept its Oscar hopes alive. The case still frames a split between a conservative regulator and a younger, more liberal creative class.

Television drama, stand-up comedy and Kiswahili-language soaps dominate local screens. Global streaming platforms now commission Kenyan series, giving Nairobi actors audiences far beyond East Africa.

Visual Artists and the Street as Gallery

Wangechi Mutu, born in Nairobi in 1972, was the first artist chosen for the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s facade commission. The Met says her works were the first art ever shown in the facade’s niches.

Her four bronze figures, The NewOnes, will free Us, filled the Fifth Avenue niches from 9 September 2019 to 8 June 2020. The commission put contemporary African sculpture on the front of a major American museum.

Much of Nairobi’s public art is on the move. Matatu crews commission airbrushed murals of musicians, footballers and film heroes, turning rush-hour traffic into an open-air gallery.

Galleries and artist collectives in the capital show contemporary painting, sculpture and photography. The Nairobi National Museum, run by the state National Museums of Kenya, holds the national collections.

Sport Icons and the Running Heartland

Distance running is where Kenya’s name travels furthest abroad. Eliud Kipchoge is a two-time Olympic champion, according to World Athletics, the sport’s governing body.

Kipchoge’s marathon personal best of 2:01:09 dates from 25 September 2022. He also lists a world title and silver medals at both the Olympics and the World Championships.

Faith Kipyegon won her third straight Olympic 1500m title in Paris on Saturday 10 August 2024, in an Olympic record of 3:51.29. World Athletics called her the first woman to win three Olympic golds in a single track discipline.

Many champions train in the Rift Valley highlands, around towns such as Iten. Schools there, such as St Patrick’s High School, have turned running into a career path.

Football is the mass spectator sport. Kenya will co-host the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), the continental championship, with Tanzania and Uganda.

The Confederation of African Football (CAF) says it runs from 19 June to 17 July 2027, both Saturdays. At home, the annual Nairobi Marathon turns the capital’s Southern Bypass into a racecourse.

Media Houses, Comedy and Festivals

Kenya’s cultural conversation runs through a few large media houses. Nation Media Group publishes the Daily Nation and the Kiswahili daily Taifa Leo; Royal Media Services owns Citizen TV.

The Standard Group and the state-owned Kenya Broadcasting Corporation complete the main players. Their comedy shows, talk shows and radio call-ins shape slang, music tastes and political satire.

Online creators now compete with them for attention. Many young Kenyans first hear new songs and jokes on short-video apps rather than on broadcast radio.

On the coast, the Lamu Cultural Festival brings ngoma drumming and dancing to the island’s seafront. Around New Year, the Beneath the Baobabs festival in Kilifi mixes music and art.

National holidays add their own rituals. Mashujaa Day on 20 October brings official ceremonies honouring the heroes of the independence struggle.

What It Means for US Readers

Many of these figures are already part of American cultural life. Ngũgĩ taught in California for over two decades, Mutu’s sculptures stood on Fifth Avenue, and Nyong’o works in Hollywood.

Travellers should check the rules first. Kenya requires visitors to apply online for an Electronic Travel Authorisation (eTA) before departure.

The US State Department rates Kenya Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, in an advisory issued on 28 July 2026. It lists Lamu County, home to Lamu Old Town, as Level 4, “do not travel”.

The same advisory also lists Nairobi’s Eastleigh and Kibera neighbourhoods as Level 4. Coastal festivals and Nairobi nightlife therefore need planning, local advice and registered transport.

Football fans eyeing AFCON 2027 should watch for ticket and venue details from the three hosts. For the wider picture, see the guides to who holds power in Kenya, who runs Kenya’s economy and Kenya’s geopolitics.

More coverage is collected on the Kenya page of The Rio Times.

What Is Not Known

Population figures here come from the 2019 census. Newer official counts by community or language were not confirmed for this guide.

Official dates for the 2026 Lamu Cultural Festival and other year-end festivals were not confirmed. AFCON 2027 venues and ticket prices in Kenya were also not confirmed as of October 2026.

No official body publishes music sales or streaming rankings for Kenyan artists, so no ranking is given. The current legal status of Rafiki in Kenya after the 2018 window was not confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kenya culture known for?

Kenya is known for distance runners, coastal Swahili heritage, Maasai traditions and writers such as Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o. Its modern scene adds Afro-pop, Sheng street rap and painted matatu minibuses.

What languages do people speak in Kenya?

Most Kenyans use Kiswahili and English alongside a home language. In Nairobi, young people also speak Sheng, a street slang mixing Kiswahili and English.

Who was Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o?

He was a leading Kenyan novelist and a Distinguished Professor at the University of California, Irvine. UC Irvine announced his death, aged 87, on 29 May 2025.

Is Mazingira Day a public holiday in Kenya?

Yes. Under the Public Holidays Act, 10 October is Mazingira Day, an environment holiday, and in 2026 it falls on a Saturday.

Is it safe to visit Kenya’s cultural sites?

The US State Department rates Kenya Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, as of July 2026. It advises against all travel to Lamu County and to Nairobi’s Eastleigh and Kibera neighbourhoods.

When does Kenya host the Africa Cup of Nations?

Kenya co-hosts AFCON 2027 with Tanzania and Uganda. CAF says it runs from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

Sources: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, 2019 census; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Kenya; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Kenya; Kenya Law, Public Holidays Act; Nobel Prize, Wangari Maathai; UC Irvine, Office of the Chancellor; Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences; Festival de Cannes, Rafiki; The Metropolitan Museum of Art; World Athletics, Eliud Kipchoge; World Athletics, Paris 2024 women’s 1500m; CAF, AFCON Pamoja 2027 dates; US State Department, Kenya advisory; Kenya eTA portal; Nation, Rafiki ruling; Nation, 10 October holidays (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Foreign Powers and Investors in Nigeria 2026
World.content:
NIGERIA · FOREIGN PLAYERS

Key Facts — The country Africa’s most populous nation, about 237.5 million people in 2025.

— Biggest lender World Bank: US$20.7 billion of US$54.5 billion owed abroad, June 2026.

— China Two Chinese state banks were owed US$5.5 billion in June 2026.

— What happened UK and US funds sent about 80% of early-2026 capital inflows.

— Diaspora Remittances reached US$22.8 billion in 2025, over five times FDI.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives Bola Tinubu a 73% chance of winning the January 2027 election (9 October, 6:09 a.m. ET).

Lenders, fund managers, oil companies, Washington and Beijing all have a stake in Africa’s most populous country, and each wants something different.

Nigeria foreign relations in 2026 run mostly on money: who lends to Abuja, who invests and who sends cash home. The biggest single creditor is the World Bank, and Nigerians abroad send home more than five times what foreign firms invest directly.

This guide maps the main foreign actors as of October 2026, what each brings and what each wants in return. Daily coverage is in the Rio Times Nigeria section.

Why Nigeria Matters to Outsiders

Nigeria had about 237.5 million people in 2025, World Bank data show, roughly 70% of the US population. Its economy was worth US$290.8 billion that year, less than a tenth of California’s output.

The dollar figure was US$487.4 billion in 2023. It fell mainly because the naira, the national currency, lost much of its value after reforms began that year.
