We never share your email.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) set its official central rate at ₦1,331.60 per US$ on 8 October 2026. That is the exchange-rate basis used throughout this guide.

Two numbers frame the foreign relationship. Nigeria owed foreign creditors US$54.5 billion on 30 June 2026.

The CBN held gross reserves of US$55.1 billion on 7 October 2026. Reserves are the dollars that pay for imports and debt service.

Having them roughly match the external debt is a buffer. But reserves can fall far faster than debt is repaid.

Who runs the domestic side of the economy is covered in a separate pillar, Who Runs Nigeria’s Economy. This guide looks outward.

Nigeria Foreign Debt by Creditor in 2026

The Debt Management Office (DMO), the federal agency that tracks public borrowing, splits the US$54.5 billion into three groups. Its figures for 30 June 2026 are the latest it has published.

Multilateral lenders: US$24.8 billion, or 45.4%, led by the World Bank.

US$24.8 billion, or 45.4%, led by the World Bank. Commercial creditors: US$23.2 billion, or 42.5%, mostly Eurobonds sold on international markets.

US$23.2 billion, or 42.5%, mostly Eurobonds sold on international markets. Bilateral lenders, meaning other governments: US$6.6 billion, or 12.1%, mostly China.

The World Bank Group is the largest single creditor. Its International Development Association (IDA), the arm that lends cheaply to poorer countries, is owed US$19.1 billion.

Add US$1.6 billion from its market-rate arm, the IBRD, and the bank holds about 38% of the external debt. Its loans usually carry policy conditions, which is how it shapes reform.

The World Bank listed 39 active projects in Nigeria as of October 2026. The newest large one, approved on 29 June 2026, is a US$1.25 billion operation to speed up investment and jobs.

Eurobonds are the second pillar. These are dollar bonds sold abroad, and investors held US$18.5 billion of them at the end of June 2026.

They trade on international markets, so their prices react quickly to Nigerian news. The DMO publishes their closing prices and yields every trading day.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the crisis lender for governments, is owed nothing. Its records show no outstanding Nigerian loans as of 30 September 2026.

Nigeria drew a pandemic emergency loan of SDR 2.45 billion (about US$3.4 billion) in April 2020 and has since repaid it. The IMF still reviews the economy and advises the government.

The African Development Bank Group, based in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, is owed about US$3.25 billion across three windows. The Islamic Development Bank holds US$406 million and IFAD, the UN farm-lending fund, US$315 million.

China, the Gulf and Europe

China is the largest government lender. The Export-Import Bank of China is owed US$4.9 billion and China Development Bank US$574 million, together about 10% of the total.

Chinese state firms are investors as well as lenders. The deep-sea port at Lekki, east of Lagos, is a joint venture led by China Harbour Engineering Company and Singapore’s Tolaram.

Lagos State and the federal ports authority also hold stakes. For Beijing, Nigeria means work for its companies and access to Africa’s most populous market.

Trade is growing too, as a Rio Times report on Nigerian exports to China sets out.

The Gulf is a quieter creditor. First Abu Dhabi Bank, from the United Arab Emirates, is owed US$3.4 billion, including a US$1.5 billion total return swap.

A total return swap is a derivative contract that works much like a secured loan. Together, the two deals make the Abu Dhabi bank a bigger creditor than the African Development Bank Group.

Cairo-based Afreximbank, the African trade-finance bank, holds US$836 million of syndicated loans. Smaller commercial creditors include Italy’s UniCredit, owed US$316 million, and Deutsche Bank, owed US$52 million.

European and Asian governments lend far less than China. France’s development agency AFD is owed US$906 million, Japan’s JICA US$127 million and Germany’s KfW US$78 million.

Foreign Investors, Fast Money Versus Factories

Foreign investors brought US$10.37 billion into Nigeria in the first quarter of 2026, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) reported. That was 83.8% more than a year earlier, according to Voice of Nigeria, the state broadcaster.

Almost all of it, US$9.86 billion or 95.1%, was portfolio money: bonds, treasury bills and shares that can be sold within days. Foreign direct investment (FDI), meaning factories, offices and company stakes, was just US$135 million.

By source, the United Kingdom sent US$5.08 billion (49%) and the United States US$3.18 billion (30.7%). South Africa followed with US$984 million (9.5%).

The UK share partly reflects London’s role as a hub through which global funds route money. Banks took US$7.55 billion of the inflows, and Standard Chartered’s Nigerian unit alone received US$4.41 billion.

Portfolio investors want high interest rates and a currency they can exit at a fair price. When those conditions slip, the money can leave as quickly as it came.

The World Bank’s balance-of-payments measure, which uses a different method, shows net FDI inflows of US$4.0 billion in 2025. That was up from US$1.6 billion in 2024.

The NBS plans to publish second-quarter 2026 figures on 21 October 2026, according to its release calendar.

Oil Majors Move Offshore

Foreign oil majors built Nigeria’s oil industry over seven decades. Since 2024, several have sold their onshore and shallow-water fields.

Shell completed the sale of its onshore subsidiary, SPDC, to Renaissance on 13 March 2025, after federal approval. ExxonMobil completed the sale of its entire shallow-water business to Seplat Energy on 12 December 2024.

Seplat, listed in Lagos and London, paid ExxonMobil US$672 million in cash at closing. Its largest shareholder at the time was France’s Maurel & Prom, with 20.46%.

The majors are not leaving entirely. Shell still operates the deepwater Bonga field with NNPC Limited, the state oil company, as a Rio Times report on Bonga explains.

Deepwater fields sit far offshore, away from the pipeline theft that has long troubled onshore production. Abuja is courting new upstream money through its latest oil licensing round.

Outside oil, foreign firms run some well-known consumer brands. MTN Nigeria, a mobile network, is part of South Africa’s MTN Group.

From Brazil, meatpacker JBS signed a memorandum in November 2024 for a US$2.5 billion plan with six plants, ThisDay reported, citing JBS. Its progress and the debate around it are covered in a separate Rio Times report.

Washington, Security and the Embassies

Security ties with the United States changed sharply in late 2025. In late October, President Donald Trump redesignated Nigeria a Country of Particular Concern over religious freedom.

That label can lead to US sanctions. Abuja denied that Christians face a genocide, as some US politicians had alleged, but chose to cooperate.

On 27 November 2025, the presidency named its members of a joint working group with Washington. National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu leads the Nigerian side.

On 25 December 2025, US Africa Command (AFRICOM) struck Islamic State camps in Sokoto State, in the north-west. It said the strikes were carried out in coordination with Nigerian authorities.

Washington also restricted visas. A presidential proclamation partly suspended new US immigrant, tourist and student visas for Nigerians from 1 January 2026.

Most large powers keep embassies in Abuja, the capital, and many also run consulates in Lagos, the commercial hub. The wider diplomatic map is in Nigeria Geopolitics Explained.

The religious-freedom talks are followed in a Rio Times report on the US working group. Trade ties are modest by comparison.

US goods exports to Nigeria were US$6.78 billion in 2025 and imports US$5.02 billion, Census Bureau data show. In 2008, the US imported US$38.1 billion of Nigerian goods, mostly crude oil.

The Diaspora and the Donors

Nigerians abroad send home more than foreign companies invest. Personal remittances reached US$22.8 billion in 2025, World Bank data show, about 7.8% of GDP.

That is more than five times the World Bank’s FDI figure for the same year. Unlike loans, the money does not have to be repaid, and much of it pays for school fees, rent and small businesses.

Many senders live in the United States and the United Kingdom. That makes US visa and immigration policy an economic issue for Nigerian households.

Classic aid is smaller than lending. Much of what donors provide now comes as cheap loans, such as World Bank IDA credits, rather than grants.

One active World Bank project, approved in August 2025, supports people displaced by conflict and the communities that host them. UN agencies and international NGOs run food, health and protection programmes, especially in the north-east.

What It Means for US Readers

US investors are already exposed. Funds from the United States sent US$3.18 billion to Nigeria in the first quarter of 2026, almost a third of all inflows.

Nigerian Eurobonds often sit in emerging-market bond funds sold to US savers. Nigerian politics can therefore move US portfolios.

For travellers and families, the visa proclamation is the bigger change. Check the State Department’s current travel advisory before any trip.

The January 2027 election matters too, because a new president could change currency and subsidy policy. The players are profiled in Nigeria Politics Explained.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bettors gave President Bola Tinubu a 73% chance of winning at 6:09 a.m. ET on Friday, 9 October 2026. Tinubu, in office since May 2023, leads the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

Peter Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress candidate and a former Anambra governor, stood at 23.5%. About US$129,700 had been bet on the market in total.

The vote for president and the National Assembly is set for Saturday, 16 January 2027, according to the electoral commission, INEC. The market offers no contract on some candidates, including Atiku Abubakar.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Second-quarter 2026 capital-importation data, due from the NBS on 21 October 2026.

External debt for 30 September 2026, which the DMO had not yet published.

How much of the UK figure is British money and how much is global funds routed through London.

The full terms of the First Abu Dhabi Bank swap, which could not be confirmed from a primary source.

How far the JBS livestock plan has advanced since 2024.

Total US government aid to Nigeria after Washington’s 2025 overhaul of foreign assistance, and total foreign NGO spending.

Whether the working group with Washington will lead to the religious-freedom designation being lifted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Nigeria’s biggest foreign creditor?

The World Bank Group, owed about US$20.7 billion on 30 June 2026, mostly through its IDA arm. That is roughly 38% of Nigeria’s US$54.5 billion external debt.

How much does Nigeria owe China?

Chinese state banks were owed about US$5.5 billion on 30 June 2026, DMO data show. That is roughly a tenth of Nigeria’s external debt.

Does Nigeria have an IMF loan?

No. IMF records show no outstanding loans to Nigeria as of 30 September 2026, after it repaid a 2020 pandemic emergency loan.

Which countries invest most in Nigeria?

In NBS data for early 2026, the United Kingdom (49%), the United States (30.7%) and South Africa (9.5%) led. Most of that money went into bonds and bills, not factories.

How much do Nigerians abroad send home?

Personal remittances reached about US$22.8 billion in 2025, according to the World Bank. That is more than five times net foreign direct investment that year.

Has the US carried out military action in Nigeria?

Yes. US Africa Command said it struck Islamic State camps in Sokoto State on 25 December 2025, in coordination with Nigerian authorities.

Are Western oil companies leaving Nigeria?

They are leaving onshore and shallow-water fields, not the country. Shell and ExxonMobil sold those assets in 2024 and 2025, but Shell still runs the deepwater Bonga field.

Sources: Debt Management Office, external debt stock as at 30 June 2026; Central Bank of Nigeria, official exchange rates; Central Bank of Nigeria, external reserves; IMF, Nigeria financial position in the Fund; World Bank, Nigeria data (population, GDP, remittances, FDI); World Bank, active projects in Nigeria; National Bureau of Statistics, release calendar; Voice of Nigeria, NBS capital importation Q1 2026; Shell, completion of SPDC sale; Maurel & Prom, Seplat completion of MPNU acquisition; Lekki Port, ownership; State House, US-Nigeria working group; US Africa Command, Sokoto strike; US House Resolution 860 on the Nigeria designation; Federal Register, Proclamation 10998; US Census Bureau, trade with Nigeria; Independent National Electoral Commission; ThisDay, JBS investment plan; Polymarket market data via its public API (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Shain Young granted $6,000 bail after nearly four months on remand for alleged sexual assault of 12-year-old girl
World.content:
Shain Young granted $6,000 bail after nearly four months on remand for alleged sexual assault of 12-year-old girl

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 33-year-old Belize City construction worker accused of sexually assaulting a 12-year-old girl during a family swimming trip has been released on bail after spending nearly four months on remand at the Belize Central Prison.

Shain Young, a resident of May Flower Street, appeared before a magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 7, where he was granted bail of $6,000, with two sureties of $3,000 each, subject to conditions imposed by the court.

Young met bail later that afternoon and is scheduled to return to court on October 30, 2026.

He was initially arraigned on June 9, 2026, on a single charge of assault of a child by penetration. No plea was taken at the time, and he was remanded after the prosecution strongly objected to bail.

The charge stems from an alleged incident on May 31, 2026, when Young accompanied several family members, including the 12-year-old complainant, on a swimming trip to a pond in the Blackberry Ridge Estate area.

According to police reports, the child alleged that Young, who was known to her family, inappropriately touched and sexually assaulted her while they were in the water.

During his initial arraignment before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison, prosecutor Sergeant Christopher Smith objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the allegation and concerns about possible interference with the complainant, given Young’s familiarity with the family.

Those objections were upheld, resulting in Young’s remand to prison until his release on bail this week.

The criminal proceedings against Young remain ongoing, and he has not been convicted of the alleged offence.

World.title: Sentencing delayed again for two men who pleaded guilty in 2018 killing of police constable Osbourne Martinez
World.content:
Sentencing delayed again for two men who pleaded guilty in 2018 killing of police constable Osbourne Martinez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly four years after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the killing of Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, Tyrique Myles and Glen Lopez remain behind bars awaiting sentencing after another adjournment in the High Court on Thursday.

The two men appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on October 8, but sentencing could not proceed because the agreed facts and formal plea agreement had not yet been filed with the court.

Justice Pilgrim gave the parties until Friday, October 9, to submit the necessary documents and adjourned the sentencing proceedings to October 27, 2026.

Both men were represented in court by attorney Norman Rodriguez.

Myles and Lopez pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter in November 2022 before then-High Court Justice Ricardo O’Neil Sandcroft. However, their sentencing has remained outstanding for almost four years.

The case stems from the November 2, 2018 murder of 27-year-old Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, who was fatally shot while responding to an armed robbery at the Belcove Hotel on Regent Street West in downtown Belize City.

Martinez and other officers responded to reports of an armed robbery involving three men. During the confrontation, Martinez was shot and later died while undergoing treatment at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Myles, Lopez and Rayford Mejia were subsequently arrested and jointly charged with murder. While Myles and Lopez eventually pleaded guilty to manslaughter, Mejia maintained his innocence and proceeded to trial.

In May 2023, Justice Sandcroft found Mejia guilty of murder, determining that the prosecution had proven his involvement in the killing.

The latest adjournment means Myles and Lopez must remain in custody for another 19 days before their sentencing proceedings are scheduled to resume, nearly eight years after Martinez was killed in the line of duty.

World.title: Anthony Carballo Jr. faces life imprisonment with minimum 20 years before parole if he pleads guilty to murder
World.content:
Anthony Carballo Jr. faces life imprisonment with minimum 20 years before parole if he pleads guilty to murder

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Anthony Carballo Jr., one of two men accused of the 2023 murder of Sylvian Nigel Swift in Belize City, has been informed that he could face life imprisonment with a minimum of 20 years before becoming eligible for parole if he chooses to plead guilty.

The sentencing indication was delivered on Thursday, October 8, by High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim, following a request made by Carballo Jr. through his attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, during a case management conference on September 29.

Justice Pilgrim considered the circumstances of the murder, agreed facts, sentencing guidelines, and relevant aggravating and mitigating factors before arriving at the proposed sentence.

Carballo Jr. has until Friday, October 23, 2026, to inform the court whether he will accept the sentencing indication and enter a guilty plea. No guilty plea has been entered at this stage.

Meanwhile, his co-accused, Christopher Pitts Jr., continues to maintain his innocence and intends to proceed with a trial before a judge sitting without a jury.

The two men are charged jointly with the murder of Swift, who was fatally shot on Antelope Street on April 27, 2023. Reports at the time indicated that Swift was standing near his home shortly before 8 p.m. when two men riding a motorcycle opened fire, striking him in the arm and neck. Police subsequently pursued the suspects and recovered a motorcycle and a 9mm firearm.

Carballo Jr. was initially arraigned on May 2, 2023, followed by Pitts Jr. on May 8. Both men were jointly indicted for murder before the High Court in March 2025.

The case is expected to return to court on October 23, when Carballo Jr. must indicate whether he intends to plead guilty or proceed to trial.

World.title: UB hosts AI discussion with renowned Belizean Mathematician Dr. Arlie Petters
World.content:
UB hosts AI discussion with renowned Belizean Mathematician Dr. Arlie Petters

By Zoila Palma: The University of Belize (UB) welcomed internationally renowned Belizean mathematical physicist and New York University Abu Dhabi Provost, Dr. Arlie Petters, for a panel discussion on artificial intelligence (AI) and higher education on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at the UB Conference Center.

The discussion explored the implications of AI for teaching and learning, as well as the opportunities and challenges it presents for the future of universities. UB faculty and staff, students and representatives of Belmopan Comprehensive School were invited to participate in the timely conversation.

UB’s President, Vice President for Academic Affairs and guests from Tuskegee University also attended the discussion. Dr. Petters, who is internationally recognized for his pioneering contributions to the mathematical study of gravitational lensing, continues to represent Belize through his achievements in science and education.

UB also recognized the contributions of IT lecturer David Garcia and Faculty of Management and Social Sciences lecturer Dr. Yasmine Andrews, who shared their perspectives during the panel.

World.title: Skiff stolen from Marina in Ladyville Village
World.content:
Skiff stolen from Marina in Ladyville Village

By Zoila Palma: A 43-foot fiberglass skiff was reported stolen from the Rusty Anchor Marina on Yellow Snapper Drive in Ladyville Village, Belize District, during the early hours of Wednesday, October 7, 2026.

The vessel, named OCEANICA, has a white hull with green stripes, a blue bottom and a cabin. It is equipped with two 200-horsepower Yamaha outboard engines and is registered as BZ-0428.

Police are asking the public to be on the lookout for the vessel and to report any information about its whereabouts.

Anyone with information can contact Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 App, or report to the nearest police station.

World.title: Minister Chebat says his approach will be of partnership, professionalism, accountability and service
World.content:
Minister Chebat says his approach will be of partnership, professionalism, accountability and service

By Zoila Palma: Today, Minister Michel Chebat issued a statement extended gratitude to Prime Minister John Briceno for the confidence entrusted to serve as Minister of National Security, Energy and Ports.

“I accept these responsibilities with a clear understanding of their importance to the security, stability and continued development of our nation. These portfolios touch directly on the safety of our citizens, the strength of our institutions, the resilience of our economy and Belize’s ability to meet both present and emerging challenges.

At the heart of our national security are the men and women who serve our country every day. I look forward to working closely with the Belize Defence Force, the Belize Police Department, the Coast Guard, our border and security personnel, and all those who dedicate themselves to protecting our people and our sovereignty,” Chebat said.

Chebat added that National security, however, does not stop at our borders. The challenges facing Belize—from transnational crime and maritime security to trafficking, cyber threats, disaster preparedness and energy security—require strong cooperation with our neighbors and trusted international partners.

“I therefore look forward to strengthening Belize’s relationships with our regional counterparts in Central America and the Caribbean, as well as with our longstanding security and development partners. Cooperation, intelligence sharing, training and mutual respect will remain essential to keeping Belize and our wider region safe.

Our ports and energy infrastructure are equally important to our national security and economic future. I intend to work closely with the professionals, regulators, private-sector stakeholders and communities involved in these sectors to ensure that they are secure, efficient, resilient and positioned to support Belize’s long-term development,” Chebat explained.

Chebat says that his approach will be one of partnership, professionalism, accountability and service.

Chebat pledged to engage constructively with stakeholders, and to build upon the important work already being done.

Minister Chebat says he plans to meet with the leadership and personnel across the respective portfolios, reviewing key priorities and gaining a full appreciation of both the challenges and opportunities.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture eyes Wambugu Apple research for local production
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture eyes Wambugu Apple research for local production

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Agriculture Rodwell Ferguson visited Jamaica last week to explore the potential of cultivating Wambugu apples in Belize.

Minister Ferguson also visited the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) in Jamaica to examine research into the tropical fruit.

Ferguson believes the research could provide a blueprint for Caribbean countries seeking to diversify agricultural production and strengthen food security.

During his October 1 visit to CASE, Ferguson inspected the Wambugu apple and expressed interest in the possibility of producing apples in tropical climates, the Jamaica Observer reports.

He noted that apples are traditionally associated with colder regions and are largely imported into Belize from countries such as the United States and Canada.

Ferguson said growing apples locally could reduce reliance on imports while creating new opportunities for farmers and agricultural businesses. He also called for greater investment in agricultural research, pointing to Brazil as an example of how innovation and research can help countries achieve food self-sufficiency while expanding their agricultural exports.

The minister was accompanied during the visit by Senior Advisor Hugh O’Brien, Latoya Panton, managing director of Summit Apple Orchards and My Jamaican Food Forest, which imports and distributes Wambugu apples from Kenya to Jamaica and other Caribbean markets.

Panton said the variety has been performing well in Jamaica, with farmers and backyard gardeners successfully cultivating the fruit, and expressed hope that production can eventually be scaled up to commercial levels across the Caribbean.

World.title: International News: Maduro and wife face new US charges over alleged torture
World.content:
International News: Maduro and wife face new US charges over alleged torture

By Zoila Palma: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been charged by U.S. prosecutors with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding new allegations to the drug trafficking case they already face.

A superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court details alleged torture involving nine people, including three U.S. citizens, Reuters report.

Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured in Caracas on January 3 during a U.S. military operation and taken to New York to face drug-related charges. Prosecutors allege that thousands of Venezuelans were threatened, arrested, tortured or killed by state forces between 1999 and 2025, with several of the alleged incidents occurring during periods of political unrest.

According to the indictment, Maduro allegedly ordered the 2013 arrest of a Venezuelan military officer suspected of plotting a coup, who prosecutors say was subsequently subjected to electric shocks and other forms of abuse. Prosecutors also allege that a U.S. citizen detained in Venezuela in 2022 was beaten and subjected to electric shocks after being accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.

Both Maduro and Flores deny the new allegations. Maduro’s attorney said the former president looks forward to his day in court, while Flores’ lawyers also rejected the charges.

World.title: MELISSA FRAUD SHIELD
World.content:
One of a number of houses in Unions Acres, St James, still waiting for repair to the damage caused by last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

LASCO Financial Services has revealed that it began holding back 30 per cent of donations made through the Government’s Hurricane Melissa relief platform after its system flagged as suspicious, a number of transactions linked to the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM).

LASCO said it remitted 70 per cent of the money received to ODPEM daily while the reserve was being held, with more than 95 per cent of all donated amounts having been paid over to the agency by the end of March, before the 30 per cent withholding was discontinued in June after the risk associated with the account returned to normal.

The disclosure provides a new explanation for the arrangement, which came under scrutiny after the Auditor General’s Department found that 30 per cent of online donations had been retained for up to 45 days by a financial services institution, without a formal written agreement governing the retention.

The audit found that $15.7 million and US$298,429 in donations withheld between October 28 and December 31, 2025 were due to be transferred to ODPEM by February 15, 2026.

However, the financial services institution told auditors on March 9 that none of the withheld funds had yet been transferred.

Four days later, ODPEM provided a transfer receipt showing that $16.1 million and US$305,292 had been sent on March 9, but the auditor general said she could not independently confirm that the money had reached ODPEM’s accounts because the agency had not provided the relevant bank statements.

LASCO Financial, in a July 31 letter to Public Accounts Committee (PAC) Chairman Julian Robinson, said the decision to retain the money followed a review of the risk associated with the account after its payment system detected suspicious activity.

According to the company, the 30 per cent was not treated as money belonging to it, but as a refundable security reserve intended to protect against possible losses arising from disputed or fraudulent card transactions.

The company said a July 8, 2024 agreement with ODPEM expressly provided for a refundable security reserve, but no reserve was instituted at the time, based on the risk assessment then in place.

LASCO Financial said the 45-day period was based on guidance from its banking partners, who advised that this was the period within which a customer could challenge a transaction.

“If a charge-back occurred due to ODPEM transactions, without reserve, LASCO would have to absorb full loss,” the company said, adding that the arrangement was “standard practice by financial institutions in these types of transactions”.

A charge-back occurs when a card transaction is challenged and the money is reversed through the banking system.

LASCO said the reserve was therefore intended to ensure that money would be available if a transaction processed through the donation platform was later disputed and reversed.

The company said the donation button remained active on the Government’s Support Jamaica website and continued to receive contributions, while the withholding arrangement was eventually discontinued in June after the risk associated with the account had returned to normal levels.

The latest explanation comes after the issue was raised during a meeting of the PAC on July 28 at which questions were asked about why a financial institution had been allowed to retain a portion of disaster donations and whether there was a formal agreement authorising the arrangement.

At that meeting, ODPEM Director General Commander Alvin Gayle told the PAC that the funds, which had prompted the auditor general’s concern, had since been received by the agency.

Gayle also acknowledged that there had been no formal arrangement specifically governing the retention of Hurricane Melissa funds, even though there was an existing agreement covering the processing of donations.

In a subsequent August 31 response from the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) to questions from the committee, the Government said the legal teams of ODPEM and LASCO were still discussing the terms of the agreement.

The OPM also told the PAC that ODPEM selected LASCO after assessing the available payment-processing options.

It said LASCO is currently the only financial services provider with which Amber Innovations Inc — the company behind the relevant licensed payment products — has granted a non-exclusive licence for a payment-based solution to merchants.

World.title: ‘I don’t shy away from court’
World.content:
Attorney Hugh Wildman speaking at a news conference on Thursday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Attorney Hugh Wildman on Thursday insisted that he would never deliberately stay way from the fraud trial of his client Fritz Pinnock in the St Andrew Parish Court, but said his involvement in the murder case of six cops in the Home Circuit Court, downtown Kingston, has been creating unavoidable scheduling clashes due to the latter matter being dragged out by the prosecution.

Wildman was defending himself at a news conference he called a day after Justice Sanchia Burrell told Pinnock that he may have to cross-examine a witness himself if no legal representation is present for him when the delay- plagued Ruel Reid and company fraud trial resumes next Monday.

“Today’s press conference is called to respond to the media reports and various comments concerning the Pinnock and Reid matter, where the judge made certain comments in my absence and gave the impression that I deliberately stayed away from the court.

I wish to make it abundantly clear that everybody in Jamaica knows my position; I don’t shy away from court,” Wildman said.

“In fact, I am known to appear in all courts and take a certain stand to defend my clients vigorously,” he said.

“The situation is this: It is a known fact that we are engaged in the trial of the six police in downtown since the 7th of January of this year.

When the case commenced, the trial judge [Sonia Bertram- Linton] made it abundantly clear that she got instructions from the chief justice that that case must be a priority case; that’s what she told us,” Wildman said.

He said that in all his years of practising law he has never seen a situation in which a murder trial is dragged out by the prosecution the way that the policemen’s matter has been.

“The case has been going on unnecessarily long because of the conduct of the prosecutor in recalling and recalling witnesses, evidence to adduce new evidence, and it goes on and on, uncontrolled.

It amounts to an abuse of process.

The case continues and continues, and nobody knows when this case will come to an end,” he said.

“Everybody in the justice system knows about this.

In fact, we have had cases in court where Supreme Court judges have said they know Mr Wildman is engaged in other matters, and they put off the case.

Up to this week…

The point is this, I explained to Ms Burrell the challenge we are having with the downtown case, which is a priority.

It’s a murder case with six policemen.

I’m representing four of the accused persons,” he said, emphasising that, “It is impossible for me to be at two places at the same time.” On Wednesday in the Parish Court, fellow defence attorney Carolyn Chuck told Justice Burrell that Wildman had advised that he would ask another attorney to hold in his stead; but no one turned up.

Chuck went on to share that Wildman had indicated that he could also have challenges with being present next week as he was given time off from the Supreme Court to deal with the arrangements for his mother’s funeral.

Justice Burrell acknowledged the sensitivity of the matter and extended condolence to Wildman’s family.

However, she queried why this had not been communicated before.

“I don’t take lightly that Mr Wildman is making funeral arrangements for his mother, and my condolence goes out to him and his family, but early information- sharing makes a huge difference,” she said.

“I have to be very sensitive because all of us who are here either have a mother or had a mother at some point…

but I am not understanding the lack of communication; the lack of communication is very unhelpful,” the judge said.

Emphasising that the case impacts four other accused, Burrell said Wildman and Pinnock are not entitled to an infinite supply of the court’s resources.

Her comments came on the one-year anniversary of the official start of the trial, which has been plagued with scheduling challenges.

“It cannot be that Mr Wildman avoids appropriate and adequate communication and expects to get what he asks for,” she said.

“How can the rights of four other people be expected to continuously and infinitely, at this point in time, … be expected to yield to Mr Wildman’s failure — I am using the word failure — to organise himself?” Justice Burrell said.

Pinnock, the former Caribbean Maritime University head; former education minister Ruel Reid; his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle; as well as Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence (Jamaica Labour Party, Brown’s Town Division) are defendants in the high-profile $25-million fraud trial in the parish court.

In the matter being heard in the Home Circuit Court, the six policemen are on trial for murder in relation to the January 12, 2013 shooting deaths of Matthew Lee, Ucliffe Dyer, and Mark Allen on Acadia Drive in St Andrew, during an alleged shoot-out.

On Thursday, Wildman said he was trying to find a solution to his problem, telling the news conference that he has written a letter to Chief Justice Bryan Sykes urging his intervention.

“I was shocked when I heard that the judge was behaving like that, as if I deliberately stayed away from court.

Everybody knows that that is not my style.

I want to be there to defend my client, Mr Pinnock, and defend him vigorously, because we maintain that there is no case against him.

But the point is that I am locked in that trial downtown.

What do I do?” he said.

“Should I have walked away from the criminal case downtown with the six policemen? I don’t know why this is taking so long.

Every day, up to yesterday, I made serious submissions in law based on the constitution, that the trial is an abuse of process with what is going on downtown,” he said.

World.title: PATCHING UP
World.content:
Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby watches as workers carry out repairs on Seaview Avenue in St Andrew on Thursday, with a line of motorists passing through the work area.

WITH potholes causing almost daily logjams in the Corporate Area, the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) has started a major road patching project across the city.

Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby says patching has started on badly damaged sections of 20 to 25 roads, including some which he said are under the control of the National Works Agency (NWA).

Swaby said the municipal corporation is targeting some of the worst-affected areas in downtown Kingston, and New Kingston, with surrounding communities also included in the programme.

“They are not only community roads but actually we are fixing some main roads, and…

it’s important for us to fix those main roads because clearly, where you have these big craters across the road it impedes traffic.

It appears you have to slow down and it builds up that traffic,” Swaby said after touring some of the road work on Thursday.

According to Swaby, the KSAMC was helping to repair some roads which are the responsibility of the NWA because of the effect their condition was having on traffic.

The decision comes against the background of a monthslong dispute between the leadership of some municipal corporations and minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan over the condition of roads and the amount of money available to repair them.

Morgan has repeatedly argued that municipal corporations must do more to maintain roads under their control.

In September, Swaby told the Jamaica Observer that most of the roads repaired by the NWA in Kingston and St Andrew were KSAMC roads and argued that the Parochial Revenue Fund — which supports road work and other municipal works — had increased significantly without a similar increase in road repairs.

Swaby has repeatedly argued that the corporation’s resources are stretched thin because the same funds used for road repairs must also support other municipal responsibilities.

On Thursday, Swaby doubled down on his position as he pointed to the funding pressure and said the KSAMC would be better able to meet its mandate if it had more money.

“Obviously, if we had more funds, we would be in a better position to respond to the people of Kingston and St Andrew, and we are trying our best to see how we can garner the funds from what is owed to us, along with what the Government gives us, to fix these roads,” he said.

“Let me remind people that the Parochial Revenue Fund not only fixes roads, but it is the same fund that is required to do other things.

So we don’t have a dedicated resource, a fund to say every month we are in a position to spend ‘x’ on roads.

There are times… we have to divert those funds in cleaning drains.

So we continue to face the challenges, and we are looking at ways of how best we can fix these roads,” Swaby said.

The mayor’s explanation came months after the KSAMC announced a $220-million road rehabilitation programme covering all 40 divisions of the municipality.

By March, the corporation said 33 roads had been repaired at a cost of $90 million, with the remaining programme intended to cover additional roads.

In June, the KSAMC also increased allocations under its Divisional Allocation Fund from $10 million to $13 million for each urban division and $13.5 million for rural divisions.

The fund covers road repairs as well as other activities, including drain cleaning, emergency work, and community programmes.

World.title: Mental health awareness push
World.content:
Mental health professionals at the National Mental Health Conference held at Golf View Hotel in Mandeville on Wednesday. (Photos: Kasey Williams)

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — As Jamaica observes Mental Health Week, a host of activities are being staged in the southern region to raise awareness and promote emotional well-being.

Dr Kevin Goulbourne, director of mental health and substance abuse services in the Ministry of Health and Wellness, and Dr Melissa Flinch, medical doctor and mental health advocate, told the Jamaica Observer that the week of activities will culminate on Friday with a Mental Wellness in the Park event at Brooks Park in Mandeville.

“For Friday’s event patrons can get screening for mental health issues like depression, anxiety, but also they can get assessment for physical illness,” Goulbourne said Wednesday on the sidelines of a National Mental Health Conference in Mandeville.

The Mental Health Week of activities is being hosted under the theme ‘Lived experiences heard: Real voices, real change’.

“For this Mental Health Week, now more than ever, we have to embrace that we are not alone.

Life has a way of throwing a lot at us, even without acknowledging how much we are already dealing with.

Moments like these allow us to pause to remember that resilience is a skill that has to be developed overtime and that support is built by making sure we reach into the various groups that are around us,” Flinch said in reference to the Lions Club of Mandeville.

The service club on Wednesday hosted its appreciation awards for the annual Men Who Cook event.

“We all experience mental health challenges.

Anxiety and depression affects all of us, whether or not it is happening enough for it to become clinical stapled as one of the things we deal more chronically,” added Flinch.

Meanwhile, Goulbourne admitted that there are resource challenges hampering the response to mental health support in communities where there is a need for an immediate response.

“We have been responding to most of those emergencies…[but] it is not at the level that we want… Sometimes there aren’t enough vehicles and/or staff to respond in a timely fashion, but as much as possible we respond to the psychiatric emergencies,” he said.

Goulbourne also called on the media to be cautious in reporting on suicides to prevent copycat scenarios.

“If responsible media reporting is not done then it may cause a negative response.

When you speak about persons who died by suicide [don’t] give the details of how it was done, because it may give an idea to persons who may be contemplating it.

Try to end the [report] by making persons know that there is help available,” he said in reference to the Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Helpline 888-639-5433.

“We are making sure our services are accessible.

We have our helpline, which is a 24/7 service manned by psychologists, where persons who have emergencies and emotional distress can call and get assistance,” added Goulbourne as he pointed out that counselling is also readily available at clinics islandwide.

“We have been trying to sensitise the public in general to actually listen to each other, because sometimes people who are contemplating suicide may start with a small issue.

If we have a community where persons are able to listen to each other more …persons wouldn’t escalate to the point of feeling hopeless and helpless and wanting to hurt themselves,” Goulbourne said.

He also issued a reminder to relatives and caregivers of people with mental challenges to maintain the prescribed dosage of medication to them.

“Ensure that the person is on their treatment, because sometimes what people do is allow their relatives to miss their appointment, not taking tablets, and watching to see if they will remain okay.

That is not ideal.

You have to maintain your treatment and maintain your appointments,” added Goulbourne.

World.title: ‘No fight against poor people’
World.content:
Central Car Park in the Mandeville town centre where the mayor says a wholesale market will no longer be permitted effective November 26. (Photos: Kasey Williams)

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Mandeville Mayor Donovan Mitchell has announced that, effective November 26, there will be a ban on the use of the Central Car Park in the town centre for a wholesale market.

“The decision follows numerous complaints received from the taxi associations.

The [Manchester Municipal] Corporation must ensure that the car park can effectively serve its intended purpose and facilitate orderly transportation,” Mitchell said during Thursday’s sitting of the corporation.

“I was there [in the car park] Tuesday evening and what I saw was not a wholesale market.

Three pounds of carrot and five pounds of Irish potato and two pounds of yam is not wholesale market.

There is space in the Mandeville Market and we intend to create additional space.

“That is the space that we want to use for vending,” Mitchell added in reference to plans to demolish an old derelict building at the back of the market.

He said the ban is among a number of measures being implemented to eliminate chaos in Mandeville.

“We are trying to bring order to the town of Mandeville… I know people tend to use this [saying] that we are ‘fighting against poor people’.

I don’t know how that works, but all we are saying is, we must start at the right place.

Not because we are poor, [should it mean that] we can’t obey the law and do things orderly.

We have to first set the example,” declared Mitchell.

“When there is chaos in the town centre, petty crimes start and I know that we have received a number of complaints about pickpocketing,” the mayor added as he reiterated that public order enforcement activities are continuing across Manchester.

“I want to make it abundantly clear that the Manchester Municipal Corporation is serious about restoring order, protecting public spaces and ensuring that development across the parish takes place in an orderly and lawful manner.

Our special enforcement team commenced operations on October 1 targeting illegal buildings, unauthorised car marts, wayside garages and the unlawful placement of building material on parochial roads.

“It is not about money, it is about order, you cannot be building a house with a veranda in the roadway.

You can’t be building houses in drains and then if it rains you get damaged and complain that Manchester [Municipal Corporation] is not doing anything.

Development must never come at the expense of public safety and progress must always be accompanied by responsibility,” added Mitchell.

World.title: Cop sounds alarm as domestic violence surges in Trelawny
World.content:
Commander of the Trelawny Police Division Superintendent Velonique Campbell makes a point to head of the Trelawny Fire Department Superintendent Roland Walters during an anti-domestic violence pop-up clinic hosted by the police force’s Trelawny Community Safety and Security Branch in historic Water Square, Falmouth, on Wednesday.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Commander of this parish’s police division, Superintendent Velonique Campbell has sounded the alarm over a worrying surge in domestic violence, warning that the sharp third-quarter increase is a grave problem and will force the constabulary to intensify its response.

The Trelawny division recorded 68 of its 94 domestic violence cases for the year during July, August, and September, with August accounting for 34 — the highest monthly tally so far this year.

“Of course, this uptick in the third quarter is of major concern to the division, and that is why we are going to improve and increase our initiative targeting this very sensitive issue,” Campbell said Wednesday afternoon at an anti-domestic violence pop-up clinic hosted by the police force’s Trelawny Community Safety and Security Branch.

The event was held in historic Water Square, Falmouth, where police and stakeholders converged with placards bearing messages including “Peace, No Violence”, “Talk It Out, Walk It Out”, “Live In, Live Out” and “Respectful Love”.

The monthly figures rose sharply as the year progressed.

There were eight cases in January, three each in February and March, one in April, seven in May and four in June.

Those were followed by 11 in July, 34 in August, and 23 in September.

Despite the spike, Campbell said police had resolved 84 of the 94 cases, giving the division an 89 per cent resolution rate.

“The remaining 10 cases, of course, we have been working on them assiduously to bring these matters to a closure,” the senior cop assured.

Campbell said the push to curb domestic violence will include — alongside police investigations — public education, counselling and community- based prevention, as well as emphasis on getting victims of abuse to seek help.

“We must encourage persons experiencing abuse to talk up, talk up, because too often we wait until somebody gets seriously injured, or somebody dies,” Campbell said.

She also encouraged people who know of someone being abused to intervene and help that person access support.

Meanwhile, head of the Trelawny Fire Department Superintendent Roland Walters said the Jamaica Fire Brigade will continue to support the police in confronting the problem.

“We have to walk handin- hand with the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

Whatever they are doing, the Jamaica Fire Brigade is on board to support,” Walters said.

Describing domestic violence as a reality affecting both women and men, he made a special appeal to males to speak out if they are victims.

He also stressed the need for early intervention before tensions boil over.

“I am encouraging all of us to speak up,” he said.

Falmouth Mayor Councillor C Junior Gager also endorsed the initiative, saying the municipality is committed to promoting peaceful communities.

“We will do what we can to make sure that everyone lives like brothers and sisters,” Gager said.

“We also want to say a big, big-up to the hard-working policemen and women of Trelawny who have been doing a very, very excellent job,” he added In addition to the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, police and fire departments, the pop-up event brought together representatives from the Peace Management Initiative, Health Services Department, Child Protection and Family Services Agency, Victim Support Department, Child Diversion, National Council on Drug Abuse, and Restorative Justice.

World.title: Bunting urges Jamalco to fund legacy project at Winston Jones High
World.content:
Member of Parliament for Manchester Southern Peter Bunting speaking at the launch of the 50th anniversary celebration at Winston Jones High School in Pratville, Manchester on Wednesday. (Photos: Kasey Williams)

PRATVILLE, Manchester — Member of Parliament for Manchester Southern Peter Bunting is calling on bauxite/alumina company Jamalco to do a legacy project at the Winston Jones High School in optoelectronics and drone technology.

“I often speak stridently about the impact of bauxite mining in southern Manchester… I know that [Pratville] has suffered over the past years, if you took at aerial shot of this school, you would see that Winston Jones [High] is an island surrounded by a sea of mining and constantly suffering from the dust and even in the rehabilitation phase, they continue to do so,” Bunting said on Wednesday during the school’s 50th anniversary celebration launch.

“I really want to use the opportunity to call on Jamalco to ensure that they leave a legacy project and put in, for example, an optoelectronics [the study and application of electronic devices and systems that source, detect, and control light] lab, a drone lab, something that speaks to the jobs of the future that are being created.

At Winston Jones, it would be a fine legacy project to leave something in the community to compensate for what has been extracted over many years,” he said.

Bunting, who previously served as the MP for Manchester Central, said he has long lobbied for communities impacted by bauxite mining to get a fair share of lucrative industry through community projects particularly in education.

“I do this in a sense of partnership and I hope that is how we will proceed…If not by partnership then by insistence that some proper legacy projects are left in Manchester from the mining and vast value that has been extracted over many years,” added Bunting.

He urged students to not limit their potential and pledged to continue pushing the technological development of Winston Jones High.

“It is an important institution within this constituency and the quality of our school will have a direct bearing on the strength of our communities and ultimately on the development of our country.

“In my first month as MP, I brought the drones in schools tour to Winston Jones High, Pratville Primary, New Forest High and New Forest Primary.

I have to expose students to what the new career opportunities will look like,” said Bunting..

He lauded the leadership at the school for moving the institution in the right direction.

“Fifty years after this institution opened its door, Winston Jones High stands as part of a legacy,” he said.

Parliamentary secretary in the Ministry of Education Senator Marlon Morgan also credited the leadership at the school for steering students towards the right path.

“We want you [students] to be creators and innovators in your own right and that is why the programme of offerings here at Winston Jones High should be grasped with both hands,” said Morgan.

He said the school is on the Ministry of Education’s Priority 2 list following the passage of Hurricane Melissa almost a year ago, but did not give a timeline for repairs works to commence at the school.

World.title: Major renewal for Jamaica’s public health-care infrastructure
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton delivering his presentation at a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday. At left is Information Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

FROM rebuilding hospitals battered by Hurricane Melissa to approving plans for four new, climate-resilient facilities, the Government is embarking on what Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton has described as a major renewal of Jamaica’s public health-care infrastructure.

Speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday, Tufton said Cabinet had approved a partnership between the Ministry of Health and Wellness and the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) to advance the climate-resilient reconstruction and modernisation of four hospitals.

The projects include new build-outs and improvements at the 250-bed Black River Hospital in St Elizabeth, classified as a Type B facility; the 250-bed Falmouth General Hospital in Trelawny and the 150-bed Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover, both designated Type C; and the 750-bed Kingston Public Hospital (KPH), which will be classified as Type A.

The facilities, he noted, are being developed according to the new Secondary Healthcare Model and the Pan American Health Organization smart health facility standard.

According to Tufton, the KPH project is intended to be rolled out in phases and will include new surgical and medical towers on Orange Street in downtown Kingston.

He said the eventual goal is for the new campus to replace the existing KPH and provide Jamaica with a modern, resilient, and dependable hospital capable of fulfilling the Type A referral and national trauma role assigned under the Secondary Healthcare Model.

As for the other facilities, Tufton said, “the locations of these facilities are, again, to be finalised, but that’s a work in progress.

What is most important is that Cabinet has now sanctioned, under the guidance of Prime Minister [Dr Andrew Holness], moving forward.

And this is historic, because it means a renewal of our infrastructure, a continuation of that renewal.

It will be bigger, better equipped, and will, therefore, hopefully, serve the purpose both for staff and for patients”.

The announcement comes as the Government continues to repair and rebuild hospitals damaged by Hurricane Melissa, which devastated sections of Western Jamaica nearly a year ago.

On Wednesday, Tufton declared to the press briefing that Black River Hospital was once more fully operational following significant reconstruction efforts.

“By the end of October, the prime minister will officially open the new, if you want to call it, new second-hand Black River Hospital male and female surgical wards.

The operating theatres and the staff quarters, which is a 20-bed staff quarter at the hospital, those have been rebuilt over the last 12 months, and this month, October, we will see the opening of those,” he said, adding that the surgical wards’ reconstruction also featured an increase in bed count from 150 to 180.

Tufton noted that the renovated facility also had newly renovated bathrooms, repurposed rooms for doctors and staff, a new nursing station, and piped oxygen extended to all areas on each ward.

“The operating theatre suite comprises two floors with two operating rooms, a recovery room area, waiting area, bathroom, changing room facilities for patients and family and staff, staff lounge, offices, storeroom, and central sterile service department,” he said.

“So this month, on the first anniversary [of Hurricane Melissa], Black River Hospital is back.

And it took a lot of effort, and I want to again recognise the team,” said the minister.

He added that renovation of the facility’s administrative building is expected to be completed in November, while construction of a 23-bed maternity ward is scheduled to begin this month.

At Savanna-la-Mar Hospital, an extension of the former COVID-19 ward has been completed and is now accommodating 28 medical patients.

The works include the renovation of the female surgical ward, painting, fixing of the roof, and upgrades to toilet facilities, as well as a 38-bed increase in the hospital’s Accident and Emergency (A&E) department which, Tufton said, will reduce overcrowding.

Meanwhile, at Falmouth Hospital, the main ward within the A&E department is approximately 90 per cent complete, and expected to be done by the end of October.

“I think they’re just waiting now to instal the air-conditioning unit, and they’re hoping to complete that this month.

The next step at Falmouth is paediatrics and dietary, and the work has started on those areas,” said Tufton.

Noel Holmes Hospital has also undergone significant reconstruction marked by the establishment of six staffing quarters, an outpatient area and a maternity ward that is 85 per cent complete.

For Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James, its main A&E building has been completed and will be officially opened this month.

The minister added that the new building is now twice the size of the current A&E department.

“It will boast modern, spacious, and integrated environment designed to support the rapid assessment, stabilisation, diagnosis, and treatment of critically ill and injured patients.

The new area will have all the full A&E services — trauma, ambulatory, walk-ins, and emergency services.

There are 10 observational beds for 24-hour observation, examination rooms, and other support services,” noted Tufton.

In addition to the hospital projects, Tufton said the Government expects to commission the Old Harbour Health Centre, St Jago Health Centre, and Portmore Health Centre under the Health Systems Strengthening Programme.

“These are mega facilities when compared to previous ones.

More space, more doctors, more services, and more smart.

This started before the hurricane, but I just want to say stay tuned and see that capacity being added in the months to come,” he told the media briefing.

World.title: Andy Burnham vows to ease non-compete clauses
World.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech during the The Innovation Nation Summit at Bruntwood SciTech on October 09, 2026 in Manchester, England. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

Drive — first reported by POLITICO Thursday — comes after intense lobbying from the startups sector.

LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed Friday he will legislate to ease restrictive non-compete clause rules for workers — but stopped short of committing to a ban.

​Burnham said in a speech in Manchester that he wants to "make sure that non-compete clauses will no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising start-ups and scaling firms" — but did has yet to set out the extent of the crackdown.

​The scope of the new rules will come later, ahead of legislation. POLITICO first reported the planned crackdown Thursday.

World.title: Hitler Mussolini wins local election
World.content:
Aerial view of the Plaza de Armas with the government palace on the left and the cathedral on the right in Lima's downtown on January 4, 2026. | Connie France/ AFP via Getty Images

Peruvian voters pick their new mayor, despite his unusual name.

Voters in the Peruvian town of Queropalca have chosen their new mayor: Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores.

The unusually named candidate for the center-left Ahora Nación party won 34% of the vote. According to local media, the top three candidates were separated by just 42 votes.

Simeon’s candidate application form gives few details (and none about his name), apart from the fact that he manages the Simeon Sac Investment Group.

World.title: EU’s new list of critical mineral projects focuses on clean energy metals
World.content:
Through these projects, Brussels wants to meet its targets under the Critical Raw Materials Act, which, by 2030, the bloc aims to mine at least 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of its own needs, while sourcing no more than 65% of any one material at any processing stage from a single non-EU country.

The list covers 15 of the 17 “strategic minerals” under the act, which the bloc needs to deliver these targets on each one.

Friday’s announcement is the second batch of strategic projects listed under the act, after the EU rolled out its first list in March 2025, featuring 47 projects and 13 non-EU country projects. The majority of those projects are behind schedule however, highlighting the complexity of getting critical mineral projects up and running.

“With the projects selected in 2025 and 2026, we could now fully meet our European extraction target for lithium, nickel, rare earths, magnesium and tungsten,” said the bloc’s industry chief, Stéphane Séjourné. “We could also meet our processing target for lithium and rare earths. And our recycling target for lithium, cobalt and rare earths.”

With over 170 applications received, the 46 projects span 16 EU member countries: Belgium, Bulgaria, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Spain, Romania and Sweden.

“Exactly one year ago, we experienced firsthand why this matters. On Oct. 9, 2025, China announced new export restrictions on rare earths,” said Séjourné. Those export controls are due to expire in January.

The “strategic project” label is meant to provide faster permitting and help secure public and private finance, with permitting deadlines of 27 months for mines and 15 months for processing and recycling projects.

The Commission will also announce strategic projects in non-EU countries later this year.

World.title: EU faces gas supply shortage as winter looms
World.content:
Those conclusions are echoed in a key report by a top European body of gas network operators that was presented to national energy officials on Thursday.

Natural gas is used widely to heat Europe's buildings, power its industry and generate its electricity. But the EU's gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level for the time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for later use in the winter.

With gas prices at near-four-year highs and supply constrained due to the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, Europe has limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the last, IEEFA found.

While that doesn't necessarily mean the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean there could be 7 billion fewer cubic meters of stored gas to draw upon. That could force countries to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets, or even require consumers to cut demand if fresh supplies are unavailable.

The EU's record-low reserves leave the bloc "with less of a buffer" against global supply disruptions, leaving it "vulnerable to price spikes," Ana Jaller-Makarewicz, IEEFA's lead European energy analyst, said in a statement. If countries are forced to exhaust stocks this year, that would also leave them with more to refill next year, continuing the feedback loop of low reserves and higher prices, she added.

The same risks were outlined in a 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if imports of liquefied natural gas are limited or even “optimal” in the context of a cold winter, storage levels could fall as low as 11%, a baseline needed for strategic reserves that can't be easily tapped into.

World.title: Elif Eralp und Friedrich Merz’ neues Berlin-Problem
World.content:
Ein drohender Linksruck in der Hauptstadt sorgt für handfesten Ärger auf Bundesebene. Während SPD und Grüne in Berlin ernsthaft mit der Linkspartei sondieren, blickt Friedrich Merz mit Sorge auf eine mögliche Regierende Bürgermeisterin Elif Eralp. Welche radikalen Forderungen im Raum stehen und warum der Antisemitismus-Streit in der Linken die Regierungsbildung zur Zerreißprobe macht, analysiert Maximilian Heimerzheim.

Beim Dauerbrenner Rentenreform verhärten sich die Fronten zwischen Union und SPD zusehends. Rasmus Buchsteiner ordnet ein, welche Kompromisse der Kanzler bis Weihnachten erwartet und wer in den Verhandlungen auf der Bremse steht.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview spricht CSU-Forschungsministerin Dorothee Bär über das europäische Kräftemessen im All. Parallel zum Staatsbesuch von Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier und Emmanuel Macron in Bordeaux erklärt sie, wie sich Deutschland in der Raumfahrt behaupten will und warum Europa beim Flug zum Mond mehr Selbstbewusstsein gegenüber der NASA braucht.

World.title: Is the EU ready for the next pandemic?
World.content:
Five years after the height of the Covid pandemic, how much better prepared is the EU for the next health crisis?

Host Sarah Wheaton is joined by POLITICO health reporter Helen Collis and global health expert Michel Kazatchkine to discuss the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, and what it tells us about international health cooperation and transparency.



They look at what became of Brussels’ post-Covid ambitions — from the EU’s HERA health-emergency authority to better coordination of research — and at Donald Trump’s push to bring down US drug prices by putting pressure on Europe to pay more.



Plus: As Brussels tries to compete with the U.S. and China on biotech and new medicines, is it focusing on the innovation patients actually need?
