World.title: Green Leader Polanski vows to fight on after Westminster gamble fails
World.content:
It is an early boost for Starmer’s replacement Andy Burnham, who has shifted the ruling Labour Party to the left since taking charge and toughened the U.K.’s stance on Israel amid criticism that his predecessor’s response to the war in Gaza was flat-footed.

And it has triggered a round of soul-searching in the left-wing Greens, already fractious over a deeply controversial motion on Zionism passed at their party conference. The party had been troubling Labour in the polls under Polanski, but has now fallen short of a high-profile target.

The north London seat has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983 — but the Greens poured significant resources into trying to get their leader elected.

Abdi-Wali got 45% of the vote – down four points on Labour’s 2024 general election result. Polanski won 33% of the votes cast — a 22-point leap on the party’s 2024 result, but still some way short of taking the traditionally-safe Labour seat.

Labour Party candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali is hugged by a supporter after winning the Holborn and St Pancras by-election in London on Oct. 9, 2026. | Carl Court/Getty Images

A defeated Polanski – who had gambled on getting a toehold in parliament to boost the Greens’ profile – insisted he would stay on as party leader, telling broadcasters: “I’ve taken a loss tonight, but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion.”

Polanski told Sky News Friday he is “disappointed” by the result, but put his defeat down to voters wanting to “give Andy Burnham a chance.”

World.title: When politicians write bad erotic fiction
World.content:
Politicians can, of course, make great writers, and several have won Nobel’s literature prize, including Britain’s Winston Churchill in 1953, and Peru’s Mario Vargas Llosa in 2010. The latter — who ran for president in 1990 — won the prize “for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual’s resistance, revolt, and defeat.” But has he ever referred to British Conservative grandee Jacob Rees-Mogg as a “Haunted Pencil”? No, he has not.

There are, however, a lot of very bad books written by politicians.

Former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson — very much the “Winston Churchill if you ordered him off Temu” — published a book in 2004 called “Seventy-Two Virgins — A Comedy of Errors” (the last four words also being the summary of his Covid policy) about a terrorist group targeting the U.S. president on a visit to London. It was described in the Guardian some 15 years later — after Johnson became prime minister — as ” sexist, racist, fundamentally undiplomatic.”

But the undisputed king when it comes to politicians letting out their inner writer is France.

In 2023, Bruno Le Maire, then the country’s economy and finance minister, published the novel “Fugue Américaine,” which drew instant criticism and mockery, mainly because of an explicit sex scene (unhappy French people were quick to point out that they had been screwed by the government for years).

Then there’s Marlène Schiappa, former government minister and writer of raunchy books under the pen name Marie Minelli, with titles such as “Osez les sexfriends,” “Sexe, mensonge et banlieues chaudes” and “Comment transformer votre mec en Brad Pitt en 30 jours.” When she was junior social affairs minister, Schiappa appeared on the cover of Playboy, although she was not naked in the magazine (great news for those who buy Playboy only for the articles).

World.title: Passport-free travel, AI agents and longevity: Key takeaways from the WTTC Global Summit
World.content:
Hundreds of the world’s biggest names in travel gathered in Malta this week for the 26th edition of the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) Global Summit to discuss the challenges and opportunities the industry is facing.

 

Covering everything from luxury travel and longevity to the future airport experience and how destinations can grow sustainably, the panels gave an insight into what governments and businesses will be focusing on in the coming years.

Euronews Travel was reporting on the ground – here’s what you may have missed.

Justin Trudeau: Tourism is the best counter to an increasingly insular world

Canada’s former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau was this year’s main speaker, joining WTTC President and CEO Gloria Guevara on stage to chat about “how to shape the opportunity ahead”.

Directly addressing the “Trump Slump”, Trudeau said in recent years “the US hasn’t been very good at making travellers feel welcome”.

He said: “There’s a tendency right now in countries around the world, and we’re seeing it to a greater or lesser extent in certain countries or governments, that are encouraging people to look inward, turn inward, to go a little more insular and be mistrustful or in opposition to the rest of the world. That’s not necessarily a productive path for the world, and the best counter to that is tourism.

“It’s getting to know people who are different. It’s wanting to travel, being curious about the world, being empathetic. These are the instincts that people need to be developing, and this is something that makes your industry so great.”

When pressed on which single destination Trudeau would recommend to visit in Canada, he suggested Montréal, his home city.

“Montrealers, we love good restaurants, we love good art. We fill our summers with festivals, in winter, it’s worth coming to see the snow,” he added.

You won’t need to use your passport to travel within the next five years

In a panel discussing the implementation of digital identity and changing the border experience, Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths said that passports will no longer be a necessity for travel within the next five years.

The barrier isn’t the technology, but a lack of coordination between the different systems that must be connected to make this happen, he added.

Panellists envisioned a future where travellers won’t need to use their passport when passing through borders, when collecting hire cars, or even checking in to hotels.

AI is already being used to plan holidays – the next stage is letting agents book your trip

Tourists across the globe are becoming “super-empowered travellers” by using AI to plan out their trips, according to Christie Travers-Smith, a director for EMEA Strategic Partnerships at Google Inc.

The next big step for AI? Building enough trust for customers to hand over their credit card information and allow AI agents to book for them.

While the luxury sector is leading the way, ‘longevity as standard’ is what all hotels should be aiming for

Bryan Johnson’s antics have brought longevity out of the fringe and into the mainstream in recent years, and luxury hotel groups have been paying attention, introducing things like hyperbaric oxygen therapy and infrared saunas.

But Tim Gray, the founder of Health Optimisation, argues that “longevity as standard” is what all hotel groups should be aiming for.

What that means is allowing travellers to stick to the basic principles of recovery – eating well, sleeping well, staying hydrated and staying active – even while away from home, and that starts from small things like adding black-out blinds and removing blinking lights, to ensuring that mini bars are stocked with healthier options.

All of the fancy tools are just meant to help “turbo charge” the basics. Having tried out HPO.TECH’s hyperbaric oxygen therapy for ourselves at the WTTC summit, we can certainly see how jet-lagged travellers could benefit.

Measuring success by value, rather than volume

For many years, the travel industry’s main measure for success was the number of tourists flowing into a destination.

Today, the indicators people are paying attention to are changing – governments are now shifting from “volume to value”, according to Michelle Fridman, Secretary of Tourism of Jalisco, Mexico.

“We are looking for those tourists that are better tourists, that stay for a longer period, that spend a bigger amount of money, that consume local products,” Fridman said during a panel on destination stewardship.

“More importantly, we are looking for those that respect and are interested in our identity.”

She added that Jalisco is “the most Mexican destination, and we want to keep it that way”.

It was a sentiment shared across the panellists, with Miguel Sanz, Director-General at Turespaña, saying that his role was now more of a “tourism curator”, with efforts being made to attract a different kind of traveller to Spain.

The idea was further explored on the “impact-oriented traveller” panel, with Mark Weingard, CEO & founder of Iniala, noting that it’s important for the industry to not become too focused on bringing in high-value travellers “because then we are almost being elitist” and “saying only the wealthy can travel”.

“At the same time, I think it's very important that we position travel that it benefits the cities that it's in, that it doesn't destroy the culture, it doesn't destroy the neighbourhoods and that we are making sure that the work that we are doing in hospitality actually gives back to the community,” he added.

World.title: What happened to OpenAI’s $20bn? Revenue scare rattles AI trade
World.content:
Wall Street looks set to recover some ground on Friday morning after confusion over how much money OpenAI, the ChatGPT maker, is actually bringing in shook investor faith in the artificial intelligence boom.

 

Nasdaq 100 futures were around 0.8% higher, and S&P 500 futures were up 0.4% in early trading on Friday.

On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI’s annualised revenue, which projects recent sales over a full year, was "approaching $50 billion (€44.6bn)" at the end of September, according to figures shared with investors.

That is about $20 billion (€17.8bn) less than the company projected last month.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.25% to around 27,193, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks major US chip stocks, sank 3.4%. A jump in oil prices added to the pressure.

Where did the $20 billion go?

In short, nowhere.

The gap does not mean OpenAI missed a target or lost sales: the roughly $70 billion (€62.5bn) figure was an estimate, not a company forecast, built on a different way of counting revenue.

According to the FT, the higher number came from OpenAI’s backers recalculating its sales to match the method of rival Anthropic, which counts what customers spend on its AI models through cloud platforms such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud as revenue, while OpenAI excludes such sales.

Taken at face value, OpenAI’s figure trails the $65 billion (€58bn) Anthropic reportedly hit at the end of July, although the different accounting methods make a direct comparison difficult. At the time of writing, OpenAI has not publicly reacted to the reports.

The figures matter as OpenAI, valued at $852 billion (€760bn) in March, is reportedly seeking at least $30 billion (€26.7bn) in fresh funding at a $1.4 trillion (€1.25tn) valuation.

FILE. Open AI CEO Sam Altman speaks at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco, 29 Sept. 2026 AP Photo/Jeff Chiu

Shares in firms that have bet big on OpenAI’s growth were among the hardest hit after the news broke on Thursday.

Oracle, which has agreed to supply OpenAI with vast computing power, slid 5.5%, while CoreWeave, an AI cloud specialist with multibillion-dollar contracts with the firm, lost nearly 8%.

Microsoft, a major OpenAI shareholder, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta all fell by more than 1%. Like Oracle, all four are hyperscalers that are pouring money into AI data centres.

Chipmakers slid too, with Nvidia down almost 3%, AMD down around 4% and Broadcom, which is building a custom chip with OpenAI, down 4.35%.

In Tokyo on Friday, shares in SoftBank Group, which owns about 13% of OpenAI, fell as much as 7.3% before paring losses.

Chip demand still strong

Despite the negative news, other signals this week suggest demand for AI hardware remains robust.

South Korea’s Samsung estimated on Thursday that its third-quarter operating profit hit a record 107.4 trillion won, or $80.2 billion (€71.5bn).

The figure, if confirmed, would be the biggest quarterly operating profit ever reported by a technology company, beating the $63.7 billion (€56.8bn) in operating income that US chip designer Nvidia booked in its latest quarter.

Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, said the same day that September sales rose 54.6% year-on-year, taking third-quarter revenue to a record NT$1.49 trillion, or $46.8 billion (€41.8bn).

Investors will get a clearer read next week, when Dutch chip equipment maker ASML reports on 14 October and TSMC on 15 October.

Potential listings by Anthropic, as soon as November, and OpenAI next year could bring their audited accounts into the open.

World.title: Iran and Russia used ChatGPT for propaganda by ‘fake journalists’, OpenAI says
World.content:
OpenAI revealed on Thursday it had shut down two influence operations — from Russia and Iran — that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly spread anti-Ukraine propaganda and foster division in the US and Israel over the war in Iran.

 

The report is the latest example of how state actors could exploit widely available AI tools to produce and disseminate sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale.

The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support false front entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging.

The Iranian operation involved seven fake journalist profiles, each claiming to be from Western countries, including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world.

"We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world," OpenAI said.

"These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East."

The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025 and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier this year.

The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added.

One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be "an American freelance writer," had social media accounts across several tech platforms, including Elon Musk's X and Meta-owned Instagram.

X's transparency information showed the account was connected via a "West Asia android app" and Instagram's transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI.

Both accounts appeared to be suspended.

The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a think-tank called the Social Research Center (SRC). It was used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said.

"The available evidence indicates that the SRC's employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group," OpenAI said.

"The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we've disrupted over the past two and a half years."

The operators used ChatGPT to write internal reports on their activities, create content for their operations and draft reports on the performance of the think tank, as well as to help design and create texts for publishing on social media as posts and comments.

Among the social media activity, say OpenAI, were reactions to Polish far-right MEP Grzegorz Braun proposing that people who showed “anti-Polishness” be declared persona non grata in Poland, in an attempt to sow divisions in Poland over the country’s support for Ukraine.

World.title: Putin offers help to end Iran war while Russia continues its own in Ukraine
World.content:
Vladimir Putin pledged to do "everything in our power" to help end the war between Iran and the US on Thursday, positioning Russia as a would-be Middle East mediator while continuing his own full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

 

The Russian president made the remarks at a bilateral meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Avazeh, on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast, praising Tehran for making what he called "genuine efforts" to resolve the war.

Pezeshkian said Iran and the US had exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Tehran was reviewing and amending them before consolidating them through mediators. Despite ongoing US attacks, he said Iran would not leave the negotiating table.

"We are talking, but every time we negotiate with the United States, they attack again," Pezeshkian said. "Nevertheless, we will not abandon the negotiating table and dialogue."

He said the revisions, once finalised, would be put to mediators. "We are supposed to sit down through the existing mediators and consolidate them," he said.

It was the seventh meeting between the two presidents since Pezeshkian took office, following a phone call on 7 October — Putin's birthday — in which the pair discussed regional developments and the Iran-US negotiations.

The two previously met in person on 1 September on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek.

Russia is not a mediator in the US-Iran negotiations. So far, Qatar and Pakistan have led the talks.

Ties further deepen

Military, diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Russia have strengthened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

The Iran war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on 28 February, has sparked more frequent consultations between Moscow and Tehran on political and material support and financial co-operation.

Since 2022, Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drone technology — which Moscow has since copied to create its own Geran-type variant, a key tool in its daily attacks on Ukrainian civilian and infrastructure targets — and short-range missiles.

Moscow also faces accusations of providing Tehran with targeting information for attacks on US interests in the Middle East.

Trade between the two countries rose by more than 21% in 2025 and continued on the same trajectory through the first seven months of 2026, Putin said, adding that relations were developing under a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed early last year.

Pezeshkian described the current situation as an opportunity to deepen co-operation and said Tehran and Moscow should coordinate "with greater speed and strength."

Billion-dollar loan delayed

Iranian state-run media reported in the days before the meeting that Russia was ready to extend a $1 billion loan to Tehran, described as the first tranche of a $20 billion package agreed at a meeting between Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani and Putin.

The semi-official IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said arrangements to disburse the sum were complete, but disagreements among Iranian authorities over how to spend the money prevented Tehran from providing the account number needed to complete the transfer.

Iran's Planning and Budget Organisation wants to use the funds to import cars and collect customs duties, the Oil Ministry wants them for oil equipment, and the Agriculture Ministry is seeking to allocate them to basic commodity imports, according to the same report.

The bilateral meeting took place on the eve of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders' summit — a gathering of nine former Soviet republic heads focused on regional co-operation — and a separate Caspian Sea environmental conference, also held in Turkmenistan, bringing together the leaders of Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

World.title: In Pictures: Weirdest and most thought-provoking statues of Donald Trump over the years
World.content:
Donald Trump has been immortalised by artists on countless occasions, with creatives using their talents to poke fun, criticise, educate, and even warn.

 

From signs and murals to carnival floats, the divisive POTUS has inspired many to remind the public that the arts are a vital way to comment, inform and inspire.

One artform which has been an effective favourite for many wishing to represent Trump is the sculpted figure. It makes sense since Trump has shown a clear preference for classical and gilded aesthetics; statues play on the man’s perception of monumentalism as being a reflection of power. Artists therefore use oversized or flashy statues to better reflect and lampoon Trump’s ego, as well as comment on the pitfalls of gaudish effigies which so often betray a sense of narcissism.

In effect, the momuments strike at the heart of Trump's sensibilities and symbolically cast him as the eagle in Aesop’s fable – a figure undone by a self-infliction. In this case, a marked proclivity for oversized effigies.

The latest example has been "The Orange Plague", the 2.6-meter statue by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt.

The Orange Plague AP Photo

Coated with 23-karat gold, the artwork also known as “The King of Injustice” shows a nude Trump holding a comically sized golf club in one hand, a set of scales in the other, all while sitting on the back of a smaller, frailer man.

Beneath the statue is a plaque which reads: "I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back. - The King of Injustice."

According to Galschiøt, the work is a “satirical outcry” against Trump’s volatile climate and foreign policies.

The statue was previously displayed at the “hands off Greenland” demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier this year and the COP30 UN Climate Summit in Belém, Brazil last year. It has just finished its short stint at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg and is heading to the COP31 UN Climate Conference next month in Antalya, Türkiye.

Before we see “The Orange Plague” once more, here are other notable statues of Trump which have amused spectators and sought to reflect what certain people think of the current leader of the free world.

"The Emperor Has No Balls"

The Emperor Has No Balls AP Photo

The Emperor Has No Balls AP Photo

Artist: Indecline

Year: 2016

Original location: Cleveland, Los Angeles, New York City, San Francisco, Seattle

Description: Not one, but five 1.95m-tall statues were installed in five major cities in the US. Made of clay and silicone, the statues show a naked Trump with bits missing. The title will clue you which. The monuments were all promptly taken down, with the greatest official statement being from the New York City Parks Department, whose phrasing was perfection. They said that it “stands firmly against any unpermitted erection in city parks, no matter how small”.

Related Best and funniest signs from mass No Kings protests against Trump

"Dump Trump"

Dump Trump Screenshot @sarahbishi - Twitter/ X

Dump Trump Screenshot Richard Gray @rugfoot - Twitter / X

Artist: Don Lessem

Year: 2019

Original location: Trafalgar Square, London

Description: The 4.9m-tall statue depicts Donald Trump sitting on a golden toilet and on his phone, wearing a MAGA hat with the words “Impeach Me!” on the headwear. The statue was spotted during Trump’s visit to the United Kingdom. It was also seen during the Trump-organised Salute To America in Washington D.C. on 4 July 2019. Also worth noting is that the effigy emitted noises of flatulence and featured audio of Trump catchphrases like “I’m a very stable genius” and “fake news”.

"Statue of Illiberty"

Statue of Illiberty AP Photo

The other side of Statue of Illiberty AP Photo

Artist: Tomaž Schlegl

Year: 2019

Original location: Near Kamnik, Slovenia

Description: The wooden statue was erected only weeks after architect / artist Tomaž Schlegl’s Melenia Trump statue, which was placed in her home town of Sevnica. That one was destroyed by fire. “Statue of Illiberty” showed Trump with his arm raised in the style of the Statue of Liberty, but featured two sides. One side was Trump’s face (with luscious red lips); the other face was an image of a “vampire”, a monstruous image which served as something of a warning. And wouldn’t you know it, this statue was also burned down a year later.

"In Honor of a Lifetime of Sexual Assault"

In Honor of a Lifetime of Sexual Assault YouTube screenshot

In Honor of a Lifetime of Sexual Assault Screenshot - YouTube

Artist: Anonymous

Year: 2024

Original location: Portland and Philadelphia

Description: Two satirical statues, approximately 2.4m tall, which were spray painted gold, showing Trump grinning and making a grabbing gesture with his right hand. The plaque accompanying the statues was a direct quote from Trump from the infamous Access Hollywood tape: “I just start kissing them. It's like a magnet. Just kiss. I don't even wait. And when you're a star they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab them by the pussy. You can do anything.”

"Best Friends Forever"

Best Friends Forever AP Photo

Best Friends Forever AP Photo

Artist: The Secret Handshake

Year: 2025

Original location: National Mall, Washington D.C.

Description: Otherwise known as “Why Can’t We Be Friends?”, this 3.7 meter-tall statue depicts Donald Trump and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein merrily holding hands and frolicking. It was created in protest of the relationship between Trump and Epstein and as a way to call out the sexual misconduct allegations against Trump and the redaction of the Epstein Files. The statue was constructed from foam, resin, wood and coloured to appear bronze. The center plaque read: "In Honor of Friendship Month – We celebrate the long-lasting bond between President Donald J. Trump and his “closest friend” Jeffrey Epstein.” It was dismantled by the US Park Police within 24 hours of installation but "Best Friends Forever" was temporarily reinstalled at various other locations in Washington D.C.

"King of the World"

King of the World AP Photo

King of the World AP Photo

Artist: The Secret Handshake

Year: 2026

Original location: National Mall, Washington D.C.

Description: The 3.6m statue was seen this year as a companion piece to "Best Friends Forever", as it also depicts Trump and Epstein. This time, the anonymous artists belonging to The Secret Handshake mimicked the Jack and Rose pose from Titanic. The plaque accompanying it read: "The tragic love story between Jack and Rose was built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches. This monument honors the bond between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein, a friendship seemingly built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches."

World.title: 'Grand odysseys': Why historic travel and legendary journeys are trending for 2027
World.content:
It’s the season when travel companies start to reveal their predictions for the following year, and now Skyscanner has launched its 2027 Travel Trends report.

 

Pairing global search insights and research from more than 28,000 travellers, the report uses data from the likes of TikTok, ClassPass, Wise, Universal Music Group for Brands, and AllTrails.

Among the new trends for 2027 is history-focussed travel, which follows on from a trend which has already seen significant traction this year thanks, in no small part, to The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of Homer's epic poem.

Skyscanner has called this particular trend “Grand Odysseys”, and suggests that its popularity is down to travellers trying to escape a fast-paced world. They’re seeking out history which offers context and grounds them in timeless human stories.

Related Follow in the footsteps of The Odyssey in Türkiye and Italy on this luxurious new tour

Next year will see tourists following sacred walking trails, exploring legendary ruins and turning to the past to enrich their often overwhelming present.

Skyscanner’s research found that cinematic releases have been driving real-world bookings, with films and TV shows including The Odyssey and Gladiator proving particularly inspiring.

Data from TikTok backs this up, too, showing that video views for cinematic travel content are up +346% year on year, while posts featuring #HeroJourney are up some +452%.

The Odyssey reportedly prompted a third of people to plan a trip inspired by the epic, and the data shows that almost half – 43% – of Millennials have been inspired by films and TV set in antiquity, from Troy to the tales of Ancient Greece.

And 24% of them have taken it further and travelled in the footsteps of ancient stories, a figure which rises to 30% among Gen Z.

Corfu’s Cape Drastis Loop is a must visit trail for history lovers Chris/Unsplash

The top historic hikes for 2027

Among Skyscanner’s partners for the report was the app AllTrails, which revealed its top five walking trails to experience historical travel on foot in 2027.

In first place is Corfu’s Cape Drastis Loop. The popular route on the Greek island is said to be ancient author Homer’s mythical land of Phaeacia, where a shipwrecked Odysseus shared the story of his epic 10-year journey home.

Next up was the route between Horcones Viewpoint, Horcones Lagoon and Espejo Lagoon in Argentina. Walkers can experience shimmering glacial lakes as they walk in the shadow of Mount Aconcagua, South America’s highest peak.

In third place was China’s Xi’an City Wall. Here, visitors can stroll along impressive Ming Dynasty walls where ancient gateways, sweeping views and centuries of history unfold below.

In fourth is Monte Santa Caterina in Favignana, Italy. Adventurous travellers can climb to Favignana’s highest point, which is home to a historic castle with a rich history linked to the island, long associated with Odysseus’ legendary voyage.

Favignana in Italy is packed full of ancient history and natural beauty Nicholas Ceglia

Finally, Rizes Cave, or the Cave of Eumaeus, in Ithaca, Greece continues The Odyssey theme. Here, walkers will pass through olive groves above the Ionian before arriving at a cave where Odysseus sought refuge after returning home in the epic tale.

“It’s grounding to visit a trail and realise you’re seeing the same rugged peaks, ancient forests, and horizons that travellers did thousands of years ago,” said Shelby Eagleburger, head of data integrity at AllTrails.

“Historic routes remind us that exploring the outdoors is a universal human experience, and it connects us across generations. How we travel evolves, but the pull of natural landscapes stays the same.”

Skyscanner’s top trends for 2027

Grand Odysseys is one of seven trends featured in the Skyscanner report, all of which show a shift in traveller behaviour.

The prediction trends also include “Signal Severance”, which is linked to the fact that one in four Gen Z travellers plan to disconnect in 2027.

Many of us are craving a less connected world and are seeking out remote travel spots, or places where it’s possible to switch off entirely.

Skyscanner found that digital detox spots in Finland, including Kittilä and Rovaniemi, are seeing rising demand.

Rovaniemi in Finland is among the best places on earth to get away from it all Dylan Shaw/Unsplash

Most of us like to bring back a keepsake from a trip – whose fridge isn’t covered in magnets? But for 2027, Skyscanner believes that the best souvenirs are the ones you have to travel for, with travellers increasingly building itineraries around unique regional apparel, artisanal crafts and location-exclusive items.

One in four travellers have taken a trip specifically for items they couldn't buy online, including the vastly popular Trader Joe's tote from the United States and merchandise from the Ritz Paris.

Weddings and travel often go hand-in-hand and, increasingly, couples are choosing to move away from gendered celebrations and are embracing the “sten do”, a combination of stag and hen parties. The report shows that 25% of travellers are opting for these combined celebrations abroad as they’re more fun, less expensive and easier to organise.

If you’re into fitness and wellbeing, you may already be an aficionado of the gym-cation, but it’s set to be a huge trend in 2027.

The report found that 67% of millennials are more likely to book a hotel which serves a nutritious breakfast, and 40% of Gen Z travellers said they prioritise hotels with gyms. TikTok data also showed a +659% year-on-year increase in video views for "Gym Hotel" content.

Increasingly, many travellers are opting to base a trip around seeing live music and experiencing unusual events.

Cultural immersion is a priority as traditional carnivals rank highly for both Gen Z (33%) and Millennials (30%), while 25% of those surveyed said the setting of a concert is almost as important as the set list, with fans hoping for gigs held in the likes of ancient caves or pyramids.

Finally, the “currency chasers” trend is set to be huge in 2027. Those keen to save cash are plumping for destinations where they can take advantage of positive foreign exchange rates.

According to the data, 45% of Gen Z and 40% of Millennial travellers have switched destinations to get more bang for their buck. Vietnam is a particularly popular choice for this trend, as the currency means tourists can spend relatively little while making the most of the beautiful Asian nation.

World.title: Inside Kazakhstan’s historic rock-hewn mosques now recognised by UNESCO
World.content:
The World Heritage Committee adopted the decision at its 48th session on 25 July in Busan, South Korea. This follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s 2024 instructions to pursue the inscription of these rock-hewn mosques on the World Heritage List.

 

Set amid the otherworldly landscapes of Mangystau, the newly recognised mosques and their associated sites are named after revered Sufi masters: Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe.

In Central Asian Sufism, ‘Ata’, meaning ‘father’ or ‘ancestor’, is used as an honorific for a revered spiritual figure.

Their spiritual lineage traces back to the 12th-century Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. His teachings helped spread Islam among the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia, connecting Islamic practices with older Tengri beliefs and local shamanistic traditions.

The mosques welcome both pilgrims and visitors seeking to explore Kazakhstan’s spiritual, cultural and architectural heritage.

Mangystau – the cradle of nomadic spirituality

According to the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, the complexes reflect the evolution of a distinctive spiritual culture.

They represent “sacred practices in which Islamic Sufi spirituality organically continued and transformed more ancient practices related to ancestor worship, the sacredness of the landscape and the role of spiritual leaders”.

Developed over many centuries, the monuments show how spiritual traditions and practices were adapted to the region’s distinctive natural environment and geological features through local architecture.

Speaking at the 48th session in July, Erlan Karin, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s National Commission to UNESCO and ICESCO, highlighted the significance of the inscription for the country.

“The inscription of the sacred monuments of Mangystau on the World Heritage List was not only a recognition of their significance for humanity as a whole, but also a tribute to the rich history, spiritual heritage and cultural identity of the Kazakh people.”

For local resident Almagul Zhaiman, the sacred sites embody a faith passed down through generations.

“These sacred sites have been preserved because of the faith passed down through generations, the knowledge of that heritage, preserving it and passing it on to our future generations. I believe that is what makes all these mosques so meaningful to us,” she said.

The Sufi masters of the mosques

Karaman-Ata was a Sufi missionary who came to spread Islam in the region. His mosque is believed to date back to the 12th or 13th century, while its associated necropolis is one of the largest and oldest in Mangystau.

For the Kazakhs and Turkmens who lived on the Mangyshlak Peninsula, the necropolis was considered a sacred place. According to local tradition, it was also a site for resolving disputes and negotiating peace. Those who made vows there were expected to honour them, as breaking a vow was believed to bring death and the end of one's lineage.

Karaman-Ata is believed to have been the grandson of Shopan-Ata, a 12th-century mystic revered as the spiritual protector of shepherds and their livestock.

According to tradition, Shopan-Ata was a disciple of the renowned Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. Once part of an ancient caravan route to Khorezm, Shopan-Ata’s site remains an important destination for Sufi pilgrims.

Beket-Ata is said to have regarded Shopan-Ata, who lived centuries earlier, as a spiritual mentor.

Local traditions attribute extraordinary abilities to the 18th-century scholar, healer and architect, including teleportation and levitation.

“He was also regarded as the last and highest-ranking spiritual master among other holy men, which is why he became known as Pir Beket,” said Bakhtiyar Esimbetov, caretaker of Beket-Ata’s mosque.

In Sufi tradition, the Persian word ‘Pir’ refers to a spiritual guide or master, often one who has attained a high level of spiritual wisdom.

The Shakpak-Ata complex served as one of the region’s principal Sufi centres for centuries. Shakpak-Ata is believed to have lived sometime between the 9th and 14th centuries.

Carved into a chalk and limestone cliff, the sanctuary is arranged around a central domed hall with a cross-shaped layout.

Local traditions say the scholar taught astrology and astronomy, as well as ideas linked to the cosmos.

Inside the mosques’ architectural layout

According to local belief, divine signs guided the Sufi masters to the places where they built their mosques.

The sanctuaries are scattered across Mangystau, in western Kazakhstan, a region shaped by its nomadic heritage and geological history. Much of the area was once covered by the ancient Tethys Ocean.

Locally known as “underground mosques”, the complexes were built in natural caves, carved into steep rock faces or dug into the ground, providing shelter in the semi-desert landscape.

Their architectural layouts vary. They include prayer halls, mihrabs, rooms for contemplation and self-reflection, multifunctional spaces and tombs of the Sufi masters, sometimes alongside those of their immediate families.

Some underground cells were carved out for silent meditation and ascetic isolation.

“These underground mosques were places of retreat from society, where people could withdraw from everyday life and devote themselves fully to spiritual purification,” said Yersultan Islam, a local sacred sites guide.

The complexes also feature courtyards, water sources, sacred trees, pathways and cemeteries, some of which date from the 10th to the 20th centuries.

Pilgrims

For centuries, Mangystau’s sacred mosques have been important destinations for pilgrims.

Visitors are expected to dress modestly, while women are required to cover their heads before entering the underground mosques as a sign of respect for the sacred sites.

The sanctuaries attract not only local worshippers but also pilgrims from abroad.

Among them is Dinara Farvazova, whose family travels from Bashkortostan, Russia, to visit Mangystau’s sacred sites year after year.

“We read the Quran here, pray and make wishes. People come here seeking healing, and many see their dreams come true. They then tell their relatives and friends about the place, who come here too.”

Some visitors come in search of a deeper understanding of Islam.

Kaahn Ozturk, a traveller from Turkey, stopped at Karaman-Ata’s mosque during a long-distance motorcycle journey across the country.

“I have lots of questions in my mind, and I just want to find answers. That’s why I’m trying to discover every mosque, every place, every idea about Islam, to understand it better.”

Rinat Aubekerov and his wife, ethnic Kazakhs from Russia, made a pilgrimage to Shopan-Ata, hoping their prayers to have children would be answered.

For Davide Passanante, a visitor from Italy, the appeal was different.

After experiencing the crowds of summer tourism at home, he found a sense of calm in the remote sanctuaries. Travelling with a group of friends across Mangystau’s Martian-like landscapes, he was struck by the region’s spiritual atmosphere.

“I'm very impressed because the religion here is very important. I see how people pray and how they feel, how they think of God every time.”

Easing travel for visitors to sacred sites

The remote sanctuaries are attracting growing numbers of pilgrims from around the world. Kazakhstan is now planning to improve access to the newly listed sites while preserving them for future generations.

A five-year comprehensive development plan, due to begin in 2027, is expected to support tourism at the sites, including restoration work and the development of new visitor infrastructure.

Each sanctuary already has basic facilities where visitors can sleep and eat free of charge, although donations are welcome to help cover maintenance costs.

Plans include building visitor centres at Shopan-Ata, Beket-Ata and Karaman-Ata, complementing the existing centre serving Sultan-Epe and Shakpak-Ata.

“An asphalt road will be built to the site as part of the development plan. We also hope that internet connectivity issues will be resolved,” said Baltabai Balapan, director of the Mangystau State Historical and Cultural Reserve.

The five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites of Mangystau, now collectively inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, are bringing the region’s spiritual heritage to a global audience, inviting visitors to discover its sacred landscapes.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: Hurricane Isaias intensifies en route to US Gulf Coast
World.content:
Oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has already been affected by the approaching hurricane, which has strengthened so far to Category 2.

Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall over the US Gulf Coast, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday. The storm's approach coud disrupt oil and gas production.

Isaias has been forecasted to cross the coast in either Florida, Alabama or Mississippi on Friday night or early Saturday.

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for coastal areas in four counties in northeastern Florida, while states of emergency are in place in parts of neighboring Alabama and Georgia.

"Isaias will be a dangerous hurricane with significant storm surge, damaging winds, and flooding rains when it reaches the northern Gulf Coast," the NHC said.

The NHC urged residents that emergency preparations to protect lives and property from high winds and storm surges "should be rushed to completion."

The Atlantic hurricane season has been remarkably quiet in 2026 Image: Octavio Jones/AP Photo/picture alliance

First Atlantic hurricane this year

Isaias has strengthened to a Category 2 storm over the Gulf of Mexico, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of the Mississippi River delta, packing maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph).

The hurricane is the very first to develop in the Atlantic this season, which began June 1.

The remarkably quiet hurricane season was caused partly due to a strong El Nino weather phenomenon. It causes strong vertical wind shear — dry air and sinking air over the Atlantic Ocean —, hampering storm formation and intensification in the area.

US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal authorities would coordinate response efforts with state and local governments.

"To everyone in the storm's path: ask that you also do your part to stand ready. Now is the time to prepare," Mullin said on X.

The NHC urged residents to complete their emergency preparations ahead of the storm Image: Octavio Jones/AP Photo/picture alliance

Storm impacts oil and gas production

The path of the storm covers some important industry points of oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico. As a result, platforms and rigs were already evacuated.

Some 63% of the oil production in the region has been temporarily suspended, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA).

Similarly, some 57% of gas production has also been suspended, the MMA said.

Offshore production in the Gulf accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

Hurricane Simon heads for Pacific

Meanwhile, the Pacific Ocean has been affected differently by the El Nino phenomenon.

El Nino's effect has left little vertical wind shear over the Pacific, creating favorable conditions for hurricanes to intensify. This has caused this year's Pacific hurricane season to be more severe than usual.

Hurricane Simon is currently moving toward Mexico's Pacific coast, with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, the NHC said.

The storm has reached Category 1 and has been forecasted to reach Jalisco state, where the popular tourist resort of Puerto Vallarta is located, on Friday night or early Saturday, the NHC says.

"Rapid intensification is expected to continue, and Simon is expected to be a very dangerous major hurricane when it approaches the coast of Mexico," the NHC said.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?
World.content:
Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?

It was billed as "the most unique stadium in the world," a key pillar of Saudi Arabia's World Cup 2034 plans. But now Neom Stadium, part of the kingdom's ambitious aims to build a 170-kilometer-long (111 miles) city in the desert known as The Line, looks set to be scrapped, with the broader project scaled back significantly.

A recent Reuters report said the stadium, which according to the country's bid book was going to be "350 meters (1,148 feet) above ground" and have "stunning vistas, and a roof created from the city itself," would no longer be built for the tournament, where it was to host a quarterfinal and several other games.

Observers of the gulf country saw this coming.

"When I was in Saudi Arabia in December there were already plenty of signals that the whole Neom project was being put on the back burner, if not abandoned altogether," F. Gregory Gause III, a regional expert from the Middle East Institute think tank in Washington D.C., told DW.

"I see it as part of a general re-evaluation of their fiscal situation, both in light of the oil market before the current war and in light of the damage that the war is doing. The draw-back from sports commitments is just part of a more general reassessment of priorities in the current, more straitened, situation."

Priorities changing, with sports losing out

Saudi Arabia's sports splurge that saw players like Cristiano Ronaldo join the country's football league and the kingdom invest in all sorts of sports in myriad ways has slowed dramatically. The country pulled funding for the multi-billion dollar LIV Golf as well as events in snooker, tennis and rugby and also withdrew from ambitious plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games in Neom.

Sports had formed a key part of Saudi Arabia's Project 2030, which aimed to diversify the country's economy away from oil and increase its soft power. But Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Saudi-government operated Public Investment Fund (PIF), which also owns Premier League football club Newcastle United, said earlier this year that the PIF was "reassessing its priorities" amid war in the region.

How the Iran war has ruined Saudi Arabia's 'Vision 2030' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The impact of the war has not only made the economic rationalization more important, but it's also accelerated the desire to rethink some of these projects in the sense that Neom is now being repurposed as an industrial center on the Red Sea, which has obviously assumed much greater urgency since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked," Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, author of "Kingdom of Football: Saudi Arabia and the Remaking of World Soccer," told DW.

Parallels between Qatar 2022 and Saudi Arabia 2034

There are, Coates Ulrichsen continued, clear parallels with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where plans to build 12 stadiums resulted in only eight being used at the tournament. The Arab Spring uprising arrived shortly after the bid was accepted by FIFA and, though it didn't impact the country directly, it destabilized the region both politically and economically.

Neither Saudi Arabia's World Cup organizing authority or Sports Ministry has responded to questions from DW about whether we may again see fewer stadiums than the planned 15 for the 2034 World Cup, which could feature 64 teams.

"We're seeing the same obviously with Saudi Arabia now," said Coates Ulrichsen, who is also a Fellow for the Middle East at Rice University in the US.

"[FIFA President] Gianni Infantino announced Saudi would be the only bidder on the 4th of October 2023. Three days later was October 7th, so within three days, the region was effectively in flames."

Saudi Arabia will host its first World Cup in 2034 but has been a regular at the tournament Image: Saudi Arabia Football Association/Handout via REUTERS

Since then, there has been the Israel-US war against Iran, while Houthi attacks continue to hit Saudi Arabia as part of the conflict in Yemen, meaning that: "This whole hosting cycle is taking place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty and kind of real tension."

World Cup will still matter to Saudi Arabia

But though the scope and cost of it may be reduced, Saudi Arabia's softening commitment to sport will not likely apply so firmly to the biggest sporting event in the world, said Gause.

"I think it continues to be a major priority, because of its global importance and because the Saudis will want to do at least as well, if not outshine, Qatar's hosting earlier."

Relations between Saudi Arabia and Qatar have improved since an agreement in 2021 but the pair remain regional rivals, something Coates Ulrichsen agrees will spur the 2034 hosts on.

As such, the 2034 tournament will still likely be a high-end affair, with Saudi Arabia building most stadiums from scratch. But, said Coates Ulrichsen, it may look somewhat different to what was planned.

Gulf Cup hosting a postivie sign before Asian Cup test

"The fact that at least the Saudis were able to host a big event with 60,000 people in the stadiums, full stadiums without any security concerns [the Gulf Cup football final which they won this week] is a good sign," he said.

The regional expert thinks more matches could end up being hosted in the two biggest Saudi cities, Riyadh and Jeddah. This may be at the expense of some venues nearer the east coast such as Al Khobar or Al Ahsa. These are separated from Iran by the Persian Gulf, which includes the Strait of Hormuz, and could be reconsidered depending on the state of political affairs.

Saudi Arabia host football's Asian Cup in January, which Coates Ulrichsen thinks will be an "early test of whether that is viable to have a weeks-long major tournament under these conditions.”

With nearly eight years until the World Cup, the political and economic situation in the country is difficult to predict. While the supposed shelving of Neom Stadium and general Saudi sporting withdrawal poses questions of commitment more broadly, it appears the World Cup show will go on. But probably not quite as billed.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: France: Investigators recover 2 stolen Renoir paintings
World.content:
Thieves had initially taken four pieces with a value of over $10 million, but dropped two as they fled. Officials praised everyone that tracked down the paintings, but didn't reveal how they found them.

Two Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in France last month have been found, authorities said on Friday.

Police have arrested six people in connection with the crime.

The two stolen paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history, our heritage," said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the Renoir Museum is located. "Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief."

The heist followed a string of high-profile robberies from European museums, including the theft of crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris last year.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Voting to begin in local elections in the Czech Republic
World.content:
The vote is being seen as a test of popularity for the Andrej Babis government.

Voters in the Czech Republic begin casting ballots in local polls on Friday to elect local representatives as well as one-third of the Senate's members.

The elections are being seen as a test of popularity for the populist billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

Babis took power last December after forming a coalition with two small political groups. His party, the ANO, or YES, won big in parliamentary elections last year after he was able to tap into people's economic frustration, playing into a sentiment that the center-right government at that time was spending too much on Ukraine.

But Babis ran into challenges as well after having formed a government, with the opposition challenging his widening budget deficit — which is when the government spends more than it earns. But he survived a no-confidence vote in parliament earlier this month.

Babis, 72, founded the Patriots for Europe in the European Parliament with former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and other far-right parties.

Housing shortage is big issue in Czech cities

More than 8 million eligible voters are set to elect municipal and town councils in more than 6,200 districts nationwide.

Housing shortages, a big theme in major European cities including Berlin and Madrid, is a top concern for voters in the Czech Republic's major cities too.

As for the Senate, a third of the seats are up for grabs, as they are every two years.

The vote will determine whether the liberal and conservative opposition can retain their majority in the chamber or whether the governing parties and their allies make gains.

President Petr Pavel drew attention ahead of the vote because he said he was not going to be able to cast his ballot since he was on a private holiday outside Europe.

"The president regrets the planning error," his spokesman said.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: South Africa pulls asylum directive after violent protests
World.content:
South Africa has withdrawn a controversial asylum directive after anti-migrant protests descended into violence and chaos on Thursday.

South Africa has halted a new directive for the processing of asylum applications after violent protests broke out in Johannesburg and Durban.

The directive was issued by the Department of Home Affairs in response to a court judgment.

The court had ruled that asylum seekers could not be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.

Offices for asylum seekers were quickly overwhelmed, and that placed officers at serious risk, the Department of Home Affairs said.

That's because the court ruling led to days of protests in the major coastal city of Durban, which then spread to Johannesburg's Soweto township on Thursday.

Rioters torched 14 cars in Durban and 10 in Soweto. Shops were looted in both locations.

Rioters torched cars and looted stores on Thursday Image: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

Police officers take control after clashes break out between groups of people Image: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

What else do we know about protests in South Africa?

The unrest in Durban followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. Vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.

Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

Police fired rubber bullets when clashes erupted between protesters and foreign nationals in Durban Image: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

What is the court ruling that sparked protests?

The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.

Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.

On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa."

Immigrants in South Africa pushed out of their own shops To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa: What to know

South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.

Amid international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.

Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.

Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Roshni Majumdar
