See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

In a joint statement on Friday some 30 cultural organisations in Groningen announced they were banning the use of smart glasses from their buildings and events.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

“This technology compromises the privacy and safety of visitors, staff, and artists, and undermines trust in an open, respectful environment,” the statement says.

Backers including the Groninger Archieven, the Groninger Museum, Noorderlicht, Stichting Kunst & Cultuur and the Grand Theatre Groningen.

Last week, eyewear chain Hans Anders announced it would stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP has warned that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR laws unless permission is given by everyone in the images.

The consumer watchdog Consumentenbond has also issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a blanket measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.

Utrecht music venue Tivoli Vredenburg banned smart glasses at its events in 2025 and has since refused entry to one man who would not take them off.

World.title: NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
World.content:
Patients who use medicinal cannabis face having to switch to imported products after the only licensed grower in the Netherlands was declared bankrupt on Thursday.

A court in Groningen declared Veendam-based Bedrocan bankrupt two weeks after the company had applied for protection from its creditors. The firm, whose main growing site is in Emmeloord, employs around 70 people.

Bedrocan ran into trouble after the health ministry ended its contract at the start of this year. All medicinal cannabis sold in Dutch pharmacies is bought and distributed by the state-run Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC).

The ministry ended the deal in anticipation of a change in the law that will let growers sell directly to pharmacies. But health minister Sophie Hermans (VVD) told MPs in July that the change is not expected to take effect until July 1, 2028.

That left Bedrocan unable to supply the BMC and not allowed to sell to pharmacies itself, the Volkskrant reported. The state was by far its largest customer.

Limited stockpile

The BMC built up a stockpile of Bedrocan cannabis before the contract ended, but the minister said it was limited and had a finite shelf life. The BMC will switch to imported cannabis during 2027, with products matching current THC and CBD levels as closely as possible.

Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed medicinal cannabis, according to the Volkskrant. They include people with multiple sclerosis (MS), severe pain, certain forms of epilepsy, and patients in palliative care.

Patients fear a different variety will not work as well for them. Cannabis contains many compounds that together determine its effect, and the mix depends on the plant and how it is grown.

The MS association has written to Hermans warning that some long-term patients depend on a specific variety.

Bedrocan also supplied patients in other European countries through the BMC. The BMC is due to stop exporting at the end of 2026. In September, Bedrocan told foreign pharmacies and wholesalers to order from it directly.

World.title: MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time
World.content:
The rainbow flag will fly at the Dutch parliament building on Sunday, Coming Out Day, after MPs overturned a decision by managers of parliament to drop the plan.

MPs backed the move by 90 votes to 36 in a vote late on Thursday night, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Parliament’s presidium, which runs its day-to-day affairs, initially agreed to the plan but changed its mind after Christian parties were told about the plan, RTL Nieuws reported on Thursday.

The orthodox Protestant SGP led the objections. “The rainbow flag is not a national flag but a flag of interest groups, which has grown into a symbol of activism,” SGP MP Diederik van Dijk told NOS.

Roll-call vote

Kati Piri, MP for opposition party Pro, then tabled a motion saying parliament should “stand up for the rights of the global LGBTI movement” and ensure “an inclusive working environment” for its staff.

Van Dijk responded by demanding a roll-call vote, in which each MP votes individually rather than by party. That meant MPs who had already gone home on Thursday had to return to The Hague.

Most MPs from D66, the VVD, CDA, PRO, PvdD, SP, ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and Volt voted in favour. The anti-immigration PVV, far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD), Denk and the SGP voted against, while MPs from JA21 and the Markuszower group were absent.

Purple Friday

The vote came on the eve of Purple Friday (Paarse Vrijdag), when schools mark LGBTI acceptance. This year it is being held in October for the first time, having been moved from December at the request of schools.

A record 3,130 schools have signed up, including 2,130 primary schools, compared with 2,890 last year, LGBTI rights organisation COC told news agency ANP.

The COC linked the rise to a survey published last month that found acceptance of homosexuality has slumped among teenagers. Only 22% of secondary school boys and 51% of girls now have a positive view, down from 40% and 78% in 2021.

World.title: MPs push for legal changes after pro-Hamas demonstration on Dam
World.content:
MPs are calling for a bill criminalising support for terrorist organisations to be pushed through faster, after demonstrators carried a “We support Hamas” banner onto the Dam on October 7, the third anniversary of the attacks in Israel.

Police and prosecutors judged that doing so was not illegal under current law. Police later stopped the marchers from heading towards the city’s Jewish quarter, home to the Portuguese Synagogue, the Jewish Museum and the Holocaust Names Monument.

Around 150 people were part of the group, according to Het Parool, with some chanting “Long live the 7th of October”. Some also carried a banner from the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PLFP), which is also on the EU terrorist list.

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema described the event “shocking and distasteful” but noted that the protests were not illegal.

Protestors only have to notify a local council to hold a demonstration, and authorities can stop or intervene in one if it poses a threat to local safety or order.

Rival political figures have criticised the lack of intervention on Halsema’s part, with JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie branding the decision to allow the protest “appalling”.

Orthodox Protestant SGP MP Diederik van Dijk submitted written questions to the justice minister David Van Weel asking why the protest was not broken up sooner.

A bill is already in parliament, submitted by Van Weel in June, proposing 3 new offences: glorifying the most serious terrorist crimes, distributing material that glorifies them, and publicly expressing support for banned terrorist organisations, which would carry a maximum sentence of 2 years in prison.

Van Weel amended the bill to meet objections from coalition party D66, which had long opposed it, so that support would only be punishable if it is aimed at winning others over to an organisation’s terrorist goals.

Peace organisation PAX has called for the bill to be scrapped, warning the law could be used against activists, journalists and protesters, and pointed to developments in the UK.

There, at least 3,070 people had been arrested by the end of April this year for showing support for Palestine Action, after the government banned the group as a terrorist organisation.

In 2024, around 320 people were arrested in Amsterdam after Halsema broke up a pro-Palestinian protest held on the same day as an October 7 commemoration on the Dam.

World.title: Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
World.content:
A new plan by care agencies and insurance companies aims to create 30 residential care zones in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area of Limburg, combining health services, activities and accessible living.

The plan, known as the Deltaplan Maastricht Heuvelland, aims to help older people live independently for longer and receive support and care closer to home, largely to tackle loneliness.

The initiative is a collaboration between municipalities, health insurers, residents, hospitals and elderly care advocacy agencies. Health insurers CZ and VGZ have provided €33.4 million for the project.

Nineteen of the 30 zones are currently under development, and organisers say the rest will be up and running next year.

“We have traditionally been accustomed to looking to nursing homes, but in this way, older people can continue living at home much longer, provided it is responsible,” Petra Lamberts, chair of Deltaplan, told regional news outlet L1.

The zones will also organise more activities, for example in a shared communal living room, to tackle loneliness. “Loneliness is a predictor of the need for care,” Lamberts told broadcaster NOS. “People notice minor ailments sooner when they are alone. When they take part in activities, they are distracted, and they are also encouraged to use their skills.”

Informal carers, such as family members, will also be able to hand over some of their tasks from time to time so they do not become overburdened.

A communal living room recently opened in Valkenburg, where local residents can take part in activities and meet for coffee.

The population of the region is ageing faster than the rest of the country. By 2030, one in four residents of South Limburg will be over 65.

According to Lamberts, a year of home care costs around €12,000, while a year in a nursing home costs more than €100,000.

World.title: Defence minister calls Russia “the enemy”, but policy unchanged
World.content:
Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz has started calling Russia “the enemy” rather than “the aggressor”, but says the change in wording does not mean any immediate change in national security policy.

The right-wing liberal VVD minister used the term during Thursday’s parliamentary debate on the defence budget. In a break in the debate, she told public broadcaster NOS that a rise in sabotage, drone incidents and intimidation in Europe meant the threat should be named plainly.

“It is very clear that Russia is presenting itself as the enemy,” she said. “That does not mean we are at war or that we will suddenly take a completely different approach.”

In August, the cabinet published a draft law that would give the domestic intelligence service AIVD and military intelligence service MIVD sweeping new powers against Russia, China and Iran.

A “new reality”

Yeşilgöz said Russia had long been the biggest threat to Europe, but the danger had grown into what she called a “new reality”. “Putin is testing how strong our alliance is,” she said. She added that experts had advised her to call things what they are.

The policy of investing more in defence and working closely with European allies has been in place since Russia invaded Ukraine, she said. “We were not naive before and we will not become naive now.”

In April, the AIVD said in its annual report that national security was under more pressure than at any time since the Second World War.

Oversight concerns

Under the draft law, the intelligence services would be able to designate “evident adversaries”, such as a Russian intelligence agency, and act against anyone believed to be working for them without asking a watchdog for permission first. A single new regulator would check afterwards whether the action was lawful.

The services would also be able to demand information from organisations such as banks, universities and online platforms.

The independent watchdogs that currently oversee the AIVD and MIVD have strongly criticised the plans. Hugo Hillenaar, who chairs the intelligence review committee CTIVD, told NOS last month that the changes could threaten the democratic rule of law itself.

World.title: Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs
World.content:
The Dutch customs service will have to endure substantial budget cuts because it is not formally counted as part of the country’s security system, its director general has told MPs, warning of the impact cutbacks could have as criminal gangs step up pressure on the country’s ports.

Customs chief Nanette van Schelven told parliament in a position paper on Wednesday that the agency will be hit by cuts planned for government departments. It will also miss out on the extra money the cabinet has made available to strengthen the national security sector.

The agency’s role in tackling organised crime “requires continuation and intensification”, Van Schelven wrote. Customs is looking for smarter ways of working, she said, “but efficiency alone will not resolve this tension.”

Customs, which comes under the finance ministry, has a budget of almost €982 million for 2027.

New smuggling methods

Customs officers seized 19,332 kilos of cocaine in the first half of this year, up 20% on the 16,104 kilos seized in the same period of 2025, according to the paper and figures provided by customs. That is already close to last year’s total of almost 24,500 kilos.

The paper also cited more than 106 million illegal cigarettes seized in the first half of the year.

Gangs adapt quickly, Van Schelven wrote, and customs has to anticipate trends rather than rely on seizures alone. She named dropping drugs at sea for collection, soaking cocaine into other materials, chemically disguising it, and smuggling via private aircraft.

The risk of drop-offs means smaller Dutch ports need to stay alert, the paper said.

Pressure on staff

Van Schelven’s “first concern” was criminal networks’ growing willingness to use violence and the pressure they put on the organisation and individual officers.

Arrests of customs staff for corruption show how concrete that threat is, she wrote.

Measures like periodic screening take a long time to introduce, and customs needs proper resources to protect its people, the paper said.

The hearing was held by parliament’s justice committee to discuss the government’s first national threat assessment of how organised crime undermines Dutch society. MPs will debate organised crime with justice minister David van Weel later this month.

World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents

Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. Kraków saw police interventions at night fall by almost half during the first six months the measures were in place, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 zloty to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding. The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024. Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers. Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine. “These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year. Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport. A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025 Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim. However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities. Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet. In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison. However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP. “Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz. Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence. They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026 Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia. In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers. The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. World.title: Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it. The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack. “We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters. “So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.” Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000. Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP. However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down. World.title: One person killed in second school knife attack in Poland in two days
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate. Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives. The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content. W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5 — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning. A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised. The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The incident comes just a day after another similar tragedy only 50 km away, in the town of Ostrołęka. On Wednesday morning, a 19-year-old attacked a vocational high school, leaving four students, two teachers and two bystanders injured before being captured. The assailant, who has been named only as Jakub Z. under Polish privacy law, is a student at the school. On Wednesday evening, national prosecutor Dariusz Korneluk told broadcaster TVN that the attacker had a homemade explosive in his backpack “that almost detonated”. “The backpack was already in the computer room and, only due to the responsible actions of the teacher and the students, was it thrown out of the window” after smoke had begun to billow out of it, he said. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek pledged that “prosecutors will ensure that the perpetrator answers for every blow inflicted and faces the legal consequences…There is no tolerance for violence in Polish schools”. Policjanci z Ostrołęki w pobliżu plaży miejskiej zatrzymali 19-letniego mężczyznę podejrzewanego o zaatakowanie ostrym narzędziem osób w pobliżu i na terenie szkoły w Ostrołęce. Ze wstępnych informacji wynika, że mogło dojść do zranienia 7 osób. Policjanci na miejscu wykonują… pic.twitter.com/cRzqMs36rD — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 7, 2026 On Thursday morning, around the same time as the attack in Leszczydół-Nowiny was unfolding, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that a 17-year-old boy had been detained by police after threatening to attack another school. The suspect, who resides in the same Masovia province where Wednesday and Thursday’s attacks took place, “was found with two knives”, said Kierwiński, quoted by news website Interia. His internet history also showed that “he was looking for information on how to carry out this type of bloody act”, added the minister. The potential incident was prevented after fellow pupils reported to teachers that the suspect announced he wanted to “do something bad at school”. Last week, a 13-year-old was detained by police after telling a fellow online gamer that he was planning an attack on his school in the village of Książki, north-central Poland. He reportedly confessed to having killed cats and said that he wanted to attack random people with a cleaver in the school halls. Dzięki przytomnej reakcji uczniów, nauczyciela oraz błyskawicznej akcji policjantów z Sierpca powstrzymano 17-latka, który zapowiadał, że „zrobi coś złego w szkole”. Policjanci zatrzymali nastolatka i zabezpieczyli należące do niego noże, a w jego telefonie natrafiono na historię… pic.twitter.com/oUkwKbHmNr — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The Polish authorities have recently warned of growing concern over radical ideas spreading among young people. Last month, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One was charged with planning an attack on a school and a mosque. Last year, a 19-year-old student was detained after it was determined he was planning an Islamic State-inspired attack on a Christmas market. In August, he was indicted to stand trial. In February, an 18-year-old was indicted over claims he planned to attack a school, also inspired by the Islamic State. Speaking on Wednesday, after the Ostrołęka incident but before today’s events, education minister Barbara Nowak warned that “we are seeing a radicalisation of young people”, reports the Onet news website. She called for “much greater control over what happens on the internet”. Earlier this year, Poland introduced a new law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour. The government is also working on measures to block children from social media and has banned the use of smartphones in schools. World.title: Poland launches €114m fund to support space technology firms
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) has announced the launch of the country’s first fund to support companies developing space technologies. Vinci Space Tech Fund will be worth 500 million zloty (€114 million), investing up to 100 million zloty each in 15-20 firms in the sector. The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence. Kosmos to nie tylko gospodarka i innowacje. Kosmos to także bezpieczeństwo Polski. 🇵🇱 Dziś w Krakowie uruchamiamy pierwszy w Polsce fundusz dla sektora kosmicznego – Vinci Space Tech Fund. 500 mln zł na rozwój sektora @BGK_pl Vinci. Mamy ambitne spółki, znakomitych naukowców i… pic.twitter.com/NQBy8HYOcY — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 6, 2026 According to the growth and technology ministry, one of the fund’s strategic partners, BGK will invest between 10 and 100 million zloty in companies with a potential for rapid growth and expansion into international markets through its Vinci investment vehicle. The fund’s other partners are the Polish Space Agency and Kraków Technology Park (KTP), where the launch took place, along with ICEYE, a world-leading Finnish microsatellite manufacturer and operator co-founded by Pole Rafał Modrzewski. Announcing the fund, Domański highlighted the space sector’s role in responding to threats, protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening energy security and monitoring Poland and its surroundings. “The money from the Vinci fund is an investment in Poland’s capacity to build its own strong companies and develop competences that will be strategically significant for our economy and security,” he said. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Mirosław Czekaj, president of the BGK management board, also noted that the development of the space industry would help “to build Poland’s technological sovereignty”, as one of the projects that are “vital to the Polish economy”. The fund is expected to invest in 15 to 20 companies, mainly Polish, although companies from elsewhere in Europe may also qualify if they have their main business operations in Poland, the ministry said. Its key investment areas include satellites, optics and Earth observation, satellite communications, electronics and photonics, rockets and propulsion systems, and artificial intelligence. In addition to funding, companies will benefit from advice and support from the fund’s partners. KPT, the city of Kraków and the Faculty of Space Technologies at AGH University are expected to provide much of the initiative’s academic, research and technical expertise. ICEYE, meanwhile, will share its experience of growing a space company and expanding into global markets. Last month, the company opened a satellite technology centre in Warsaw, and it plans to invest more than 120 million zloty in Poland by 2028, reports industry website Space News. Modrzewski said that raising capital in Poland was difficult when the company was founded 12 years ago, but that it has become easier as space has emerged as one of the country’s “strategic domains”. “The availability of capital in Poland will allow our companies to build their position on the global market without needing to leave the country at an early stage,” Modrzewski said, quoted by financial news site Bankier.pl. Vinci has previously invested in ICEYE as part of its private equity fund. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. Once limited to making components for others, Poland is now building its own spacecraft and participating in missions https://t.co/TmQiD91IzZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2025 Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems. A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight. The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security. In July this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency centre focusing on civil security and resilience. World.title: Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data. The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013. Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%. The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030. At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%). After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU. In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%). And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%). Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%. The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation. At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts. World.title: Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, finds UN study
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte. The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study. “Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte. 📉Facts matter. Refugees from Ukraine contributed 2.4% of Poland’s GDP in 2025, says new analysis by UNHCR and Deloitte. This is what happens when people forced to flee are given the opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity. The full report: https://t.co/egUp8jjCwc pic.twitter.com/CSNONqdKGU — UNHCR Polska (@UNHCRPoland) October 1, 2026 The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025. Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further. The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before. The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data. The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens. However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens. Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland. Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise. The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million. Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026 Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity. Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”. Indeed, in 2025, they paid around 2.8 billion zloty more in health-insurance contributions than the cost of the services they received. At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives. Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work. Ukrainian immigrants pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits, a report by Poland's National Development Bank has concluded. The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2025 The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status. Meanwhile, surveys show a weakening of refugees’ intentions to eventually return to Ukraine. Research by the National Bank of Poland (NBP) found that the proportion who plan to settle permanently in Poland rose from 21% to 25% between 2024 and 2025. However, UNHRC’s report also highlights the negative shift in attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees in recent months, with a July poll showing for the first time that a majority of Poles are opposed to accepting refugees from Ukraine. World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: National Assembly speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer meets US delegation in Budapest
World.content:
Ágnes Forsthoffer welcomed a delegation led by Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx to Hungary’s Parliament, where discussions focused on strengthening bilateral parliamentary ties and addressing the country’s key challenges.

Hungarian National Assembly Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer met an American delegation led by Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx at the Hungarian Parliament building on Thursday, calling for closer cooperation between the two countries’ legislatures.

In a Facebook post published on Friday, Forsthoffer said the US delegation had praised the results of Hungary’s spring election and asked about the most pressing challenges facing the country.

Trust, the budget and energy diversification

Forsthoffer said she had highlighted several priorities during the meeting, including restoring public trust both domestically and internationally, stabilising the difficult budgetary situation inherited by the new government, and diversifying the country’s energy sources.

She also stressed the importance of ensuring that the state operates transparently and economically. According to the Speaker, the American delegation offered cooperation and support in parliamentary affairs, an offer she said she welcomed and was keen to build upon.

The meeting comes as Hungary seeks to strengthen its international relationships and address economic and energy-related challenges. However, Forsthoffer’s statement did not provide further details about specific agreements or initiatives discussed during the talks.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

New Hungarian-American parliamentary friendship group planned

Forsthoffer also announced that a Hungarian-American parliamentary friendship group would soon be established. According to her post, 34 MPs have already indicated their intention to join, making it potentially the largest such group. The initiative is intended to help develop relations between the two countries, with the Speaker highlighting potential opportunities in areas including the economy and innovation.

“We trust in the further development of Hungarian-American relations, which will open doors between the two countries, including in the fields of the economy and innovation,” Forsthoffer wrote. She thanked the visiting delegation for its visit and what she described as its supportive trust.

While the meeting signalled an interest in closer parliamentary cooperation, Forsthoffer’s public account focused on the broad direction of future relations rather than outlining concrete policy commitments. The planned friendship group could provide a parliamentary framework for maintaining dialogue and exploring areas of shared interest between Hungarian and American lawmakers.

World.title: Hungary considers ‘exit tax’ on wealthy citizens moving their money abroad
World.content:
Hungary’s government is considering a 15 per cent tax on unrealised gains for wealthy Hungarians who change their tax residency and move abroad. The proposed measure would apply to assets worth more than HUF 500 million, although the details have yet to be finalised.

Taxing the rich for moving money abroad?

Hungary’s government is considering introducing an ‘exit tax’ targeting wealthy citizens who move abroad and take their assets with them, according to reports on the government’s proposed tax reforms. The measure would apply to Hungarian citizens who change their tax residency and have wealth or savings exceeding HUF 500 million (approximately EUR 1.37 million).

Under the proposal, they would face a 15 per cent personal income tax on gains accumulated since acquiring their assets, even if those gains had not yet been realised through a sale. The tax would effectively treat the assets as if they had been sold at the time of departure, triggering a tax liability on the increase in their value, writes Népszabadság.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Different deadlines for moving within and outside the EU

The proposed rules would distinguish between those relocating within the European Union and those moving to countries outside the bloc. Hungarians moving to another EU member state would reportedly receive a ten-year deferral before having to pay the tax. Those relocating outside the EU, however, would be required to settle their tax bill in the year they leave, provided their assets exceed the HUF 500 million threshold.

The proposal is not yet final, and its details could still change. The government is expected to complete its tax package within the next week or two if it intends the new rules to take effect in January. The proposed exit tax would be separate from the government’s planned wealth tax, which is also open to public consultation.

More on the economy: An exact date of Hungary adopting the euro emerged with new roadmap proposed

Hungary’s wealth tax aims to raise HUF 200 billion

Finance Minister András Kármán has argued that Hungary’s tax system places a disproportionate burden on lower-income households because consumption is taxed heavily, while wealth is taxed relatively lightly. According to the minister, wealth inequality has increased in recent years, making a wealth tax necessary to create a fairer distribution of the tax burden.

Under the current proposal, individuals with assets worth more than HUF 1 billion (around EUR 2.74 million) would pay an annual wealth tax of one per cent. A higher rate of 1.5 per cent would apply to fortunes exceeding HUF 100 billion (close to EUR 274 million), with the first payments scheduled for 2027. The government expects the wealth tax to generate HUF 200 billion (around EUR 548 million) in annual revenue, describing this as a conservative estimate.

Kármán has said the wealth tax was designed to make transferring assets abroad unnecessary, arguing that wealthy individuals could face higher corporate and income taxes in other countries. Nevertheless, officials have reportedly begun developing the separate exit-tax proposal as a safeguard against the transfer of wealth overseas. The plans remain subject to change, and it is not yet clear what the final legislation will look like.
