World.title: 18-year-old Budapest student missing for three days as police appeal for information
World.content:
An 18-year-old secondary school student has been missing from Budapest for three days, with police appealing to the public for information about his whereabouts.

Bauer Dénes left his home in the Hungarian capital’s Zugló district at around 6 PM on 6 October and has not been located since, according to the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK).

The 14th District Police Department has issued a missing person notice and is continuing to search for the teenager. Police are asking anyone who may have seen the young man or has information about his disappearance to come forward.

What does the missing student look like?

According to the police description, Bauer is approximately 182 centimetres tall, with short brown hair and green eyes. When he left his home, he was reportedly wearing a blue hooded sweatshirt, greyish jeans and dark blue trainers with white soles.

Authorities have not provided further details about the circumstances of his disappearance in the available reports.

Dénes Bauer. Have you seen him? Photo: police.hu

Police appeal for public assistance

The Budapest police are urging anyone with information about Bauer’s current whereabouts or the circumstances surrounding his disappearance to contact the authorities.

Information can be provided anonymously through Hungary’s free, round-the-clock Witness Hotline on +36-80-555-111. Anyone with information can also call the national emergency number, 112.

Police have stressed that even seemingly minor information could help establish where the missing teenager may be.

Anyone who recognises Bauer from the description or may have encountered him since he left home on 6 October is encouraged to contact the authorities as soon as possible. The search remains ongoing.

World.title: Hungary’s once-banned newspaper returns after 10 years – Népszabadság is back
World.content:
Exactly ten years after it was shut down, the online edition of Népszabadság, a former popular daily, was relaunched on Thursday, with the weekly print edition set to reach readers a week later, its editor-in-chief has said.

The publisher’s management announced the relaunch of the news outlet on 24 September. According to the announcement, the publication’s website, nszo.hu, will cover Hungarian and international public life and the major current affairs of society and the economy, with background pieces, analyses, reports and interviews.

A weekly print edition will follow the week’s most important topics and events, while the daily Népszava will also be part of the media group, with its content appearing in Népszabadság’s weekly edition in future.

According to the statement, the relaunched Népszabadság is published by Liberty Press, which also holds the publishing rights to Jelen and Népszava. Fully, 90 percent of the company is held by 4Sight Media Group, currently being registered, and 10 percent by Ákos Tóth, Népszabadság’s editor-in-chief. The group, founded by four Hungarian private individuals, is providing sufficient funds at launch for two years of operation.

Read Daily News Hungary’s article published on the day of the suspension of Népszabadság: Publisher of daily Népszabadság suspends paper’s operations

Tóth told MTI after the announcement of the relaunch that the paper’s motto is: “It changes with the world.” The editorial team is built largely on Népszava’s staff, which has taken on many former Népszabadság journalists, he said. Nepszava’s existing website will be restructured in the coming weeks, Tóth added.

In 2014, Austrian businessman Heinrich Pecina bought part of Ringier and Axel Springer’s Hungarian interests, including Népszabadság, and created Mediaworks Hungary.

On October 8, 2016, Népszabadság’s journalists were preparing to move offices when the paper’s owner, Mediaworks, abruptly suspended publication and switched off its website. That same month Mediaworks was bought by Opimus Press, part of the business empire of Lőrinc Mészáros, who had close ties to the former prime minister.

Mészáros said at the time that he had nothing to do with the media group’s purchase. Pecina wound up his Hungarian media interests within months. Several proceedings were launched against him in Austria, and he was eventually handed a legally binding suspended prison sentence and a fine for embezzlement and fraud in connection with a banking scandal.

World.title: Taxi driver clings to bonnet for more than 100 metres after crash in Budapest – Video
World.content:
A traffic dispute in Budapest reportedly escalated into a chaotic confrontation after a woman drove for more than 100 metres with a taxi driver clinging to the bonnet of her car.

The incident happened on Üllői Road and began with what appeared to be a minor collision, according to RTL Híradó. The woman’s car reportedly hit the back of a taxi driven by the man. The two drivers initially pulled over to discuss the incident, but failed to reach an agreement. The woman then reportedly got back into her car and drove away.

Taxi driver ends up on bonnet

According to police information cited by RTL, the taxi driver grabbed onto the bonnet as the car began moving. A witness who filmed the extraordinary scene said he initially thought he was watching a film being shot.

“I thought it was a film shoot, but they don’t usually shoot films on Üllői Road,” the witness said, according to RTL. The driver reportedly travelled at around 30 km/h while the man remained on the bonnet. The witness said the woman appeared to be trying to move towards the side of the road.

The car eventually turned into a side street, where the incident came to an end. The taxi driver, who was reportedly around 30 years old, complained of pain in his hand and leg. Witnesses called an ambulance, and he was taken to hospital for examination.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Passenger claims taxi driver feared being hit

RTL also spoke to a passenger who had been travelling in the taxi. According to the passenger’s account, the woman had allegedly attempted to hit the taxi driver with her car after the dispute. The passenger said the man climbed onto the bonnet because he feared for his safety.

This account has not been independently confirmed, and the circumstances surrounding the confrontation remain under investigation. Video footage of the incident showed the man holding onto the front of the moving vehicle as it travelled along the busy Budapest road.

More on the Hungarian capital’s traffic: Disabled parking space in the middle of the road in Budapest

Police investigating road safety offence

Witnesses called both the police and emergency services after seeing what was happening. Police have launched an investigation on suspicion of endangering road traffic. It remains unclear from the available reports whether further charges will be brought in connection with the incident.

What began as a minor rear-end collision therefore escalated into a highly unusual and potentially dangerous confrontation, with one driver being carried on the bonnet of another vehicle for more than 100 metres through the streets of Budapest.

World.title: 15-year-old boy beaten with branches in Hungary after refusing to give up his property
World.content:
A 15-year-old boy suffered serious-looking injuries after several youths allegedly attacked him with willow branches in a park in Pilis, near Budapest, on Wednesday. The boy had reportedly refused to hand over a carabiner attached to his keys. His friend was also injured.

According to a report by TV2 Híradó, the incident happened in broad daylight in a park that also contains a playground. The confrontation reportedly began when another teenager took an interest in the carabiner attached to the 15-year-old’s keyring and tried to take it from him.

The boy refused and managed to take back his property. Several people then allegedly attacked him.

The attackers reportedly broke branches from a nearby willow tree and used them to hit the two boys. The 15-year-old was left with long, bloody marks across his back and what appeared to be a large red handprint, while his friend suffered an injury to his calf.

Photographs taken after the incident showed the extent of the injuries.

Mayor arrived before authorities

The injured boy’s family remained in contact with him by phone before asking Pilis Mayor Attila László for help. The mayor said he and his colleagues reached the scene before municipal wardens.

“We arrived before the wardens and told the group that nobody could leave the area,”

László told TV2 Híradó. He said he took photographs and videos at the scene and gathered information about what had happened. According to the mayor’s account, the boy had attempted to defend himself after the carabiner was taken from him and eventually managed to recover it.

A crowd soon gathered at the park, including relatives of both the injured boys and those allegedly involved in the attack. László later addressed the incident on social media, saying that the town should have zero tolerance for violent acts. He called for the circumstances to be thoroughly investigated and for anyone found responsible to face the consequences under the law.

Police investigation expected

The mayor also raised concerns about information allegedly given to the victims’ families at the Monor Police Station. According to his account, one parent was reportedly told that a criminal complaint could be made after obtaining medical documentation of the injuries, but that little would come of the case because the alleged perpetrators were under 16.

László questioned this information, pointing out that the general minimum age of criminal responsibility in Hungary is 14. Being under 18 can result in different procedures and sanctions, but does not automatically rule out criminal responsibility.

He called on the Monor police to clarify exactly what information had been given to the parents and what action would be taken. The mayor later said he had been contacted by the Monor Police Station and informed that proceedings would be launched against those allegedly involved.

The investigation will determine the precise circumstances of the incident, including whether the initial attempt to take the boy’s property and the subsequent assault could amount to robbery or other offences.

The case also comes with a political and social controversy, as László’s public statement included inflammatory comments about the alleged attackers’ ethnic background and called for members of their community to leave Pilis and Hungary. Those remarks are separate from the factual question of what happened during the alleged assault, which will have to be established by the authorities.

World.title: Orbán-era oligarchs reportedly seek immunity deals as corruption arrests grow – UPDATE
World.content:
Some members of Hungary’s former economic elite are reportedly looking to make deals with the new Tisza government, with one wealthy oligarch allegedly offering to return assets and money in exchange for protection from prosecution.

Oligarch reportedly offers assets in exchange for immunity

Some members of the economic elite associated with the former Orbán era are already seeking ways to reach an agreement with Hungary’s new government as several prominent figures face criminal investigations and arrests, according to the latest edition of the VSquare newsletter Goulash.

A senior member of the Tisza government told VSquare that one unnamed, wealthy and influential oligarch has reportedly been sending messages to the government through intermediaries. According to the source, the businessman would be prepared to return assets and money in exchange for immunity from prosecution.

The source did not identify the oligarch or specify the amount of money or assets allegedly involved. It is also unclear whether the government led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar is willing to consider such an arrangement.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Another oligarch reportedly chooses a different strategy

According to the same source, another member of the former economic elite has chosen a different approach. Rather than attempting to negotiate immunity, the oligarch is reportedly keeping a low profile, returning whatever the government demands and trying to remain in business through bids from foreign subcontractors.

The source compared this strategy to that previously used by Austrian construction company Strabag, which operated while being placed on a blacklist by the previous Orbán government. The reports come amid a series of high-profile arrests involving figures linked to Hungary’s former political and economic establishment.

High-profile arrests shake former elite

In September, Dániel Jellinek, Hungary’s seventh-richest person and CEO of property company Indotek, was detained together with former state asset manager chief Norbert Szivek over alleged bribery linked to public transport bus purchases.

A court ordered Jellinek to remain in pre-trial detention for a month. His company has denied wrongdoing on his behalf, and the detention order is under appeal.

Two weeks later, former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták were arrested within hours of Parliament lifting their immunity. Courts subsequently ordered 30 days of detention for both men in separate corruption-related cases.

The arrests have contributed to growing uncertainty among members of the economic elite who built their fortunes or political connections during the previous governing era.

Will the new government make deals?

The VSquare source said it remains unclear how willing Magyar’s government will be to negotiate with former oligarchs and potentially spare them from prosecution in exchange for the return of assets. Any such agreements would raise significant questions about accountability and the treatment of wealth accumulated during the previous political era.

UPDATE: Magyar reacts

“There will be no deal with Orbán’s oligarchs,” the prime minister wrote on his Facebook page on Friday, quickly putting an end to the speculation. Magyar wrote, “You cannot buy immunity by returning certain assets. The only option is to return all stolen public assets. This could be considered a mitigating factor in court.”

World.title: Wizz Air cancels several Eastern flights for the entire winter season
World.content:
Wizz Air has scrapped its planned winter return to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, citing ongoing airspace restrictions that have made the routes commercially unviable.

Wizz Air postpones Middle East return

Wizz Air will not resume its planned flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai this winter after cancelling all services to and from the two UAE destinations for the season. The airline had originally planned to operate the routes between 25 October and 27 March, following an earlier announcement that it would return to the UAE alongside services to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan.

The latest decision comes just days after Wizz Air initially announced that some Abu Dhabi routes would be postponed until January following updated safety guidance from Europe’s aviation regulator. The airline has now cancelled the Abu Dhabi and Dubai services for the entire winter season.

Longer routes make flights too expensive

Wizz Air said the decision was prompted by regional airspace restrictions that were extended on 30 September. The restrictions mean aircraft would have to take significantly longer routes to reach their destinations, increasing both flight times and operating costs.

According to the airline, the resulting costs make operating the routes commercially unviable under current conditions, including with its Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft.

“We regret the disruption to travel plans and will continue to monitor developments, reassessing operations as safety guidance and operating conditions evolve,” Wizz Air said in a statement to The National.

The airline also confirmed that its planned flights to and from Amman are affected by the latest conflict-zone guidance from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which recommends that airlines do not operate within Jordanian airspace.

Have you heard? Wizz Air rethink could reshape ticket prices and routes across Europe

Wizz Air had planned a major Middle East comeback

The cancelled UAE services were part of a much bigger planned return to the Middle East. For the winter season, Wizz Air had announced plans for 12 routes and 49 weekly flights connecting nine European cities with destinations in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

The planned network would have offered around 470,000 seats across the three countries. Wizz Air had suspended its European-operated Middle East services in late February following the escalation of the regional conflict.

The planned return came after the airline’s low-cost subsidiary Wizz Air Abu Dhabi ceased operations in September 2025. The continuing airspace restrictions have also forced other international airlines to adjust their schedules and routes across the region.

For passengers who had been planning to fly Wizz Air to Abu Dhabi or Dubai this winter, the latest announcement means the airline’s much-anticipated return will have to wait.

World.title: For the Trump Administration, Kosovo is Now Just a Bargaining Chip
World.content:
Kosovo has finally broken its political deadlock, with parliament electing a new President after 20 months of wrangling that produced two early elections and brought the country to the brink of a third.

But the political turmoil is far from over. Demonstrations have erupted over the indictment of four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders and the country remains deeply divided over its political future.

For a young country still struggling to find its political footing, one thing has been conspicuously missing: the United States. Washington once played a parental role for Kosovo, stepping in to broker deals and settle disputes, as US Ambassador Christopher Dell famously did in 2011, when he helped propose a presidential candidate after Kosovo’s political leaders could not agree on one. Today, Washington appears reluctant to play that role.

Since the end of the Kosovo war, Washington has envisioned its role as having a defined endpoint: the US would win the war, and Europe would take responsibility for maintaining the peace. Kosovo, and more broadly the Balkans, would eventually become a European responsibility.

World.title: Montenegro Detains Co-Founders of Pro-Russian Telegram Channel
World.content:
Montenegrin police on Friday arrested the two co-founders of the pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Rybar, Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk, along with three associates, accusing them of malicious political meddling in the Balkan state.

Founded in 2018, Rybar is a prominent Russian digital propaganda and geopolitical analysis network centred around a channel on Telegram, which is reported to have more than 1.3 million followers.

The Telegram channel administrators confirmed that the Zvinchuks had been detained along with other Russian citizens. They insisted that all of them were in Montenegro legally.

“Specifically, their plans included filming the Cetinje Monastery, for which a completely official request had previously been submitted. At present, the project team is in contact with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, which is working to resolve the situation,” the channel administrators wrote on Telegram.

“Since there were no violations of local legislation, we are awaiting the release of all those detained,” they added.

Mikhail Zvinchuk is a prominent Russian military blogger who has been under EU sanctions since 2023 for allegedly spreading “disinformation and pro-Russian propaganda”.

He was a member of a working group set up by Russian President Vladimir Putin in December 2022 to coordinate Russia’s mobilisation efforts in support of the war in Ukraine.

Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk are officially designated on the British sanctions list.

In October 2024, the US State Department offered a $10-million reward for intelligence on Rybar over allegations that it was involved in interference in the American presidential elections intended to “sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence”.

The State Department accused Rybar of “bolstering Russia’s military capabilities and advancing pro-Russian and anti-Western narratives”. Zvinchuk was one of nine named people about whom the US was seeking information.

In June 2024, Bosnian Serb authorities announced a collaboration with Zvinchuk during his visit to Bosnia’s Serb-majority Republika Srpska entity, where he met Drazen Visnjic, director of the entity’s Agency for Information and Communication Technologies.

The Agency at the time said Zvinchuk and Visnjic had agreed to cooperate on establishing a media school, as well as other projects.

World.title: Albania Parliament Approves Municipal Reform Plan Amid Protests
World.content:
The Albanian parliament in session. Photo: Photo: Malton Dibra/LSA.



After a tense session lasting more than 12 hours, Albania’s parliament voted in the early hours of Friday morning for territorial reform legislation, as people protested against the outside the building and clashed with police.

Police said eight protesters were arrested during the clashes.

Opposition Democratic Party MPs opposed the reform. One MP, Gazment Bardhi, threw bottles of water at Prime Minister Edi Rama during the vote.

The government argues that the current map of 61 municipalities no longer reflects Albania’s demographic and economic reality.

Critics, however, say the only result will be greater centralisation and the further isolation of rural communities from public services, spurring even greater depopulation.

There was some criticism of the reform within Rama’s ruling Socialist Party, too, with MP Erion Brace expressing opposition but finally voting in favour. Asked why by journalists, he said: “I am still against the reform … I will tell you tomorrow about the motives for my vote.”

The law needed 84 votes to pass. The Socialists have 83 seats. According to media, Rama ordered Socialist MPs to “either vote in favour or leave the party”. With votes from the Social Democratic Party MPs, the law passed with 85 votes in favour.

Rama later on Friday said that the vote in parliament “gave Albania another modernising push”.

Albania’s municipalities have responsibility for waste management, drinking water, urban planning, public transport, social services, environmental protection, energy efficiency, climate adaptation, civil protection and local public procurement.

The reform comes 12 years after the last shake-up in which the number of municipalities was slashed from 400 to 61.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Reports of Trump’s Attempt to Reshape Poland’s Govt Spark Political Row
World.content:
Hungary tables wealth tax; Budapest mulls bid to host 2036 Olympics

Fulfilling a campaign promise, PM Peter Magyar announced this week his government would introduce a special wealth tax on individuals whose assets exceed 1 billion forints (2.7 million euros). The draft legislation – which is still subject to debate – uses a broad interpretation of private wealth, including real estate, assets in companies, shares, and savings held in both domestic and foreign banks. Those affected would have to pay an additional 1 per cent tax, effective from August 2027, over the 1-billion-forint threshold. For wealth exceeding 100 billion forints (272.5 million euros), the tax rate would be 1.5 per cent. The government expects the wealth tax to affect around 15,000 people in Hungary and generate an additional 800 billion forints (2.2 billion euros) in revenue over the next four years. According to Forbes magazine, the number of ultra-wealthy individuals who would come under the 1.5 per cent threshold is only around 35 or 36. As the wealth tax would be imposed on individuals, many families can breathe a sigh of relief, as their wealth would be assessed on an individual basis. Critics, however, warn that wealth taxes imposed on billionaires have not necessarily been successful internationally and could trigger an exodus of some individuals. To prevent people from circumventing the system, the Hungarian government would introduce a ten-year period during which those whose wealth was accumulated in Hungary would remain liable for the tax, regardless of their country of residence.

Hungary has expressed interested in hosting the 2036 Olympic Games, as was revealed by the International Olympic Committee this week. Under the previous government of Viktor Orban, which was keen to use international sporting events to burnish Hungary’s reputation, the country considered bidding to host the 2024 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw its application in 2017 after the newly established Momentum party collected more than 260,000 signatures in support of a referendum against the plan. Experts say that most of the sports infrastructure needed to host the Olympics has already been built over the past decade, largely due to Orban’s strong interest in sports. Budapest – and Hungary more generally – would now be well suited to hosting the Games, they say. The capital has already hosted the World Athletics Championship in 2023, while its swimming facilities are due to host the 2027 World Aquatics Championships, meaning that organising the Olympics would not require massive additional investment in sports infrastructure. A so-called Budapest Olympics Masterplan was already submitted in March by the previous government. The plan envisages a “regional Games”, with some basketball and golf events staged in Austria and Slovakia hosting equestrian events. Surfing would be held in Ericeira, Portugal. Gergely Karacsony, the mayor of Budapest, has cautiously floated the plans several times throughout the year, while PM Magyar also expressed support for hosting the Olympics in earlier interviews. “As the sports infrastructure required to host the Olympic Games has already been built in Hungary in recent years, an Olympic bid that involves no stadium construction and requires no significant investment in sports infrastructure is both feasible and realistic,” hvg.hu quoted the mayor’s office as saying. The costs are estimated at 5.5 billion euros, with 90 per cent expected to come from the private sector, while the projected economic benefits are estimated at 4.7 billion euros. According to a recent Median poll, 64 per cent of Hungarians would support hosting the Olympics. This is a considerable increase from the 50 per cent polled only two years ago. The list of countries competing with Hungary for the 2036 Games currently includes Germany, Turkey, South Africa, South Korea and Qatar.

World.title: Kosovo President’s Election Kindles Hope of Return to Stability
World.content:
Justina Shiroka Pula was inaugurated as Kosovo’s President on Wednesday after two days of unrest, three weeks of peaceful protests, and almost two years of political crisis.

The day before, Pristina woke up to the lingering smell of tear gas, which the Kosovo police had used to disperse a protest that turned violent on Monday night.

The protesters were demanding legal changes to curb the jurisdiction of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, after it convicted four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders of war crimes.

On Tuesday, Kosovo also braced for the announcement of a new snap parliamentary election, as October 6 was the deadline for MPs to elect a new head of state. If the deadline expired, new polls would have been obligatory under the constitution.

World.title: ‘ChatGPT Diagnosed Me’: Patients’ Faith in AI Leaves Albania’s Doctors Feeling Frustrated
World.content:
After three intensive sessions and a series of specialised tests, Albanian psychologist Sonila Jaupbashi realised that the patient sitting across from her was not suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder, or OCD.

The young woman, a third-year medical student in Germany, insisted she had been suffering from OCD for years.

“I had spent time and three difficult sessions, using specialised tests and questionnaires that are used to establish this diagnosis, and she had spent quite a lot of money,” Jaupbashi recalled to BIRN.

“Later, she admitted that she had been diagnosed by ChatGPT.”

World.title: Stench from Bosnia’s Ramici Landfill Indicates Mounting Waste Challenges
World.content:
Scorching temperatures were followed by rain, and a heavy, suffocating stench of decay filled the air around the Ramici Regional Landfill, near Banja Luka in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

A viscous black liquid, a mix of rain, wastewater and sewage, is absorbed into the ground and, eventually, the stream that runs nearby.

The landfill cassette – an isolated, underground ‘cell’ with impermeable lining, drainage system, and gas control system – is full, according to local resident Dragan Bajic, and so, he said, the landfill should be closed.

“Data gathered by residents and activists indicate that the maximum capacity of the cassette was reached a year or a year and a half ago,” said Bajic, who is part of a group of concerned residents.

“Given this, the conditions for operating a regional landfill no longer exist. In the environmental permit we reviewed, in coordination with a legal team, we found that the method of animal waste disposal currently practiced at the landfill is not recognised by the applicable legislation.”

At Ramici, animal waste is dumped in an open meadow and mixed with the other waste using excavators, even when the summer temperatures are nudging 40 degrees Celsius.

Bajic said he and other residents live in fear of an environmental catastrophe.

“We are not asking for anything special, nor do we have political motives or wish to score points for the elections,” Bajic said, speaking ahead of elections held on October 4.

World.title: Serbian Watchdog Claims Voters’ Rights Under Threat Ahead of Elections
World.content:
Serbian election watchdog CRTA asserted on Thursday that citizens’ electoral rights and freedoms are being undermined by intimidation, violence and unlawful surveillance ahead of the October 25 parliamentary elections.

CRTA’s election monitoring report claimed that opposition figures have been subjected to unlawful surveillance and police operations.

It also claimed that pro-government politicians and media had spread “manipulative narratives” about alleged opposition plans to incite unrest and overthrow the constitutional order.

CRTA’s monitoring found that nearly 1,500 articles in pro-government online media warned of chaos and violence on election day, while an average of seven articles daily portrayed opposition activities as an attempted “colour revolution”, referencing the popular revolts that toppled authoritarian, pro-Moscow governments in Ukraine and elsewhere.

CRTA programme director Rasa Nedeljkov said another key issue was “widespread electoral engineering” , which “clearly involves Serbia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs”.

According to CRTA, around 22,000 Serbian citizens living abroad could effectively be denied the right to vote because of the decision not to open polling stations in all countries where sufficient numbers of voters had registered.

“The ministry made a poorly explained, vague and unconvincing decision not to open polling stations in countries where a sufficient number of voters had registered to vote,” Nedeljkov said.

Nedeljkov said another example of “electoral engineering” was the “unrealistic decision by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) requiring voters in all time zones to cast their ballots according to Serbian time, making it even more difficult for them to exercise their right to vote”.

The new rule rule obliging voters abroad to follow polling hours based on Central European Time means some diaspora Serbians would have to cast ballots in the middle of the night.

The report also highlighted unequal media coverage, saying opposition parties have received half as much airtime as the ruling parties on national television, much of it negative. On the public broadcaster, RTS, the opposition has received just 15 per cent of airtime devoted to political actors, largely due to mandatory election coverage segments.

Nedeljkov said the mission was alarmed by persistent efforts to incite hostility towards independent election observers like CRTA.

“Allegations that first appear on marginal social media accounts, often newly created, quickly gain traction in pro-government media outlets and even in statements by senior state officials. CRTA is portrayed as a tool of foreign intelligence services, a covert political actor and a participant in a conspiracy to overthrow the state,” Nedeljkov said.

He said such actions threaten not only citizens’ rights and freedoms but also the safety of everyone “who wishes to devote their time and energy to election monitoring in the interest of democracy in this country, with the aim of ensuring free and fair elections”.

CRTA reported that one in three campaign activities by the ruling “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list monitored on the ground had involved elements of manipulation or potential legal violations, including suspected signature forgery, misuse of public resources and public office, and offering money, assistance or jobs in exchange for political support.

The watchdog also accused the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media, REM, and the Anti-Corruption Agency of contributing to the ruling party’s advantage by failing to consistently enforce the law.

World.title: EU Seeks Strict Classification of Toxic Compound Found in Croatian Subjects
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – The EU is seeking much stricter classification of the toxic compound discovered in the blood of Croatian subjects.

The European Chemicals Agency has announced that its Committee for Risk Assessment recommends that trifluoroacetic acid, known as TFA, and its inorganic salts be classified as substances toxic to reproduction. Index reports that this is one of the concerning PFAS compounds that was recently found in the blood of all 110 participants in a study conducted by the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament. Among the test subjects were ten people from Croatia, from Gospić, Knin and Pula.

It is important to emphasise that ECHA has not yet adopted a final, legally binding ban or classification. The Committee for Risk Assessment (RAC) adopted an expert opinion and sent it to the European Commission, which still has to decide whether to introduce such a classification into European legislation.

what is being sought?

RAC recommends that TFA and its inorganic salts be classified in category 1B for adverse effects on development and in category 2 for adverse effects on sexual function and fertility. Their classification as persistent, mobile and toxic substances (PMT) and as very persistent and very mobile substances (vPvM) has also been recommended. This means that they are difficult to break down, move easily through soil and water, and can pollute water resources over a long period. Such a classification does not mean that every measured amount of TFA will automatically cause a health problem in humans. It indicates the hazardous properties of the substance itself, while the actual health risk also depends on the level and duration of exposure.

tfa was discovered in the blood of all 100 subjects

The Greens/EFA study covered 110 volunteers from nine European countries. TFA was detected in the blood of all participants. The authors of the study emphasise that this is an exploratory study that is not representative of the population of individual countries and that the results should be interpreted with caution. There is currently also no appropriate health reference value for the concentration of TFA in blood serum on the basis of which it could be concluded from the finding alone that an individual is health-endangered. In the Croatian part of the testing, ten people from Gospić, Knin and Pula participated, who travelled to Brussels for testing organised by Možemo! MEP Gordan Bosanac.

should the ec react more quickly?

After ECHA’s announcement, Bosanac called on the European Commission to speed up the procedure. “I welcome this decision of the European Chemicals Agency, which comes a few days after our study showed that TFA is present in the blood of European Union citizens,” he said. He announced that together with Greens/EFA MEPs he will demand that the Commission react within the next three to six months, instead of the procedure, as he claims, being stretched out until the end of the decade. Bosanac had earlier also requested a broader restriction of PFAS compounds, the gradual phase-out of their production and use, and European funds for more extensive population testing.

ECHA’s expert opinion is now with the European Commission. If the Commission, after consultations with Member States and other interested parties, accepts the recommendation, TFA and its salts would receive a harmonised and legally binding classification at EU level. Such a decision could then trigger additional restrictions under European chemicals regulations and other sectoral laws.

World.title: Friends of Animals Demand a Ban on Loud Pyrotechnics in Croatia
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – The Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) Association is seeking a ban on all loud pyrotechnics in Croatia after the Netherlands set the ball rolling.

Friends of Animals have called on the Croatian Government to further restrict the use of loud pyrotechnics, after the Netherlands banned citizens from buying, possessing and using category F2 and F3 pyrotechnic products from the 1st of August this year. Index reports that in Croatia, firecrackers and string firecrackers from those categories have been banned for personal use since 2021, but other F2 and F3 products are still permitted under prescribed conditions. The association is demanding that the ban be extended to all category F2 and F3 pyrotechnics whose main effect is a strong explosion and noise.

“It isn’t logical to ban one product because of the noise and allow others that produce an equally strong or even stronger bang, just because they are not called a firecracker but, for example, an aerial bomb,” said Snježana Klopotan Kačavenda from Friends of Animals.

According to the association, the Dutch ban covers entire categories F2 and F3 for private users, while citizens still have access to category F1 pyrotechnics, which pose a very low risk and produce negligible noise. Professional fireworks remain possible under special conditions, and exceptions can be approved for some organised New Year’s celebrations. Friends of Animals believe that such a model would reduce the number of injuries, fires, material damage, noise and stress for people and animals.

The association has already proposed amendments to the Act on Explosive Substances and the Production and Trade of Weapons to the Ministry of the Interior. In addition to the ban on loud category F2 and F3 pyrotechnics, they are demanding that the use of the remaining permitted pyrotechnics for citizens be limited to only two hours around midnight on New Year’s Eve. They also propose that sales be allowed only on the 29th, 30th and 31st of December, that advertising of pyrotechnics and their sale in mixed-goods stores be banned, and that places of use and the number of public fireworks displays be further restricted.

Friends of Animals state that their petition for a ban on loud pyrotechnics has so far been supported by more than 40,000 citizens. “Croatia already has experience with the ban on firecrackers, a concrete proposal for amendments to the law and more than 40,000 citizens’ signatures for a ban on loud pyrotechnics,” the association concluded.

World.title: More Issues Arise for Ambitious Croatian Toll Collection System
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – More issues have arisen for the ambitious future Croatian toll collection system due to come into function in March 2027.

Croatian Motorways (HAC) has now cancelled the public procurement procedure for the development of a sales web portal, a mobile application for end users and an integration data bus as part of the new Crolibertas toll collection system. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this raises the question of whether the new system can indeed start operating on 1 March 2027, as prescribed by the Toll Collection Act.

how will crolibertas work?

The new Crolibertas toll collection system should completely change the way motorway tolls are paid in Croatia. Instead of stopping at toll booths, vehicles will pass without stopping, and collection will be carried out via ENC devices or automatic reading of registration plates. A total of 212 portals with cameras and antennas are being installed on the motorways, along with new IT infrastructure and data processing centres. The main contract for the implementation of the system, worth almost 80 million euros excluding VAT, was signed by HAC with the consortium of SkyToll and TollNet. According to the government’s decision, of the total 160.5 million euros, 115.6 million euros of eligible costs will be financed by non-repayable funds from the Recovery and Resilience Mechanism, while 44.9 million euros of ineligible costs will be borne by Croatian Motorways.

what procurement issues have arisen?

After the cancellation of the procurement procedure, the question now arises whether it will be possible to implement it on time at all. In May, HAC initially selected the consortium of Bos Projekt, Infinum and the British AMR CyberSecurity, whose bid amounted to 329,500 euros excluding VAT. The estimated value of the procurement was 330 thousand euros. The State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures cancelled the initial selection decision following an appeal by the Zagreb company Abysalto, whose bid amounted to 379,000 euros excluding VAT, and returned the matter to HAC for a new decision.

hac has now also rejected the bid it initially chose

HAC rejected this bid because it was higher than the estimated value of the procurement, while it also rejected the bid it had initially selected. The minutes state that this consortium did not meet the conditions for key experts. For two mobile app development engineers, diplomas from the Faculty of Organisation and Informatics in Varaždin were submitted, and for one database engineer a diploma from the Faculty of Science in Zagreb. The tender, however, required diplomas in the field of technical sciences. The consortium of bidders, according to the minutes, did not satisfy the condition relating to the quality standard. The submitted ISO 9001:2015 certificate relates to cybersecurity and assurance services, and it is not evident from it that it covers software production and the integration of information and communication solutions.

The third bid, from the Zagreb craft H&D Info i trgovina, amounted to 410,000 euros excluding VAT. It was rejected because the bidder did not meet the conditions for key experts, and the price was higher than the planned funds.

deadlines are now the big issue

In the cancelled procedure, HAC envisaged six months for the realisation of the work. It should be said that the cancellation decision is not yet final because the appeal deadline is ongoing, and any new procedure could follow only after the completion of that part of the procedure. Less than five months remain until the legally prescribed start of Crolibertas operations, which is a potential problem. HAC has previously emphasised that this is an implementation-complex and multidisciplinary project that requires the coordination of technological, legal and operational segments. Precisely for this reason it is clear that after this additional complication time is increasingly running out, and there is less and less room for new delays.

Jutarnji reported back at the beginning of September, citing a source, that the procurement had been incorrectly set up from the beginning. According to the claims, the development of the application was initially included in the tender for the selection of the contractor for the new toll collection system, but was subsequently, for unknown reasons, separated and a separate procurement procedure was decided upon for it. It is also stated that DKOM accepted the appeal because HAC did not adhere to the conditions it itself prescribed. In the event of the cancellation of the tender, HAC can contract this service by direct agreement with a contractor who will carry out the work for a lower amount than the estimated value in the tender and guarantee that everything will be completed by January next year.

hac: the project is proceeding according to plan

We contacted HAC and asked them whether the new toll collection system can still start operating on the 1st of March 2027, when they plan to launch a new procurement procedure, and whether that date will remain final or whether there is a possibility of it being postponed. We also asked them whether the web portal, mobile application and integration data bus are necessary for putting Crolibertas into operation. “In accordance with the Public Procurement Act, the decision on the cancellation of the procedure has not yet become final and the deadline for lodging an appeal is ongoing. Therefore, at this moment HAC cannot comment on possible further steps or models for the realisation of the subject functionalities.

The project of the new electronic toll collection system is being carried out according to plan, and HAC is undertaking all necessary activities so that the system is established within the deadline established by the Toll Collection Act. The public will be timely informed about all future decisions and activities,” Croatian Motorways explained. The question also arises at what stage the remaining parts of the infrastructure are, how many systems are already interconnected and how much time will be needed for final testing before commissioning.

According to the latest information published in the media, of the total of 212 planned portals, 111 have been installed. But the portals are only one part of the infrastructure. HAC officially states that the project also includes cameras, antennas, advanced IT equipment, construction works and back-office centres for data processing, and after the installation of all portals and related equipment a comprehensive system test will follow at the level of the entire network.

the deadline has already been postponed once before

It should also be noted that the deadline for the introduction of the system has already been postponed once. When the main contract with SkyToll and TollNet was signed in September 2024, HAC stated a works completion deadline of 24 months, i.e. until September 2026, and the Government at that time announced that the new system would be in function after the summer of 2026. The Act later set the start of full application for the 1st of March 2027, which is now once again under a very large question mark.

World.title: Rijeka Saw More Tourists in September 2026 Than September 2025
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – Rijeka recorded 22,690 tourist arrivals in September, which is two percent more than in September 2025.

In addition to encouraging growth in arrivals, Rijeka’s number of overnight stays remained almost unchanged at 61,672. The strongest growth was achieved among domestic guests. Index reports that there were 4,035 of them recorded in September, or 17 percent more than last year, and they recorded 7,604 overnight stays, a rise of 15 percent. Foreign tourists accounted for 82 percent of all arrivals in September, and domestic guests for 18 percent.

From the beginning of the year to the end of September, Rijeka achieved 193,716 tourist arrivals and 568,868 overnight stays. The number of arrivals remained at last year’s level, while overnight stays were one percent lower. Domestic tourists also recorded strong growth in this period. They achieved 38,747 arrivals, 14 percent more than last year, and 76,655 overnight stays, a rise of 13 percent. Foreign guests recorded 154,969 arrivals and 492,213 overnight stays and account for 80 percent of all arrivals and 87 percent of overnight stays.

Among foreign markets, Germany leads with 71,764 overnight stays in the first nine months. It is followed by Poland with 56,842 overnight stays, Italy with 41,053, Hungary with 30,437 and Austria with 25,932 overnight stays. In September, Germans were also in first place with 9,945 overnight stays, ahead of Poles, Italians and Austrians. The most overnight stays in the first nine months were recorded by guests aged 19 to 30, a total of 137,776, or 24.22 percent of all overnight stays. They are followed by guests aged 41 to 50 with 103,645 overnight stays and those aged 31 to 40 with 97,749.

Foreign tourists in Rijeka stayed on average 3.18 days, domestic guests 1.98 days, while the overall average was 2.94 days. The largest share of overnight stays was recorded in private accommodation – 335,776, or 59.02 percent of total traffic. Hotels had 145,876 overnight stays, hostels 41,573, and non-commercial accommodation 43,094 overnight stays. The data shows that Rijeka still achieves the largest part of its tourist traffic from foreign guests, while the domestic market is recording noticeably faster growth this year.

World.title: Hvar in Conde Nast Top 10 Islands for 8th Consecutive Year
World.content:
October 8, 2026 – More strengthening of the American love for Croatia’s premier island, as Hvar once more in top 10 islands in Europe in Conde Nast Traveler Readers Choice Awards.

These are good times for the relationship between Hvar Town and the sought-after American tourism market, with a marked shift in approach resulting in a boom in American tourism arrivals in recent years. According to official statistics, American tourists were the biggest number of arrivals and overnight stays in the town last year, and those numbers show no sign of slowing, with overnight stays from the USA in September up an impressive 17.83% year on year.

The success has been down to a number of key factors, including better promotion to the USA market, the introduction of the first direct flight from New York to Split this April, meaning one can get from New York to Hvar (with the aid of a good speedboat) in under 10 hours. So successful has the flight connection been that plans are being discussion to prolong the flight season as well as frequency of flights for 2027.

An additional factor has been the positive media coverage that the town has been attracting since moving away from its party focus in search of more upmarket tourism focused on families and couples, as well as adventure tourism. Arguably the most influential travel publication for American travellers is Conde Nast Traveler, which every year holds the prestigious Conde Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards, a publication which known Hvar very well.

Often named one of the 10 most beautiful islands in the world, that claim has its roots in a Conde Nast award in the late 1990s (you can see a list of the islands on the map on the Jelsa waterfront), and the American publication’s readers’ love for Hvar has been pretty constant ever since. Indeed, this year’s 9th place as the best island in Europe is the 8th consecutive year that Hvar has featured in the sought-after top ten list, including 2019 and 2021, when Hvar was voted the best island in Europe.

Breakfast at Sirena Resort

American interest has been mirrored by a raising of standards in the hotel sector, which is also attracting plenty of international column inches. The latest addition is the superb Sirena Resort from Suncani Hvar Hotels, 1.4 km north of the town, set in an idyllic bay without neighbours, and offering access to the vibe of Hvar Town, as well as the laidback calm of the nature of Hvar, the island. Within weeks of opening, Sirena Resort was featured in the New York Times as one of the top 5 new hotels in Europe for an autumn getaway.

The main season may be over, but there is still plenty of life in the town, with this weekend hosting the Spartan World Championship, with around 3,000 competitors expected. All the signs are there for a bumper 2027 for Americans visiting one of Europe’s most perfect spots.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport Could Surpass 3.2 Million Passengers
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Dubrovnik Airport might surpass the figure of 3.2 million passengers, with passenger numbers climbing even during the month of September this year.

Dubrovnik Airport continued its passenger traffic growth throughout September this year as well. According to data from the airport itself, Dubrovnik Airport handled 474,212 passengers in September, which is almost 31 thousand more passengers than in the same month last year. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that for comparison, in September 2025 a total of 443,444 passengers passed through Dubrovnik Airport.

Compared to September 2025, the number of passengers increased by 6.9 percent, while the number of operations also rose. Dubrovnik recorded 3,718 operations in September this year, compared to 3,564 operations in the same month last year, which represents growth of approximately 4.3 percent. Growth is also recorded in the first nine months of this year. From the beginning of January to the end of September 2026, Dubrovnik handled a total of 2,820,860 passengers. In the same period last year 2,692,873 passengers were recorded, meaning that Dubrovnik handled almost 128 thousand more passengers in the first nine months of this year, or 4.8 percent more.

Last year, the airport handled a total of 3,090,245 passengers, which means that by the end of September 2026 more than 91 percent of last year’s total traffic had already been achieved, and the airport still has three months ahead of it. While significantly lower traffic is expected in November and December, October should bring strong numbers. Consequently, it would be no surprise if Dubrovnik Airport already matches last year’s figures by the end of October.

World.title: Radioactive Strontium in Gospić Jumps by a Staggering 961%
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Radioactive strontium found in the soil in the Gospić area has jumped by an extremely concerning 961 percent, but what is being done about it?

In the surface layer of soil at the measuring point in Gospić last year, an almost 11 times higher concentration of radioactive strontium-90 per square metre was recorded than in 2023, according to the regular annual reports of the Zagreb Institute for Medical Research and Occupational Health (IMI), published on the Ministry of the Interior’s website. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that the published activity per square metre rose from 24.5 to 260 becquerels, or by as much as 961 percent. The concentration of strontium-90 (Sr-90) per kilogram of material at the Gospić measuring point also rose drastically: from 0.605 becquerels per kilogram in 2023 to 4.08 becquerels in 2025, or almost seven times.

has radioactive contamination occurred?

It should be emphasised immediately that there is no evidence pointing to a connection between strontium-90 and the illegal waste at the former PPK Velebit in Bilajska Street in Gospić, nor does this change in itself mean that radioactive contamination has occurred or that the health of residents is endangered. The measuring point in Gospić is located about 7.6 kilometres southwest of PPK Velebit and so far there is no evidence that would confirm a link between the two locations.

Strontium-90 is a radioactive form of the chemical element of the same name, a silvery-white metal. This means that its atomic nucleus decays over time and in doing so releases radiation that can damage living cells. Strontium-90 does not exist originally in nature, but is created by the fission of atomic nuclei, for example in nuclear reactors and during nuclear weapons explosions. “All Sr-90 in the environment on Croatian territory is a consequence of the Chernobyl disaster back in 1986. Sr-90 has a half-life of 28.8 years. After the half-life has elapsed, the activity and quantity of the radionuclide fall to half of the initial amount, so it is not surprising that Sr-90 is still present in Croatia – there is still approximately 38% of the quantity that was initially deposited.

This radionuclide is anthropogenic; it is created by the fission of uranium-235. Sr-90 entered the environment from the atmosphere, via the radioactive cloud, and accumulated in the surface layer. Therefore it is not surprising that it is most present there, because it spreads into deeper layers by the slow process of diffusion,” states the response of IMI’s Radiation Protection Department.

Gospić is the only area to record an increase since 2023…

The origin of strontium-90 has been explained, but there is no adequate answer as to why its concentration on the surface has enormously increased only in Gospić over the last three years. Among the five measuring locations we compared, Gospić had the lowest surface value of strontium-90 in 2023, and two years later the highest. While between 2023 and 2025 that value fell in Zadar, Osijek, Buzet/Pula and Opuzen, in Zagreb it rose by approximately 92 percent, and in Gospić by 961 percent. Becquerel per kilogram (Bq/kg) indicates how much radioactivity is concentrated in a kilogram of soil, while becquerel per square metre (Bq/m²) indicates how much total radioactivity of Sr-90 exists under one square metre of surface. Since Bq/kg can fluctuate considerably if the sample one year is a little lighter, denser or richer in organic matter, Bq/m² is to some extent a better indicator.

If there is no new input or soil erosion, the total Sr-90 expressed in Bq/m² should mostly gradually decrease due to radioactive decay, and not increase as in the Gospić case. It should also be added that in the deeper layers of the earth, below the surface five centimetres, the opposite occurred: the concentration of Sr-90 is strongly declining.

The Radiation Protection Department offered this answer to the question about the professional interpretation of the increase in Sr-90 concentration: “In Gospić soil Sr-90 is continuously monitored, with a break in the period 2014–2022. It was reintroduced into the environmental radioactivity monitoring programme in the Republic of Croatia in 2023 and continues to be monitored. The measured values varied and no year-on-year upward trend was observed. For example, in 2003 440 Bq/m² was measured, in 2004 280 Bq/m², in 2005 180 Bq/m², and in 2007 270 Bq/m². In order to establish whether the increase in the period 2023–2025 represents the beginning of an upward trend, more time needs to pass.” The last measured and published value of 260 Bq/m² is not in itself a historical maximum in Gospić, but such a sudden jump from 24.5 to 260 in only two years is shocking. An additional problem is that IMI did not carry out measurements in Gospić from 2007 to 2023.

Although IMI wrote in its 2024 report that only in Gospić “is the activity concentration of Sr-90 is several times higher than last year’s”, there’s no data that because of this obvious anomaly, which was repeated in 2025, a new control measurement was proposed or requested.

nobody requested or paid for additional monitoring

“Sampling within the framework of environmental radioactivity monitoring is carried out in agreement with the client of the work, in this case the Ministry of the Interior. IMI cannot itself define where and how often sampling will take place. We have not received a request from the client for additional or extraordinary sampling in Gospić.

Every year, sampling for the following year is agreed with the Ministry of the Interior. We may propose the mentioned, but the Ministry of the Interior will decide. That is open for now. It should be emphasised that it is possible to carry out detailed research outside the regular monitoring; we have often done that so far. Someone has to order and pay for it,” the Radiation Protection Department replied to the question whether it would recommend to the Ministry of the Interior more sampling points, more frequent sampling, analysis of water, vegetation, food or sediment. An interpretation of this sensitive issue was sought from a renowned Croatian scientific institution, without revealing what it was about. A radioactivity expert, who requested not to be named, answered the question whether a multiple increase in the concentration of strontium-90 on the soil is possible without a new source of contamination: “NO. That would be a perpetual motion machine.”

When we explained to him what it was actually about, he said that the only reasonable explanation could be deficient sampling, or inadequate laboratory analysis: “Measuring low activities is very delicate and it can happen that laboratories have different instrumentation, so measurements near the detection limits can deviate significantly. This is especially the case with measuring Sr-90, which is quite complicated. The analysis takes about three weeks.”

no answers have come from institutions about potential health risks…

From the existing data, it is not possible to draw a concrete and reliable conclusion about the impact of the strontium-90 concentration on people in Gospić. The surface increase refers to activity per square metre of soil, and not to the radiation dose received by citizens. To assess the health risk it is necessary to determine what dose residents receive due to radiation from the environment and the possible intake of radioactive substances through food, water and inhalation of particles. The soil finding alone is not sufficient either for the claim that there is a danger to health or for the claim that it is completely ruled out.

Interestingly, the Radiation Protection Department did not want to comment on the possible danger to human health: “The assessment of the threat from a particular radionuclide, which includes the ways of its propagation through the environment and the food chain, is not part of our contract in monitoring environmental radioactivity. That topic is quite complex and requires an interdisciplinary approach that would consider all relevant aspects.”

There was no concrete answer from the Croatian Institute of Public Health to Index’s inquiry. Unofficially we received the message: “We do not deal with that.” And the Ministry of the Interior’s Civil Protection Directorate completely ignored several inquiries on this topic; that is, even after two weeks no answer arrived. The key question in this story is not the concentration of strontium-90 itself and its possible impact on human health, but the inertia and disinterest of the competent institutions in reacting and additionally checking findings that clearly deviate from trends and expectations. Just as in the case of the illegal waste at Bilajska 50.

World.title: For 75% of Croatians, a Dignified Salary Starts From 2,000 Euros
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – For 75% of Croatians, a dignified salary starts from 2,000 euros, but the reality of what salaries are actually paid out in Croatia is starkly different.

The topic of the average wage in Croatia is a frequent topic, and we talk about the minimum wage most often when another increase is announced. The real question for many, however, is just how much should a Croatian wage be to enable workers a fully dignified life? What some would be one in which, after paying rent, utilities and food, there remains room for socialising, going to the cinema, an annual holiday or putting some savings away for a rainy day. A life in which an unexpected expense does not mean that we have to spend the rest of the month counting every single euro.

Alma Career Croatia, the international company known for the MojPosao/MyJob brand, addressed precisely this question in a new survey in which more than 500 people participated. Poslovni reports that just two years ago participants said that a dignified wage should not be less than 1,500 euros. Given the constant increases in the cost of living, we checked where they set that boundary today.

Is 1,500 euros enough for a month, but not for a peaceful life? The minimum wage in Croatia currently amounts to 1,050 euros gross, or around 800 euros net, depending on the worker’s tax circumstances. But the legal minimum and the amount that survey participants consider sufficient for a dignified life are clearly quite distant, because none of them chose a wage lower than 1,000 euros. The next range did not receive many more votes either. Only 3% of participants believe that it is possible to live with dignity on a wage between 1,000 and 1,500 euros.

A somewhat larger number, approximately every fifth person (22%), chooses the range from 1,500 to 2,000 euros. For them 1,500 euros is the lower limit which, with inflation and rising living costs, still leaves the possibility of a life above merely covering obligations. Everything below that, they believe, means living ‘from month to month’. Everything below 2,000 euros is not enough for the vast majority.

The largest number of participants, 50% of them, place a dignified wage in the range from 2,000 to 2,500 euros. However, they note that even that amount does not tell the whole story. A lot depends on whether we have solved our housing situation or whether every month we have to set aside money from the same wage for rent or a loan. For every fourth person (25%) the boundary is even higher. A dignified life in Croatia, they emphasise, requires a monthly wage of at least 2,500 euros.

Compared with the survey from 2024, the change is visible. Then the largest number of participants, 47% of them, chose the range from 1,500 to 2,000 euros, while a third selected amounts from 2,000 to 2,500 euros. Today precisely that higher range gathers half of the answers.

World.title: Northeastern Estonian cities question value of participatory budgeting
World.content:
Narva and Narva-Jõesuu are both reconsidering participatory budgeting as residents' proposals continue to prove too costly or vague to carry out.

Narva-Jõesuu has run the process nine times, spending €30,000 a year on projects including sidewalk repairs, fountains and a shorefront Wisdom Trail dotted with display boards featuring quotes from famous figures. But city officials say public interest is waning, ideas are getting repetitive and many proposals are simply too expensive.

"Over the past three years at least, the same proposal has come up again and again: let's renovate the resort hall," Mayor Maksim Iljin said, noting that €30,000 is nowhere near enough to overhaul the long-abandoned building.

"It's clear participatory budgeting has run its course in Narva-Jõesuu," he added.

Iljin said the city should instead focus on supporting local nonprofits and community organizations.

Narva, meanwhile, has spent up to €300,000 a year on participatory budgeting, but some winning projects have proved too expensive to complete, including Paju Park on Rakvere tänav and a boat ramp on Jõe tänav.

No new big projects

The city paused the collection of new proposals two years ago and now believes the annual participatory budget should be slashed to a tenth of its current size to focus on smaller projects.

"That's the problem — people come up with these big ideas that end up requiring public procurements and quotes," said Narva City Council chair Urbo Vaarmann.

He argued that unfinished projects should be completed before the city starts over with a new approach focused on "nice little projects."

In Narva-Jõesuu, the fate of participatory budgeting is on the city council agenda later this month. Narva city officials, meanwhile, are expected to make a decision within the next four months.

World.title: Defense Intel Chief: Russia targeting Ukraine's railways and Dnipro bridges in escalating strike campaign
World.content:
Moscow has introduced a new tactic and is attempting, through extensive long‑range strikes, to break Ukraine's infrastructure and the population's psychological resilience, says Col. Ants Kiviselg, head of the EDF Intelligence Center.

Kiviselg said at Estonian MoD briefing on Friday that in the battlespace, the downward trend in the number of combat contacts has continued, Russia continues to suffer heavy losses, and both sides continue long‑range strikes into each other's rear areas.

During this week, about 200 combat contacts per day have taken place, he noted.

"The most intense fighting has occurred in the same areas as in recent weeks: in Donetsk, the Pokrovsk and Konstantynivka directions; in Kharkiv oblast, the Southern Slobozhanske direction; in Zaporizhzhia, the Hulyaipole direction; and in Donetsk also the Lyman direction. Ukraine's counterattacks have continued in the Kupiansk direction in Kharkiv oblast, and in Donetsk in the Sloviansk, Lyman, and Kramatorsk directions," Kiviselg said.

"Losses of the Russian Federation have remained at an average of around 1,700 soldiers per day, which means the sixth consecutive week with more than 10,000 killed or wounded fighters per week. In response, Russia is slightly changing its behavior pattern: attempts are being made to break Ukraine's unity with intensive and very long‑lasting long‑range strikes," the military intel chief said.

Kiviselg pointed out that on 4 October Russia announced its intention to intensify long‑range strikes on Ukraine, and during the past 241st week such strikes hit various targets in 13 Ukrainian oblasts, followed in many places by power outages.

Ukraine setting up air defenses

Russia also repeatedly attacked bridges over the Dnipro River — both in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia — attempting to intimidate civilians, hinder everyday life in Ukraine, and thereby affect the economy.

"In Kyiv, air‑defense systems operating with artificial intelligence have begun to be placed to protect the bridges, and alternative solutions are being sought in case traffic on the bridges is halted for a longer period; the possibility of installing pontoon bridges over the Dnipro river is also being examined," Kiviselg said.

Kiviselg noted that according to Ukrainian data, about 330 educational institutions in Kyiv have been damaged in airstrikes during the war — roughly one‑third of all educational institutions there — and in the first eight months of this year, 107 educational institutions have been hit.

"Ukraine's rail transport is also in a very difficult situation. More than 500 locomotives have been damaged during the war, and this year alone 60 percent of them have been hit. Attacks against railway infrastructure are 40 percent higher this year than during the entire year 2025. So we see that Russia has intensified attacks both against educational institutions and against railway and transport hubs," Kiviselg said.

"Ukraine, for its part, has carried out medium‑ and long‑range strikes against Russian fuel‑industry facilities in Volgograd, Nizhny Novgorod, Samara, and Moscow oblast. Military‑strategic targets have also been attacked in occupied areas in Krasnodar, and in Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, and in the Republic of Adygea," he said.

Russia's fuel exports diminished

According to Kiviselg, the impact of Ukraine's long‑range strikes has begun to clearly appear in Russia's fuel exports. If in 2025 Black Sea ports exported an average of 200,000 tons of fuel per week, then according to public data this transport fell to zero in the third week of September. "Russia's diesel and gas‑oil exports are currently taking place through the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk and amount to about 81,000 tons," Kiviselg said.

Kiviselg said that between 1 and 30 September, Ukraine liberated, according to public sources, 25 to 80 square kilometers of territory, compared with last September, when Russia occupied 258 square kilometers.

"The trend is changing significantly, and last September Russia did not suffer such extensive losses as this year. Speaking of Operation Vivaldi, which began by the Ukrainians in late spring, it is likely that much larger areas have been liberated there — we are talking about more than 100 square kilometers," Kiviselg said.

Kiviselg emphasized that the Russian Federation has not come any closer to its stated goal of occupying the entire Donetsk oblast.

"Large personnel losses reflect rather that unit leaders and commanders on the ground are trying to fight their way to lines that have already been reported to higher leadership as occupied areas. We will likely see similar intensity in the coming weeks — perhaps intensity will decrease, but personnel losses on the front will continue. From this we also see that Putin's statements, as if Russians had additionally occupied 1,300 square kilometers during September, are not true; these are rather doomed attempts by commanders to achieve previously advertised results," Kiviselg commented.

World.title: Developers crowd into Lüganuse as municipality navigates project surge
World.content:
Lüganuse municipality in Ida‑Viru County has become a favorite location for various developers, which has forced the municipality to hire additional staff to process planning applications.

In Lüganuse, VKG and Kiviõli Keemiatööstus are expanding their oil‑shale mines; the state wants to establish two defense‑industry parks in the municipality; both a nuclear power plant and a VKG limestone‑product factory are being planned for the area.

A large part of the new Haljala–Kukruse section of the Tallinn–Narva highway, which will be publicly presented on Monday, also falls within Lüganuse's borders. In addition, various wind‑farm developers are showing active interest in the municipality, said Lüganuse Municipal Council Chairman Mart Kivistik.

"At the moment we have five detailed plans, four special plans, and one has been established — Evecon Energia's. In reality, this is an enormous burden for our small municipality. Initially more than 160 positions were launched. I think the real number will remain around one hundred, because so many locations will fall away," Kivistik said.

According to Gregor Raudvere, board member of Varja Windfarm, which wants to build wind farms in Lüganuse, the municipality's advantage is its favorable location and the low level of local opposition.

"In Lüganuse, I would say the attitude of residents is certainly one factor that speaks in its favor — this has been mentioned a lot elsewhere too. But Lüganuse also has very good wind conditions, Lüganuse has the Püssi substation, which is one of the largest node substations in Estonia, and there is a lot of free land and people who are willing to allow turbines to be erected on their land," Raudvere said.

Chairman of the Lüganuse Municipal Council Mart Kivistik. Source: Lüganuse municipality

For the municipality, the interest of various industries means that additional workforce is needed to make the proceedings run more smoothly, Kivistik noted.

"It is quite a large resource cost to answer all kinds of inquiries and matters that come with all of this. In that sense, we have created additional positions," Kivistik said.

In various proceedings, the municipal council chairman has been bothered by the fact that the experts assessing impacts tend to view the processes more from the developer's perspective than from that of the local resident.

"I would say from my own experience, since I have attended many of these meetings, that experts should explain more substantively and the presentations should be better, more prepared and impartial," Kivistik said.

Lüganuse municipality was formed by the merger of the former Lüganuse, Sonda and Maidla municipalities and the towns of Püssi and Kiviõli. The municipality has almost 8,000 residents, most of whom live in the town of Kiviõli.

World.title: Parties struggle to navigate new EU rules on political advertising
World.content:
With five months to go until the elections, parties are still unsure how they may legally run political ads this year. A new European Union rule meant to increase funding transparency has also created confusion and added bureaucracy.

Under the new requirement, an  must include who ordered it, with what money, and who paid. The idea of increasing transparency of funding in this way is considered good by the parties, but the implementation not so much.

Tõnis Kons, board member of Parempoolsed, gave the example of radio advertising. "If its length is ten seconds and it is followed by five to ten seconds of a declaration that this is paid advertising, then probably every Estonian understands that if it is a party , it is paid political advertising," he explained. The same applies to television.

"With TV ads it is somewhat unclear that if it is a TV ad featuring Reform Party people, promises, colors, then we must additionally state both in audio and visually that this is political advertising," explained Reform Party secretary‑general Kristo Enn Vaga.

It becomes complicated when the  is not so direct. With only five months left until the elections, politicians are still asking the consumer protection officials whether, for example, singer Stig Rästa must inform the audience during a concert that he is a politician, how to behave with opinion pieces, and whether a pen or flyer must also be supplemented with information.

"With one sentence it is unfortunately not possible to bring all of this out," noted Merike Koppel, deputy director‑general of the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority.

She said that if a politician distributes something in public space during the campaign period and does not use a service provider for it, then it is internal activity and does not need to be marked. "The same applies to pens, flyers, and political merchandise," added Koppel.

Although the authority does not plan to start punishing anyone, the fines are still large and the room for error small.

Viljar Voog, communications manager of Isamaa, said that in case of confusion both parties and advertising sellers choose the strictest interpretation so they would not have to pay a large fine later.

Parempoolsed, the first party to start with outdoor advertising, has already had to replace its posters once following an order from the consumer protection authority.
