World.title: How Export Growth Helped Kazakhstan Return to Current Account Surplus
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan recorded a $2.4 billion current account surplus in the first half of 2026, equivalent to 1.6% of gross domestic product (GDP), reversing a $3.6 billion deficit in the same period last year, as export growth outpaced imports, according to the National Bank.

The improvement follows a $13.1 billion current account deficit in 2025. The current account had been in deficit in nine of the 10 years from 2016 to 2025, averaging around 2.7% of GDP annually. The balance improved by nearly $6 billion year on year, with the strongest contribution coming in the second quarter, when the surplus reached $3.2 billion.

What the surplus means for Kazakhstan

The current account records a country’s transactions with the rest of the world, including trade in goods and services, investment income and current transfers. A surplus means that receipts from these transactions exceed payments abroad. For Kazakhstan, the shift into surplus reduces the economy’s reliance on external financing to cover current international payments. Stronger export receipts can also support the supply of foreign currency and create conditions for accumulating external assets.

Historically, Kazakhstan’s goods trade has generated a surplus, but payments of income to foreign investors have often offset a significant share of it. The current account last recorded a substantial surplus in 2022, reaching $6.4 billion, before returning to deficit in subsequent years.

Export growth drives external balance

A key factor behind the improvement was the expansion of Kazakhstan’s trade surplus. In the first half of 2026, the surplus in goods trade more than doubled, from $7.7 billion to $16.2 billion.

Exports of goods, measured using the National Bank’s balance-of-payments methodology, rose 27.1% to $48.5 billion. Growth was recorded across more than 80% of commodity categories.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, exports of copper and copper cathodes increased 58%, copper ores and concentrates rose 42.9%, uranium grew 15.1% and wheat increased 28.2%. Sulfur exports nearly tripled, while silver exports more than doubled.

The positive trend continued over the first seven months of the year. Goods exports increased 15.8% to $50.9 billion, while the foreign trade surplus reached $14 billion, up $5.4 billion from the same period in 2025.

Non-commodity exports also expanded amid growth in manufacturing output. They rose 19.5% to $18.6 billion, while manufacturing production increased 9% over the period.

Agricultural exports grew 34.8%, from $3.7 billion to $5 billion. Key contributors included wheat, up 25.5%, sunflower oil, up 49.1%, animal feed, up 68.2%, flax seeds, which more than doubled, and flour, up 37.1%. These products accounted for nearly 60% of agricultural exports.

Imports shift toward production and investment

Imports also increased, but at a considerably slower pace than exports. Under the National Bank’s balance-of-payments methodology, goods imports rose 6.2% to $32.3 billion in the first half of 2026.

The composition of imports changed, with higher purchases of production inputs and equipment alongside a decline in consumer goods. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, imports increased 5.5% to $31.5 billion. Intermediate goods accounted for 47.6% of the total, with imports in this category rising 14% to $15 billion.

Imports of investment goods increased 10.6% to $8.1 billion. Purchases of electricity-generating units rose 83%, machinery for lifting and handling goods increased 70.1%, and equipment for sorting and crushing soil more than doubled.

Intermediate goods imports also grew, including natural gas, up 96.3%, turbojet engines and gas turbines, up 2.7 times; petroleum products, up 41.6%, uranium, up 2.6 times, and gold, up sixfold.

The increase in equipment purchases coincided with higher investment in fixed capital, which grew 9.6% in real terms to 9.5 trillion tenge (US$21.2 billion). Investment in manufacturing rose 33.3% to 1.43 trillion tenge (US$3.2 billion), accounting for 15% of total fixed-capital investment.

Manufacturing output increased 9.8%, while machinery production grew 23.1% and chemical industry output rose 20.7%.

The figures suggest that part of the import growth is linked to the construction of new facilities, the expansion of existing production and technological upgrades. The economic returns from these investments will depend on the capacity being brought into operation and its contribution to domestic production.

Consumer imports decline

In contrast to purchases of equipment and production inputs, imports of consumer goods declined. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, consumer goods imports fell 10.5% to $8.3 billion in the first half of 2026. Imports of passenger cars decreased 21.9%, pharmaceuticals fell 18.7%, suitcases and bags dropped 49.4%, women’s textile clothing declined 38.9%, and air conditioners fell 34.3%.

The National Bank reported that imports of non-food consumer goods had been declining for 11 consecutive quarters, beginning in the fourth quarter of 2023.

The decline in passenger car imports coincided with an increase in domestic production. From January to June, Kazakhstan produced 88,886 passenger cars, up 37.2% year on year, while sales in the official dealership segment remained stable. This points to partial import substitution through domestic vehicle assembly.

World.title: Rybakina Confirms Participation in 2026 WTA Finals in Indian Wells
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has confirmed her participation in the 2026 WTA Finals, which will take place in Indian Wells, California, from Nov. 8 to 15.

In a video message published on the Women’s Tennis Association’s (WTA) official social media accounts, the world No. 1 expressed her excitement about qualifying for the season-ending tournament.

“I’m very happy to qualify for the WTA Finals. Come and watch us play in Indian Wells,” Rybakina said.

Rybakina secured her place in the tournament ahead of schedule, becoming the first player to qualify for this year’s edition. She will return to defend her title after winning the WTA Finals last season. The Kazakh player has enjoyed an outstanding season, winning the Australian Open and the US Open before reaching the top of the world rankings for the first time in her career.

Aryna Sabalenka and Mirra Andreeva have also secured places in the singles competition. The remaining five spots will be determined over the coming weeks.

Rybakina’s participation comes after concerns over a back injury forced her to withdraw from a recent tournament in Wuhan, China. She took time off to recover following a demanding North American swing.

The WTA Finals bring together the leading players of the season. This year’s tournament is scheduled to run from Nov. 8 to 15 at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

World.title: Kazakhstan Bridges Distances With Major Transport Upgrades
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan built, reconstructed and repaired more than 19,000 kilometers of roads between 2023 and 2025, while expanding railway infrastructure and domestic flight connections to improve regional connectivity and strengthen its transit capacity.

The modernization program includes major infrastructure projects and digital technologies aimed at reducing travel times, improving passenger mobility and accelerating freight transportation along international corridors, according to the Kazakh government’s press office.

Road upgrades improve regional access

Road construction, reconstruction and repairs covered 5,656 kilometers in 2023, increasing to 7,306 kilometers in 2024 before reaching 6,178 kilometers in 2025.

In 2026, work is underway on more than 11,000 kilometers of roads, including 3,400 kilometers of national highway construction and reconstruction, 5,000 kilometers of major and medium-scale repairs on national roads and 2,400 kilometers of local road repairs.

The upgrades come amid growing demand for road transport. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the number of passengers transported by road rose from 1.5 billion in 2023 to 1.7 billion in 2024 and 1.9 billion in 2025. In the first eight months of 2026, the figure reached 1.3 billion, up 3.9% from the same period in 2025.

Efforts to improve rural accessibility have also advanced. Between 2023 and 2025, work was completed on 10,200 kilometers of local roads, including 556 kilometers of newly built roads, providing year-round connections to district and regional centers.

The government expects 95% of national highways and 92% of local roads to meet technical standards by the end of 2026, up from 92% and 86%, respectively, in 2023. The targets for 2029 are 97% and 94%.

Major highway projects are expected to further reduce travel times and expand interregional and transit connections. Among them is the 896-kilometer Center-West route, which will connect Astana with western Kazakhstan through Arkalyk and Yrgyz.

Railway expansion strengthens passenger and freight transport

Kazakhstan has laid 911 kilometers of new railway tracks over the past five years, with another 800 kilometers under construction and approximately 2,600 kilometers of existing tracks undergoing modernization.

Railways carried a combined 60.2 million passengers between 2023 and 2025. Since the beginning of 2026, Passenger Transportation, a national passenger rail operator, has served 7.5 million passengers, with the highest passenger volumes recorded in Almaty, Astana, Shymkent and the Abai, Aktobe, Karagandy, Kyzylorda and Zhambyl Regions.

Passenger services have also become more accessible. Women-only carriages now operate on 13 routes and have carried 946,000 passengers since their introduction. Passengers with disabilities and their companions are eligible for a 50% fare discount on socially significant routes, while 396,000 tickets for designated accessible spaces were issued in the first seven months of 2026.

Digitalization is also accelerating international freight transportation. The Digital Trade Corridor platform integrates railway systems in Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Georgia along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, through a single-window system.

Its Tez (fast in Kazakh) Customs module enables paperless customs transit procedures, reducing clearance times from eight hours to 30 minutes. Combined with other infrastructure and operational improvements, cargo delivery times along the corridor have fallen from 38 days to 13-17 days, according to the government. The next target is to achieve consistent delivery times of 10-12 days for shipments from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Domestic aviation network expands to 890 weekly flights

Kazakhstan’s domestic aviation network has grown steadily, with airlines operating 630 weekly flights across 51 routes in 2023. This increased to 669 flights across 57 routes in 2024 and 821 flights across 60 routes in 2025. As of September 2026, approximately 890 weekly flights operated across 60 domestic routes.

The expansion has been accompanied by the restoration of regional airports. On Aug. 22, subsidized flights began operating between Arkalyk and Astana, Almaty and Kostanai following the reopening of Arkalyk Airport. Each route operates twice a week, with flights between Arkalyk and Astana taking approximately 40 minutes.

Airport modernization is continuing elsewhere in the country. The runway at Pavlodar Airport was upgraded in 2026, while construction of new airports in Zaisan, Katon-Karagai and the Kenderli resort area is scheduled for completion by the end of the year.

Further runway construction and reconstruction projects are planned through 2029 in Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Taraz, Aktobe, Oral and Zhezkazgan, alongside terminal upgrades at major airports.

To support air cargo transportation, the government has introduced a 12-year duty-free regime for cargo aircraft and simplified export procedures for selected goods, including aviation-related products, to countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Nuclear Legacy Offers Lessons in Age of AI and Geopolitical Rivalry
World.content:
ASTANA – Thirty-five years after Kazakhstan closed the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site and began giving up the nuclear arsenal it inherited from the Soviet Union, the world is moving back toward a security environment in which nuclear weapons are again seen by some as an answer rather than a danger. That was one of the central concerns raised during the Sept. 22 online discussion dedicated to what Kazakhstan’s nuclear experience can teach the world today.

Organized by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and the Council on Strategic Risks, the discussion brought together Kazakh and United States officials and experts who were directly involved in the nuclear threat reduction efforts of the 1990s. Their focus was not only on what Kazakhstan did after independence, but on whether the lessons of that period can still work in a world defined by geopolitical rivalry, weakening arms control and rapidly developing artificial intelligence.

The answer was not straightforward. The environment that allowed Kazakhstan and the U.S. to cooperate on eliminating nuclear dangers was unusually favorable. Today, major powers are again competing militarily, key arms control agreements have lapsed or been abandoned, and new technologies are making strategic calculations more complex. But Kazakhstan’s experience offers one lesson that remains relevant: security does not necessarily become stronger when a country possesses more nuclear weapons.

When a nuclear arsenal was seen as a risk, not an asset

When Kazakhstan became independent, it inherited the world’s fourth-largest nuclear arsenal. The country also inherited the consequences of the Soviet nuclear program. Between 1949 and 1989, the Soviet Union conducted 456 nuclear tests at the Semipalatinsk site, affecting approximately 1.5 million people. Kazakhstan closed the site on Aug. 29, 1991, and subsequently relinquished the nuclear weapons and delivery systems left on its territory.

For Laura Holgate, former U.S. ambassador to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the significance of that decision goes beyond disarmament. She noted that Kazakhstan’s leaders recognized that the weapons were not necessarily an asset that would protect the newly independent country. They could instead make Kazakhstan more vulnerable to confrontation with other major powers.

“To recognize that that was a source of weakness or risk of insecurity rather than a source of security,” Holgate said, was an “incredibly bold and courageous decision.”

That point is particularly relevant today because nuclear deterrence continues to shape how states think about security. Magzhan Ilyassov, Kazakhstan’s ambassador to the U.S., recalled a conversation he had as a young exchange student in the U.S. in the early 1990s. Americans he met had grown up fearing that the Soviet Union might attack them. Kazakh Soviet people had grown up with a similar fear of the U.S. Yet on both sides, nuclear weapons were understood as defensive.

“I never thought that we would drop it on you. It was our defense,” Ilyassov recalled.

That contradiction remains at the heart of the nuclear debate: if every country sees its own nuclear weapons as defensive, but another country’s arsenal as a threat, the logic of deterrence can become an argument for more proliferation.

Ilyassov warned that the more countries come to believe they need nuclear weapons for deterrence, the more difficult it becomes to maintain the credibility of the system itself.

“The whole deterrence concept sounds solid,” he said, but the more countries seek nuclear weapons, “the whole deterrence thing starts losing its credibility.”

Corey Hinderstein, vice president for studies at the Carnegie Endowment, similarly noted that nuclear weapons should not be discussed as a stand-alone security issue. In countries where public support for acquiring nuclear weapons is rising, she said, the question changes when people are asked to consider what that choice would mean for national spending, alliances, economic stability and society.

“It’s not a nuclear trade-off. It’s a societal trade-off,” Hinderstein added.

That is one of the lessons Kazakhstan’s experience puts back on the table: nuclear disarmament was not simply about removing weapons. It was about redefining what security meant.

From a Soviet nuclear legacy to a role in global security

Kazakhstan’s decision did not end with the closure of Semipalatinsk. The country worked with the U.S. under the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction program to dismantle nuclear weapons and delivery systems, eliminate nuclear infrastructure, seal test tunnels and secure dangerous materials.

One of the most significant operations was Project Sapphire in 1994, when nearly 600 kilograms of highly enriched uranium were removed from Kazakhstan: enough material for approximately 25 nuclear weapons. The operation was carried out through close cooperation between the two countries and was kept secret until the material had been safely transported.

Andrew Weber, former U.S. assistant secretary of defense for nuclear, chemical and biological defense programs, was directly involved in that effort. He described Project Sapphire as an example of what can happen when governments focus on solving a specific security problem rather than allowing political differences to prevent cooperation. The operation, he said, required technical and security cooperation over several weeks to safely package and transport the material.

For Corey Hinderstein, the broader lesson was that Kazakhstan’s leadership in the anti-nuclear field was not something imposed on the country by its Soviet past.

“The nuclear legacy was imposed on Kazakhstan from Moscow. Kazakhstan didn’t have to do what it did. It certainly did not have to give up its inherited nuclear weapons. But even once that moment and that decision came, nuclear leadership was selected, was embraced and has been sustained,” she said.

That distinction matters because Kazakhstan did not simply dismantle an inherited arsenal and move on. It continued to build its role in nuclear non-proliferation, including through the IAEA low-enriched uranium bank, its participation in international negotiations on Iran and its support for the global nuclear non-proliferation regime. The country’s experience could again become relevant in dealing with Iran’s nuclear material.

Ilyassov said Kazakhstan remains ready to provide a neutral venue and, if Washington and Tehran reach an agreement, potentially assist with the secure handling of Iran’s enriched uranium under international legal, technical and verification arrangements. Weber said such a process would need to involve international partners and UN and IAEA supervision rather than being treated as a unilateral U.S. operation. That willingness is part of what Weber described as Kazakhstan’s “tremendous moral authority” on nuclear issues.

The forgotten public movement behind the decision

The discussion also highlighted a part of Kazakhstan’s nuclear history that receives less international attention: the role of civil society. Ilyassov pointed to the Nevada-Semipalatinsk movement, which brought the consequences of nuclear testing into public debate and created pressure for political action. The movement, he said, did not itself make the political decision to close the test site. But it put the issue on the political agenda and made it impossible for politicians to ignore.

“That was a public driving force that actually didn’t make the politicians take the decision, but it put this topic onto the agenda,” Ilyassov said, adding that this grassroots dimension deserves renewed attention today.

Nuclear weapons have become strangely disconnected from everyday public debate despite their continued existence. Social media can turn relatively trivial subjects into global trends within hours, while nuclear disarmament rarely becomes a mainstream issue among younger generations or public figures.

“This is your world. This is real. These weapons exist,” Ilyassov said.

The challenge is therefore not only diplomatic. It is also political and societal: how to make nuclear risks visible enough for the public to understand the stakes before a crisis forces the issue back into the headlines.

AI makes human responsibility more important

The most difficult question for the future may be how nuclear security will work once artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded in military decision-making. AI can improve analysis of satellite imagery, identify unusual activity, support safeguards and help detect illicit networks. But the same technology can accelerate decision-making, amplify false information and make deception more convincing. In a nuclear crisis, that could reduce the time available for diplomacy and increase the consequences of a technical error.

For Kazakhstan, the lesson is not that AI should be excluded from nuclear security. It is that technology cannot replace the person who ultimately has to take responsibility for an irreversible decision. Ilyassov put the distinction bluntly: an algorithm can calculate the probability of escalation, but it cannot understand its human cost. It does not feel fear, grief or hesitation, and it cannot carry moral responsibility. That is why, he said, “meaningful human control” and clear accountability must remain central to decisions involving nuclear weapons.

The issue is becoming more urgent as the global nuclear consensus weakens. Hinderstein warned that the idea that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” is itself losing ground. Discussions of limited nuclear war, tactical nuclear use and contained exchanges can make nuclear use appear more manageable than it actually is.

At the same time, countries without nuclear weapons are increasingly reconsidering whether they should acquire them, particularly when confidence in security guarantees declines. Hinderstein said that a broader public discussion of the economic, social and political costs of nuclear weapons could change that calculation.

That concern was echoed just days later at the UN General Assembly, where Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi linked the country’s nuclear disarmament experience to the current erosion of international trust.

“Our experience of renouncing the world’s fourth largest nuclear arsenal did not weaken our state. To the contrary, through international trust, it strengthens sovereignty, enhances security and promotes development,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, the experience of the 1990s offers a different reference point. She highlighted that the country did not have to keep the nuclear weapons it inherited. It chose to give them up. It did not have to become a long-term advocate of nuclear threat reduction. It chose to take on that role. And it did not do so through one decision alone. The process involved political leadership, public pressure, international cooperation and years of practical work.

The circumstances today are very different from those of the previous millennia. The U.S., Russia and China are strategic competitors, arms control mechanisms are under pressure, and AI is adding a new layer of uncertainty to nuclear decision-making. But the question raised by Kazakhstan’s experience remains much the same: whether security is best achieved by accumulating more instruments of destruction, or by finding ways to make those instruments less necessary. For Kazakhstan, the answer was decided 35 years ago. The discussion in Washington suggested that the rest of the world may need to revisit that choice.

World.title: Jackie Chan Highlights Kazakhstan’s Film Potential After ‘Armour of God IV: Ultimatum’ Shoot
World.content:
ASTANA – Filming of the international action film “Armour of God IV: Ultimatum,” starring legendary actor Jackie Chan, has concluded in Kazakhstan, showcasing the country’s potential as a destination for major international film productions.

The project, Salem Entertainment’s first international production, was filmed in Almaty and the Almaty and Mangystau Regions, with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information and China Film Group Corporation.

Speaking at a press conference on Oct. 6, Chan said the idea was first discussed during a meeting with Kazakhstan’s Vice President Erlan Karin in China in 2017 or 2018, when Karin served as State Counselor, Kazinform reported.

“I was surprised that the team had already started working on the script and selected a director,” Chan said, noting that the project moved from an initial proposal to production much faster than he had expected.

He also praised the shoot’s organization and government support.

Kazakh actor and producer Rustem Omarov said Chan sustained a shoulder injury and later fractured a rib during filming. Despite doctors advising him to rest, Chan returned to the set within days.

Filming will continue in Shanghai, with the film scheduled for international release in 2027.

The project is expected to promote Kazakhstan’s tourism and cultural potential and help attract further international film productions to the country.

World.title: Abkhazia plans pension reform, new law to take work history into account
World.content:
The government of Abkhazia has drafted a pension reform bill aimed at streamlining pension legislation, taking employment history into account when calculating pension payments and introducing specific support measures for socially vulnerable groups.

The draft pension law was prepared by the Ministry of Social Welfare and Demographic Policy. According to Minister Kama Adzynba, the bill aims to streamline regulations governing employment-related, insurance-based and funded pensions, as well as payments for special services to the country.

One of the key principles of the proposed reform is to take individuals’ employment history into account when determining pension payments. Currently, pensions in Abkhazia stand at 6,000 roubles [approximately $70], a standard amount paid to everyone, regardless of whether they have worked for many years or have never been formally employed.

Pensioners who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship and also receive a Russian pension have their Abkhaz pension reduced to a largely symbolic 500 roubles [around $6].

The new system is intended to address this “injustice”. It also provides for survivor’s pensions and other social benefits, which are expected to exceed the basic social pension.

The bill also introduces special pensions for distinguished service to the country. Recipients of state orders and veterans of the 1992-93 Georgian-Abkhaz war are among those proposed for inclusion in this category.

The draft law will be submitted to parliament for consideration.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s foreign currency reserves

Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of Azerbaijan’s Republican Alternative (ReAl) party, has criticised the country’s accumulation of $90bn in foreign currency reserves. In a Facebook post, he argued that there was little reason to take pride in such substantial reserves when some elderly citizens were forced to survive on modest social benefits.

Mammadov proposed using part of the reserves to improve living standards while expanding economic freedoms.

“There are no reasonable grounds for a country like Azerbaijan to hold $90bn in foreign currency reserves,” the politician wrote.

What makes up Azerbaijan’s $90bn in foreign currency reserves?

Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign currency reserves comprise the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). According to figures published by the State Statistical Committee, their combined value stood at $90.77bn as of 1 September 2026. This represents the total value of funds held in various financial assets.

The two institutions’ reserves serve different purposes. The Central Bank’s reserves are used to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market and mitigate risks associated with external payments.

The State Oil Fund accumulates revenues from oil and gas production, invests them, makes transfers to the state budget and builds up savings for future generations. Its assets are invested in bonds, equities, gold and property.

The authorities regard the substantial reserves as an indicator of the country’s financial resilience. Speaking at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September, President Ilham Aliyev stressed that the reserves were approximately 20 times greater than the country’s external public debt.

According to Aliyev, this demonstrates the strength of Azerbaijan’s financial system and the stability of its national currency.

‘These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace’

Mammadov also approaches the issue from the perspective of public welfare. He argues that elderly citizens have contributed to the creation of national wealth not only through formal employment but also through domestic and agricultural work.

“Only the government of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) can proudly boast of having $90bn in foreign currency reserves in a country where 180,000 elderly citizens receive no retirement pension and are forced to make do with an old-age allowance of $130. This is simply shameful.

“People over the age of 65 have contributed to society throughout their lives through their labour and their role as consumers in the economy, helping to create the conditions for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves.

“Whether it was a housewife who spent years supporting her husband as he worked as a labourer or engineer, or a man who worked in the fields for a pittance, supplying city residents with fresh fruit and vegetables, they all contributed to building up these reserves.

“This is a hardworking generation that the YAP authorities have left with virtually no means of subsistence in old age, while continuing to boast about the country’s foreign currency reserves.”

Mammadov argues that taking pride in growing reserves while this generation faces financial hardship is also morally unacceptable.

“Viewed from this perspective, even the question of economic efficiency becomes secondary. These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace.”

Assets held abroad and dependence on oil

Mammadov also argues that holding substantial foreign currency reserves abroad carries political risks. He cites Iraq and Libya as examples, pointing to the depletion of their financial resources during wars and the freezing of their assets. He links these events to the interests of external powers and suggests that Azerbaijan could face similar risks.

“By maintaining foreign currency reserves on this scale, Azerbaijan is merely provoking major players in the current world order, who are accustomed to playing by their own rules. It is like putting on our most expensive jacket, stuffing its pockets with bundles of cash and going for a walk at night down the most crime-ridden street in the city.

“There are plenty of historical examples. In 1980, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves stood at 36bn–40bn. In today’s money, that is just over $90bn. And what happened? A war with Iran was soon orchestrated, partly for the sake of that money, though not exclusively. As a result, all the money was spent on purchasing weapons from abroad, and the reserves were exhausted. Who benefited? The arms dealers.

“In 2011, Libya’s foreign currency reserves had barely reached $150bn when the country was plunged into turmoil. Some of the money was spent on arming the sides in the civil war, while around a third of the assets were frozen in foreign financial institutions (and someone is still profiting from them). The rest has never been traced.

“In today’s world, where the law of the jungle prevails, there is no point in keeping such substantial foreign currency reserves abroad. One day, a provocation could be staged against us too, and the money could be seized,” he wrote.

Mammadov also sees a potential collapse in financial markets as a serious threat. He believes securities are significantly overvalued and that a sharp fall in their prices could result in substantial losses for Azerbaijan.

Another of his arguments concerns the economy’s dependence on oil. Recalling the currency devaluations of 2015, he notes that the country’s foreign currency reserves failed to prevent the sharp depreciation of the manat.

“The reason reserves are rapidly depleted during a crisis and cannot serve as a financial safety net lies in the unhealthy state of our economy and its dependence on oil.”

According to Mammadov, if oil prices remain low for a prolonged period, substantial foreign currency reserves alone cannot guarantee economic security.

What does Mammadov propose?

Mammadov is not calling for Azerbaijan to spend all its foreign currency reserves. He believes some funds should be retained to deal with economic crises and natural disasters, although he does not specify how much should be set aside.

“There is an urgent need to improve people’s living standards, particularly those of the elderly. At the same time, economic freedoms must be expanded without delay so that citizens can realise their creative and entrepreneurial potential and generate new wealth,” the politician wrote.

Mammadov sees the rule of law as a fundamental prerequisite for these reforms. He concluded his post by urging voters to support the Republican Alternative (ReAl) party.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

World.title: ‘Light rosè’, or why claim that Abkhazia has no good wine is outdated. VIDEO
World.content:
Wine in Abkhazia

For a long time, Abkhazia was known mainly for its basic range of wines. The region’s unpredictable climate, with annual rainfall of up to 2,000 mm, was seen as a challenge, as was the popularity of mass-produced semi-sweet wines.

However, modern winemaking practices have challenged this perception. Today, Abkhaz wine producers are shifting their focus towards premium wines.

The Association of Winemakers is actively reviving local indigenous grape varieties. It says fermentation control and modern scientific methods now make it possible to produce delicate, dry and fresh rosé wines.

World.title: European Parliament resolution on banning opposition parties in Georgia: what it says
World.content:
On 8 October, the European Parliament adopted its latest — and seventh — critical resolution on Georgia. This time, it focuses on the ruling Georgian Dream party’s attempts to ban five opposition parties and political groups.

In the resolution, the European Parliament strongly condemns the attempts to outlaw these opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them.

The draft resolution also once again calls for the release of political prisoners and sanctions against those responsible for Georgia’s democratic backsliding. It specifically names Georgian Dream founder and honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, party secretary-general Kakha Kaladze, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili.

The document says that the actions of Georgian Dream have caused the situation in Georgia to deteriorate further. Democracy and media freedom have declined, while human rights and the rule of law face growing violations. The document says this increasingly conflicts with Georgia’s international obligations and responsibilities, including the Copenhagen criteria.

The draft resolution also notes that two German foundations — the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation — had to close their offices in Tbilisi after the authorities rejected their funding applications under the grants law.

The draft resolution also again refers to the persecution of journalists in Georgia who covered the authorities’ repression of the opposition and civil society.

According to the draft resolution, the European Parliament:

Strongly condemns the attempt to outlaw Georgia’s opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them. It stresses that a functioning political opposition is an indispensable pillar of democracy and that using judicial mechanisms to eliminate legitimate political opposition is incompatible with democracy. It notes that banning the only opposition party represented in the Georgian parliament undermines the government’s previous narrative that it targeted only parties “under boycott”;

Since October 2024, the European Parliament has adopted six critical resolutions concerning the Georgian government. In these documents, MEPs have criticised Georgian Dream’s policies on democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the country’s European integration.

World.title: UN Human Rights Council adopts resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
UNHRC resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories

On 7 October, the UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution in Geneva concerning Georgia‘s occupied regions.

According to Georgia’s Foreign Ministry, the resolution, entitled “Cooperation with Georgia”, addresses the human rights situation in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The UN Human Rights Council calls for unhindered access to the occupied territories for the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as international and regional human rights mechanisms.

The resolution also condemns Russia’s actions aimed at annexing Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, and reaffirms support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

It expresses concern over discrimination and human rights violations against ethnic Georgians in the Russian-occupied regions.

The document also highlights the importance of the Geneva International Discussions, established under the ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008.

The resolution, submitted by Georgia, was adopted by consensus, as it was last year.

World.title: ‘No right to enter classroom’: Teacher beats pupil at Armenian school
World.content:
Teacher beats pupil at school in Armenia

A video showing a teacher beating a second-grade pupil at a school in the Armenian village of Vardadzor has shocked people across Armenia. A relative of the girl told journalists that she was so frightened by the incident that she had refused to return to school.

The girl’s parents appealed to the Gegharkunik regional administration, demanding that the teacher be dismissed. However, they were told that this would only be possible if complaints were filed by at least seven parents.

Social media users responding to the video called on the Interior Ministry to investigate the incident and launch criminal proceedings.

The Education Ministry said it had contacted the Interior Ministry, the Education Inspectorate and the National Centre for Educational and Psychological Support to ensure a thorough investigation.

“Relevant legal procedures will begin shortly to strip this teacher of the right to teach,” the ministry said.

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, described the violence against the schoolgirl as “unacceptable and deeply concerning”.

The Investigative Committee opened a criminal case over allegations of “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”.

By the time of publication, reports had emerged that the teacher had been detained.

What happened

A relative of the second-grade pupil told Shamshyan.com that the class teacher had first beaten the girl in the classroom. The violence continued in the corridor after the pupil left the classroom. The girl returned home with swollen eyes and marks from the blows on her neck and arms.

“There had been slaps before, but never beatings like this – with hands and a pointer,” the relative said.

The girl has not attended school since the incident. According to family members, she later encountered the teacher by chance in the street and ran home in terror.

The girl’s mother said she did not want the teacher to face criminal prosecution but insisted that she be dismissed.

Armenian media reported that the incident was discussed at the school the following day.

“The teacher admits her guilt. She submitted a written statement acknowledging what she had done and asked not to be punished. As a result, I issued her a written reprimand,” school headteacher Gevorg Nersesyan said.

He also said such incidents were unacceptable and expressed surprise that a teacher with 30 years of experience could have treated a second-grade pupil in this way.

‘Schools must be a safe environment for children’

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, stressed that schools must provide a safe environment for children.

“Any form of violence against a child or any other form of inappropriate treatment is fundamentally incompatible with respect for the child’s dignity, safety and rights,” she said.

According to Manasyan, children must be protected not only through responses to individual incidents, but also through effective measures to prevent and address potential cases of violence.

Manasyan also questioned the effectiveness of mechanisms designed to protect pupils in schools, particularly the work of pupil protection groups.

“The effectiveness of these mechanisms should be assessed primarily on the basis of how they work in practice,” she said.

Pupil protection groups were established in all schools on 1 September 2026 by order of the Minister of Education, Science, Culture and Sport. They were specifically set up to prevent violence, bullying and other high-risk situations. Following the incident at the school in Vardadzor, the pupil protection group held a meeting. However, according to the girl’s relatives, no steps were taken to help her return to school.

The Office of the Human Rights Defender said it had launched an investigation into the incident.

Not the first case of violence since start of school year

Two weeks ago, a maths teacher at a school in the village of Berdavan in Armenia’s Tavush region slapped a 13-year-old boy across the face. He also pushed the pupil, forcibly made him sit at his desk and hit him on the head with a notebook, striking the child’s eye with its edge.

According to the boy’s mother, the teacher’s wife, who is the school’s deputy headteacher, also treated him harshly. She slapped him across the face, pushed him into her office and made him stand in the corner.

Although the boy continues to attend school, his mother told journalists that he had been left psychologically distressed by the incident.

The teacher has also been charged with “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”. He has been released on an undertaking not to leave the country and suspended from his duties.

Social media reactions

“A written reprimand is not enough. A teacher like this should be barred from working in education.”

“If people like this were prosecuted, teachers would think twice before raising a hand against someone else’s child.”

“Someone who displays such aggressive and unacceptable behaviour simply has no right to call themselves a teacher. What can such a person teach children – respect, kindness or compassion for others?“

“If a similar incident had happened in Germany, for example, the teacher could have faced up to five years in prison. Moreover, if the headteacher had seen the footage – had seen a child being beaten – but failed to take appropriate action, questions would also arise about his professional responsibility.“

“If the teacher behaves so brazenly in front of a camera, it is frightening to imagine what she might have done in a classroom without cameras. She should be dismissed, made to apologise to the child and permanently banned from teaching.”

“The situation is much the same in almost every school. In some, there is physical violence; in others, psychological pressure; and in some, children are simply ignored. At parents’ request, cameras should be installed not only in school corridors but also in classrooms.”

“When such incidents become public, headteachers condemn the teacher’s actions and express utter surprise that someone with more than 30 years of teaching experience could behave this way. But before things reach that point, when we ask for cameras to be installed, those same headteachers come up with a thousand excuses to prevent it.”

“They just don’t want teachers to be embarrassed or parents to see how often a teacher talks on the phone during lessons.“

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Everything is in place for Prime Minister Kobakhidze’s resignation’
World.content:
Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili predicts that Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could resign soon. The analyst focuses on Kobakhidze’s remarks at a government meeting on 7 October, where he spoke about projects completed and currently under way during his time as prime minister.

Also on 7 October, Kobakhidze appointed Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili as deputy prime minister. Khukhashvili sees this as a possible signal of upcoming changes in the government. He believes Kvrivishvili could eventually replace Kobakhidze.

On 7 October, the government held its first meeting in a month. Irakli Kobakhidze spoke about projects completed and currently under way in various sectors during his time as prime minister. Kobakhidze spent more than half an hour reviewing the government’s record.

Gia Khukhashvili: “Everything is in place for his [Kobakhidze’s] resignation. In fact, he has been powerless for a long time. No minister in the executive branch feels accountable to him. A purely technical government has been formed.

I would not rule out the possibility that [his lengthy speech at today’s government meeting] means exactly that. I can support this with the fact that Mariam Kvrivishvili has been promoted to deputy prime minister. That also happened today, and it is another sign that the end of his premiership is near.

It is possible that during the transition period, Mariam Kvrivishvili could become acting prime minister to ensure continuity until a new prime minister takes office. However, I would not rule out the possibility that Kvrivishvili herself could become the new prime minister.”

“Anything is possible — these are games at the royal court, after all. I do not see either Kobakhidze or [former prime minister] Garibashvili as real actors in the political process. There have been periods when they were given more room to manoeuvre, but they are not real players.

Anything is possible. The main and most important decisions, the fundamental ones, are made elsewhere. Someone else decides whom to hang and whom to pardon, and we all know his first and last name [Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream — JAMnews].

And this is just some petty squabbling among small-time people.”

Gia Khukhashvili on possible resignation of Kobakhidze

World.title: Turkish company ready to expand modern irrigation technology in Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Türkiye's Sezer Tarım ve Sağım Teknolojileri company is interested in collaborating on the implementation of modern irrigation technologies, increasing agricultural productivity, and ensuring the sustainability of production in Azerbaijan, the company’s head, Kağan Hişim, said at the 3rd International Agro Business Forum, held in Baku on Friday, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

According to him, the application of modern technologies is crucial for increasing production efficiency in both livestock farming and irrigation systems.

Hişim emphasized that the global pandemic and wars have demonstrated that food security is not limited to merely building up reserves; establishing sustainable production capabilities is also essential.

"Food security doesn’t simply mean having stocks of barley and wheat in our warehouses. These reserves can be depleted during a war or a pandemic. We can ensure food security through sustainable production. To achieve this, we must possess state-of-the-art production facilities and technologies for both livestock farming and irrigation," he explained.

The company head highlighted the importance of studying the experience of leading nations to boost agricultural productivity. Citing the Netherlands as an example, he pointed out that despite its limited land area, the country achieves high yields, meets domestic demand, and exports agricultural products to global markets.

According to Hişim, countries with agricultural traditions, such as Azerbaijan and Turkey, can further develop their production capabilities in this sector by expanding the application of modern technologies.

He also briefed on the areas of activity of the company he leads. He noted that Sezer Tarım, established in 1978, specializes in livestock farming and milking systems. For the past 20 years, the company has been active in the field of drum-type irrigation machines, and in the last two years, it has begun manufacturing pivot irrigation systems.

Hişim pointed out that the company does not intend to limit its cooperation with Azerbaijan to mere equipment sales. According to him, alongside the application of modern technologies, the training of specialists, the transfer of technical knowledge, and the continuous supply of spare parts are essential for ensuring uninterrupted agricultural production.

"We don’t want to be a partner that simply sells products to Azerbaijan and leaves. We aim to contribute to the continuity of production by conducting training sessions and organizing a steady supply of spare parts here. As Sezer Tarım, we are ready to take on this mission," he said.

The head of the company also focused on the price difference that arises as agricultural products move from the producer to the final consumer. He noted that intermediaries operating between producers and consumers can cause a significant increase in the final retail price of the products.

"Sometimes a producer creates a product for 1 manat ($0.59), yet the consumer purchases it for 3 manat ($1.76). Consequently, neither the producer nor the consumer is satisfied. If Azerbaijan learns from this experience and implements a model that mitigates the price hikes caused by intermediaries, it could make more rapid progress in the agricultural sector," Hişim stressed.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s view of Caspian Sea: Shared wealth, shared responsibility
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev’s address at the First Caspian Ecological Summit, held today in the Turkmen city of Turkmenbashi, should be viewed as a renewed expression of Azerbaijan’s principled stance regarding the future of the Caspian Sea on the international stage. The head of state highlighted the accelerating shallowing of the Caspian Sea, noting that the sea's surface area has shrunk by more than 20,000 square kilometers and that approximately 30,000 hectares of land have emerged in Azerbaijan’s sector of the sea. These figures demonstrate that the issue is no longer merely a subject of theoretical discussion but is producing real, measurable consequences.

A key point in the President’s speech is that the drop in the Caspian’s water level is not presented solely as an environmental issue. As the Head of State emphasized, this process directly impacts the lives of coastal populations, the economy, transport, and port infrastructure. For Azerbaijan, the shallowing of the Caspian also concerns the preservation of strategic transport capabilities, East-West cargo transportation, and the country’s position as a regional logistics hub.

In this context, a comprehensive investigation into the causes of the problem is of particular importance. Climate change, evaporation, precipitation, and river inflows influence the Caspian Sea's water balance. However, the management of river waters and the impact of human activity on natural flows must not be overlooked. The fact that the Volga River accounts for the majority of the river water entering the Caspian makes changes within this basin particularly significant. A reduction in the Volga's flow is a key factor capable of affecting the Caspian's water balance.

For this reason, the issues surrounding reservoirs built on the Volga, hydraulic structures, and water abstraction for irrigation and other economic needs require serious scientific and political attention. The primary objective here is not to preemptively assign blame to any specific country, but to transparently examine all factors influencing the flow of water from its source to the Caspian Sea. Comparative data must be obtained regarding water resource management in the Volga basin (located within Russian territory), the impact of reservoir operations on seasonal flow patterns, and how the volume of water reaching the Caspian has changed over time.

Open discussion of this issue is entirely legitimate from the perspective of Azerbaijan's national interests. If all littoral states are experiencing the consequences of the Caspian Sea's falling water levels, then information regarding the factors affecting the water balance should be accessible to all. Decisions concerning the future of the Caspian must not be limited to general environmental statements; rather, they should be grounded in concrete scientific findings regarding river basin management, reservoir operations, and the volume of water flowing into the sea.

The concern voiced by President Ilham Aliyev at the summit holds political significance precisely in this context. Azerbaijan illustrates the scale of the problem with figures and highlights the risks its consequences pose to the economy, transport, and coastal areas. The emergence of nearly 30,000 hectares of new land in Azerbaijan’s sector of the Caspian Sea serves as a concrete indicator of the changing coastline. This shift necessitates long-term planning across various sectors, ranging from port operations to coastal ecosystems.

In particular, the future of the Baku International Sea Trade Port and cargo transportation across the Caspian Sea requires a strategic approach. The receding sea level could impact shipping routes, vessel loading capacities, port access conditions, and infrastructure costs. If the decline in the Caspian’s water level continues, Azerbaijan will need to allocate significant resources toward adapting its transport system and mitigating associated environmental and economic risks. Consequently, this issue must be placed on the agenda not only of environmental protection agencies but also of state institutions responsible for economic and strategic planning.

Another critical aspect is the preservation of the Caspian’s unique ecosystem. A drop in sea level could alter coastal wetlands and shallow-water areas, disrupt fish habitats and breeding grounds, and diminish biodiversity. This process will inevitably affect the livelihoods of populations dependent on the Caspian Sea’s natural resources. Thus, the decline in water levels represents a complex crisis with interconnected environmental, social, and economic consequences. Under these circumstances, Azerbaijan's position calls for the establishment of concrete regional mechanisms. A permanent scientific monitoring system should be set up among the Caspian littoral states, data regarding the water balance should be shared regularly, and joint research programs should be implemented. Comparative assessments must be conducted concerning the flow, water withdrawal, and operational regimes of the major rivers discharging into the Caspian, including the Volga. Based on the findings, an action plan agreed upon by the states should be developed, and clear mechanisms for the fulfillment of obligations must be established.

President Ilham Aliyev’s call to preserve the Caspian Sea as a zone of peace, stability, and constructive partnership forms the political basis of this approach. Cooperation among the Caspian littoral states should not be limited solely to transport and energy projects. Since the deterioration of the sea's ecological condition affects the long-term interests of all parties, its preservation must also become a priority area for regional cooperation.

Ultimately, the views expressed by President Ilham Aliyev at the Turkmenbashi summit demonstrate that Azerbaijan is not indifferent to the fate of the Caspian Sea and considers international cooperation essential to resolving the issue. Azerbaijan’s position is clear: the causes of the Caspian’s receding water levels must be scientifically determined, human activities impacting river flows and water resources must be transparently investigated, and the responsibilities of all littoral states must be defined through concrete measures.

For Azerbaijan, preserving the Caspian Sea isn't simply an environmental choice. This is a matter of safeguarding national economic interests, transport security, the well-being of coastal populations, and the natural resources for future generations. As the level of the Caspian Sea drops, the need for timely and coordinated measures becomes increasingly urgent. Azerbaijan must maintain an active stance in keeping this issue on the international agenda, developing scientifically grounded solutions, and strengthening the principle of regional responsibility.

World.title: Azerbaijan to host Caspian Sea level commission’s first meeting in 2027
World.content:
TURKMENBASHI, Turkmenistan, October 9. The first meeting of a commission on the Caspian Sea level drop will be held in Azerbaijan in the first half of 2027, and the commission’s regulations will be approved, Trend’s special correspondent reports.

This was reflected in the Decision of the Heads of the Caspian Littoral States on the outcomes of the Caspian Ecological Summit signed following the event held in Turkmenbashi city, at the Avaza National Tourist Zone on October 9, 2026.

During his working visit to Turkmenistan, the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, participated in the summit.

The decision notes that the Presidents of Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Turkmenistan have decided on the following measures to enhance the effectiveness of five-party cooperation in addressing issues related to the drop in the Caspian Sea level:

The establishment of a commission at the level of deputy heads of government of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan, and high-ranking representatives of Iran and Russia.

The primary objective of the commission is to ensure the identification of the causes behind the drop in the Caspian Sea level, as well as the development and implementation of coordinated, comprehensive measures to combat the negative processes resulting from the sea's shallowing.

The creation of necessary specialized working groups, comprising representatives, experts, and specialists from the state agencies of the Caspian littoral states, to support the commission's activities.

The designation by the governments, within three months, of authorized representatives to represent their states in the aforementioned Commission.

The holding of subsequent meetings on a rotating basis within the territories of the Caspian littoral states, in accordance with the alphabetical order of the English language.

The initiative to establish a commission or working/expert groups regarding this matter was put forward by the President of Azerbaijan. At the 6th Summit of the Heads of State of the Caspian Littoral States held in Ashgabat on June 29, 2022, President Ilham Aliyev, placing special emphasis on the problem of the rapid drop in the Caspian Sea level and the resulting shallowing, proposed the creation of joint expert groups comprising specialists from the Caspian littoral countries to investigate the causes of this environmental disaster and to prevent its consequences.
