World.title: Kazakhstan’s KPI expands cooperation with local polypropylene processors
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Kazakhstan Petrochemical Industries Inc. (KPI) has signed agreements with local companies FIBC and Taraz Plastic to expand the use of domestically produced polypropylene in finished goods manufacturing.

This was reported by Kazakhstan's national oil and gas company KazMunayGas today.

The agreements were signed under the Investment Acceleration program, which aims to support domestic enterprises, expand production capacity and increase the use of Kazakh polypropylene in manufacturing.

FIBC already uses KPI's polypropylene to produce bags. Under the program, the company has expanded its bag production capacity and installed equipment for manufacturing multifilament yarn, a product that was not previously produced in Kazakhstan, the report says.

According to the publication, the new agreement will enable FIBC to further develop its cooperation with KPI and increase its monthly polypropylene consumption.

“Cooperation with KPI allows us to ensure a stable supply of domestic raw materials for our production and plan further increases in output. Developing the production of polymer packaging and multifilament yarn will enable us to expand our product range and strengthen the company's production capabilities,” said Kairat Taibukenov, Commercial Director of FIBC.

Taraz Plastic is also an existing processor of KPI's polypropylene, using the raw material to manufacture baling twine for hay. Under the program, the company is developing its production capacity and plans to further expand output, as well as increase its purchases of KPI's polypropylene.

The Investment Acceleration program is one of the instruments used to support domestic polypropylene processors. Under the initiative, KPI helps companies implement projects involving equipment purchases and production capacity expansion.

World.title: Uzbekistan, EU discuss stronger ties in high-level talks
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Uzbekistan and the European Union discussed prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation and preparations for upcoming high-level meetings during talks in Tashkent on Oct. 8.

This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, following a meeting between Uzbek Deputy Foreign Minister Muzaffar Madrakhimov and Eduards Stiprais, the European Union’s special representative for Central Asia, to review the current state of relations and identify opportunities for further cooperation.

The discussions focused on organizing upcoming joint events at the highest and senior levels, including their agendas and substantive priorities.

The sides also emphasized the importance of expanding practical cooperation in areas of mutual interest and making more effective use of existing bilateral engagement mechanisms.

Following the meeting, the parties agreed to maintain regular dialogue to further strengthen relations between Uzbekistan and the EU.

The European Union and Uzbekistan have maintained diplomatic and economic relations since Uzbekistan gained independence in 1991. On Oct. 24, 2025, the two sides signed an Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (EPCA) to broaden cooperation and modernize the framework governing their relations, including trade and economic ties. The agreement has been provisionally applied since March 1, 2026, providing a broader basis for cooperation in areas including investment, governance and sustainable development.

World.title: Tokayev proposes CIS artificial intelligence forum in Astana for 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed establishing a mechanism for sharing experience and best practices in artificial intelligence and holding a CIS AI forum in Astana in the first quarter of 2027.

This was reflected in a press release published by the press office of the Kazakh president. He made the proposals today during a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State in Turkmenistan.

Tokayev emphasized the growing role of digitalization and artificial intelligence, noting that the ability to adopt new technologies and develop domestic solutions is becoming a key factor in the competitiveness of CIS economies.

The proposed exchange mechanism would cover AI strategies, legislation and government support measures, bringing together research centers, universities, companies and startups. The planned forum in Astana would provide an additional platform for specialists to discuss cooperation in the field, the press release says.

Tokayev also highlighted the importance of cultural and humanitarian ties among CIS countries, citing interpersonal connections, mutual trust, shared cultural characteristics and the Russian language as important elements of the Commonwealth's identity.

“It is also important to note the tremendous significance of the Russian language in relations between our countries. This language fosters mutual understanding and expands educational, scientific, and interpersonal contacts. This is an indisputable fact. Therefore, I ask my esteemed colleagues to support the activities of the International Organization for the Russian Language. This organization has a promising future. I am confident of this, given that approximately 300 million people worldwide speak this language to varying degrees,” Tokayev said.

At the same time, he stressed the importance of respecting the linguistic and cultural diversity of CIS member states and finding more effective ways to strengthen humanitarian cooperation.

He noted that, at Kazakhstan's initiative, the CIS heads of state had adopted a statement on cultural cooperation and established the CIS Volunteer Forum, which was held for the first time in Astana in August 2026.

Tokayev further called for promoting reading among young people, arguing that literature plays an important role in education, critical thinking and personal development.

“In Kazakhstan, a National Book Day has been established, and the ‘100 Readable Books’ project is being implemented. I propose developing this idea further and creating a ‘Golden Library Collection of the CIS,’ including outstanding literary works of our peoples,” Tokayev said.

He proposed that the collection be housed in the Presidential Library, whose construction in Astana is scheduled for completion in mid-2027. The project could include professional translations and an accessible digital library, he added.

According to Tokayev, promoting the best literary works and encouraging the mutual study of the history, culture and spiritual heritage of CIS peoples could help younger generations better understand one another and maintain closer ties amid global instability.

World.title: Fiona O'Byrne wins 2026 Lester Prize with painting of daughter
World.content:
Melbourne-based artist Fiona O'Byrne has won the $50,000 Richard Lester Prize for Portraiture for an oil-on-linen painting of her daughter.

O'Byrne has been painting her children for more than a decade and her winning work — titled Luci, now — depicts her 20-year-old daughter sitting on a stool with a neutral expression on her face.

"Sitting together, you really see time move, and you see how the relationship changes," O'Byrne wrote about the piece.

The Lester Prize is held at WA Museum Boola Bardip. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

"It's an opportunity for me to stop and spend time observing her in this moment of her life.

" Painting her was just a way of holding onto that fierce, generous heart. "

Judges Alan Dodge, John McDonald and Bryony Nainby said they were captivated by the softness and tenderness of the portrait conveyed through an "unlaboured handling of paint".

They highlighted the intimacy between the sitter and artist reflected through the apparent ease in the subject's expression, the way light was captured in the work, and the details of the jacket and nail varnish.

O'Byrne picked up a paintbrush for the first time at 36 and has spent the past 10 years dividing her time between painting and landscape architecture.

Emerging artists in the spotlight

Perth-based artist Yasamin Khadembashi won the $10,000 Ashurst Emerging Artist Prize for her two-metre long re-imagined self portrait Immoral Warrior.

Yasamin Khadembashi's Immoral Warrior is inspired by Iranian folklore. (Supplied: Lester Prize)

The judges commended Khadembashi's bold and adventurous use of materials, including rhinestones, synthetic eyelash extensions and metal leaf.

"The artist did not play it safe, but their bravery paid off," the judges said.

Sky Parra's Portrait of Scott Austic, Sharon Billinge's painting titled Celeste 3, Kim Harding's Kim with Black Cockatoo and Dapeng Liu's Guido were also awarded prizes.

Loading

The Lester Prize is one of Australia's most lucrative portraiture prizes, with a total prize pool of $140,000.

It received more than 1,100 submissions this year, the most in the prize's history.

Founding partner of The Lester Prize, Russell Lester, said this reflected the impact the prize had on the arts community.

"Our ongoing stewardship of Australian talent and creativity is of utmost importance," Mr Lester said.

The exhibition of the 40 finalist pieces is on display at Perth's WA Museum Boola Bardip until November 29.

World.title: Two stolen Renoir paintings found, six people arrested
World.content:
Two Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in southern France last month have been found, and six people arrested, local authorities said on Friday.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the town that hosts the Renoir Museum, Bryan Masson, issued a statement praising investigators who tracked down the paintings and suspects.

"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history, our heritage," Mr Masson said.

" Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief. "

Mayor Bryan Masson addressed the press outside Musée Renoir after the heist. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The statement did not elaborate on how the paintings were tracked down.

The two missing paintings were Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well.

Police officers patrolled the front entrance of the Musée Renoir after the early-morning heist. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The thieves sliced through a fence, climbed through a window and initially stole four valuable Renoir paintings in the heist last month, but abandoned two of the artworks as they fled, authorities said.

How thieves stole paintings worth millions in Renoir heist Thieves sliced through a fence, grabbed 9 million euros worth of art, dumped half of them in a garden and escaped in under three minutes.

The whole operation took less than 3 minutes and targeted the most valuable works in the Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the regional prosecutor’s office said.

Investigators launched a national search for the perpetrators.

The theft conjured up painful memories of the spectacular heist of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and revived calls for better security and better funding for the many cultural sites large and small that dot France’s landscape.

AP

World.title: Litchfield fireworks help Australia to ODI victory over Bangladesh
World.content:
A Phoebe Litchfield masterclass has ensured Australia remains undefeated in 22 ODIs at Allan Border Field after seamer Megan Schutt joined an elite club of bowling greats.

Opener Litchfield's 77 off 57 deliveries ensured Australia polished off the meagre 166 all out set by Bangladesh in just 25.4 overs for the loss of three wickets.

Litchfield combined ramps, glides, clips, exquisite drives, lofted pitching wedges, reverse hockey thumps and thunderous wallops in another knock that confirmed she is unique in world cricket and an absolute joy to watch.

The left-hander was unstoppable in racing to her 12th ODI half-century.

All-rounder Annabel Sutherland, player of the match, finished the chase with 26 not out after earlier taking four wickets.

Australia pace bowler Schutt earlier snared her 150th ODI wicket in a probing opening spell to put the hosts on top.

Stand-in captain Tahlia McGrath invited the visitors to have first use of the surface and Schutt struck with the first ball of the innings, a vicious lifter that had opener Fargana Hoque edging to slip.

A Schutt inswinger trapped Sarmin Sultana (four) in front and from that moment the bowlers kept a vice-like grip on the run rate and picked up steady wickets to dismiss Bangladesh with the fourth ball of the final over.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The wicket of Sultana was the milestone 150th for Schutt. Only legendary speed demon Cathryn Fitzpatrick (180) and current all-rounder Ellyse Perry (166) have more wickets for Australia in the format.

Schutt finished with 2-19 from her 10 overs with medium pacer Sutherland (4-30) proving a handful when she hit the pitch hard.

Spinners Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham and Alana King bowled with class.

The visitors had several cameos but nothing substantial. No.3 Sharmin Akhter made a classy and breezy 24, captain Nigar Sultana (29 off 86 balls) was brave but stodgy.

Veteran all-rounder Ritu Moni (45 off 63) showcased her experience and nous and was the best of a mediocre bunch.

Schutt has relished playing at AB Field throughout her career, where she now has 20 wickets.

The quick was initially left out of the ODI side in February against India before a quad injury to Kim Garth opened the door for a recall.

Schutt took 5-19 at AB Field on that occasion to provide a timely reminder of her talents.

McGrath, usually a vice-captain, has been elevated to lead due to injury to regular skipper Sophie Molineux and rotated her bowlers with panache.

The opener of three ODIs at the same venue, Friday's clash is the first match of the summer on home soil for Australia's victorious T20 World Cup side since lifting the trophy in July.

AAP

World.title: Couple jailed for torturing 14-week-old puppy to death
World.content:
A West Australian couple who fatally tortured a puppy have been jailed.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of animal abuse, which some readers may find distressing.

Nathan James Dekkers and Isabel Maree Busher, both 26, admitted to torturing the bull terrier, Douglas, in Busselton in late 2024.

Facing the Bunbury Magistrates Court on Friday for sentencing, Dekkers was handed an 11-month jail term, and Busher was jailed for eight months.

The pair have also been permanently banned from owning another animal.

Both Dekkers and Busher had previously pleaded guilty to more than a dozen animal cruelty charges, including beating and tormenting the puppy and lying to RSPCA investigators.

They were due to be sentenced in May, but that was adjourned for Busher to undergo more psychiatric assessment.

Neighbours reported cruelty

The court heard the pair purchased the eight-week-old bull terrier puppy from a breeder in November 2024.

A neighbour overheard the couple abusing the dog on multiple occasions between December 8 and 23 and recorded audio of the incidents, which they later handed over to authorities.

While the tapes were not played in court, they were said to have captured the puppy's terrified whimpers and yelps as he was beaten and taunted.

Busher and Dekkers tortured and killed 14-week-old puppy Douglas in 2024. (Supplied: RSPCA)

On one occasion, an audio recording captured Douglas being strangled, while Busher taunted the puppy by growling and yelling at him.

On December 23, the couple was observed by neighbours driving off in a vehicle, returning about an hour later, with Douglas never seen again.

RSPCA inspectors and police attended the property that day, where they observed a yard that was small and fully paved, with a build-up of dog faeces and dried blood on the pavement.

The court heard the pair at first told authorities they had taken the puppy to a family member's farm; however, the relative later denied the claim.

'Sadistic and cruel'

Busher's defence lawyer Michelle Huber submitted there was no planning that had gone into Douglas' harm, but acknowledged the poor behaviour.

RSPCA prosecutor Ruby Harris described the offending as callous and wicked.

"The conduct was unwarranted, sadistic and cruel," she said.

The pair were sentenced at the Bunbury Magistrates Court. (ABC South West: Gian De Poloni)

In his decision, Magistrate Stephen Butcher said that while Dekkers was the one to strangle and slap the dog on at least one occasion, both were equally culpable in their offending.

He said he took into account intense community backlash toward the pair, including harassment they faced while attending court.

He also acknowledged a psychiatric assessment of Busher; however, he said it did not explain her offending.

"Her psychological profile explains some of the circumstances that have arisen here, but it doesn't excuse it," he said.

Authorities welcome decision

Outside court, RSPCA inspector Genna Haines welcomed the decision.

Genna Haines spoke outside court in Bunbury. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Ms Haines said it was one of the worst cases of animal cruelty she had seen in her career.

"We're pleased with the sentencing; the court has recognised the level of cruelty here," she said.

"The pain and terror Douglas was experiencing throughout the seven recorded beatings is evident."

Busher and Dekkers will be eligible for parole after serving half their sentences.

World.title: Anthony De Ceglie steps down as Perth Bears CEO
World.content:
Anthony De Ceglie, the inaugural chief executive of the Perth Bears, has decided to step down, the rugby league club announced today.

Mr De Ceglie, a former Seven West media executive, was appointed in May 2025 to help put the club together ahead of its entry into the NRL next year as the 18th team in the competition and the first from Western Australia since 1997.

"I'm extremely proud of what the hard-working Perth Bears team has achieved in the past year," Mr De Ceglie said in a statement.

"I have no doubt that the Perth Bears will continue to grow and grow, and become a behemoth of the national sporting stage."

Anthony De Ceglie held several senior roles at Seven West Media before joining the Bears. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

The Perth Bears have not said why Mr De Ceglie is leaving.

It had been reported that the board was seeking to have him replaced.

Mr De Ceglie's decision to leave the club comes after the departure of former head of football David Sharpe, who quit in April.

Club chair Ben Morton thanked Mr De Ceglie.

What awaits the NRL in Perth? This weekend marks the final NRL game in Perth before the city has its own team in the big league and as the beginning of forever looms, rugby league in the west is ready for its close-up.

"I thank Anthony for his leadership of the Perth Bears in our startup phase and we will now turn our attention to the leadership of our organisation as we enter the next phase of our story," he said.

Perth Bears general manager of football Gareth Holmes will act as chief executive until a permanent appointment is made.

Mr De Ceglie was previously the director of news and current affairs at Seven West Media, a role he held after overseeing Western Australia's flagship newspaper.

Channel 7 holds the rights to the AFL, while rival Channel 9 has the rights to the NRL.

World.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Judge Navi Pillay
World.content:
The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay for significantly enlarging the scope and impact of international law.

The South African-born former UN human rights chief was recognised for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

Ms Pillay, 85, served as a judge at the International Criminal Court, the High Court of South Africa and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

She was the first non-white woman to serve on South Africa's High Court.

She was also chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that last year found that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous".

Navi Pillay visits the Nazi death camp at Auschwitz, Poland, during her tenure as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. (Reuters: Mateusz Skwarczes via Agencja Gazeta)

Her work "is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world," Mr Watne Frydnes said, announcing her win.

Loading...

When the committee announced the recipient, it had not yet been able to reach Ms Pillay to inform her she had received the peace prize.

But Ms Pillay has since joked that she might "share the prize" with US President Donald Trump if people kept applauding her.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," Pillay said in a video posted by the Secretary General of Amnesty International, which showed Ms Pillay being applauded in Nuremberg.

"Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this."

Navi Pillay on a visit to Sri Lanka when she was UN Human Rights Commissioner in 2013. (Reuters: Dinuka Liyanawatte)

The award is often considered the most prestigious honour on the planet.

"At a time when the number of wars and conflicts is rising, and when judges and institutions of international law are under political attack, the Nobel Committee wishes to issue a reminder that the ability to resolve conflicts without force or violence is dependent on the international rule of law," the committee wrote in a news release.

" An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account, and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world. "

The Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo received nominations for 287 candidates for this year's prize.

Experts say the committee typically focuses on the durability of peace, the promotion of international fraternity and the quiet work of institutions that strengthen those goals.

UN human rights chief Volker Turk described Ms Pillay's award as "a collective win for human rights and for all those seeking justice and accountability".

"It's clear that we need international criminal accountability mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court, and it's clear that we have a very strong signal that this is absolutely critical in today's world," he said.

Navi Pillay was a former UN Human Rights Commissioner. (Reuters: Ruben Sprich)

"At a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law, this recognition carries particular significance," said ICC President Tomoko Akane in a statement congratulating Ms Pillay.

The Hague-based ICC has been the target of an escalating campaign by US President Donald Trump, who last month urged countries to leave it.

Acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo Haakon Gjerloew said the committee was not directly criticising Mr Trump by rewarding Ms Pillay, a former judge on it.

"I think it's generally rather a promotion of an international legal world order. Of course, he might react to someone who has been part of the ICC, but it's not a direct attack on Trump," he said.

The Nobel Peace Prize, often considered the most prestigious award, was announced in Oslo, Norway. (AP: Angela Weiss/Pool Photo File)

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness".

Ms Machado gave Mr Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-president Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: the Nobel Committee has said the honour itself cannot be transferred.

Nobel prizes awarded this week

Four of this year's Nobel prizes were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

The physics award recognised a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare type of neutrino.

The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling the mystery of mirror-image molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.718 million).

AP

World.title: Person of interest given alibi in schoolgirl's disappearance
World.content:
A person of interest in the disappearance of schoolgirl Marilyn Wallman was seen working more than 100 kilometres away at a Queensland coalmine on the day she went missing, a court has heard.

The 14-year-old's bicycle was discovered by her brothers on March 21, 1972, after she left to catch a school bus in Mackay, north Queensland, at 7:42am.

A fragment of her skull was found two years later at McGregor Creek, about 40km from where she was last seen.

At the time, Marilyn's brother, Rex Wallman, recalled hearing a young girl's voice behind a cane field near the bike and then a man speaking.

During a coronial inquest this week in Mackay, the girl's relative Noel Morris — who has not yet appeared before the inquiry — was named as a person of interest in the investigation.

On Friday, Noel's uncle, Barry Morris, told the inquest that his nephew had been at work on that day 54 years ago.

Noel Morris was the husband of Marilyn Wallman's cousin, Ann Morris. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Barry told the court via video link that he remembered seeing Noel "hauling coal from the coal face" at Goonyella mine where they worked about 145km south-west of Mackay.

The 81-year-old said he also saw his nephew playing cards in a break room, though he did not speak to him.

"[There] was sort of no need for me to have any recollection on it, except that Noel told my wife, which she told me when I got home, that Marilyn had been missing," he said.

Barry Morris said he could not remember where Noel was on the days before and after March 21 and did not know anyone else alive who could have seen his nephew at work that day.

Friction in the family

The court heard Noel had been "like a brother" to Barry, but in the years following Marilyn's disappearance there had been friction in the wider family group.

Barry said he recalled his brother, Lionel Morris, telling family members at a gathering, "Noel done it", referring to Marilyn's disappearance.

Questioned by counsel assisting the coroner, John Aberdeen, why he did not defend his nephew, Barry said: "I knew it was crap."

Witness Jenny Goode told the court she had known Lionel Morris, her uncle, to be a heavy drinker who "always exaggerated things".

Ms Goode said family often visited her house at Bucasia, including Noel and his wife, Ann Morris.

Leslie Goode and Jenny Good leaving Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The court heard Ms Morris had been staying at the home before and after she gave birth to her daughter, Jodie, on March 16, 1972 — five days before Marilyn Wallman went missing.

Ms Goode said she could not recall if Noel had visited them in Mackay that week.

"I know Ann definitely stayed with me, and I would assume that Noel would have come down from time to time," she said.

"He was still working out at Moranbah."

Family denies overnight party

Mr Aberdeen read evidence on Friday from Noel's wife, Ann.

In the statement, Ann said she had been told by Noel's uncle, Robert Morris, known as "Squizzy", that he and his nephew had been drinking together at the Bucasia home the night before Marilyn disappeared.

"Squizzy also says that they drank on till the early hours of the morning," Mr Aberdeen said.

Ms Goode and her husband, Leslie, said that no party had taken place that night.

Mr Goode told the court they had "never" had a party there at that time of the morning, on a working day.

The inquest, which is to determine the cause of Marilyn Wallman's death and whether any person was involved, will continue on Monday.

World.title: More than 65,000 Canberrans are waiting to see a medical specialist
World.content:
Canberra grandmother Billie Spencer says her five-year-old granddaughter will have to wait more than three years for a publicly funded specialist appointment, joining thousands on an invisible waitlist ahead of another inevitable waitlist.

Ms Spencer said her granddaughter suffers from excessive fatigue and struggles to keep her eyes open at school and concentrate.

"She needs to be assessed by a specialist, and we've had to wait months," she said.

Billie Spencer says she is frustrated that the health system forces patients to choose between long waits for public care and costly but timely private care. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The family concluded they had no other choice but to choice private healthcare.

"I believe in quality healthcare access for everybody regardless of your financial status, and I feel it's so disgusting that this is where we're at," she said.

"[I can't] believe that children are having to wait, or parents, grandparents are having to pay huge amounts of money to have their health needs met.

" I just feel really frustrated and really sad that our public health system is in this situation. It's not ok. "

Canberrans 'gobsmacked' by waitlists

Michael Hickey says he did not expect the wait time for a public specialist appointment to be so long. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Michael Hickey knows this story all too well.

He has already waited more than four years to see a specialist and was "gobsmacked" when he was told he would have to wait another two and a half years.

Mr Hickey has been living with a genetic hand condition which gradually leads to a loss of function if not treated.

He joined the public specialist waitlist expecting a fairly smooth process, but the reality did not align with his expectations.

Michael Hickey says a known public waiting list would ensure patients could make more informed decisions about whether to seek private care. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"There's nothing but an acknowledgement to say, 'Thank you, we've received your note, your call is important to us, we'll get back to you,' and then crickets," he said.

Mr Hickey said he did not think the wait time would be so long.

"Why aren't the figures made known up front? Why isn't there a known waiting list so I can decide to go private if I wished to," he asked.

" I know it's expensive but I could've saved my pennies, paid cash, and had the operation and been done and dusted. "

Mr Hickey said his injury was not debilitating, but was frustrated that it made hobbies and everyday activities "just that little more difficult".

Michael Hickey says that without treatment for his genetic hand condition, engaging in his hobbies is made more difficult. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

'Big number' of people waiting for outpatient appointments

Mr Hickey and Ms Spencer's granddaughter are among about 65,000 people who are waiting for outpatient appointments across public hospitals in the ACT.

The figure, which Canberra Health Services (CHS) has disclosed publicly for the first time, means more than 10 per cent of Canberrans are currently waiting.

That is despite nearly 18,000 elective surgeries completed in Canberra last financial year, according to government data.

This week, CHS launched a review of specialist and outpatient services. The review follows an independent inquiry into the territory's health system, which proposed 49 recommendations.

CHS said its review will examine outpatient services and referral pathways to better understand demand.

Alison Derrett acknowledged that the current waitlist to see a specialist through the public system was "not acceptable". (ABC News: Mark Moore)

CHS chief operating officer Alison Derritt said demand for outpatient services had been growing with a "big number" of people waiting for appointments.

"We do know that this is a problem," she said.

"It is not an acceptable position for us to have people on a wait list for an extended period of time, and our clinicians take this very seriously, and I take this very seriously.

"It's going to be one of those things that is a constant challenge for us … this is not something that will be done in a couple of weeks.

"This will be something that will take us weeks, months, and possibly up to 12 months."

The health body said patients would be contacted in the next couple of months to assess their conditions and confirm whether they still required an appointment.

For people like Mr Hickey and Ms Spencer's granddaughter, the wait for an appointment could hardly feel longer.

World.title: Australia vs South Africa cricket LIVE: Renshaw, Cummins take Australia to tea after batting collapse
World.content:
Matt Renshaw and Pat Cummins have got Australia to the tea break without losing any more wickes but the team’s chances of a big score took some critical blows in the second session.

Losing Steve Smith in the first over after lunch was heartbreaking and then losing Alex Carey and Beau Webster within the on Nortje over was a painful strike.

But Renshaw is hanging in there and he’s taking up much of a strike.

Nortje, Jansen and Mulder all have two wickets each.

World.title: Perth Bears chief executive Anthony De Ceglie quits
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 Perth Bears chief executive Anthony De Ceglie quits Joel Gould October 9, 2026 — 9:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The rise and fall of Anthony De Ceglie as a rugby league administrator is complete after the former TV and newspaper executive stepped down from his fraught tenure as Perth Bears chief executive. Perth announced the departure of De Ceglie - former director of news and current affairs at Seven West Media after being editor-in-chief of the West Australian newspaper - in a press release on Friday evening. Gone: Perth Bears chief executive Anthony De Ceglie. Trevor Collens Several well-connected sources in recent months said that De Ceglie did not have the support of the board and that his tenure was not sustainable long-term, ahead of the Bears’ entry to the competition in 2027. The Australian Rugby League Commission owns the Bears franchise and the body’s chairman Peter V’landys appointed De Ceglie.



Related Article NRL 2026 The Perth Bears have been written off. Mal Meninga says they can become an NRL superpower V’landys was reported by News Corp to have given De Ceglie a virtual stay of execution in recent days, and time to solidify his position. Bears coach Mal Meninga, who has worked as a commentator for Fox Sports, was bemused by the reports. “It’s been an ongoing battle, it’s him and I around who’s going to get sacked next,” Meninga told Fox Sports. “I know I’ve got great support and Anthony has got great support, internally, so we just get on with our business.



“We can only control what we control and that’s the internal things. We don’t want to fight any external battles.” De Ceglie has ensured there will be no external or internal battles with his resignation as inaugural CEO, just weeks before the squad starts to prepare for the 2027 season. “I’m extremely proud of what the hard-working Perth Bears team has achieved in the past year,” De Ceglie said in the club statement. “I have no doubt that the Perth Bears will continue to grow and grow, and become a behemoth of the national sporting stage.



“The club is in exceptional hands under the leadership of head coach Mal Meninga and assistant coach Ben Gardiner. Getting to work alongside both of them for the past year has been one of the greatest highlights of my professional life.” Perth’s general manager of football Gareth Holmes will act as interim CEO, with the club to make public its future plans in coming days. Happier times: Mal Meninga and Anthony De Ceglie on the Bear Walk in Perth in August. Cass Edwards The appointment of a chief executive from a media background - before the club even had a board in place - was notable, given the NRL conceded it could face a battle for exposure in AFL-mad Perth. De Ceglie had most recently been director of news and current affairs at Seven West Media, having been promoted after overseeing Western Australia’s flagship newspaper.



It is understood that V’landys and the then-NRL chief Andrew Abdo met with Seven West Media chairman Kerry Stokes on the eve of the announcement that the competition would be expanded to include the Bears. Related Article Updated

World.title: Asking the right questions is an underrated skill
World.content:
NationalVictoriaNote From The Editor Asking the right questions is an underrated skill Patrick Elligett October 9, 2026 — 7:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The right question can leave a person pondering for days. The right question, at the right time, can change a life. It can spark a thought that leads to the formation of a strategy, a business or a movement. The ABC obviously recognises that power, given it has framed its latest promotional campaign around questions. Journalism is, in part, about harnessing the power of questions asked of the right people, in the right way, at the right time. It is often the simplest, most direct questions that have the greatest impact. When my colleague Bevan Shields, then the Europe correspondent for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, asked French President Emmanuel Macron “Do you think he lied to you?” he wouldn’t have expected an equally direct answer, but he got one. “I don’t think, I know.” Loading



Those five words of diplomatic dynamite, said about then-prime minister Scott Morrison after Australia cancelled a submarine-building contract with France in 2021, has been pinpointed by some as the moment Morrison’s leadership “started unravelling”. Journalists don’t have a monopoly on questions. We just have the established networks and access to ask them of the right people. Some of the best questions we ask come from our subscribers and contacts. Comments on stories, letters to the editor, and direct feedback to journalists and editors are rich with excellent questions we should be asking. At the risk of sounding obsequious, the intelligence and passion of our subscribers was one of the motivating factors for putting on our public forum, the Melbourne Assembly, which you have been hearing about in recent weeks thanks to my newsroom colleagues. Click here to explore the trove of stories on the topic. The Melbourne Assembly, presented by The Age in partnership with the University of Melbourne, is now little more than one week away and I’m thrilled with how it has come together. We have some seriously impressive people lining up to share their thoughts on what Melbourne needs to do to continue thriving as it hurtles towards becoming a city the size of present-day London by the middle of this century.



We have assembled a depth of expertise that has the potential to live up to the event’s tagline by generating crucial conversations for the future of our city. We’ve made sure that participants at the assembly have the same opportunity as our journalists to ask the right questions and spark a conversation that could help shape Melbourne’s future. All participants will have access to an app that will allow them to suggest questions to our moderators in real time, so they can be put to our speakers and panellists. We are aiming for genuine civic engagement. That means real dialogue with some of the world’s leading thinkers such as two-term New York mayor Bill de Blasio and 15-minute city pioneer Carlos Moreno. Then there are Victoria’s decision-makers. The people with the power to shape our state and its institutions. Premier Ben Carroll, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Lord Mayor Nick Reece will all be speaking – and listening – at the Assembly. They are complemented by a line-up of local speakers with serious clout. Among them is Carolyn Evans, the newly minted vice chancellor of the University of Melbourne, who will be speaking in one of her first public appearances since taking on the role.



Melbourne University’s new vice chancellor Carolyn Evans will be speaking in one of her first public appearances since taking on the role. Dominic Lorrimer Across four key pillars of the event, we have assembled a depth of expertise that has the potential to live up to the event’s tagline by generating “crucial conversations for the future of our city”. Our Shaping the City panel, hosted by The Age’s city editor Cara Waters, features a former premier who reshaped our state and one of the sharpest public policy minds in the country. On the Education and Innovation panel, hosted by acting business editor Supratim Adhikari, we will discuss some of the biggest challenges of our generation with leading thinkers on education and the people aiming to realise the untapped potential of our city’s collective intelligence. Healthy Places and People, hosted by Channel Nine news anchor Alicia Loxley, will pose tough questions about the place we live and whether the environment is set up for Melburnians to thrive. Those questions will be answered by the people building our cities and making sure they run the way they should.



Related Article Opinion

City life Melbourne has a rare gift, but barely anyone is aware of it Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic We will finish with a discussion about Sport and the Arts, hosted by Waleed Aly, which should be as entertaining as one would expect of any discussion about Melbourne’s cultural capital. That discussion will hear from the people leading our city’s most important cultural precincts and institutions. To read more about the program and our speakers, or to buy a ticket if you haven’t yet done so, head to the Melbourne Assembly website. Speaking of the power of questions, I want to leave you with the question that got me thinking this week. One of our panellists asked me: “What does success look like for the Melbourne Assembly?” Like Shields’ Macron question, it was simple and direct. And it left me thinking about the answer for days. Ultimately, I arrived at this one: “It will be successful if, in five or 10 years, we can look back and say it was the moment when a conversation started that ultimately resulted in some public good.”



All we need to do now is ask the right questions. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of the best homes in Sydney from a bygone era Shona Hendley October 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Whether it’s art deco, Federation, Victorian, or Tudor, homes from a bygone era are often conveniently located in or near the inner city and offer both lifestyle and investment appeal. With ornate craftsmanship, large proportions, quality materials, and often steeped in history, these residences have character and personality and there is much to appreciate in them. Here are five of the best period properties on the market in Sydney. 77-79 George Street, Avalon Beach NSW “Leontine”, a late-1930s Spanish Colonial residence, sits on approximately 1636 square metres of expansive lawns and established gardens.



The double-storey home blends restored original period character, including white-rendered walls, high ceilings, original hardwood floors and a sandstone fireplace. Modern updates cater to contemporary living and include a marble-finished kitchen, a dedicated children’s wing and an entire upper level, perfect for a private parents’ retreat. Outside, you will find a 14.5 metre tiled pool and a fully self-contained cabana. 2 School Street, Balmain East NSW



Balmain East’s “Kaikoura” offers spectacular views of Sydney Harbour, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the CBD, from each of its three levels. Built circa 1840, the colonial sandstone home is integral to the peninsula’s maritime history, and many of its architectural features are beautifully preserved, including rich timber floors, restored fireplaces and iron lacework. Other features include the renovated kitchen, a luxurious master bedroom with a top-floor retreat, and a secure, gated forecourt with triple parking. 73 Ku-Ring-Gai Avenue, Turramurra NSW



This circa 1927 home offers a sense of period luxury through its original facade, rich timber detailing and soaring decorative ceilings. The designer Corian kitchen includes a butler’s pantry, polyurethane soft-close shaker cabinetry, double ovens, a breakfast island, premium Miele appliances, and three contemporary bathrooms, including two with underfloor heating. Set on a level parcel of land measuring approximately 1252 square metres, the property features an enclosed rear garden with an in-ground pool and, perhaps the highlight, a poolside pavilion with its own bathroom. 4 Matong Street, Gordon NSW



The apartment block “Stoneyhurst” was once the family estate of the Love family, who were behind the company that created Uncle Tobys. Built in 1890 and offered to the market for the first time in more than 70 years, the residence features beautifully maintained period details, including a generous floorplan, a timber staircase, four-metre-high ceilings, ornate cornices, ceiling roses, architraves and original marble fireplaces. Each apartment has its own character, yet all share large living areas, formal entertaining rooms and private outdoor spaces. 25 Sunnyside Place, Bayview NSW



This sandstone manor was built circa 1915 and has been renovated to honour the home’s period features, including ornate high ceilings, classic fireplaces, timber floors, bespoke joinery and a billiard room. Modern updates include a gourmet Carrara marble kitchen with premium Miele appliances, a temperature-controlled wine cellar and indoor-outdoor living spaces. Outdoors, you will find water gardens, a resort-style pool and an entertainer’s pavilion with a bar and outdoor barbecue. “Inglewood” features northerly views extending down Pittwater towards Lion Island and offers lower-level accommodation, ideal for guests.

World.title: Chalmers’ credit card back-down unedifying and concerning
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ intervention to temporarily halt the Australian Taxation Office’s controversial banning of credit card payments to help small businesses is management of a crisis of the Albanese government’s own making.

Chalmers is to allocate additional funds to the ATO after the ban – set to come into effect on November 30 – came under heavy criticism from the business community, opposition parties and some Labor backbenchers. “We’ve stepped in to ensure that the tax office can take credit card payments until the end of June next year,” Chalmers said. “This will give them the time to consult more with small business and to get it right. We try not to interfere with the RBA or the ATO … but it’s really important that we have stepped in today.”

Treasurer Jim Chalmers. Louie Douvis

Credit and debit card surcharges were a vexed issue when banking and financial services were the target of a royal commission nine years ago. Since then, despite a run on cash during the COVID years when money was hoarded, banks have made a motza as the declining use of cash largely helped to lower security expenditure and enabling eftpos, Visa or Mastercard to become king.

The Albanese government announced in 2024 it was prepared to ban credit card charges. The aim was to take pressure off consumers and businesses and help with the cost of living. Following a review by the Reserve Bank of Australia, on October 1 credit card surcharges were banned and interchange fees lowered, with businesses no longer able to add a surcharge when customers pay with plastic. The RBA estimated the move would save consumers about $1.6 billion annually.

World.title: ‘Imagine if I stuffed this up’: Sam Wood had the world, now it’s crashing down around him
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Millionaire lifestyle and fitness entrepreneur Sam Wood was living the picture-perfect life. The personal trainer had a reality TV star wife and he sat atop a self-made business empire, valued at $71 million, that he’d just sold to a Melbourne billionaire. The 46-year-old entrepreneur shouldn’t have had a care in the world, but Wood was anxious. “When you’ve gone from nothing … to something like that, there’s a bit of imposter syndrome, there’s a fear that one day something could happen, the bubble could burst and the dream could be over,” he told a NZ podcast in 2024. Lifestyle and fitness entrepreneur Sam Wood has been moved to a high-security prison in Brisbane after being denied bail on domestic violence charges. Matt Davidson “It’s funny, I had more anxious moments with money than I perhaps did with this sort of optimistic, youthful enthusiasm when I had none, you know, because I was like, you have something to lose. “It’s like, ‘f---, imagine if I lost all of this now or something happened or this wasn’t real or I somehow stuffed this up.’”



Wood’s anxiety would prove prophetic. A Triple Zero call from his stepdaughter to Queensland police on Saturday night, in which she described Wood allegedly strangling his wife, Snezana, has brought his world crashing down. Related Video Video icon 0:23 Sam Wood moved to correctional centre following failed bail application Locked up in a watch-house cell at Maroochydore, near Noosa, after being refused bail this week, Wood will have plenty of time to reflect on how it all came to this. A TV romance Wood was a 34-year-old personal trainer when he went looking for love on The Bachelor Australia in 2015. Snezana, also 34 at the time, was a single mother from Perth, a scientific sales representative from a tight-knit Macedonian family and the oldest woman in that season’s cast of hopefuls.



“I remember the first time I touched her. It was a hug for a photo shoot on the first group date and I could feel something there,” Wood told Jules Sebastian in an episode of podcast Tea With Jules in 2016. “That was the first time when I realised there is really something special about her.” Wood embraced his new partner’s young daughter Eve and the child was given her stepfather’s surname. He had a ready-made, photogenic family. Snezana and Sam Wood in 2016. Hausmann Communications For more than a decade the genetically blessed couple were high-voltage social media and red carpet mega-stars. Wood amassed almost 250,000 followers on his personal Instagram account and Snezana gathered 330,000 followers of her own. They graced the cover of the likes of Who magazine, Stellar and NW, built out their fairytale to include three more young daughters and struck partnerships with brands including Weetbix, Mercedes-Benz, Bupa, 2XU and Under Armour. The trappings of their wealth included multimillion-dollar homes in Melbourne’s affluent Brighton and on the Mornington Peninsula, and expensive European cars.



Even Eve, just nine years old when her mother appeared on The Bachelor, grew to become an influencer herself. The reality of business Wood leveraged his fame to build an empire, targeting women with his at-home fitness and nutrition business, 28 by Sam Wood. It offered pregnancy and postnatal plans, as well as a 12-week menopause program. Months ago, Wood launched Ollo for Women, a medical and physical weight-loss program targeting women in midlife. When Wood eventually sold his fitness business to Bastas for a reported $71 million, the deal included retention of Wood as the face (and body) of the rapidly expanding enterprise. The rise and fall over 10 years of Wood’s online empire was extraordinary. “I’d had no social media following before (The Bachelor), and it just went bananas, you know, went from 20 followers to 250,000 in a number of weeks, and so did Snez,” he told The Dom Harvey Podcast in April 2024.



After Wood launched the fitness platform in February 2016, 5000 people signed up in the first month, at $50 a month: “$250,000 a month revenue, and it was me and a few tech guys in an office, and I was filming the videos in my gym,” he said. “By the third month, we had 10,000. [It] just absolutely exploded.” Wood told Paul Spain on NZ Tech Podcast in February 2024 that the business eventually grew to more than 1 million subscribers globally, at the time of recording, with an influx of subscriptions during the COVID-19 pandemic, giving locked down Australians an at-home fitness option. Bupa, one of Australia’s biggest health insurers, noticed and offered their customers three months’ access to Wood’s online program for free. The insurer expected an extra 10,000 sign-ups, but instead 130,000 joined in three days, Wood said. “We went from 30,000 to 160,000 almost overnight,” he recalled. After several offers to buy the platform, Bastas’ DBG Health stepped in, buying the operation’s parent, Australian Life Tech. Wood clarified in the podcast that while he sold the business to Bastas for $71 million, he pocketed $15 million himself. Dennis Bastas, chairman and CEO of DBG Health, bought Sam Wood’s fitness business. AFR

Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. HIGH COURT Your letters page (″⁣Government needs to resist as miners dig in″⁣ 9/10) demonstrates the division in opinion over the High Court’s decision to impose consequential effect analysis on coal miners when seeking planning approval. Chris Bowen keeps batting away questions over this decision by saying it’s merely a tweaking of NSW state planning laws, but the implications are enormous.

Thankfully, unlike the USA, where Supreme Court appointments have become intensely political, our High Court has remained independent with appointments usually receiving bipartisan support.

So, now we have a precedent for considering the consequences of all planning applications. It seems the question of whether projects will have deleterious effect here or globally must be a factor when granting planning permits.

Mining is obviously one industry where this will shape the future of our extractive industries but other controversial developments such as data centres, housing and commercial developments may also come under the spotlight.

For once, the question ‘Is this for the greater good of humanity?’ could be front of our planning.

Graeme Lechte, Pascoe Vale No, court is not indulging in activism

Your correspondent (Letters, ″⁣Astonishing activism″⁣ 9/10) questions the reasoning of the High Court regarding coal export emissions, and accuses it of ″⁣judicial activism at its zenith″⁣. However, the legal basis of the decision was not on the merits of the coal exports. It was a ‘judicial review’ case.

Judicial review has long been a critical part of our legal system, ensuring that administrative decision makers (eg. government ministers) are accountable for following proper processes.

The High Court ruled that the minister had failed to consider a material and mandatory consideration (according to the NSW legislation), and by extension had departed from their democratically-granted power.

If those considerations need to be adjusted, the NSW parliament is now free to adjust them. A large factor in that decision will be the wishes of the NSW voting population. The High Court has played an important role in bringing the issue to their attention.

Michael Radywonik, Moonee Ponds



Supply and demand at work

Your Letters correspondent claims that our coal customers will find alternative suppliers and that “not a gram less will be burnt” (“What were they thinking?” 9/10). This is the same distorted reasoning used to justify inaction on illegal drugs, alcohol and tobacco. It also ignores the economics of supply and demand. Reducing supply, other things being equal, increases prices and reduces demand. Other suppliers may fill some of the gap, but to claim that Australian coal production has no effect whatsoever on global consumption is simply untenable. As for the economic benefits of coal exports, these will pale into insignificance when weighed against the environmental costs of ‘business as usual’.

David Fox, Beaumaris THE FORUM Not as friendly list

Anyone who thinks Melbourne is the world’s friendliest city clearly hasn’t travelled much. Would a Melburnian spontaneously buy four museum tickets for a small group of travellers in the ticket queue?

Would a Melburnian offer his home and a meal to six travellers who turned up on his doorstop out of the blue, or, quietly pay for an international visitor’s meal in a restaurant or tear his fresh bread in half to offer to a passing traveller? Or, go completely out of his way at night to walk three lost visitors to a location?

I can recall many more acts of kindness I have received from overseas strangers that I know would never happen in Australia. These few examples occurred in Iran, Mongolia, Syria and Morocco.

Julie Christensen, Blackburn Nth Art and sport mix

My Australian history professor, Ian Turner, would have heartily agreed with Waleed Aly’s analysis of the strong connection between sport and art when he delivered The Ron Barassi Memorial at a packed out Robert Blackwood Hall at Monash University in the early 1970s.

His erudite, affectionate and humorous theorising about Aussie Rules still resonates, and highlighted to this country girl that the halls of academia can be as passionate about sport as they can be about the Arts.

To this day, I treasure the opportunity to walk from the ‘G after the footy to the Arts Centre and enjoy a production or exhibition there. And that’s Melbourne.

Brenda Innes, Camberwell Convictions, not slogans

The main problem with things being the way they are at the moment, is that politicians have lost how to be politicians. All they want is the power and the prestige. Once they’re in – Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison-style – they have no idea what to do. Anthony Albanese seemed to be an old school type, someone who knew how to get the job, but has ended up proving himself as useless as the others.

The last politician to get anything real done was Julia Gillard, and we don’t have another of her on the horizon. So what do we do? If you really want to send a message, forget One Nation. Look – really look – at any independent candidates, teal candidates, people who really want to make change.

Give the balance of power to a David Pocock, or even a Jacqui Lambie; give us someone with real conviction, rather than a catchy slogan.

David Jeffery, East Geelong



Moses isn’t coming

I read another article this week and another journalist declaring people want change, that voters are searching for someone to fix their problems.

Reading between the lines, what they’re really describing is a hunger for a messiah. And when a politician inevitably turns out to be human, the media turns its considerable resources on their flaws, repeating them again and again until the flaws are all anyone remembers.

I have some grim news. Moses isn’t coming down the mountain. Pauline isn’t a prophet. No leader, from any party, is going to arrive with tablets of stone and set everything right.

Change doesn’t come from the top. It comes from us: house by house, street by street, suburb by suburb. It comes from neighbours sitting down to discuss, debate and decide what’s best for their schools, their roads, their hospitals, their town. That work is slow, unglamorous and often frustrating. But it’s the only kind that lasts.

Tom Pagonis, Hawthorn Fast track doubts

Why would any planning minister so ruthlessly turn their back on local planning expertise when we have such an urgent need to adapt to global warming as well as increase housing? (“Yes, Minister”, 7/10).

We have an approved ‘Fast Track’ seven-level proposal near us where apartments have been advertised from $1,650,000 to several million. Those most dismayed and outraged were young workers in the pub opposite. They had naively believed they were looking at a plan for affordable housing.

Fast Track planning decisions have not provided affordable buildings where young people want and need to live. Locations with ready access to trams, buses and an abundance of local amenities should be earmarked for those wishing to go car-free and enjoy the reduced costs of an apartment without a garage. This is the congested inner-city, after all.

How long can we tolerate threats to Melbourne’s liveability without questioning who is benefitting from this planning fiasco?

Susan Mahar, Fitzroy North Child crime

We can get to the moon, but it seems that as a community, we can’t even begin to realise that our youth has been contaminated, and we have lost control.

We are treating the children who are causing so much harm as “they”. We are distancing ourselves from them, and ultimately all children. We institute more and more rigorous disciplinary

measures which are not working.

Surely, there are leaders who will step up to point out the folly of allowing alternative ‘values’ which undermine social norms to seep into the minds of the emerging citizens of our community.

Australia, at least is trying to force some restraints on the tech companies whose tools allow vile ideas to penetrate our children’s psyches.

Means much more dramatic and effective have to be found to turn around the technology so that our children are imbued with the values we know, will keep society bonded and harmonious.

Geraldine Colson, Mentone American values

We align ourselves with countries we decide are civilised and scorn those we consider barbaric.

In one country this week we have heard of a string of abuses of human rights regarding capital punishment. A woman who has served 30 years in prison waiting “on death row” was scheduled to be killed by lethal injection. She survived two injections and was taken to hospital to be revived. She has recovered consciousness and awaits her fate. Tragically, the state does not automatically commute the death sentence in such cases.

Then, the defence department of that same country has announced that the execution by firing squad of a mass murderer will be live streamed. Live streamed! This country is the US, one of our closest allies.

We are quick to call out human rights abuses in countries such as Iran; where is the outcry about these abhorrent practices in our “great friend”?

Pauline Brown, Woodend Taking low road

The US is slipping into a dark age. First, a botched execution and the possibility that the prisoner will face a third attempt to kill her. And now, the public execution of a soldier who shot 13 of his compatriots.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth says the execution by firing squad will be broadcast online. How much lower can America sink?

Damien Ryan, Berwick



AI for everyone

Artificial intelligence is usually discussed as either a technological miracle or an existential threat. The fundamental question is political: who will control it, and for whose benefit?

AI is being developed by corporations, governments and military establishments competing for profit and strategic advantage. At the same time, automation threatens capitalism’s dependence on wage labour.

If machines produce more with fewer workers, society becomes richer in productive capacity while many people lose the wages needed to live. Technology that could free us from drudgery instead threatens unemployment and poverty.

The answer is not to halt AI, but to bring it under democratic control. Frontier systems need independent safety testing and enforceable international standards.

Governments should establish publicly funded, open AI research centres and a universal digital library, giving everyone access to knowledge while fairly remunerating creators.

AI is the product of humanity’s accumulated knowledge and labour. It should become a global public utility, used to shorten working time, expand knowledge and improve human life – not to enrich a few corporations or strengthen military power.

Barry York, O’Connor, ACT AND ANOTHER THING A society of ills

America is a sick society. Christa Pike is shackled to her bed. The woman was on her way to dying – are they worried she may leap out of bed and attempt to escape? Meanwhile, Pete Hegseth has authorised the live streaming of the execution by firing squad of the Fort Hood shooter. How will the young and vulnerable be protected from the footage?

Pam McConnell, Boronia Furthermore

Should I buy a bigger purse so that I can pay my tax to the ATO in cash?

Heather Barker, Albert Park Please bring back the surcharge. My local cafe decided that dropping it enabled him to increase the price of a coffee from $5 to $6, whereas the previous cost including surcharge was $5.07. I’m no mathematician, but I’m tipping he’s taking us for a ride.

Paul Thomas, Essendon



Your correspondent’s letter (9/10) about Coalition rhetoric, “we need to take back our country” etc. could have just as easily been the ‘rhetoric’ that our First Nations people might have used when the settlers began spreading through the nation.

Pepe Salvatore, North Fitzroy Re ″⁣Greens kick off campaign with public supermarket plan″⁣ (8/10). I am old enough to remember the ACTU store at the top end of Swanston Street in the 60s. It was a gallant attempt to provide goods at cheaper prices to the working class. It was doomed to fail. Marketing is best left to capitalists.

Dan Drummond, Leongatha Cricket

Quote of the year from Travis Head: “I think it’s fairly unfairly judged a fair bit from a group of past players, pretty much that put the bullet through a lot of players, which I think is unfair” (“Test star hits out at ex-players”, 8/10). Fair call Travis. I think I have a fairly, fair grasp of your grievance.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick Test not on free to air? That’s not cricket!

Luise Mock, Tawonga South Finally

A 16-letter word (Letters 9/10)? A mere bagatelle. I have one with 28: antidisestablishmentarianism. It sounds deliciously subversive.

Jane Ross, San Remo The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Asking the right questions is an underrated skill
World.content:
NationalVictoriaNote From The Editor Asking the right questions is an underrated skill Patrick Elligett October 9, 2026 — 7:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The right question can leave a person pondering for days. The right question, at the right time, can change a life. It can spark a thought that leads to the formation of a strategy, a business or a movement. The ABC obviously recognises that power, given it has framed its latest promotional campaign around questions. Journalism is, in part, about harnessing the power of questions asked of the right people, in the right way, at the right time. It is often the simplest, most direct questions that have the greatest impact. When my colleague Bevan Shields, then the Europe correspondent for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, asked French President Emmanuel Macron “Do you think he lied to you?” he wouldn’t have expected an equally direct answer, but he got one. “I don’t think, I know.” Loading



Those five words of diplomatic dynamite, said about then-prime minister Scott Morrison after Australia cancelled a submarine-building contract with France in 2021, has been pinpointed by some as the moment Morrison’s leadership “started unravelling”. Journalists don’t have a monopoly on questions. We just have the established networks and access to ask them of the right people. Some of the best questions we ask come from our subscribers and contacts. Comments on stories, letters to the editor, and direct feedback to journalists and editors are rich with excellent questions we should be asking. At the risk of sounding obsequious, the intelligence and passion of our subscribers was one of the motivating factors for putting on our public forum, the Melbourne Assembly, which you have been hearing about in recent weeks thanks to my newsroom colleagues. Click here to explore the trove of stories on the topic. The Melbourne Assembly, presented by The Age in partnership with the University of Melbourne, is now little more than one week away and I’m thrilled with how it has come together. We have some seriously impressive people lining up to share their thoughts on what Melbourne needs to do to continue thriving as it hurtles towards becoming a city the size of present-day London by the middle of this century.



We have assembled a depth of expertise that has the potential to live up to the event’s tagline by generating crucial conversations for the future of our city. We’ve made sure that participants at the assembly have the same opportunity as our journalists to ask the right questions and spark a conversation that could help shape Melbourne’s future. All participants will have access to an app that will allow them to suggest questions to our moderators in real time, so they can be put to our speakers and panellists. We are aiming for genuine civic engagement. That means real dialogue with some of the world’s leading thinkers such as two-term New York mayor Bill de Blasio and 15-minute city pioneer Carlos Moreno. Then there are Victoria’s decision-makers. The people with the power to shape our state and its institutions. Premier Ben Carroll, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Lord Mayor Nick Reece will all be speaking – and listening – at the Assembly. They are complemented by a line-up of local speakers with serious clout. Among them is Carolyn Evans, the newly minted vice chancellor of the University of Melbourne, who will be speaking in one of her first public appearances since taking on the role.



Melbourne University’s new vice chancellor Carolyn Evans will be speaking in one of her first public appearances since taking on the role. Dominic Lorrimer Across four key pillars of the event, we have assembled a depth of expertise that has the potential to live up to the event’s tagline by generating “crucial conversations for the future of our city”. Our Shaping the City panel, hosted by The Age’s city editor Cara Waters, features a former premier who reshaped our state and one of the sharpest public policy minds in the country. On the Education and Innovation panel, hosted by acting business editor Supratim Adhikari, we will discuss some of the biggest challenges of our generation with leading thinkers on education and the people aiming to realise the untapped potential of our city’s collective intelligence. Healthy Places and People, hosted by Channel Nine news anchor Alicia Loxley, will pose tough questions about the place we live and whether the environment is set up for Melburnians to thrive. Those questions will be answered by the people building our cities and making sure they run the way they should.



Related Article Opinion

City life Melbourne has a rare gift, but barely anyone is aware of it Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic We will finish with a discussion about Sport and the Arts, hosted by Waleed Aly, which should be as entertaining as one would expect of any discussion about Melbourne’s cultural capital. That discussion will hear from the people leading our city’s most important cultural precincts and institutions. To read more about the program and our speakers, or to buy a ticket if you haven’t yet done so, head to the Melbourne Assembly website. Speaking of the power of questions, I want to leave you with the question that got me thinking this week. One of our panellists asked me: “What does success look like for the Melbourne Assembly?” Like Shields’ Macron question, it was simple and direct. And it left me thinking about the answer for days. Ultimately, I arrived at this one: “It will be successful if, in five or 10 years, we can look back and say it was the moment when a conversation started that ultimately resulted in some public good.”



All we need to do now is ask the right questions. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Five of the best homes in Sydney from a bygone era
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of the best homes in Sydney from a bygone era Shona Hendley October 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Whether it’s art deco, Federation, Victorian, or Tudor, homes from a bygone era are often conveniently located in or near the inner city and offer both lifestyle and investment appeal. With ornate craftsmanship, large proportions, quality materials, and often steeped in history, these residences have character and personality and there is much to appreciate in them. Here are five of the best period properties on the market in Sydney. 77-79 George Street, Avalon Beach NSW “Leontine”, a late-1930s Spanish Colonial residence, sits on approximately 1636 square metres of expansive lawns and established gardens.



The double-storey home blends restored original period character, including white-rendered walls, high ceilings, original hardwood floors and a sandstone fireplace. Modern updates cater to contemporary living and include a marble-finished kitchen, a dedicated children’s wing and an entire upper level, perfect for a private parents’ retreat. Outside, you will find a 14.5 metre tiled pool and a fully self-contained cabana. 2 School Street, Balmain East NSW



Balmain East’s “Kaikoura” offers spectacular views of Sydney Harbour, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the CBD, from each of its three levels. Built circa 1840, the colonial sandstone home is integral to the peninsula’s maritime history, and many of its architectural features are beautifully preserved, including rich timber floors, restored fireplaces and iron lacework. Other features include the renovated kitchen, a luxurious master bedroom with a top-floor retreat, and a secure, gated forecourt with triple parking. 73 Ku-Ring-Gai Avenue, Turramurra NSW



This circa 1927 home offers a sense of period luxury through its original facade, rich timber detailing and soaring decorative ceilings. The designer Corian kitchen includes a butler’s pantry, polyurethane soft-close shaker cabinetry, double ovens, a breakfast island, premium Miele appliances, and three contemporary bathrooms, including two with underfloor heating. Set on a level parcel of land measuring approximately 1252 square metres, the property features an enclosed rear garden with an in-ground pool and, perhaps the highlight, a poolside pavilion with its own bathroom. 4 Matong Street, Gordon NSW



The apartment block “Stoneyhurst” was once the family estate of the Love family, who were behind the company that created Uncle Tobys. Built in 1890 and offered to the market for the first time in more than 70 years, the residence features beautifully maintained period details, including a generous floorplan, a timber staircase, four-metre-high ceilings, ornate cornices, ceiling roses, architraves and original marble fireplaces. Each apartment has its own character, yet all share large living areas, formal entertaining rooms and private outdoor spaces. 25 Sunnyside Place, Bayview NSW



This sandstone manor was built circa 1915 and has been renovated to honour the home’s period features, including ornate high ceilings, classic fireplaces, timber floors, bespoke joinery and a billiard room. Modern updates include a gourmet Carrara marble kitchen with premium Miele appliances, a temperature-controlled wine cellar and indoor-outdoor living spaces. Outdoors, you will find water gardens, a resort-style pool and an entertainer’s pavilion with a bar and outdoor barbecue. “Inglewood” features northerly views extending down Pittwater towards Lion Island and offers lower-level accommodation, ideal for guests.
