Tech.title: How to Tell if a New Neighborhood Device Is a Flock Surveillance Camera
Tech.content:
When a Flock camera shows up on a nearby street corner or sidewalk, it spells a new era of surveillance for your area. These license-plate reading cams can also use AI to identify vehicles and people by their appearance, or even listen to nearby sounds of screaming, depending on the add-ons that the users have chosen. Those features and how Flock cameras have used are raising serious privacy concerns, and a tug-of-war between cities forced to cancel their Flock networks and other towns embracing new Flock setups.

The problem is that while there’s so much concern over Flock cameras and various abuses by law enforcement, people aren’t always great at spotting Flock cams in the real world. It leads to lots of mistaken fears about radar, traffic cameras, trail cams and other various, nontracking devices. That’s one reason I’m not a huge fan of crowdsource-dependent apps such as DeFlock, which can give conflicting information based on what people think is Flock.

That’s why I’m breaking down exactly what a Flock installation looks like — and how to tell whether you’re looking at one, a similar automated license plate reader camera or something else entirely.

More from CNET

Look for the telltale Flock camera shape and logo

You can still most Flock cameras by their distinctive design. Allen J. Schaben/Contributor/Getty Images

Flock Safety’s brand has a very clear camera shape, so with a closer look, it’s typically easy to tell if it’s a Flock automatic license plate reader camera or something else.

Watch for the classic oval, hooded shape of the camera with a circular lens, a near-universal mark of Flock camera.

Notice this competitor brand Obvio has a distinctly different design than Flock, and may not offer the same surveillance services.

Not all license plate cameras are Flock, and that can matter for your privacy. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Keep in mind, Flock offers a variety of surveillance technology, including cameras that can recognize human attributes like clothes and beards, as well as devices that can detect sounds like gunshots, so not every device will look the same. But this is still one of the first and simplest ways to detect a Flock brand camera. If you get very close, you can also small, shiny, stem-like Flock logo on the front of the cameras.

Some Flock cameras don’t have the slim hood, but the color, general design and logo still give them away. Bloomberg/Getty Images

I have seen reports of other ALPR cameras hidden inside objects like fake plants, but this doesn’t appear to be Flock’s typical approach and is very rare so far.

Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

Look for Flock’s visible solar panel arrays

Flock’s solar panels often have a distinctive look. Bloomberg/Getty Images

Next, look for Flock’s large, dark-colored solar panels, which are typically angled above the camera or close by on the same mount. Many ALPR cameras use solar panels so they can be installed nearly anywhere, but Flock’s have a unique design that’s more noticeable the longer you look at the cameras.

If you see what you think is a surveillance device without a solar panel, it probably isn’t one, or at least not one associated with Flock and its camera competitors like Axon or Obvio.

For example, red-light or speed cameras may be wired into traffic-light mounts, but they are used for traffic enforcement and don’t carry the same surveillance baggage as general ALPR cameras. While they automate certain aspects of traffic enforcement and take pictures of license plates, they don’t typically have the AI recognition, broad police search capabilities, or ways to recognize individual vehicles and people like Flock can (although they can still make communities uncomfortable).

Red light and traffic cameras aren’t Flock, and don’t have the same surveillance capabilities as Flock. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc./Getty Images

Remember, Flock and ALPR solar panels are always larger and more public than the panels people use for their home security cameras. Fortunately, there are other ways to make sure.

Check what surveillance equipment local law enforcement has bought

Searching the Atlas of Surveillance by city or county can surface Flock Safety camera locations, contract details and any reported data-sharing agreements with federal agencies. EFF

I recommend confirming your community is using Flock cameras even if you think you’ve spotted one. One of the best ways is with the Atlas of Surveillance website, which uses dedicated research to collect the different surveillance technologies that cities, police and sheriff departments have bought and are using.

The Atlas of Surveillance tries to stay as current as possible, and you can search by town or county in just a few seconds. It links to reports or public records to confirm use if possible. I’ve used it frequently to trace Flock activity in certain areas, not only with cameras but with growing numbers of surveillance drones, too. It works with multiple types of devices and platforms that law enforcement uses, making it one of the most dependable ways to corroborate that your local government recently started using Flock cameras.

When I talked to senior research Beryl Lipton from the Electronic Frontier Foundation about using the website, she said, “People should start by searching for their town and county to see what technology is in play close to home. While folks may expect some larger cities to use some of these devices, I think people will be surprised to see how common they’ve become in mid-sized and rural areas too.”

Lipton also recommended using a similar tool, the Street-Level Surveillance hub, which is more focused on the complex ways today’s agencies use surveillance technology. With both tools together, you should have a good idea what your community is facing.

Check who owns the property and what contracts they may have

Private companies like Home Depot can use Flock too, which makes it confusing when cameras are posted around parking lots. Bloomberg/Getty Images

Flock doesn’t just contract with cities or police departments. That means that while a city government may have canceled Flock Safety cameras, local businesses can use them on their private property, which can cause a lot of confusion among worried people.

If it doesn’t appear your local government is using Flock cameras, try to find out who owns the property with a camera on it, and if they contract with Flock. Home Depot and Lowe’s, for example, are very open about using ALPR cameras, including Flock’s, in their parking lots, and sometimes share that data with police.

Local businesses and neighborhood entities like HOAs can also contract with Flock, but you can often ask them directly if they have AI surveillance cameras and why.

Ask your city council

Asking your city government and showing up to meetings is a great way to find out what’s going on with Flock. The Washington Post/Getty Images

Going to your city council, especially in person, can also be helpful (even Darth Vader thinks so). You can find out about present or future connections with Flock and make your opinion heard. You may also discover that, as I’ve seen before, cities have canceled their Flock contracts and no longer use the cameras, but they still stay up because no one is sure how to legally remove them.

I’ve also seen city councils unsure what Flock cameras are or how police use them, essentially signing off on police and sheriff budgets without knowing what they’re paying for, which is a sign that auditing and accountability practices are lacking. Or, I’ve noticed some cities announce new camera or surveillance programs but carefully avoid using the word “Flock” even though they are contracting with Flock Safety.

Asking direct questions to public servants can help handle issues like these. Look for council meetings where the public is welcome, and try writing or calling your city council to ask about their plans for Flock, if any.

File a public records request

Check if your city or state supports public records requests. You may be able to use a government website to formally request access to information about ALPR cameras, installations and contract documents.

Depending on the public records portal, you may have to be very specific about the kind of information you want, and which government body has it — the police department vs. the city, for example. My other steps are a good start to the research you need if you want to access public records like this.

While not every camera is from Flock, knowing which are — and which have ALPR or person detection capabilities — is a key step in avoiding confusion and protecting your privacy.

Tech.title: If You’re Still on iOS 26, You Need to Download iOS 26.7.1 Now for This Zero-Day Patch
Tech.content:
If your iPhone isn’t running iOS 27, you need to download iOS 26.7.1 now to patch a zero-day flaw. Apple wrote online that this update patches a security issue on devices running iOS versions prior to iOS 27 that might have been actively exploited in an “extremely sophisticated attack.”

Zero-day exploits are newly discovered vulnerabilities with no existing protections. Updating to software versions that patch those vulnerabilities is generally the only way to guard your devices.

You can download iOS 26.7.1 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

According to Apple’s release notes, iOS 26.7.1 patches a security issue in CoreGraphics, a framework that handles low-level, lightweight 2D renderings. Apple wrote that this issue could lead to arbitrary code execution, which could allow a third party to steal your data or hack your device for other nefarious purposes.

“Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals,” the company wrote online.

Apple’s description suggests this flaw was used in a targeted attack as opposed to a widespread campaign, so most people probably aren’t the intended target of this attack. However, you should still download iOS 26.7.1 to remove the possibility entirely.

If you’re running iOS 27, you should already be protected from this issue since Apple wrote online the flaw affected iOS versions prior to iOS 27. If you are on iOS 27, I still recommend downloading iOS 27.0.1 now to give yourself the most up-to-date software.

For more on iOS, here’s what to know about iOS 27, why you might not see iOS 27.1 on your device and what iOS 27.2 could bring to your device.

Tech.title: From Zuck to Musk: Big Tech’s Scandals and Scammers Are Coming to the Big Screen
Tech.content:
Hollywood is unleashing a handful of movies this fall, pulling the curtain back to shine a light on some of the big names in tech: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg; Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk; Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes; and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Plenty of movies have tackled themes of techno-pessimism and dug into the deep well of science fiction. Remember 2001: A Space Odyssey? Blade Runner? M3GAN? But apocalyptic threats and human-versus-machine scenarios feel much more prescient in 2026.

What’s changed is that there seems to be an appetite for Big Tech to get its comeuppance. The movies being released are real stories about the scandals and scammers affecting our daily lives.

More from CNET

The Social Reckoning (Oct. 9)

The Social Reckoning continues the story Aaron Sorkin began with the 2010 film The Social Network about Facebook. The Oscar and Emmy-winning screenwriter stepped behind the camera to helm the movie, which he once again wrote.

The Social Reckoning highlights the societal damage caused by Zuckerberg’s social media empire. Based on thousands of leaked documents from former Facebook engineer Frances Haugen, the movie draws inspiration from the 2021 Wall Street Journal article The Facebook Files, which documents the whistleblower’s actions and the subsequent fallout.

Succession star Jeremy Strong now plays Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg played the bright-eyed college student 16 years ago). The film also stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Billy Magnussen, Bill Burr and Betty Gilpin.

The Social Reckoning hits theaters Friday.

Musk (Oct. 16)

The upcoming documentary Musk is by lauded filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose work includes Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.

Running about 4 hours, the movie delves into the life and legend of Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, and (cue Dr. Evil’s theme music) the richest man in the world. Given that the film seems to dismantle the mythos he built and sold along the way, Musk hasn’t had kind words to say, calling the movie a “hit piece” and Gibney a “douchebag” in a social media rant.

For a brief period, ads for the movie were barred from social media platforms Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. Google and Meta have since cleared the way for promotional materials for Musk, while the other platforms have remained silent.

Musk hits theaters on Oct. 16 and will stream on HBO Max next year.

You Can See Everything (Oct. 16)

In case you’re unfamiliar with the story of Holmes, Gibney’s 2019 movie is a good place to start. You could also try the 2022 Hulu original series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried. Holmes, who was the face of Theranos, a short-lived blood-testing company, was indicted in June 2018 for fraud and conspiracy.

You Can See Everything is a nearly 3-hour-long documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (the director of the Chris Hanson drama Primetime), which appears more like a psychological horror film than a nonfiction narrative. The new movie follows Fielder into the private life of Holmes and her family, roughly a month before she was to report to prison. You Can See Everything has a hefty amount of buzz behind it and is turning into one of fall’s must-see theatrical releases.

You Can See Everything is released Oct. 16.

Artificial (Dec. 25)

Italian film director Luca Guadagnino (Call Me By Your Name and Queer) turns his eye on OpenAI’s Altman in his upcoming biopic, Artificial. Just like The Social Reckoning, this isn’t a documentary, and it’s already generating substantial Oscar buzz.

Artificial takes place in 2023 and follows the tumultuous period when Altman was fired by OpenAI and then rehired five days later. Amazon MGM Studios was originally set to distribute the movie, but after signing a multiyear partnership with OpenAI, it stepped away from the project. Neon came in and picked up the film, which also stars Billie Lourd, Monica Barbaro, Chris O’Dowd, Jason Schwartzman, Zozia Mamet and Ike Barinholtz (who plays Musk).

Artificial will premiere in theaters on Christmas Day.

What to stream

If you’re watching from home, you can also cash in on the Big Tech dystopia genre.

AMC’s The Audacity is a fictional account of the Silicon Valley tech bubble. Netflix has the documentary The AI Doc or How I Became an Apocaloptimist and will soon release AI Gone Wild, a new Instadoc about the rather infamous Hugging Face cyberattack. The streamer will also debut The Altruists, an eight-episode true-crime series about the 2022 collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s cryptocurrency empire, FTX, on Nov. 19. There’s even a legal procedural called Cupertino coming to CBS this week that is about Silicon Valley lawyers.

Tech.title: I Let AI Plan My Days and Nights. It Doesn’t Understand Happiness
Tech.content:
True happiness may seem a little hard to come by these days. We’ve got to balance our budgets with the tantalizing prospects of shiny new iPhones, stay on top of seemingly endless work tasks and surf the turbulent waves of wild news cycles.

What might be bliss for one person could feel like an exercise in tedium for another. I put three AI tools — ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude AI — to the test to see if they could curate two days filled with hour-by-hour happiness for me. The results revealed a fundamental misunderstanding of what it means for this particular human to be happy.

I used a single prompt for each tool: Plan my life, by the hour, for the next two days. Be very detailed and plan everything I should do from the time I wake up, including when I should wake up, to the time I go to bed. Optimize for happiness.

More from CNET

The chatbots plan my days

Morning happiness level: Cranky toddler

All three AI tools I used had me waking up around 7 a.m., with Claude adding a 15-minute earlier rise and shine deadline to fill with stretching/yoga, gratitude journaling and a jaunt outdoors. By 9 a.m., all three had put me to work crafting a “real,” “substantial,” “vibrant” breakfast and tackling either creative projects or writing and researching for my gig here at CNET.

Claude recommended I start my morning at 6:45 a.m. and swap screen time for cat stretches. Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT had me rise and shine with my dog and coffee outside. OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini made a note to take in that crisp Los Angeles air first thing. I don’t know how “crisp” 72 degrees can be, but the deep breaths were nice. Google Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Afternoon happiness level: Annoyed and bored

The consistent marker among the afternoon plans was a light, healthy lunch with plenty of veggies, followed by a 45-minute to hour-long walking session. After I’d exercised for the second time in five hours, I was directed to dive right back into work mode, with little 10- to 15-minute breaks in between sessions.

This focus on work really irked me, because while I understand this is the typical workday for many Americans, I didn’t ask AI to make my days productive. I asked for the tools to optimize two days for happiness. I’m only left to assume that an AI views a human who is not productive for even a moment as being deeply unhappy. On days when all I do is eat ice cream and cackle at internet videos, I would disagree.

Gemini was big on healthy eating and exercising throughout the day. Google Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT offering the option of a good, long sniff walk in the middle of the day. OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET

Claude allowed for a luxurious, 15-minute snack and text break block in between productivity and exercise.

Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET

Nighttime happiness level: Lonely and resentful

Right before dinner time, I was instructed to get moving yet again, for either a 45-minute or hour-long walk. For my final meal of the day, I was allowed to cook dinner, order in or have leftovers, because why would I want to go out for a romantic meal at my favorite restaurant or see friends for drinks at a new bar and tapas place?

By 9 p.m., I had wound down with a bit of hands-on hobbying like doing a puzzle, more gardening or reading a book. ChatGPT allowed for some Baldur’s Gate and TV time in the evening before settling down, and Claude asked me to jot down “one sentence on the best moment of the day” at 10 p.m. before my 10:15 p.m. bedtime. “Watching my dog sleep,” was what I wrote. Now, I love my dog, but for a day that was supposed to be optimized to make me as happy as possible, that’s pretty lame.

ChatGPT coming in hot with the exercise and a nice gaming session. OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET

Claude recommended I work on some productive hobbies for an hour and do some cleaning. Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini thought weeding and checking on my garden would be happy-making in the evening. Google/Screenshot by CNET

Missing modern life

None of the AI tools built in any time on the internet. No browsing the local and national news. No social media moments. No YouTube scrolling. This might be because reading the news, checking up on social media and seeing the latest updates, or lack thereof, on the new Fable game were unlikely to make me happy. It seems more likely to me that it’s a huge blind spot in how the modern person spends their time and finds comfort and amusement.

ChatGPT allowed for a “quiet internet” podcast or audiobook hour at the end of the day in bed, but no other instruction to use online amusements. According to Claude and Gemini, I was only allowed to look at the internet for work, with explicit instructions at times to not engage with screens at all.

No meaningful human contact

The AI tools also managed to plan a two-day schedule for me in which I rarely spoke to or had contact with another human being, with the exception of a single text to a single friend and meals, which gave me the option to invite a coworker or friend to my one-hour lunch break or eat with a companion at dinner. I suspect this advice had more to do with avoiding watching TV or looking at my phone than getting human contact.

The chatbots almost never suggested reaching out to check on friends, family, co-workers or loved ones as a standalone activity. Just a relentless onslaught of work, manual labor and healthful activities. It would seem like humans don’t need to interact with each other deliberately to be happy, according to these AI tools.

Overall, the AI tools I used seemed to be optimizing my days for wellness and productivity rather than happiness, which is what I requested. Doing laundry, washing dishes, weeding the yard, exercising multiple times a day and maybe squeezing in a few hours for book learning, all while never truly engaging socially or prioritizing fun, sounds more like a light punishment than a schedule built for glee.

It occurs to me that the models are being trained on texts created to appeal to people who might struggle to simply get out of bed in the morning, and the definition of happiness in that realm may not include a whole lot of mirth. But these tools should be able to discern between being asked to craft a schedule built for mental health improvement and creating a two-day run of fun.

AI tools might be good at a lot of things, such as doing homework and doling out compliments, but I’d leave engineering human happiness to the pros at Disneyland and the pharmaceutical companies.

Tech.title: Super Skygazing: Step Outside to See October’s Meteor Showers, Views of All 8 Planets and More
Tech.content:
As October moves on, we’re being showered with skygazing events, and there are plenty of reasons to step outside at night and check out the universe. This month features an action-packed lineup of meteor showers and celestial showcases.

You can see all eight planets this month

Mercury is visible just before sunset for several days in October. Stellarium

Every planet in the solar system is easily seen at some point this month, with Mercury being the most difficult. That’s not unusual, thanks to its proximity to the sun. Here’s a quick rundown on the best times to view each planet in October.

Mercury: Mercury is in elongation (the farthest it can get from the sun) on Monday, making that day and the two or so days before and after the best possible time to view Mercury.

More from CNET

Venus: Venus will spend most of the month right next to the sun, making it virtually impossible to see. However, by the end of the month, it will begin to separate from the sun, making it visible just after sunset. The best view will be on Oct. 31, but the view will get better going into November.

Mars: Mars will be visible in the night sky every night in October. It rises from the eastern horizon right around 2 a.m. ET and stays there until the sun comes up.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are going to be pretty close together all month, so most of the same rules apply, except that Jupiter rises about two hours later than Mars on most nights in October.

Saturn: Saturn is living its best life in October. It’s visible almost right at sunset ET and stays visible in the night sky until sunrise.

Neptune: Neptune is also visible every day in October and follows a very similar path to Saturn. It rises in the east, streaks across the sky and sets in the west right around sunrise. They’re actually pretty close together in the night sky every night during the month, so if you can find Saturn, Neptune isn’t far off, but you’ll definitely need magnification to see it.

Uranus: Uranus is visible the entire month and follows a very similar path through the sky as Saturn and Neptune, but its trek happens later at night. It rises on the eastern horizon about two hours after Saturn and follows it across the sky, but never really catches up, ending up in the high western sky when sunrise comes.

Through Oct. 10: Draconids Meteor Shower

The Draconids meteor shower is in the Draco constellation near Vega. Stellarium

The Draconids meteor shower is a minor meteor shower that occurs every year around the first week of October. It officially started on Oct. 6 and runs until Oct. 10, making it one of the shortest meteor showers of the season. It’s fed by the 21P/Giacobini-Zinner comet, which is part of the Jupiter family of comets.

Draconids meteors appear to originate from the Draco constellation. It sits high in the western sky in the northern hemisphere this time of year, with a slight lean to the north. If you’re using a sky map app, all you need to do is find Vega, and you’re already in the right neighborhood to catch Draconids.

The peak is a little tame, at around 10 meteors per hour most years, but it has a history of surprising astronomers. In 1933 and 1946, Draconids spat out thousands of meteors an hour in what were two of the most intense meteor showers of the 20th century. On the plus side, the moon is below the horizon for this meteor shower, so you won’t need to worry about light pollution from the moon.

Oct. 10: The last good chance to see the Milky Way

The Milky Way captured with the Tiny1 camera. TinyMOS

The very best time to view the Milky Way is at a new moon in the warm months of the year, from May to August. This is when the Milky Way is high in the sky all night, giving night owls great views and plenty of time to photograph it. The problem is that it’s best viewed on nights with a new moon between midnight and 4 a.m. local time, which can be a bit late for some folks.

September and October are great for this because the Milky Way is at its highest point between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. local time, giving the early birds a chance to snap some sweet photographs of the Milky Way. After October, the Milky Way is too low on the horizon to allow really good pictures of it until the following May. So, if you have a camera and are in some place that’s dark, the new moon on Saturday is probably your last chance to capture a striking photo before next spring.

Oct. 21: Orionids meteor shower

The Orionids meteor shower will be low to the horizon in the east when its peak occurs.

Orionids is the better-known of the two October meteor showers. This one officially started on Friday and runs until Nov. 7. It’s possible to spot a meteor from Orionids any night during the month, but the shower reaches its peak on the evening of Oct. 21. Meteors for this shower come from the 1P/Halley comet, which also feeds the Eta Aquariids meteor shower that happens every year in May.

This is a slightly more active meteor shower than the Draconids, and you can expect about 10 to 20 meteors per hour. The moon is set to be about 76% full that night, so you can probably expect to see fewer meteors thanks to lunar light pollution. The Orion constellation, where the meteor shower will appear to originate, doesn’t pop up over the eastern horizon until after midnight, so make sure to pack some coffee if you’re staying up late for this one. If you can find the stars Betelgeuse, Capella and Rigel, then you should be able to find Orion easily. They’re in the same general area.

The Orionids meteor shower is best known for its bright, fast-moving meteors, which leave long trails that can last for over a minute and sometimes result in fireballs. Their brightness will be a boon, with the three-quarters-full moon in the sky hindering viewing.

Oct. 26: The Hunter’s moon

A full moon rises behind the Washington Monument. NASA/Bill Ingalls

October’s full moon falls close to Halloween this year, perfect for spooky views. According to The Old Farmer’s Almanac, October’s full moon reaches its peak on Oct. 26 at 12:12 a.m. ET. It’ll also be over 90% full for a couple of days before and after, giving you a solid five days to check it out.

October’s full moon isn’t quite a supermoon. A full moon is only classified as a supermoon when the moon is in perigee and full at roughly the same time, and October’s full moon misses the mark by a couple of days. October’s full moon is the last normal full moon of the year. November and December close out 2026 with supermoons before January opens with the final supermoon of this cycle.

Oct. 27: The moon eclipses the Pleiades

The moon will eclipse the Pleiades before either rises in the sky, but most people will still get to see part of it. Stellarium

Pleiades is one of the best star clusters to view in the night sky. They’re known as the Seven Sisters, and in terms of clusters of stars, it’s one of the easiest to see. The exception is on Oct. 27, when the moon will cross in front of them, blocking them almost entirely from view. When this happens depends on where you’re located.

The moon begins passing in front of them before sunset in Eastern time, and moves out of the way around midnight. Those on the East Coast will start the night in the middle of this little eclipse, while those on the West Coast will glimpse it at the very end. Finding it should be simple enough since the moon is the easiest thing to see in the night sky.

All month: Constellations and asterisms

The sky is continuing its rearrangement from summer into autumn, and there are tons of constellations to gaze at over the course of the month. Many of September’s constellations appear again, including both Dippers, Aquarius, Pegasus, Pisces and many others. October plays host to a few new ones in the night sky cycle, including Taurus, Cetus, Auriga and Orion, which will appear low on the horizon as they begin their months-long ascent into the sky for the winter.

There are some smaller asterisms to observe as well, including the Coffin of Delphinus, the Circlet of Pisces and the Northern Cross. We recommend using a sky map to find them all, as there are quite a lot. That’s good news, because even if you don’t go out during one of the big events in October, you’ll still have plenty of objects to look for in the night sky.

Tech.title: The Time Is Now to File Your Claim for Apple’s $250M AI iPhone Settlement
Tech.content:
If you bought a new iPhone 16 expecting to use AI like Apple’s ads demonstrated at the time, you were probably disappointed since Apple Intelligence didn’t arrive until later and lacked those features.

Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The form to opt-in is available only for a limited time, though, so get your name into the pool before it closes.

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

“False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. Bridget Carey/CNET

How to claim your portion of the settlement

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

Who is eligible for the $250 million settlement?

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

iPhone 16

iPhone 16E

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 16 Pro

iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

Why is there a lawsuit over Apple Intelligence?

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

When can you expect to receive a settlement payment?

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

Tech.title: Everything We Expect From Apple’s Surprise Smart Home Event Next Week
Tech.content:
We finally have confirmation of Apple’s massive smart home event, which is happening on Tuesday. So many things are expected to be announced, centering on Apple and Siri entering the home tech space in all-new ways. The tech giant’s smart home devices will face serious competition from Amazon, Google and other players.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been collecting the reports, insider claims and possible leaks to see just what Apple could be announcing. It all points to a major shake-up for home security, smart home devices and how Siri AI can be used. CNET will be there in person to see what Apple has cooked up, but in the meantime, here are the latest rumors.

A representative from Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

More from CNET

A Siri smart display at last

An Apple smart display could allow Siri to get much more creative. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be near the release of a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home. This display would focus heavily on Siri AI and compete with products like Amazon’s Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub line.

Smart displays can add a lot of functionality to smart speakers, if you don’t mind using voice assistants. Rumors say the display could swivel and/or be attached to a wall, be at least several inches wide and allow Siri to recognize different people when multiple users are having a conversation.

Smart display touchscreens are great for getting visual information, watching videos or viewing to-do lists, so a display like this is likely to have a bit of Apple TV and Safari in it, too.

Is it likely? I think it’s quite likely, based on how many insider reports have mentioned this smart display, but I don’t think we have a good idea how it will look yet.

Updates to the HomePod line

Is a new HomePod mini on the way? Chris Monroe/CNET

Along with a smart display, rumors are flying that Apple will give its HomePod smart speaker line the first major update in years. It’s the ideal time to update the HomePod line, too, although it’s possible some of these reports have confused plans for a smart display with a new smart speaker, both of which could fall under the HomePod label.

If a new HomePod speaker is on the horizon, reports indicate that it would be a new type of HomePod mini. That’s not surprising — the original HomePod has often been critiqued for being over $300, which is why Apple focused on the less expensive mini model afterward.

Is it likely? Yes, I’d say this is about as likely as a Siri smart display, if Apple wants to continue developing the HomePod line.

A new Apple TV

Apple TV is due for an upgrade, too. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The same reports that say a smart display and new HomePod are on the way also mention Apple is planning to release a new Apple TV model.

It’s a product line that’s sort of connected to the smart home, especially if Apple is launching a smart display. The company hasn’t released a new set-top box since 2022, so it’s about time for another. This could also give the Apple TV new hardware for extra Siri AI tricks.

Is it likely? I think it’s less likely than a speaker or display. It’s not quite as much of a smart home gadget, and it seems to have gotten swept into the wide net of rumors, but without as many reports.

Little Apple security cams — with no recording

Recent rumors says Apple is ready to enter the home security world with its own products. Although we don’t know much, reports from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman say these will be tiny cameras that, interestingly, won’t record any video. No recording means Apple won’t have to worry about cloud storage and may be able to avoid charging extra subscriptions for them.

The cameras are rumored to have some kind of presence-sensing or human-recognizing technology as well as AI video descriptions, suggesting Apple Home will be running analysis on the video even if it won’t record permanently. The phrase “facial recognition” was also mentioned, but this doesn’t seem nearly as likely to me.

Is it likely? I’m betting on some kind of home security announcement, and I expect Apple would like to have its own camera line, but I don’t know if this exact product will be released. However, the extra details do lend this rumor legitimacy.

An LG collab for a new thermostat

Apple may be partnering with LG for some smart home devices, and there are even reportedly leaked product concept photos circulating on the internet. One of the biggest potential releases is an Apple-friendly thermostat. The photos show a round, Nest-like thermostat dial, and rumors say it will include far-sight presence sensing, a humidity sensor and several temperature calibration options.

Alongside the thermostat, the Apple/LG combo is expected to release a sensor that can measure the temperature at specific locations and feed that information back to the thermostat hub. That would be no surprise, because models from Nest, Ecobee and others have similar satellite sensors, although Apple’s may have adhesive strips to attach its version to the wall.

Interestingly, Apple partnered with LG years ago to support Apple-friendly security cameras, but those lines were rarely updated and quickly became obsolete. Maybe Apple is ready to try again with a different approach.

Is it likely? If Apple really is partnering with LG for a new wave of home devices, I think a thermostat is likely. But this is starting to be a lot of products to announce at a single October event that won’t be publicly streamed.

2. LG Smart Thermostat



• Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.

• Calibrated Temperature/Temperature Offset options. pic.twitter.com/Q8AAaxy4ey — pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026

Further LG collabs for smart lock and maybe more

The other big rumor centering around an LG collaboration is an Apple smart lock. While many smart locks work with Apple and Apple Home Keys, the tech giant hasn’t been involved in the development of a smart lock before.

It could have automatic unlocking, tapping your phone to unlock and a variety of keypad management options. That’s not surprising, but the rumored product images show a round, twist-to-unlock, light-up outdoor keypad, and I haven’t seen anything like that before.

If Apple does release a smart lock, Ring will have beaten it to the punch with its own announcement of its first-ever lock, which will include Alexa compatibility and a unique thumbturn that can generate a charge when the battery dies.

Other rumors and purported product images suggest the LG partnership could also yield a video doorbell, floodlight camera, outdoor camera and indoor camera.

Is it likely? Now this is a lot of new gadgets to announce at once. I think a smart lock is about as likely as a smart thermostat; those are both strong fields for Apple to enter. For the rest of the cameras, I’m doubtful. The indoor camera could be connected to the rumors of Apple’s no-video model. If the LG partnership line is this large, I wouldn’t be surprised if Apple is saving it for a separate announcement later on.

What role will Apple Intelligence play in all this?

Apple Intelligence will fuel many Siri AI capabilities in the Apple Home app. That’s especially true of AI video descriptions, which Apple is bringing to supported security cameras (there are very few right now, but some of Aqara’s camera hubs are compatible). I’m testing these uses of Apple Intelligence now, but if Apple releases any of its own security cameras, you can bet they’ll use AI features in the same way.

Will there be any iPad news at this event?

There are rumors that Apple will announce an iPad mini sometime this month, but it probably doesn’t have much to do with this event. This is a strictly smart home-focused release.

Tech.title: This ‘Mind-Reading’ AI Is a Wiz at Figuring Out What You See
Tech.content:
Israeli scientists have devised an AI model that can reconstruct and even predict what people are seeing with startling accuracy, likening the results to mind reading.

Their work still exists largely in lab settings, though the researchers are hopeful that advances down the line could be extended even as far as reading people’s dreams. More immediately, the technology could have potential for medical purposes, like helping people communicate who otherwise can’t due to injury or disability.

The AI model, called Brain-IT, was developed by professor Michal Irani and fellow researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. They’ve documented their work on GitHub and in a paper presented at a scientific conference earlier this year.

More from CNET

Brain-IT takes advantage of the thing that AI is best at, which is pattern recognition. It takes in data from functional MRI brain scans, which track changes in blood flow and oxygen in the brain to measure brain activity, and then uses that data to recreate the images the person was thinking about when the scans took place.

It also works in reverse, predicting what a brain scan would look like if shown a specific image.

According to Irani, other AI models can translate brain activity into images and preserve the general vibe of an image.

“However, they tend to make mistakes in basic features such as composition and color,” Irani said in a statement. “The new model we developed outperforms them in reconstructing both the content of the image and its details.”

Brain-IT is also substantially faster. The researchers say that it needs only 1 hour of fMRI data from a new subject to match the results achieved by other methods trained on 40 hours of recording.

The Brain-IT image reconstructions — the right side of each paired image — clearly aren’t perfect but they are largely true to the original. Weizmann Institute of Science

How does the Brain-IT AI model work?

The Weizmann Institute researchers trained the AI model on thousands of brain scans from the publicly available Natural Scenes Dataset that came from eight volunteers who were told to look at specific images while they were being scanned. This allowed the AI to identify patterns in brain activity.

The researchers noted that different regions of the brain light up on scans when people think about specific things and identified 128 “functional regions.” For example, Irani said, some regions light up in scans when someone looks at food and others when a person views sports. These patterns helped the AI figure out what the person being scanned was witnessing.

Some of these regions were already known by neuroscientists. Research has shown that dogs’ brains light up like Christmas trees in the presence of their owners and that dogs can differentiate between a human’s facial expressions. It’s also been observed that humans use the same neurons in recalling an image as they do looking at them.

As impressive as Brain-IT is, it’s also quite limited. It can currently only generate images from fMRI brain scans. This takes time and requires a person to willingly put themselves into an MRI machine.

Irani and other scientists are also looking into whether a simpler EEG device could deliver similar results more easily, according to MIT Technology Review.

So is it mind reading? Not really — nothing in this technology is capturing thoughts, memory or language. What the Weizmann Institute researchers have built is essentially a more efficient and reliable method of reconstructing a scene based on the brain activity of the person viewing it.

In an interview with MIT Technology Review, Irani acknowledged that “mind-reading” is a “cute, jazzy name.”

Irani and her team now want to see if they can achieve similar results with auditory information.

Beyond that lies a more mysterious realm: dreams. That, Irani said in a statement, would require conquering the challenges of decoding video.

“Dozens of images change every second while an fMRI scan takes about two minutes,” she said. “If we overcome all these obstacles, it’s possible that in the future, we may even be able to read dreams.”
